title: Ludwig review – cosy crime at its bumbling best  | Television | The Guardian
description: David Mitchell and Anna Maxwell Martin are back and having a blast nerding around Cambridge solving low-stakes murders. Long may this whimsical, corduroy-clad mystery continue!
Author: Sarah Dempster
Headline: David Mitchell and Anna Maxwell Martin are back and having a blast nerding around Cambridge solving low-stakes murders. Long may this whimsical, corduroy-clad mystery continue!
Content: Don’t mention his piles … David Mitchell as John ‘Ludwig’ Taylor.Photograph: BBC/Big Talk Studios/Olly CourtneyView image in fullscreenDon’t mention his piles … David Mitchell as John ‘Ludwig’ Taylor.Photograph: BBC/Big Talk Studios/Olly CourtneyTV reviewTelevisionReviewLudwig review – cosy crime at its bumbling bestDavid Mitchell and Anna Maxwell Martin are back and having a blast nerding around Cambridge solving low-stakes murders. Long may this whimsical, corduroy-clad mystery continue!Sarah DempsterThu 20 Aug 2026 17.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOh, Ludwig – how do I love thee? Let me count the ways.Or at least allow me to hold your favourite biro as you scurry around Cambridge in a state of rumpled exasperation, like a Womble that’s just been chased out of Ryman following a misunderstanding over a hole-punch.Missed the first series of this endearingly nerdish crime caper? Panic not. The second arrives bearing that most traditional of housewarming gifts – a recap. And very welcome it is too, given Ludwig’s fondness for befuddling conspiracies, impenetrable ciphers, and scenes in which corduroy-clad David Mitchell points at a graph while spluttering things like “the whole thing is dichotomous!”.The recap, then: Mitchell is John “Ludwig” Taylor, a crossword-setting introvert who has been posing as his identical twin, James – a DCI – in order to uncover the reasons for the latter’s mysterious disappearance. Though swiftly rumbled by the fuzz, John’s extraordinary knack for solving low-stakes murders has seen the bumbler hired as a “crime scene consultant”.Meanwhile, James has left cryptic clues re the covered-up murder of a journalist named Sinclair. The key to the conundrum, it seems, lies in Sinclair’s innumerable files, which currently reside in James’s wife Lucy’s (Anna Maxwell Martin) spare room.View image in fullscreenBumbler in chief … Mitchell as John with Dipo Ola as DI Russell Carter, Ben Ashenden as DS Ethan Cole and Rumi Sutton as DC Caitlin Sullivan.Photograph: BBC/Big Talk Studios/Colin HuttonAnd now? John is diligently organising the folders into what he calls, with touching fondness, “my piles”.“Do this enough times,” he explains, “and we’ll find the one file that Sinclair died for and the reason for my brother’s disappearance!” A pause. “Probably!”All clear? Splendid. And so to the theatre, where a narky pensioner has been stabbed by one of her daughters. But which one? “I did it,” honks Portia (Doon Mackichan). Oh no she didn’t, counter-honks her sister, Patricia (Rebecca Front). “It was me.” The reason? “Mummy wouldn’t let me have a bichon frisé.”John is flustered. “This one’s really hard,” he splutters, his expression, as always, that of a mole startled to learn that the last UK branch of Tie Rack closed in 2013 and not, as he was convinced, 2021.“Whichever one didn’t do it knows that the other one did and is protecting her. While the one that did do it knows we can’t prove that the one who didn’t do it, didn’t do it.”There is a lot of this sort of thing in Ludwig. That is, John holding forth on the impossibly convoluted ins and outs of each preposterous case-of-the-week, oblivious to the bewilderment of all concerned. Frankly, there is not much room here for the armchair detective. Magnifying glasses will remain unwielded; pipes resolutely un-puffed. It’s simply too idiosyncratic. Too … Ludwig. Instead, the fun lies in the sight of John boggling at each low-stakes murder before dissolving into radiant, childlike grins as he realises he has – gosh, really? How marvellous! – solved said low-stakes murder all by himself. How? A combination, usually, of a) accident b) preternatural boffinry and c) shouting about his piles into a cretaceous-era Nokia.Like all cosy crime series, Ludwig is up to its elbow patches in nostalgia. There is a tangible yearning for a time before the impertinences of modern drama; a time of corniced accents and iced-sponge values, of labradors in padded gilets upbraiding menials on gravel driveways. But Ludwig is as sharp as it is cuddly, its bobbly pullover concealing a script (by series creator Mark Brotherhood) that revels in wordplay and the infinite micro-horrors of social awkwardness.View image in fullscreenWhat fun she’s having! Anna Maxwell Martin as Lucy in Ludwig.Photograph: BBC/Big TalkBest of all is the ever-expanding friendship between John and the gloriously direct Lucy, who has finally and rightly been elevated from underused supporting character to giddily eccentric co-lead. And what fun Maxwell Martin is having; bounding around Cambridge in her dinky ankle socks, her schoolgirl bob bouncing with investigative zeal.John and Lucy are clearly perfect for one another. So much so that you occasionally find yourself wishing James would remain buggered-off to let nature take its course (even if any exertion in the spare room department would play havoc with John’s piles).How best to describe Ludwig’s blend of whimsical mystery and cerebral silliness? Midsomer Murders meets Monk? No, that would be awful. Jonathan Geek? If anything, that would be worse. Instead, let’s leave it at this: Ludwig is Ludwig, and hurrah for that. Long may it bumble.Ludwig aired on BBC One and is on iPlayer nowExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform UK hates ‘Mickey Mouse’ degrees – apprenticeships in dodgy crypto, anyone? | John Crace | The Guardian
description: Dicky Tice recalls digging trenches with a JCB as a young man, omitting to say the firm he went on to run was founded by his grandfather
Author: John Crace
Headline: Dicky Tice recalls digging trenches with a JCB as a young man, omitting to say the firm he went on to run was founded by his grandfather
Content: Reform UK’s Suella Braverman and Richard Tice hold a press conference at a decorating company in Enfield.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAView image in fullscreenReform UK’s Suella Braverman and Richard Tice hold a press conference at a decorating company in Enfield.Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PAThe politics sketchReform UKReform UK hates ‘Mickey Mouse’ degrees – apprenticeships in dodgy crypto, anyone?John CraceDicky Tice recalls digging trenches with a JCB as a young man, omitting to say the firm he went on to run was founded by his grandfatherThu 20 Aug 2026 14.07 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareYou have to hand it to them. Most political parties would have chosen to go quiet, what with it being the middle of August and having next to nothing to say. But Reform are made of stronger stuff. They aren’t bothered that the only interesting thing about them at the moment is that they are fighting like rats in a sack. They seem to wear that as a badge of honour. A coming of age sophistication. So for the second time in a week they called a press conference.Obviously there was no sign of Nigel Farage. He is still in hiding, avoiding answering questions onReform’s unusual funding modelsand perhaps having therapy to recover from hishumiliating byelection adventure. Nor were we to be graced with Zia Yusuf who is now close to becoming a persona non grata in the party having picked fights with almost everyone. It’s just that no one, least of all Tim Montgomerie, is allowed to say so until Nige works out what to do about him.So that left this presser in the shaky hands of Richard Tice andSuella Braverman. Dicky is ubiquitous these days. Mainly because he’s too dim not to realise that not all publicity is good publicity. Perhaps he can’t resist the attention or feeling of freedom he gets when not umbilically attached to Nige. It allows him to believe that he is a fully sentient, independent being. Rather than one of the last clowns standing in the circus.It was Dicky who got us under way, trying not to look too grumpy that the weather had turned and rain was forecast. He seems to prefer the smell of smoke, the thrill offire-fighters risking their livesto but put wildfires and the threat of drought. Speaking at the headquarters of a decorating company in Enfield, Dicky didn’t mince his words. He wasn’t going to congratulate those students who had got their A-level results last week or their GCSE results today.Why? Because almost certainly 80% of them had either underperformed or wasted their time on taking “Mickey Mouse” subjects. Why bother with modern languages? It’s foreigners who should be learning English. And they could forget history. Just a load of crap about stuff that had happened a long time ago. The trouble with school was that you end up learning a whole lot of stuff you’ll never need. All this bullshit about learning to think was completely over-rated.Dicky was here to extol the benefits of being an apprentice. Now he came over positively dreamy. He had been an apprentice once, he said. He could clearly remember his first day on a construction site digging trenches with a JCB. It had been the making of him. Why, it was only a matter of a few years before he was CEO of his own property company. He omitted to mention that the business he was running was the family firm started by his grandfather. But don’t think for a minute that Dicky was just another nepo baby. He had got where he had in life on merit. It takes skill to turn a large fortune into a small one.Here was the thing. Children were being held back by their schools. By their own limited imaginations. These days kids should learn to choose their own parents a bit better. That’s a life skill children should be taught in school. And start to think outside the box. When most people thought of apprenticeships they turned to manual labour. But the possibilities were so much greater than that. Today’s kids should get with the programme. There must be hundreds of apprenticeships in dodgy crypto deals, money laundering and offshore accounts.Suella had tried and failed not to look too patronising; while Dicky had been wittering on. You get the feeling she still feels apprenticeships are something for other people’s kids rather than her own. But she was starting at a huge disadvantage when explaining the new Reform offering. It obviously didn’t help that the government had already spelled out its own rather more thought-through apprenticeship scheme, so the morning was something of a waste of everyone’s time.But what really stuck in the throat was that Suella spent the first five or so minutes saying that the government had let down students over the past 15 years. Now either Suella is suffering from extreme memory loss or she imagines the rest of us are. Because until January this year she had been a Tory MP and a senior cabinet minister in successive Conservative governments. And now she was expecting us to take her seriously.Then Suella got to the nitty gritty. Businesses were to be helped to take on apprenticeships. Much like they were under Labour. And she was going to cancel any degrees that weren’t strictly vocational and close down almost every university because they were a waste of time. Mere generators of student debt. She spat out the phrase “gender studies”. She wouldn’t be happy until she had annihilated a higher education sector worth billions of pounds. Her legacy would be to turn Oxford University into Oxford Technical College.It was Dicky who fielded most of the questions. After all, why wouldn’t you get the most half-witted person in the room to clarify your education policies? The BBC pointed out that student loans actually qualified as borrowing on the government balance sheet. This seemed to take Dicky by surprise but, like the bullshitter he is, he chose to plough on anyway. “Cash is cash,” he declared triumphantly as if revealing a wonder of the universe. It certainly is for Reform. This will be written on the party’s gravestone.We moved on to Reform’s latest contributions to the light entertainment industry. The squabbles. The fuck ups. Dicky’s eyes lit up. Things were going great. Had never been better. The infighting was just day-to-day disagreements. And Nige had had a huge triumph in Clacton. No one had ever beaten a man with a bin on his head so comprehensively. It had been such a success that Reform was looking forward to going through the whole process again if a recall petition is triggered following the conclusion of aparliamentary standards investigation. The summer of fun just gets better and better.Explore more on these topicsReform UKThe politics sketchSuella BravermanRichard TiceNigel FaragecommentShareReuse this content

title: Fat people cannot win, regardless of what we do. And I’ve had enough | Rebecca Shaw | The Guardian
description: Using weight loss drugs like Ozempic is not ‘cheating’ – and why does it matter how a person changes their body anyway?
Author: Rebecca Shaw
Headline: Using weight loss drugs like Ozempic is not ‘cheating’ – and why does it matter how a person changes their body anyway?
Content: ‘If you’re fat, that’s a moral failing, if you lose weight with drugs, you didn’t earn it,’ Rebecca Shaw writes. Pictured: Actor John Goodman, whose weight loss has drawn media attention after a photo of him went viral.Photograph: Lev Radin/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreen‘If you’re fat, that’s a moral failing, if you lose weight with drugs, you didn’t earn it,’ Rebecca Shaw writes. Pictured: Actor John Goodman, whose weight loss has drawn media attention after a photo of him went viral.Photograph: Lev Radin/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.OpinionLife and styleFat people cannot win, regardless of what we do. And I’ve had enoughRebecca ShawUsing weight loss drugs like Ozempic is not ‘cheating’ – and why does it matter how a person changes their body anyway?Thu 20 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 16.28 EDTShareAs you might know if you read my columns, see me a mile away, or talk to me for five seconds, I am a card-carrying lifelong member of the Fat Lesbian Club. However, ever since I first laid eyes on the television show Roseanne (very important to me) as a small child, the actor John Goodman has held a special place in my heart. It was confusing for me: did I want to be Dan Conner, or be with Dan Conner? I’m still not sure. He has always been so hot to me, from Dan on Roseanne toFred Flintstoneto Walter in The Big Lebowski. His body has now drawn attention in the last week or so, after aphoto of himshowing significant weight loss went viral.It’s not Goodman’s 74-year-old body (his choice) I want to discuss, but instead the arguments that broke out abouthowhe lost the weight. On one side there were many people congratulating him on his hard work. Then there were people claiming he had taken Ozempic so it wasn’t actually hard work, and then there were people defending that by saying he’d been losing weight for years, so he’d done it the “right way”, actually.The social media algorithm has left me behind. I’m unc and I’m chopped – and that’s OKRead moreI don’t know the details and I don’t care, but none of this is good. This is a common sentiment, but now it seems to be snowballing. There’s this idea that fat people who use weight loss drugs are “cheating” or “taking the easy way”. What it means, as usual, is that fat people cannot win, regardless of what we do. And I’ve had enough.I’m a fat person. We areconstantlybadgered and tortured by a society that tells us to lose weight, at all costs. If you’re fat, that’s a moral failing: you’re lazy and unhealthy. If you’re fat at the gym, or jogging down the street, you’re an object of ridicule. If you lose weight with drugs, you didn’t earn it. If you’re fat and not self-flagellating at every moment, you’re glorifying obesity. If you lose weight for any reason, it then proves you were never really happy with yourself; it proves that fat is bad, that thinness was always the real goal. If you stay fat, we want you to admit you’re unhealthy. If you say you’re happy, we want to diagnose you with denial. So much of the condescension as well as plain cruelty towards fat people is packaged as “we just want you to be healthy”. If this were true (and if being skinny were the only marker of health, which it isn’t), nobody would be criticisingJohn Goodmanor other fat people for using medication, by saying it’s cheating.“Cheating” implies you’re competing against someone. Who is being cheated if a fat person changes their body? What game are we playing? Why does it matterhowa person changes their body – and why does any of it matter at all to non-fat people anyway? Just like basically every other human condition, there are a million reasons people’s bodies are different sizes and respond differently to different things. When someone quits smoking with medication, we don’t say they’ve cheated. We know that medication can be a tool. We don’t insist they go cold turkey to prove that theyreally wanted to quit. We understand in all other cases that making something easier, with less suffering, doesn’t make the outcome less legitimate. But when the body in question is fat, suddenly we become moral arbiters. Suddenly it mattershowthey do what we have savagely demanded they do.‘Ozempic face’ and hair loss: what evidence is there for weight-loss drug side-effects?Read moreSociety has spent decades telling fat people that our value depends on our ability to control our weight. Now there is medicine that can make that control easier, and suddenly the problem is not the weight but whether the person has suffered sufficiently to “deserve” it. People resent us for being fat, and they resent us for getting thin. They just want us to suffer. All of this, as ever, is only about punishing fat people. People just hate us and our bodies, and they feel no shame about demonstrating that hatred, largely (no pun intended) because they are safe from being called out. It is perfectly socially acceptable to hate fat people.This is not even about weight loss drugs – I don’t think everyone should take Ozempic, and I certainly worry about all the relatively thin people who seem to be taking it purely to get even thinner. I also don’t think being fat is inherently bad or good. I just think we should be treated like human beings. Is that really so much to ask? Apparently it is.We should be allowed to lose weight without having to provide you with a moral explanation for how we did it. We should be allowed to remain fat without having to convince you that we are sufficiently miserable about it. We should be allowed to exercise, eat, dress, date, and just go about our lives without our bodies becoming public property. Fat people should not have to audition for your approval. We are human beings, our bodies are none of your business, and you need to keep your big fat noses out of our lives.Rebecca Shaw is a writer based in SydneyExplore more on these topicsLife and styleOpinionCelebrityJohn GoodmanWeight-loss drugscommentShareReuse this content

title: Premier League returns and Arsenal sense opportunity with rivals in flux | Premier League | The Guardian
description: New managers galore suggest many of the usual suspects will struggle to dethrone the champions but their own hunger could be the key
Author: David Hytner
Headline: New managers galore suggest many of the usual suspects will struggle to dethrone the champions but their own hunger could be the key
Content: Declan Rice did more than most last season to ensure Arsenal ended their 22-year wait for the Premier League title.Photograph: David Price/AFC/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDeclan Rice did more than most last season to ensure Arsenal ended their 22-year wait for the Premier League title.Photograph: David Price/AFC/Getty ImagesPremier LeaguePremier League returns and Arsenal sense opportunity with rivals in fluxNew managers galore suggest many of the usual suspects will struggle to dethrone the champions, but their own hunger could be the keyDavid HytnerThu 20 Aug 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMikel Arteta wants to get his messaging absolutely right. According to him, Arsenal are not about to defend theirPremier Leaguetitle. They are set to attack another one.Remember Win the dog, who the manager brought in to the club’s training ground a few years back? She must now be called “Won”. But it is when Arteta quibbles over another bout of semantics that he highlights why he is entering the new season with such energy and optimism.Do not talk to him about Arsenal’s stability. He prefers the word “consistency” along with more thrusting ones like “ambition”. The overall theme is clear. When Arteta surveys the landscape at the top end of the English game, he sees a settled environment at his club and flux elsewhere.Premier League: nine newcomers to watch in the top flight this seasonRead moreIn terms of the so-called Big Six – the richest clubs in the country, as ranked by Deloitte – there are new managers at Manchester City, Liverpool and Chelsea; a virtually new one at Tottenham and a relatively new one atManchester United. It has been a summer of unprecedented change in the Premier League with nine clubs with a new man in charge. Of those who hold out hope of a title challenge, only Aston Villa have a fully bedded-in manager in Unai Emery.Rather abruptly, Arteta finds himself as the longest-serving manager in the division;he took over from Emeryat Arsenal in December 2019. Emery is second on the list,having been at Villafor three years and nine months, and only one other –Daniel Farke at Leeds– has been at his club for more than three years.When Arteta was given the job at Arsenal, Pep Guardiola was two titles into his storied City tenure, Jürgen Klopp had won the Champions League atLiverpooland was on his way to winning the league that season and José Mourinho had just joined Spurs.View image in fullscreenMikel Arteta and Arsenal held their nerve to hold off the challenge from Manchester City last season.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianArteta has seen them all off, withGuardiola’s departure from Cityat the end of last season being the most significant single shift in the dynamics for the forthcoming campaign.Arteta is nowthe big beast, the only current manager to have won the Premier League, and as Arsenal prepare for the curtain-raiser at home to Coventry on Friday night, it is hard to ignore the confidence they are projecting. With virtually of all their rivals in transition, uncertainty undercutting the excitement, predictions difficult to make in the face of little actual evidence, Arsenal are reassured by their firm foundations. They sense opportunity, another title; the creation of a dynasty. That is the ultimate goal.There is something more. Namely how everything changed for them in the closing weeks of last season. City had done the hard work, clawing back a nine-point deficit from the middle of March – a period when they had a game in hand. But in the five-match shootout that followed, City blinked first,drawing at Everton. Most know how nerve-racking it was for Arsenal. Not least Arteta. The Emirates Stadium was a sea of anxiety when Arsenal last played there – against Burnley in the penultimate game of the season. They gota 1-0 win over the line.View image in fullscreenBruno Guimarães is a high-quality arrival from Newcastle to boost Arsenal’s midfield ranks.Photograph: Mark Leech/Offside/Getty ImagesThenCity drew at Bournemouthand it was over; Arsenal’s 22-year wait, the oppressive weight. It is impossible to underestimate the feeling of liberation. Nobody can question the bottle of this team. Nobody will taunt them with the cry of “second again, olé, olé.” It is plain Arteta and his players will feed off it and perhaps it will lead to a more expansive style of football. The fear of falling short inhibited their game as the heat rose last time out.Arsenal have made changes behind the scenes, looking for the marginal gains, most notably in the medical department where the head doctor, Zafar Iqbal, was mutually consented in early June. Arnaldo Abrantes has come in from Aston Villa to replace him. If the players can stay fitter for longer, Arsenal believe they can stay ahead. They have protected themselves with moves to deepen an already well-stocked squad.Bruno Guimarãesis the most eye-catching addition, withEzri Konsa about to follow.Arsenal versus City still feels like the primary head-to-head. Guardiola had Arteta’s number last season, winning two and drawing one of the three meetings between the clubs. City were much the better team in theCarabao Cup final that they won 2-0. But that was under Guardiola and that was with Rodri and Bernardo Silva. If Guardiola’s exit has hit City the hardest, then those of the commanding midfielders to Barcelona and Real Madrid, respectively, is not far behind.City’s faith in their new manager, Enzo Maresca, is rooted in what they saw of him when he worked on their coaching staff; he was an assistant to Guardiola in the treble-winning season of 2022-23. Previously, he coached the Under‑23s to the Premier League 2 title in 2020-21.View image in fullscreenElliot Anderson has arrived at Manchester City for £116m, but, like his manager, he has big shoes to fill.Photograph: Alex Pantling/FA/Getty ImagesIt is a well-thought-through appointment; the kind a well-run club makes. Yet at the same time, it is not one to quicken the pulse. Maresca, quite simply, has enormous shoes to fill. Ditto Elliot Anderson, the impressive young midfielder upon whomCity have bet the house. Can City be better given the personnel losses they have sustained? They must surely do so given the direction of travel at Arsenal. City do retain the cheat code that is Erling Haaland.There are parallels between City and Liverpool, who want their new manager, Andoni Iraola, to have a similar impact in his first season that Arne Slot managed in 2024-25. Slot took Klopp’s teamand glided to the title. Maybe consistency in the dugout is not everything?On the other hand, Slot was given only one new player – Federico Chiesa – who barely played that season and he essentially stuck with what had made the Klopp collective so successful. It was evolution not revolution. When he tried the latter last season, Slot found that his tenure unravelled, although his rotten luck with injuries must be acknowledged. There was also the death of Diogo Jota.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLiverpool have moved onAndy Robertson, Ibrahima Konaté and, most crucially,Mohamed Salah, even if he was a shadow of his former self last season. Salah has not yet been replaced; it would be impossible to replace the prime-years version of him and Iraola, who has a number of injury concerns, has it all to do.Coaxing more from Florian Wirtz and Alexander Isak is fundamental. Iraola’s style has the capacity to hold Anfield in thrall; the aggression, the front-foot slickness, the boldness to go one-versus-one all over the pitch. How quickly can he impose it?Chelsea will be interesting under Xabi Alonso, who has been allowed to add players to fit into the 3-4-2-1 he used to such stunning effect at Bayer Leverkusen. Alonso has also been permitted to break from the club’s youth-first signing model and bring in much-needed experience.View image in fullscreenMorgan Rogers celebrates scoring in pre-season, after his £117m move from Aston Villa.Photograph: Anthony Hanc/Wired Photos/ShutterstockMorgan Rogers, alongside Cole Palmer and behind João Pedro, with Moisés Caicedo and maybe Reece James in the deep midfield roles, has a very nice feel to it. There is talent in central defence. The lack of European football will be a temporary blessing.Ask any chief executive what supporters want at the start of a season and the answer is invariably the same: be better than last season. Which will not be a problem for Chelsea after the implosion to limp home in 10th. Or Spurs, who finished 17th for the second campaign in a row and narrowly avoided relegation. Roberto De Zerbi, who was appointed as the manager with seven games to go,kept them upand in the first summer since the end of Daniel Levy’s near 25-year as chair, the new hierarchy have been determined to act decisively. Their heavy spend on Premier League-proven players has allowed the fanbase to dream.De Zerbi is a man to generate buy-in. In him they trust. Ditto a midfield that will feature Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes. With Conor Gallagher or James Maddison expected to fill the No 10 role, Spurs look to have a proper unit to hold things together. They will also benefit from no European football.Premier League fans’ previews: our club-by-club guide to 2026-27Read moreWhat about United, for whom everything suddenly came together afterthe appointment of Michael Carrickin January, initially for an interim spell? His record meant the club had to give him the jobon a permanent basis– he finished the season with 12 wins and three draws from 17 league matches. It was 2.3 points per game. Transpose that over a 38-match campaign and you get 87 points. Arsenal won the title with 85. Are United dark horses for glory?Concerns remain. Carrick was largely untroubled by injuries and when United have their best XI on the field they are a match for anybody. When they miss a few, as they normally did under Ruben Amorim, they can flatline. United were always going to have to add a good number of signings this summer, particularly as they prepare to go from a Europe-free season to a return to the Champions League. They have not yet done enough; the final week-and-a-half of the transfer window could be crucial. As Mike Tyson almost said, everybody has a plan until they are punched in the face by the Champions League.View image in fullscreenMarcus Rashford is back at Manchester United after falling out of favour during Ruben Amorim’s reign.Photograph: Grzegorz Wajda/SOPA/Getty ImagesAre Villa really about to take another step forward after the highs of last season when they finished fourth andwon the Europa League? It feels unlikely given the departures, headlined by those ofRogers,Youri TielemansandLucas Digne, with Konsa primed to go, too. Strangely, there is a whiff of transition about them. It is possible to find reasons to fret about every team. Apart from Arsenal.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueArsenalLiverpoolManchester UnitedManchester CityTottenham HotspurAston VillafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I need to think like a CEO’: Weezer on the shifting sands of success, ugly feelings and the joy of spreadsheets | Weezer | The Guardian
description: As the self-professed geeky rockers release their conceptual 20th album, Rivers Cuomo and Patrick Wilson discuss dodging failure, being saved by fans and their obsessive creativity
Author: Stevie Chick
Headline: As the self-professed geeky rockers release their conceptual 20th album, Rivers Cuomo and Patrick Wilson discuss dodging failure, being saved by fans and their obsessive creativity
Content: ‘We have perspective on everything now’ …(from left)Weezer’s Patrick Wilson, Rivers Cuomo, Brian Bell and Scott Shriner.Photograph: Brendan WalterView image in fullscreen‘We have perspective on everything now’ …(from left)Weezer’s Patrick Wilson, Rivers Cuomo, Brian Bell and Scott Shriner.Photograph: Brendan WalterWeezerInterview‘I need to think like a CEO’: Weezer on the shifting sands of success, ugly feelings and the joy of spreadsheetsStevie ChickAs the self-professed geeky rockers release their conceptual 20th album, Rivers Cuomo and Patrick Wilson discuss dodging failure, being saved by fans and their obsessive creativityThu 20 Aug 2026 10.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 13.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song Rivers Cuomo wrote for Weezer’s new album, their 20th, blatantly mimics the US rockers’ 1994 debut single, Undone (The Sweater Song). On the track CEO, the singer-guitarist grumbles over a slow, Velvets-y backing about having to crank out “another 90s jam” and wishing he could do “something new – but nobody wants to hearthat”. It’s a deliciously meta moment, but also one that allows Cuomo to gently vent “my frustrations over people wanting me to just write songs about our first two albums”.Cuomo wrote the song straight after SZNZ, the four-album song-cycle Weezer released throughout 2022, each album named after a season. That project fed his notoriously intense, analytic and occasionally obsessive approach to songwriting. Thanks to the kind of data artists have at their fingertips in the streaming age, though, he realised that, with each subsequent SZNZ, “fewer and fewer people were listening to them”.His response was to “think strategically”. On a video call from his home in Santa Monica, California, where Cuomo, 56, lives with his wife and children, he says he realised: “If I want people to listen to my music, I need to think less like a mad scientist in the research and development department and more like a CEO.” Accordingly, he took several years off from releasing any new material (“to build up demand”), ditched the high concepts of SZNZ and focused on creating what he thinks the fans want.Gently venting their frustrations … CEO, from Weezer’s 20th album.Like six previous albums, the new album is titled Weezer. It has already been dubbed the “gold” album by fans, due to its sleeve colour. While the arch lyrics to CEO might suggest it is a cynical exercise in pandering to his audience, the Gold Album is a more complex, sophisticated beast.Cuomo is driven by his obsession with songwriting. “It’s like building sonic architecture, such a cool, stimulating experience,” he says, although he prefers to describe himself as a “composer”. “The term ‘songwriter’ feels like Paul Simon’s about to explain a sombre part of life,” adds his bandmate Patrick Wilson, 57, who plays drums and guitar and joins the interview from the garage of his California home. “What we do is more visceral: busting out a sick riff and saying to each other: ‘Dude, checkthisout!’”Cuomo’s approach is methodical to a degree that feels antithetical to rock music; he has boasted that Google Sheets is integral to his process. (One spreadsheet, which he has named “The Encyclopedia o’ Riffs”, keeps track of all his unused and unfinished ideas and is legendary among Weezer fans.) He also can’t resist a kooky conceptual hook to guide his songwriting – see the group’s 2021 heavy metal set, Van Weezer, or OK Human, their orchestral rock opus of the same year, or, obviously, SZNZ.The Gold Album is similarly conceptual, this time the concept being the creation of an album the Weezer faithful will love. Cuomo’s process has been typically analytical and methodical – and it’s clear he has loved the challenge. He views their live shows as the testing ground for the new material – “where the rubber meets the road”, he says. “I want the people in the room to want to hear these new songs as well as our old hits, and to sing along. I wanted them to be reallyfunlive, to have substantial riffs and guitar parts.” Accordingly, he has taken inspiration from his favourite band of the moment, the Swedish heavy rockers Ghost, whom he says restored his understanding of “the power of stadium-rock riffage”. Nevertheless, much of the Gold Album channels the loud guitars and pop-oriented tuneage of Weezer’s eponymous 1994 debut, often brilliantly so.View image in fullscreenAlmost over before they began …(from left)Cuomo, Wilson, Matt Sharp and Bell in 1996.Photograph: Martyn Goodacre/Getty ImagesThe new album is shaped by deeper wounds than those occasioned by SZNZ’s reception, however. The line in CEO where Cuomo says he has “gotta keep this rocket in the sky” references the moment when the failure of Weezer’s second album, 1996’s Pinkerton, seemed to hobble their career before it began – a foundational trauma for the group’s leader.He remains the pilot of his bandmates’ fortunes as much as his own and, while the Gold Album sounds bold and confident, there are moments in our interview when his anxiety over this responsibility surfaces. They collaborated more as a group on the songwriting of the Gold Album than any previous Weezer release; while Cuomo talks about how their positive feedback was “a real good sign” he might be on the right track with an idea, it’s clear he chiefly prized their solidarity as a group “to give us the strength to face any pushback from the audience”.Raised in a Buddhist ashram in Connecticut, which taught him methods to “calm down my body and mind”, Cuomo became a teenage metalhead and, in his late teens, under the influence of the Swedish poodle-rocker Yngwie Malmsteen, formed the hair-metal group Avant Garde. That group renamed itself Zoom and relocated to Los Angeles to make it big, but within a year they had imploded and Cuomo began working at Tower Records in West Hollywood.This disappointment – alluded to on The LA Sound, a song from the Gold Album, written by guitarist Brian Bell, about a no-hoper metal band running aground on the Sunset Strip circuit – was “heartbreaking”, says Cuomo. But it proved the making of him. “If Zoom had ‘happened’, if my dreams had come true, I would just be the lead guitar player – thesecondlead guitar player, excuse me – in a heavy metal band that would have been woefully out of style by 1992. Instead, my heart got broken and that led to something a lot bigger and better: singing, and expressing myself, and focusing on songs rather than shredding.”Weezer formed shortly after Nirvana’s fateful breakthrough. Cuomo had been seduced by the Pixies’ “big crunchy guitars, melody and heaviness” – one of numerous artists he discovered through his Tower co-workers. On Weezer’s earliest demos, he “tried singing like Black Francis or Kurt Cobain or Perry Farrell, more of a ‘rock’ voice. It took months before I finally gave up and sang with my natural, pure voice. I’d sung in school choirs; to my surprise, it still worked, even over the big guitars.”It wasn’t just Cuomo’s voice that set Weezer against the grain. They wore glasses and unhip clothes, while Cuomo sang about comic books and Dungeons & Dragons. The rock press identified them as nerds, a label they never quite shook loose and ended up embracing: they kicked off this year’s Weezer: The Gathering tour, named after the fantasy card game Magic: The Gathering, with a pickleball tournament with their fans. Regarding this resistance to cool, Cuomo says they “just felt it was very uncool to try and be something you’re not”.“The kids today would call it ‘being a sweat’,” says Wilson, un-coolly. “In hip-hop, they would have called it ‘fronting’.”View image in fullscreenStill unapologetically nerdy …(from left)Bell, Cuomo, Wilson and Shriner.Photograph: Brendan WalterThis honesty – along with Cuomo’s infallible gift for pop songcraft – struck a chord in the post-Nirvana cash grab. But as their debut began its ascent to quintuple-platinum status, via a punishing schedule of touring and promotion, Cuomo’s morale plummeted. In his diaries, he wrote of his dissatisfaction with this new rock’n’roll life. Addressing an imaginary rock-star-in-waiting, he gloomily advised: “Youwillget lonely … It’s not all cocaine, chicks and limos.”His face is mostly obscured by shadow on our call, but Cuomo’s disillusionment remains palpable three decades on. “All my life. I’d figured that if I got a record deal – if we got on MTV and radio – then I would feel fulfilled and loved,” he says. “We achieved all those things. But I still felt unseen and unheard and misunderstood and lonely.”Cuomo abruptly ditched the tour bus for Harvard, where he studied classical composition alongside students sporting Weezer T-shirts, oblivious to his presence. The course deepened his feel for songwriting. “Creatively, I was feeling incredibly confident. I was not happy about my personal life, but believed if I isolated myself – and, to an extent, tortured myself – I would be able to create something really great.” He pauses. “I was probably overconfident.”Inspired by the antihero in Puccini’s Madama Butterfly, he wrote Pinkerton, an ambitious, strikingly unguarded confession that success had left Cuomo engulfed by loneliness, disaffection and sexual confusion. Before the album’s 1996 release, he warned the Weezer fanclub that it included “all the parts of myself that I was either afraid or embarrassed to think about before. So there’s some pretty nasty stuff on there.”View image in fullscreen‘A chaotic era’ …(from left)Bell, Cuomo, Wilson and Sharp in 1996.Photograph: Martyn Goodacre/Getty ImagesSure enough, Across the Sea depicts him falling in love with a Japanese teenager who wrote him a fan letter (“I wonder what clothes you wear to school … I wonder how you touch yourself”); on Pink Triangle, he grumbles about a lesbian who doesn’t fancy him; and, on The Good Life, he’s “a pig, I’m a dog, so ’scuse me if I drool”.The album was, he says, an act of catharsis. “It’s always been hard for me to communicate feelings in words, in conversation,” he sighs. “But if I can play them through melodies and chords and lyrics, I feel thistremendousemotional release.”It was all done with lashings of self-mockery and knowing awfulness, but plenty of fans recoiled. Even Ric Ocasek, the producer of their debut, didn’t seem to like it.Pinkerton flopped; Cuomo put Weezer on hiatus and went into hiding. It was “a chaotic era”, says Wilson, who worried about the impact of Weezer’s steep arc on Cuomo. “I wondered how child stars dealt with success. And I realised: they’re all insane, because it’s a ridiculous process. That period was overwhelming.”“I’d keep feeling like I’d found my way out, that the way back was just around the corner,” Cuomo remembers, of the struggle to write a third Weezer album. “But each time, just as I’d be about to announce to the guys I had songs I felt confident in, my confidence would collapse again: these songs are terrible. Let me start over. Give me a few months.”Salvation came in 2000, in the form of an unexpected six-figure offer to play Japan. After four years of darkness and frustration, Cuomo remembers being “in tears” when his manager called with the news. Next, the band jumped aboard that summer’s Warped tour and discovered that, in their absence, Pinkerton had found an audience that treasured its confessional intensity. “Our fans were out of their minds, chanting: ‘Weezer! Weezer!’ all through the bands on before us,” remembers Wilson. “I knew something was up. Like: oh. We’re going to be OK.”Today, Pinkerton is recognised as a pivotal emo album. Its follow-up – 2001’s Green Album, again produced by Ocasek and containing the single Hash Pipe – was a platinum-selling hit. “I remember thinking: if we can survive the last five years of solitude and self-doubt and come back to this, we can get throughanything,” Cuomo says. “Our fans pulled us out of our self-doubt.” Today, those fans log in to Cuomo’s personal Discord server and watch him practice vocal warm-ups or play Beethoven on his piano. “There’s always this group of people online that love me and appreciate me and are looking forward to hearing anything I’m doing, so I never have to feel alone,” he says.The fans have stayed loyal as Cuomo has explored unexpected directions – such as the heavy metal of Van Weezer and the orchestral rock of OK Human – and collaborated with songwriters outside his realm, including Linda Perry, Jermaine Dupri and Justin Hawkins of the Darkness. He confesses his obsession with songwriting isn’t always healthy: “There were times where my wife was going through troubles and she really could have used my help. And I would spend all day in my room, just working – super-deep, detailed work – and I told her, like: ‘I can’t help you right now, I’m on a roll here, I really need to focus.’ There has been some conflict.”View image in fullscreenFor ever a frontman … Cuomo performs at the Coachella festival in 2025.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for CoachellaThis hasn’t happened recently, though, he says. Three decades after the existential wobble of Pinkerton, Cuomo seems happy keeping Weezer’s rocket in the sky. He feels lucky to “have this vocation with these three other guys. We can get in a room together and work on stuff that feels important to us. As you get older, it can be hard to have those kinds of relationships. But we have them.”‘There is an alternative to capitalism’: after addiction and losing a home to LA wildfires, indie rockers Diiv start againRead moreThe relationships have held strong through traumas that might have destabilised other groups, such as the 2011 death of bassistMikey Welshfrom a suspected drug overdose. The bandmates all “get along pretty great now”, says Wilson. “We all have perspective on everything now. We see how everything unfolded and how deeply unusual it was, and we recognise it.”Can Cuomo see a time in his life when Weezer isn’t a thing? On the sleeve to 2005’s Make Believe – released during a period of emotional anxiety and voluntary celibacy, for spiritual reasons – he included the soliloquy from The Tempest, where Prospero abandons his magic and commits to “drown my book”.“At the time, I wasn’t sure I was gonna go on making music,” Cuomo says. “I wanted to try a really intense spiritual path and then start a family. I wanted to step away from the spotlight, from being an artist, even from being creative, and see what else there is in life. So I included that speech, like: OK, maybe this is my retirement statement.” He stops. For one of the few times during our chat, he looks up from the shadows and into his laptop camera, smiling. “But it’s obvious, isn’t it? Come on, Rivers. You can’t escape this.”Weezer is released via Reprise/Warner on 21 AugustExplore more on these topicsWeezerPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Hazy sunshine, factor-50 smiles and Cliff Richard at the wheel: the 20 best summer holiday movies – ranked! | Movies | The Guardian
description: From feelgood romances to heated interactions, here are the films that best capture the seasonal moment
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: From feelgood romances to heated interactions, here are the films that best capture the seasonal moment
Content: Paul Mescal and Frankie Corio in Aftersun.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyView image in fullscreenPaul Mescal and Frankie Corio in Aftersun.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyRankedMoviesHazy sunshine, factor-50 smiles and Cliff Richard at the wheel: the 20 best summer holiday movies – ranked!From feelgood romances to heated interactions, here are the films that best capture the seasonal momentXan BrooksThu 20 Aug 2026 08.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 12.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. American Graffiti (1973)Let’s begin at the end. 2 September 1962: the final night of the summer vacation; one last big blowout before adult life intervenes. George Lucas’s rambunctious salute to footloose youth paints vivid vignettes of Modesto, California, rocking around the clock with its loose-knit gaggle of characters. But this has one eye on the meter and knows that time is running short.19. The Lost Daughter (2021)“It’s a working holiday,” insists Olivia Colman’s brittle academic, blasting her factor-50 smile at the bemused guests and staff of a Greek island resort. She’s in flight from her past and liable to combust any second. Paradise here offers little rest or respite. The professor has made a clean getaway, but she’s brought along all her baggage.18. My Summer of Love (2004)View image in fullscreenWild at heart … Emily Blunt and Natalie Press in My Summer of Love.In which Natalie Press’s working-class Yorkshire lass finds an exotic foreign land just a hop and a skip across the moor in the form of the ivy-clad house of Emily Blunt’s boarding-school princess. Director Paweł Pawlikowski slowly turns up the temperature as the girls lean into the season, lounging in the dry grass and listening to Edith Piaf. They’re at once stickily close and a thousand miles apart.17. Summertime (1955)David Lean’s tender Technicolor romance was one of the first British films to be shot entirely on location, strolling around beautiful, dirty Venice in the company of Katharine Hepburn’s middle-aged Miss Lonelyheart. Lean called for her to step backwards into the green canal at Campo San Barnaba. Hepburn gamely obliged and clambered out with conjunctivitis.16. Y Tu Mamá También (2001)View image in fullscreenA place in the sun … Gael García Bernal, Maribel Verdu and Diego Luna in Y Tu Mamá También.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamySex and death ride shotgun in Alfonso Cuarón’s lustful field trip through turn-of-the-century Mexico. Gael García Bernal and Diego Luna are teenage buddies who light out for the beach with their engines overheating; Maribel Verdú co-stars as the exacting older woman who, if not quite steering them straight, at least helps point them in interesting new directions.15. Summer Holiday (1963)A summer holiday list without Summer Holiday? It would be like the Tower without the ravens or mistletoe without the wine. Directed with an easy swing by Peter Yates (his debut, and he would go on to make Bullitt and Breaking Away), this now stands as a colourful blast from the past, an innocent postcard from postwar, pre-Brexit Europe. A blue-collar bus mechanic – embodied byCliff Richard– magics up a new route from Hertfordshire down to Athens, complete with entertainment and a flurry of comic misadventures. Only a churl wouldn’t get on board.14. Tomboy (2011)Céline Sciamma makes small rousing films about secret lives, sanctuaries and precious stolen moments. Tomboy is one of her best: a gorgeous coming-of-age tale about 10-year-old Laure (Zoé Héran), who – bouncing between schools, the new kid on the block – introduces herself as Mickaël and effectively becomes another person. Sciamma’s implied message? That the humble summer break can be a transformational timeout, with September’s child only distantly related to July’s.13. La Piscine (1969)View image in fullscreenBody of water … Alain Delon and Romy Schneider in La Piscine.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyThe pool is a mirror in Jacques Deray’s dazzling, depthless thriller pungently set on the French Riviera and tapping the off-screen tensions of co-stars Romy Schneider and Alain Delon. If La Piscine’s air of modish ennui now feels overused, that’s because it’s a design classic, most notably lifted and adapted by both François Ozon’s Swimming Pool and Luca Guadagnino’s A Bigger Splash.12. Roman Holiday (1953)“Rome. By all means, Rome,” declares Audrey Hepburn’s runaway princess after spending a liberative, life-changing few days in the eternal city with Gregory Peck’s US newsman. As for the movie, this might be the ultimate European and American meet-cute. Shot on location, skipping between the tourist sights, Roman Holiday wedded old-school Hollywood romance with the looser rhythm of Italian neorealism.11. A Summer’s Tale (1996)Eric Rohmer was the poet laureate of French dreamers, the creator of films that feel flyweight and then linger for a lifetime. A Summer’s Tale is his semi-autobiographical account of a lost summer spent on the coast of Brittany pursuing sea shanties and women with the same awkward stumble. It’s a hazy, lazy joy of a film, brimming with sunlight and rocked by the backwash of chatter and song.View image in fullscreenHot times … Jennifer Grey and Patrick Swayze in Dirty Dancing.Photograph: Vestron Pictures/Allstar10. Dirty Dancing (1987)Everything’s big in this Borscht Belt summer classic. Big gestures, big emotions, big drums on the soundtrack, big hair. It’s 1963 and Baby (Jennifer Grey) is getting whisked off her feet by Patrick Swayze’s bad-boy dance instructor. The Catskills are a cauldron of class and ethnic tensions; first love is an intoxicating, disorientating hot mess. Resistance is futile: the film lifts and spins us. Grand finale, big reward.9. Sundown (2021)The best holidays are the ones that you never, ever want to end. Michel Franco’s Sundown casts Tim Roth as mild-mannered Neil, whose Mexican vacation is interrupted by the news of his mother’s sudden death. The trouble is that Neil would really prefer not to leave. So he pretends he’s lost his passport, shoves his tear-stained family through the departure gate and then circles back to the beach with the satisfied air of a man who’s just put out all the bins. Who is this Neil? What the hell is he thinking? He’s the shadow beneath the parasol, the chip of ice in the cocktail glass and the finest existential antihero this side of L’Étranger.8. The Go-Between (1971)LP Hartley’s source novel was elegant and reflective, weighed down by the heat as it traces the illicit exchange of letters via a lovestruck schoolboy. Joseph Losey and Harold Pinter make the mood more jangly and atonal, perpetually on the verge of panic. What a wonderfully treacherous period drama this is, the filmic equivalent of a strip of flypaper. All the characters are stuck and squirming. None of them are getting away unscathed.7. Les Vacances de Monsieur Hulot (1953)View image in fullscreenBeside the seaside … Jacques Tati in Les Vacances de Monsieur Hulot.Photograph: Ronald GrantThis was initially lower on the list, as befits its musty antique status, but then I watched it again and it’s flawless – there’s nothing else quite like it. Jacques Tati is the hapless holidaymaker who haunts the wings of a seaside town sometimes as a mute witness, sometimes as an agent of gentle chaos. If anything, Tati’s comedy grows more cherishable with each passing decade. Watching it is like peering into a forgotten tide-pool ecosystem: the rumble-tumble lost world of the postwar French resort.View image in fullscreenAngry young men … Jeremy Fox, Esteban Powell, Wiley Wiggins and Mark Vandermeulen in Dazed and Confused.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/Alamy6. Dazed and Confused (1993)Where its spiritual ancestor, American Graffiti, began at the end, the uproarious Dazed and Confused wraps up at the start. It’s the first full day of the 1976 summer break. The high-school kids are wafting groggily back to earth, buffeted and elated after a wild night around town. They’ve drunk beer and shot pool, run amok and made out, and now there’s nothing on the horizon except an Aerosmith concert and the month of June. Sunrise on the football field; the golden morning of their lives.5. Summer with Monika (1953)Flee your family, feel the city; steer a boat around the archipelago. Ingmar Bergman’s jolting kitchen-sink romance casts Harriet Andersson and Lars Ekborg as working-class Stockholm kids who make a bold bid for freedom and yet are bound for the rocks. Bergman was always drawn to life’s extremes – its sunlight and shadow, its ecstasies and agonies – but rarely made them feel as purely relatable as here.4. Days and Nights in the Forest (1970)View image in fullscreenInto the woods … Days and Nights in the Forest by Satyajit Ray.Photograph: Album/AlamyForget the beach and the island retreat – it is the forest where summer breaks tend to deepen and darken. Four Kolkata bachelors drive into the backwoods of Bihar only to realise that there is more than one way to get lost. What follows is an antic meditation on all the big stuff: friendship, responsibility, class and cultural divisions. Writer-director Satyajit Ray takes a humdrum off-the-peg concept – the buddy hangout comedy – and makes it mythic, mysterious and borderline elemental.3. The Green Ray (1986)The second Rohmer film on the list is a small miracle about a small miracle. Specifically it’s about thirtysomething Delphine (Marie Rivière), who is newly single and drifting in a kind of semi-ostracised state across France. But it is also about the green ray, which can reputedly be glimpsed for a split second at sunset and might quietly, magically make everything right. Rohmer employed a skeleton crew and encouraged his cast to improvise, ensuring that his film remained unencumbered and almost weightless, open to the world’s possibilities and the happy accidents it might send our way.2. Aftersun (2022)View image in fullscreenSlow burn … Paul Mescal and Frankie Corio in Aftersun.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyCharlotte Wells’s rapturous family album is still relatively recent and may yet fade out as the years go by. Then again maybe not, because if Aftersun tells us anything it’s that memory only intensifies an experience and that lost summers burn brighter the older we get. On screen it’s for ever 1999 and Paul Mescal’s young father is in Turkey with his daughter (Frankie Corio), browsing for rugs and lounging by the pool, searching for sunshine and averting their gaze from the shadows. Wells’s astonishing debut feature doesn’t feel directed so much as recovered and resurrected. It’s an impressionistic, deeply felt and finally devastating tour de force.1. Before Sunrise (1995)View image in fullscreenTrue romance … Julie Delpy And Ethan Hawke in Before Sunrise.Photograph: Hulton Archive/Getty ImagesThe summer holiday can be a time of freedom and escape, romance and self-discovery. It is all of these things in Richard Linklater’s mid-90s masterpiece about a pair of garrulous Interrailers (Julie Delpy and Ethan Hawke) who steal a few precious hours and wander around Vienna for the night. But the best summer holiday movies are also about time itself. They’re about how we choose to use it and what comes out of those choices.Before Sunrise, a joyous film about footloose youth, tellingly went on to spark a pair of excellent sequels that caught up with its lovers many years down the line. But that awareness of time was baked into the tale from the start. I agonised at some length over what should be number one on this list – and what probably swung it was the bittersweet flourish of Before Sunrise’s last moments, when Linklater’s camera beats back like a ghost to show us the places where Céline and Jesse were idling just a few hours before. The fountain and the ferris wheel. The forlorn little alley with the stacked wooden pallets. The Interrailers have already left them behind and moved on – except that they haven’t, not really. They’ll be haunting them happily for the rest of their lives.Explore more on these topicsFilmRankedMusicalsRomance filmsCliff RichardFilm adaptationsAudrey HepburnBefore SunrisefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Racism and sexism have become normalised in Britain, says equalities minister | Bridget Phillipson | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Bridget Phillipson says politicians have helped fuel hatred and that police are not taking violence against women and girls seriously enough
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Bridget Phillipson says politicians have helped fuel hatred and that police are not taking violence against women and girls seriously enough
Content: 32:10UK minister criticises misogynistic social media culture | Politics WeeklyBridget PhillipsonRacism and sexism have become normalised in Britain, says equalities ministerExclusive: Bridget Phillipson says politicians have helped fuel hatred and that police are not taking violence against women and girls seriously enoughKiran StaceyPolicy editorThu 20 Aug 2026 10.36 EDTFirst published on Thu 20 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRacism and sexism have become normalised in Britain, the equalities minister has said, as she warned that young men were being sucked into violent misogyny by the “cesspit” of social media.Bridget Phillipson said she was increasingly worried about how commonplace misogyny and racism had become, fuelled by online interactions and statements by politicians she said would not have been acceptable a few years ago.She accused senior MPs from Reform and theConservativesof having made racist statements in recent years, and accused the police of not taking violence against women and girls seriously enough.Speaking to the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast, she said: “I worry that we are at kind of a ground zero in terms of attitudes around violence against women and girls. Things that not very long ago felt totally unacceptable are becoming normal. I think we’re seeing that in terms of attitudes towards women, and I think we see that in terms of attitudes around racism.”She accused the shadow justice secretary, Nick Timothy, and Reform’s economic spokesperson, Robert Jenrick, of having made racist statements in recent years.Earlier this year, Timothy called Muslims praying in Trafalgar Square an“act of domination”, while Jenrick came under fire in October afterthe Guardian revealedhe had complained he “didn’t see another white face” on a trip to an area of Birmingham.“We’ve had pretty despicable things that the likes of Robert Jenrick have said in the past on his visit to Birmingham,” she said. “We had Nick Timothy, who said some appalling things about Muslim prayer.“Apparently I’m calling him names when I say that’s racist. I think it is fundamentally racist because I don’t think he would say that about any other group.”Neither Reform nor the Conservatives responded to requests for comment.Labour has been accused in recent years of shying away from criticising statements by Reform and Conservative MPs for fear of alienating their own voters. Phillipson’s comments suggest that underAndy Burnhamministers will be freer to take on their opponents more directly, even on sensitive issues such as race and gender equality.Her comments about online misogyny underline the government’s determination to push through theunder-16 social media ban, which was one of Keir Starmer’s last announcements in office and which ministers have promised will be in place by next spring.View image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch accused Bridget Phillipson, who raised taxes on private school fees as education secretary, of being a ‘spiteful class warrior’.Photograph: The GuardianThe women and equalities minister also criticised the police for not taking violence against women and girls seriously enough. “We’ve seen some pretty shocking failings in terms of the police response over decades and sadly we’re not seeing the progress that we should in terms of how the police will often respond to this,” she said.Labour itself is facing accusations of not taking violence against women seriously withits planto release 5,000 prisoners earlyto free up space in crowded prisons.More women will die if domestic abusers leave prison early, victim’s parents warnRead moreSome in the partyalso thinkthe government is veering into xenophobia with its proposals to toughen the immigration system and even deport children forcibly if their families refuse to move.Phillipson defended the policies of the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, saying they were necessary to restore faith in the migration system. “Having public consent for migration and having a system that is fair is absolutely essential,” she said. “If you don’t have that, then everything falls away.”Phillipson’s criticisms of other parties in part reflect her second role as party chair, which involves coordinating attack lines against Labour’s opposition. But it is also a sign of the personal animosity between her and senior Tory politicians, including the opposition leader, Kemi Badenoch.Badenoch has accused Phillipson, who raised taxes on private school fees as education secretary, of being a “spiteful class warrior”. The comments causeda rowin the Commons chamber this year as the two MPs traded remarks.Phillipson spoke in depth about that row for the first time since it happened, saying: “When she had her say, I just kind of said that people would find her out for who she really was.”She added: “I’m from an ordinary working-class family in the north-east. They don’t like people like me making the argument for what I believe. For some of them, I guess they think I should just get back in my box.”Having been moved by Burnham from her previous role, Phillipson said she was sad to leave her education brief, but said the new prime minister had lifted the mood within the party.“There is a real sense of energy and hope and purpose,” she said. “My reflection on where we began in July 2024 is that a bit more of that would have probably got us a long way down the line.”She added that Burnham had brought “a sense of hopefulness and optimism that I think people have felt has been lacking, not just actually since we came into government, but for years before that”.She denied the party was planning to usethe polling bounceit has seen since Burnham entered Downing Street to launch an early election. “We were elected with a five-year mandate in 2024, and I see no reason that we would depart from that,” she said.Explore more on these topicsBridget PhillipsonViolence against women and girlsWomenSocial mediaAndy BurnhamMigrationLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Leaders attack ‘demotivating’ plan to make pupils who fail GCSEs retake maths and English | Education | The Guardian
description: Government announce plan for ‘stepping stone’ qualification as 620,000 year 11 students face retaking maths or English after failure to achieve grade 4
Author: Richard Adams
Headline: Government announce plan for ‘stepping stone’ qualification as 620,000 year 11 students face retaking maths or English after failure to achieve grade 4
Content: Experts have criticised the plan, saying the number of young people not in education, employment or training is likely to increase as long as GCSE failure rates remains high.Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenExperts have criticised the plan, saying the number of young people not in education, employment or training is likely to increase as long as GCSE failure rates remains high.Photograph: Matthew Horwood/Getty ImagesEducationLeaders attack ‘demotivating’ plan to make pupils who fail GCSEs retake maths and EnglishGovernment announce plan for ‘stepping stone’ qualification as 620,000 year 11 students face retaking maths or English after failure to achieve grade 4Richard AdamsandSally WealeThu 20 Aug 2026 14.21 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe government’s plans to make young people continue studying maths and English if they failGCSEscould be demotivating and ineffective, according to education experts and school leaders after retake pass rates slumped this year.Only one in seven students in the age group retaking GCSE maths after a previous failure got a grade 4 or above this summer, while only one in six managed to pass English, meaning the majority will have to retake the exams next year if they remain in education or training.The lower than expected results for older students came against a more positive national picture in which students in year 11 achieved record high grades in GCSE examinations across England.Compulsory GCSE resits in England harm teenagers’ mental wellbeing, study findsRead moreWhile seven in 10 of 16-year-olds achieved pass grades in maths and English, the remaining 620,000 year 11 students face retaking GCSE maths or English next year after failing to reach grade 4.Lucy Powell, the education secretary in England, said the government would be sticking with plans for a new “stepping stone” qualification aimed at those who got a grade 2 or worse in their first attempt at GCSEs.Powell described the current policy as “a hamster wheel” and said: “There’s got to be a better way to give young people the skills and confidence that they need to succeed, not just branding them a failure, and also allowing them to gain other qualifications that show they have a strong foundation in English and maths.“So that’s why I want to bring in a new level-one qualification so they’ve got a strong foundation in English and maths that gives them that passport to go on for further study or an apprenticeship or a training place.”But the plan, first announced in last year’s skills white paper, has been met with scepticism by experts and school leaders, who warned that the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) was likely to increase as long as GCSE failure rates remained high.Pepe Di’Iasio, general secretary of the Association of School and College Leaders, said: “This year’s post-16 resit results reinforce the fact that the government policy of force-feeding them a relentless diet of GCSE English and maths in post-16 education is simply not working.“Tinkering at the edges of the qualification system will not solve this problem. As long as we continue to grade students in this way in these gateway subjects of English and maths, we will continue to damage their future prospects.“If the government is serious about tackling the Neet crisis it must grasp this nettle and rethink how we assess English and maths.”Lee Elliot Major, a professor of social mobility at the University of Exeter, warned that the new qualification would “need a strong fairness test to ensure this doesn’t create a two-tier system in which pupils from under-resourced backgrounds are disproportionately directed onto lower-level routes.“With around a third of young people not achieving the grade 4 benchmark in both English and maths, the system itself needs reform. This is the cruel injustice of narrow expectations: we need different pathways, but not different ceilings.”The Department for Education’sconsultationpositions the new “stepping stone” qualification as preparation for a later GCSE resit, meaning young people will still face multiple examinations while they remain in education.Paul Whiteman, head of the National Association of Head Teachers, said: “We have long called for an end to the current policy which forces students into dispiriting rounds of repeated, demotivating resits.“What is needed are more appropriate and engaging alternatives to GCSEs in English and maths at key stage 4 which enable students to study for qualifications that better suit their needs and aspirations.”GCSE results: almost one in four boys in England get top grades in mathsRead moreThis year, the results revealed a strong performance in maths among boys in England, with a new high of 24% achieving grade 7 or above, while 20.5% of girls reached the same level. However, girls maintained their lead in top grades across all subjects, with 25.5% of their exam entries being awarded grade 7 or above compared with 20.7% of boys.The proportion of exam results at the top grade, 9, remained at 5.2%, unchanged from 2025.GCSEs in England award grades on a scale of 9 to 1, while many in Northern Ireland and Wales continue to award letter grades with A* at the peak. Education policy is devolved to UK national governments, making it difficult to directly compare GCSE results between them due to different content, marking and regulation.In Northern Ireland 31.5% of entries by 16-year-olds gained A or grade 7 and above, a slight improvement over last year, while 84.4% gained C or grade 4 and above.In Wales, 20.2% of grades for 16 year-olds were awarded A or better, and 63.7% of entries gained at least a C, slightly below the 2025 pass rate.Explore more on these topicsEducationGCSEsExamsSecondary schoolsLucy PowellSchoolsDepartment for EducationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Jailed ex-Pakistani PM Imran Khan in hospital after uproar over health | Imran Khan | The Guardian
description: Supreme court ordered transfer of ex-leader whose health is reportedly deteriorating and following public protests
Author: Shah Meer Baloch
Headline: Supreme court ordered transfer of ex-leader whose health is reportedly deteriorating and following public protests
Content: Police officers on guard on Thursday at a barricaded road near the Shifa international hospital where Imran Khan was transferred.Photograph: Anjum Naveed/APView image in fullscreenPolice officers on guard on Thursday at a barricaded road near the Shifa international hospital where Imran Khan was transferred.Photograph: Anjum Naveed/APImran KhanJailed ex-Pakistani PM Imran Khan in hospital after uproar over healthSupreme court ordered transfer of ex-leader whose health is reportedly  deteriorating and following public protestsShah Meer Balochin IslamabadThu 20 Aug 2026 19.07 EDTFirst published on Thu 20 Aug 2026 17.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePakistan’s jailed former prime ministerImran Khanhas been taken to a hospital in the country’s capital on supreme court orders after weeks of uproar about his deteriorating health.A spokesperson for Khan’s party, Zulfikar Bukhari, said: “Imran Khan has been shifted from Adiala jail to International Shifa hospital in Islamabad following the supreme court’s order.”Bukhari said that as per the court order, family should be allowed to meet Khan.“The next phase must therefore go beyond Imran Khan’s immediate medical treatment. It must ensure independent medical oversight, access to qualified specialists, respect for family and legal rights, and complete transparency regarding his health,” Bukhari said.Security was beefed up in Islamabad, and hundreds of security personnel were posted around the hospital before Khan was taken there.Prisoner number 804: the plot to erase Imran Khan – podcastRead moreThe government had to comply with the order by a three-judge panel of the supreme court that ordered the government to take Khan to the private hospital within 48 hours to be examined by physicians. Initially, the government seemed divided on whether to do so or not.Khan has been suffering from health issues including poor eyesight, and his family and party have been demanding he has access to specialist medical care for months. The family eventually took the case to the supreme court.In February, officials at Khan’s party, Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf, said he wasfacing severe eye damageand had only 15% eyesight, and was being kept in solitary confinement. He was also being denied basic medical care and meetings with family and lawyers.For months, Adiala jail has been a protest site, where Khan’s family and dozens of protesters would gather to demand medical care for him and for him to be allowed to meet his sisters.On Tuesday the judges said that they would involve an eye specialist for Khan’s treatment. The order read: “We are mindful of the constitutional and legal obligation … to safeguard the life, health, dignity and security of the prisoner.”Khan’s party assured the judges that his supporters would not gather in front of the hospital and would allow treatment to go smoothly. In the early hours of Friday, Asad Qaiser, the former speaker of the national assembly and a close aide of Khan, wrote on X that it had been decided by the party that no worker would gather in front of the hospital after Khan is taken to Shifa.Hewrote“if anyone attempts to gather in front of the hospital and violating the party’s decision, he would have no affiliation with the party.”Khan was arrested in2023 and sentenced to three yearsin jail on corruption charges and disqualified from politics for five years.Khan, who is facing more than 100 cases, was sentenced to 14 years in 2025 on corruption charges and accused of obtaining lucrative plots of land worth billions of rupees through a corrupt deal with a Pakistani property tycoon when he was the prime minister. Khan and his party denied the charges and said cases were politically motivated.He was Pakistan’s cricket captain before becoming a politician, and served as the prime minister of Pakistan from 2018 to 2022. He was ousted in a vote of no confidence. Khan had enjoyed good relations with Pakistan’s powerful military before he came to power.Once he was removed from office in 2022, he blamed the US for his removal initially and then Pakistan’s then army chief Gen Bajwa. Both have denied his accusations. After his brief arrest and release in May 2023, Khan in an interview withthe Guardian accused Pakistan’s army chief Asim Munirof harbouring a “personal grudge” against him and ordering his arrest and a crackdown on his party.Explore more on these topicsImran KhanPakistanSouth and central AsianewsShareReuse this content

title: Harry and Meghan’s security funding on UK return is private matter, Burnham says | Prince Harry | The Guardian
description: Prime minister wishes couple well in their move back from the US to a non-royal residence outside London
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Prime minister wishes couple well in their move back from the US to a non-royal residence outside London
Content: The Duke and Duchess of Sussex  flanked by security during a recent visit to Melbourne in April 2026.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Duke and Duchess of Sussex  flanked by security during a recent visit to Melbourne in April 2026.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyPrince HarryHarry and Meghan’s security funding on UK return is private matter, Burnham saysPrime minister wishes couple well in their move back from the US to a non-royal residence outside LondonHarry and Meghan: key moments and controversies since US moveCaroline DaviesThu 20 Aug 2026 13.50 EDTFirst published on Thu 20 Aug 2026 08.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSecurity arrangements for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex while living in the UK are a “private matter”,Andy Burnhamhas said, after news that Harry and Meghan intend to relocate to Britain from the US this month.Harry and Meghan: the key moments, conflicts and controversies since their US moveRead moreThe UK prime minister refused to be drawn on security funding, saying: “This is a private matter. It’s a matter for Harry and Meghan, and we wish them well in the moves that they’re making.”The couple, whomoved to North Americamore than six years ago, will make their home in a non-royal residence outside London. Their children, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, are already enrolled at British schools and due to start in September.King Charles, who was told of the decision on Sunday, is said to welcome the opportunity to see more of his family in a personal capacity. There will be no change in their status as private individuals and non-working royals who do not carry out royal engagements. There is said to be no half-in, half-out option.11:35Why are Prince Harry and Meghan moving back to the UK? – The LatestSecurity funding has been a long-running source of tension between Harry and the Home Office, the government department that would decide on such measures. The Times has reported that there are no plans to provide the couple and their family with taxpayer-funded armed protection.Last year, Harrylost a protracted court battleover what security he and his family would be entitled to while visiting the UK after automatic taxpayer-funded security was withdrawn when the couple stood down as working royals.During the legal challenge against the Home Office, Harry said in his witness statement: “The UK is my home. The UK is central to the heritage of my children and a place I want them to feel at home as much as where they live at the moment in the US. That cannot happen if it’s not possible to keep them safe when they are on UK soil.
