I cannot put my wife in danger like that and, given my experiences in life, I am reluctant to unnecessarily put myself in harm’s way too.”A senior judge later ruled that his “sense of grievance” over the decision about his security was not sufficient as grounds for an appeal.The prince later told the BBC that he “can’t see a world” in which he would bring his family to the UK.He was understood to be already awaiting a fresh risk-management assessment, but his new circumstances may now have to be factored in. Decisions on the security of royals are taken by the royal and VIP executive committee, an independent body overseen by the Home Office. The prime minister does not decide about security for the royal family.After the couple left the UK, Harry was granted a “bespoke” security arrangement. He may no longer qualify for the level of protection he previously had as a working royal but he is a high-profile figure and former military serviceman who has served in Afghanistan, which may be considered in any assessment.A Home Office spokesperson said: “The UK government’s protective security system is rigorous and proportionate. It is our long-standing policy not to provide detailed information on those arrangements, as doing so could compromise their integrity and affect individuals’ security.”In the US, the Sussexes paid for their own private security team.View image in fullscreenHarry and Meghan meeting people at the Royal children’s hospital in Melbourne during a tour of Australia in April.Photograph: William West/AFP/GettyThere has been no statement from the Sussexes on why they are choosing to return to the UK, but a source close to them said they had had a great time during their visit in July, and that “stars are aligning with work” to make this a good time to move. This may include Harry’s Invictus Games, which are to be held in Birmingham next year.The couple intend to retain their properties in Montecito, California, and in Portugal. Meghan is expected to run her lifestyle brand As Ever from the UK, but it is not yet known whether she will begin undertaking charity visits as a non-working royal or embark on other ventures.Harry has recently made it clear that he would like to spend more time with his father, who has cancer. Next year also marks the 30th anniversary of the death of his mother, Diana, which will include commemorations and events in the UK. Harry and his family stayed at home of Diana’s family, the Spencers, in Althorp, Northamptonshire, during their visit to the UK last month.A YouGov poll of 5,810 adults carried out the day after the Sussex’s surprise news, showed 33% believe Harry and Meghan should not return to the UK, while 45% do not know. Less than a quarter (21%) are in favour of the Sussexes relocating to the UK.Explore more on these topicsPrince HarryMeghan, the Duchess of SussexAndy BurnhamMonarchyUK security and counter-terrorismKing Charles IIInewsShareReuse this content

title: More than 16 killed as Kyiv comes under intense Russian bombardment | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: Missile and drone attack one of heaviest since war began, with children’s hospital and residential areas hit
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Missile and drone attack one of heaviest since war began, with children’s hospital and residential areas hit
Content: 1:12Barrage of Russian strikes devastates Kyiv – videoUkraineMore than 16 killed as Kyiv comes under intense Russian bombardmentMissile and drone attack one of heaviest since war began, with children’s hospital and residential areas hitDan Sabbaghin KyivThu 20 Aug 2026 18.15 EDTFirst published on Wed 19 Aug 2026 23.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA heavy Russian missile and drone bombardment has killed at least 16 people in and around Kyiv in one of the most intense aerial attacks on Ukraine’s capital since the start of the war.Vitali Klitschko, the city’s mayor, said homes, a school and a children’s medical centre were among the buildings damaged overnight in an attack that began at about midnight and was continuing into the early afternoon.Sixteen people were reported killed in the city, officials said, while other authorities said 33 had been injured.The Ukrainian president,Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said: “It was a massive attack – the Russians had been preparing for a long time, combining different types of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones, aiming to cause as much damage as possible to civilian infrastructure.”View image in fullscreenFirefighters work to put out a fire at a residential building hit by a Russian missile in Kyiv.Photograph: ReutersExplosions could be clearly heard from the city centre within minutes of the first warning at 11.51pm on Wednesday, earlier than the normal timing of Russian missile strikes. A further wave of attacks followed after 6am on Thursday, and drone threats continued throughout the morning.Ukraine’s air force said Russia had launched dozens of ballistic, cruise and hypersonic missiles and 168 drones in the overnight attack. Later it reported shooting down 41 out of 46 cruise missiles and 145 drones, although none of an unspecified number of high-speed ballistic missiles was intercepted.A shortage of Patriot interceptors means that Ukraine is struggling to defend itself from attack from high-speed ballistics, which can arrive within minutes of an air raid warning. Earlier this month, the air force decided to stop announcing how many ballistics had been launched, citing security concerns.Eight people were reported killed in the Solomianskyi district to the west of the centre of the capital. A multistorey apartment building in a residential area was struck and flats on the top floor destroyed, killing two, rescuers said.View image in fullscreenAn emergency rescuer attends the scene at an apartment block in the Solomianskyi district, Kyiv.Photograph: Ukrinform/ShutterstockAn empty building, sometimes used informally as a shelter, in the middle of a car park was destroyed in a strike at about midnight. Nobody was reported killed, though several cars were burnt out and bricks from the building scattered several metres across the open space nearby.Oleksandr, a car park attendant, was on duty at the time of the attack and escaped with light injuries. The next morning, still shocked, covered in cuts, his shorts torn into strips, he waited by his destroyed booth and said he could not remember what had happened to him immediately after the blast.Andriy, 57, a driver, said he first heard an explosion close by and was in his vehicle when the strike on the building in the car park took place. He said he believed his life was saved by the tinted plastic sheeting he had stuck on to his car windows. “I was only scratched on the back of my head,” he added.View image in fullscreenOleksandr, a car park attendant on duty at the time of the attack, was still shocked the next morning and could not remember what had happened to him after the blast.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianThere was no sign of any military or industrial activity in the local area. The car park was used by residents of the nearby apartment blocks, and the non-residential buildings largely disused.Zelenskyy urged a global response to the attacks. “While Moscow is investing in ballistic missiles and escalation, such strikes do not always receive the response they should. And as long as Ukraine does not have enough anti-ballistic defence, Russia will not consider peace seriously,” Zelenskyy said on social media.An attack in Brovary district in the widerKyivregion killed one man and wounded another, said the regional governor, Tymur Tkachenko. “One industrial facility has been damaged. All relevant services are on site, working to extinguish the fire,” he said.Warehouses in Boryspil, east of Kyiv, were also attacked, including a facility operated by the Ukrainian Red Cross, Ukraine’s prime minister, Sergiy Koretsky, said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBoth sides have been escalating long-range attacks while air defences remain short. Ukraine has attacked oil refineries and warehouses close to Moscow using newly developed cruise missiles and drones, while Russia has stepped up its attacks on Kyiv, making heavy use of hard ballistics.View image in fullscreenA rescuer evacuates a woman from an apartment building in Kyiv on Thursday.Photograph: Anatolii Stepanov/ReutersThe Ukrainian air force said Kinzhal and Zircon hypersonic missiles were used in the attack, as well as Iskander and North Korean KN-23 ballistic missiles, sea-launched Kalibr cruise missiles andShahed drones.Ukraine’s air force had earlier warned of Russian Kalibr missiles passing over the regional village of Kaharlyk and heading towards the capital. Eight of the missiles had been launched from warships in the Black Sea, though all were shot down.Romania’s defence ministry said radar systems detected aerial targets near the Ukrainian border overnight, prompting the scrambling of two Spanish fighter jets deployed on Nato missions and a Romanian air force helicopter. The ministry said a drone entered Romanian airspace near Galați before crashing in an unpopulated area in Tulcea county.Ukraine war briefing: Russia running on imported gasoline, government confirmsRead morePoland’s military command said it had mobilised aircraft and activated air defences aimed at protecting Polish airspace, particularly in areas bordering Ukraine.Finland’s defence ministry said on Thursday evening that it suspected a Russian aircraft had violated its airspace earlier in the day.Russia also reported a large Ukrainian drone attack. Moscow’s mayor, Sergei Sobyanin, said 250 drones had flown toward the Moscow region between Wednesday night and Thursday morning, and that most had been destroyed at a significant distance from the capital itself.Moscow confirmed on Wednesday thatRussia was having to import refined petroleum productsto try to stabilise supply following Ukraine’s attacks on its refineries. The Reuters news agency used industry contacts and market data to establish that a tanker from India had recently arrived and unloaded, while supplies were also being sourced from east Asia.Explore more on these topicsUkraineEuropeRussiaKyivVolodymyr ZelenskyynewsShareReuse this content

title: Reform’s new economic adviser has called for end of pensioners’ triple lock  | Reform UK | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Mitchell Palmer has also argued for privatising the NHS and immigration as way of cutting poverty
Author: Kiran Stacey
Headline: Exclusive: Mitchell Palmer has also argued for privatising the NHS and immigration as way of cutting poverty
Content: Mitchell Palmer was appointed by Robert Jenrick and  is a rightwing economist at the Adam Smith Institute.Photograph: Adam Smith InstituteView image in fullscreenMitchell Palmer was appointed by Robert Jenrick and  is a rightwing economist at the Adam Smith Institute.Photograph: Adam Smith InstituteReform UKReform’s new economic adviser has called for end of pensioners’ triple lockExclusive: Mitchell Palmer has also argued for privatising the NHS and immigration as way of cutting povertyKiran StaceyPolicy editorThu 20 Aug 2026 13.36 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleReform UK’s new economic adviser has previously called the pensions triple lock unsustainable, advocated privatising the NHS and welcomed migration as a poverty alleviation tool, the Guardian can reveal.Robert Jenrick, Reform’s economic spokesperson, has appointed Mitchell Palmer, a rightwing economist at the free-market Adam Smith Institute, as one of his key aides.Palmer’s background is as a champion of economic liberalism, in many cases putting him to the right of Reform’s existing policy platform. His appointment comes amid tensions within the party between those who want to lean into its tax-cutting agenda and those who worry that steep cuts to welfare and other government spending will alienate voters.Palmer has previously called for the abolition of the triple lock, arguing it is an expensive and unsustainable way to protect pensioners.Tice defends suspension of Reform UK activist over Farage criticismRead moreHe toldGB Newsin April that he disagreed with Jenrick’s decision to back the triple lock, which guarantees that the state pension will rise by the highest of earnings, inflation and 2.5% every year. Nigel Farage, the Reform leader, had previously suggested the policy would be “up for debate”.Palmer told the news channel: “The triple lock is an expensive way to ensure that pensioners have dignity in their retirement. There are ways that you can do that without the unpredictable ratcheting effect that the triple lock has.“Pensioners almost by definition are made better off in real terms than workers and that obviously is, one, unsustainable as the number of pensioners that each worker has to pay for increases, but, two, can be seen by those younger generations as somewhat unfair.”In a separate media appearance, this time on a podcast hosted by the former Conservative MP Steve Baker,he arguedfor the privatisation of the NHS. Asked by Baker if it was time to privatise the service, he replied: “Well it’s long past time, Steve.”He went on to add: “The reality is the NHS is a horrifically performing system. It establishes much lower cancer survival rates. It has obvious rationing – we all know that when we try and get a GP appointment or a specialist appointment. It has a pretty bad safety record – that’s not for lack of spending.”At times his commitment to liberal economics seems to go against Reform’s main policy positions. In 2020, when working in the New Zealand parliament, he argued online for the benefits of economic migration,posting: “Hot take: Allowing people in from abroad who choose to come to NZ and earn *significantly* more than they would at home is not slavery. In fact, it is one of the best contributions we can make to global poverty alleviation.”Some of his other views include ending VAT exemptions and imposing a land tax.A Reform spokesperson said: “Unlike the Guardian, Robert believes in hiring smart people with whom he disagrees.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA Labour source said: “Reform have long talked up selling off the NHS to the highest bidder and going after ordinary people’s rights. It’s no surprise they’re hiring a brainchild of those types of damaging policies. Nigel Farage’s party have already shown the public who they are. It’s time to believe them.”Jenrick is bolstering his team at the same time as he is looking to stamp his authority on his party’s economic agenda.Earlier this weekhe announcedReform would make steep cuts to welfare if it was elected, which he said would total £50bn a year by 2030. Those cuts mean even people with terminal illnesses and permanent disabilities would be likely to have their incomes slashed by up to £10,000 a year, according to a leaked government analysis seen by the Guardian.There are signs of resistance to Jenrick’s position from within Reform, however.Earlier this week the party’s home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf,posted on X: “Have you noticed the people with ‘Right Honourable’ in their titles are among the most dishonourable people in the country?”Jenrick has the title of “right honourable”, which denotes membership of the privy council, as do several others who have defected from the Conservatives to Reform, including Suella Braverman and Nadine Dorries.Explore more on these topicsReform UKRobert JenrickEconomic policyPensionsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Academic who accused Jason Arday of plagiarism suspended by his university | Jason Arday | The Guardian
description: Researcher Nathan Cofnas previously claimed Black people would hold few high-profile positions in a meritocracy
Author: Chris Osuh
Headline: Researcher Nathan Cofnas previously claimed Black people would hold few high-profile positions in a meritocracy
Content: Nathan Cofnas was sacked from his role at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, in 2024 and has now been suspended by Ghent University in Belgium.Photograph: Adam Gerrard/MirrorpixView image in fullscreenNathan Cofnas was sacked from his role at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, in 2024 and has now been suspended by Ghent University in Belgium.Photograph: Adam Gerrard/MirrorpixJason ArdayAcademic who accused Jason Arday of plagiarism suspended by his universityResearcher Nathan Cofnas previously claimed Black people would hold few high-profile positions in a meritocracyChris Osuhand agenciesThu 20 Aug 2026 14.12 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNathan Cofnas, the academic who made plagiarism allegations against ProfJason Ardaybefore his death, has been suspended by a university.Arday, 41, resigned from his role at theUniversity of Cambridgethis month after coverage of Cofnas’s accusations of plagiarism. The allegations, which were not proven in any formal investigation, triggered questions about Arday’s achievements.There has been stiff criticism of Cambridge over its handling of the affair, but also of the coverage by some media. The university’s chancellor, Chris Smith, described it as a “racist feeding frenzy”. Arday, who became Cambridge’s youngest black professor in 2023, wasfound deadin Battersea, south London, on Friday.View image in fullscreenTributes to Jason Arday have been left at the gates of the Senate House in Cambridge this week.Photograph: Chris Radburn/AFP/Getty ImagesThe “American anti-woke” blogger Cofnas is a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University’s department of philosophy and moral sciences, according to his website.In a post on X on Thursday, Cofnas said: “I am under investigation by my university for discriminating against Arday.” He added in a separate post: “I was just suspended by Ghent University. They will almost certainly fire me.”Ghent University confirmed his suspension after saying they had been “shocked” by Arday’s death and that it “should prompt reflection”, adding that the institution “opposes discrimination, hatred and racism”.In a joint statement on Wednesday, Ghent University’s rector, Petra De Sutter, and vice-rector, Herwig Reynaert, said: “We attach great importance to academic freedom and to open academic debate, even when views are controversial. However, that freedom is not unlimited.“It goes hand in hand with responsibility and may be restricted in order to protect the rights of others. For this reason, the university takes the recent public statements made by a postdoctoral researcher at Ghent University regarding this matter very seriously.“Ghent University has decided to take appropriate action within its powers and the applicable framework.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA rightwing witch-hunt focused on Jason Arday – but so did legitimate journalism | Hugh MuirRead moreThe rector and vice-rector said that while it was “important to be transparent”, they did not want to “pre-empt any potential decisions at this stage”.In an update on Thursday, a spokesperson said: “Ghent University formally notified the staff member concerned of the launch of a preliminary disciplinary investigation.“As part of this process, the university is assessing whether there are sufficient grounds to refer the case to the competent disciplinary body for further consideration. Pending this preliminary investigation, Ghent University has suspended the staff member as a precautionary measure.”Earlier this week, organisers said more than 30,000 people had attended a vigil for Arday in Trafalgar Square, central London.1:27‘There needs to be some reckoning’: thousands attend Jason Arday vigil in London – videoCofnas wassacked from his role at Emmanuel College, Cambridge, in 2024. In blog posts, he had said that, in a meritocracy: “Blacks would disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment.” In a piecetitled “Don’t Scapegoat Women”, published in January this year, Cofnas claimed “women but not men can get people fired by pointing and crying”.He added: “To meet de facto quotas, employers have had to reach deeper into the pool of less qualified female candidates. For obvious reasons, affirmative action hires often have a chip on their shoulder. Many of them turn to social justice activism to distract from the fact that they aren’t as good at their job as the straight white men who earned their position based on merit, or weren’t hired at all.”Explore more on these topicsJason ArdayHigher educationUniversitiesDEI policiesBelgiumUniversity of CambridgenewsShareReuse this content

title: Mark Zuckerberg buys 440-acre Strancally castle estate in Ireland | Ireland | The Guardian
description: Meta chief executive paid roughly €20m for gothic-style mansion built in 1830 and its surroundings
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Meta chief executive paid roughly €20m for gothic-style mansion built in 1830 and its surroundings
Content: Strancally castle in Waterford, Ireland, has changed hands after 25 years.Photograph: Patrick Kenealy/ReutersView image in fullscreenStrancally castle in Waterford, Ireland, has changed hands after 25 years.Photograph: Patrick Kenealy/ReutersIrelandMark Zuckerberg buys 440-acre Strancally castle estate in IrelandMeta chief executive paid roughly €20m for gothic-style mansion built in 1830 and its surroundingsRory CarrollIreland correspondentThu 20 Aug 2026 13.39 EDTFirst published on Thu 20 Aug 2026 13.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt stretches the definition of pied-à-terre butMark Zuckerbergnow has a pad inIreland: Strancally castle.TheMetachief executive and his wife, Priscilla Chan, have bought the gothic-style mansion and its 178-hectare (440-acre) estate in county Waterford to use as a base during visits to Ireland.“Mark and his family are excited to continue caring for this historic home and look forward to spending time inIreland, where Meta maintains its international headquarters,” a spokesperson said on Thursday.The price paid in the off-market deal is not known but the Irish Times, whichfirst reported the sale, estimated a value between €20m (£17m) and €30m: approximately 10% of the cost of his387ft superyacht.View image in fullscreenMark Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, will stay at Strancally when visiting Ireland.Photograph: title: US aircraft carrier arrives in Middle East to relieve troubled USS Lincoln | US military | The Guardian
description: USS George Washington will replace warship families say suffers from shortages, plumbing problems and low morale
Author: Anna Betts
Headline: USS George Washington will replace warship families say suffers from shortages, plumbing problems and low morale
Content: The US navy Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS George Washington transits the strait of Malacca on 13 August.Photograph: US Navy/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe US navy Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS George Washington transits the strait of Malacca on 13 August.Photograph: US Navy/ReutersUS militaryUS aircraft carrier arrives in Middle East to relieve troubled USS LincolnUSS George Washington will replace warship families say suffers from shortages, plumbing problems and low moraleAnna BettsThu 20 Aug 2026 14.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 14.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe USS George Washington aircraft carrier has arrived in the Middle East, where it is expected to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln from its record deployment amidconcernsabout poor living conditions and morale.US Central Commandannouncedon Thursday that the Washington arrived in the area on Wednesday, and posted an image of sailors working on the flight deck as the ship transited the Arabian Sea. No date has yet been announced for the Lincoln to return to the US.In an interview this week, the wife of a sailor onboard theUSS Abraham Lincolntold the Guardian that she has been getting brief glimpses over the past few months of what life is like on the aircraft carrier, mostly through text messages. And that as the deployment has stretched on, and on, she has noticed a change in her husband’s messages.“There’s less hope in the way he talks and less positive things that he has to say,” she said. “You can just tell the little things.“He’s just exhausted,” she added. “It’s a long, long deployment and it takes a toll.”The woman, who spoke on the condition of anonymity out of fear of retribution, said that her husband rarely complained. But photographs he sent of what she described as his sometimes sparse meals as supplies ran low have left her worried. One meal she described as just a “couple of pieces of bacon and three or four chicken wings”.“He’s never complaining. It’s just when I ask him a question, I’m like, OK, wait a minute, that’s not right,” she said. “To put it plainly, I just don’t think they’re getting enough calories.”double quotation markTo put it plainly, I just don’t think they’re getting enough caloriesWife of USS Lincoln sailorHer account comes as recent reports have rung alarm bells about conditions onboard the Lincoln, which has spentmore than 250days at sea supportingUS operationsagainst Iran without a significant port visit or date to return home for the 5,000 sailors aboard.Reports from families of crew members published in theNavy TimesandStars and Stripesmilitary newspapersdescribedfood and water shortages, disrupted mail services, plumbing problems, low morale and worsening mental health,promptingDemocratic lawmakersto demandanswers from the Pentagon.“I just don’t really think they’re treating them like people. I think they’re treating them like a uniform, like a pawn on a chessboard,” the wife said in a telephone interview.Over the weekend, Adm Brad Cooper of US Central Command visited the ship, and released astatementsaying the Lincoln “currently has among the lowest number of cases related to mental health” of the navy’s 11 active aircraft carriers, but acknowledged “that doesn’t mean all is perfect”, describing long deployments at sea as “uniquely challenging and tough”.A navy official, in a statement last week, alsorecognizedthat the war had disrupted traditional supply hubs, but said that “current reports from the ship confirm continuous access to clean water, functional [air conditioning] and healthy meal options”.But the wife of the sailor still worries for her husband and his shipmates.“He has not point-blank said anything, but I feel like I can tell through text it’s getting hard … being deployed without having any stops, and just kind of doing the same thing over and over again for months is exhausting,” she said, adding: “especially when you’re dealing with high stress” in a war zone.The couple are in their early 20s and he works on the planes on the flight deck. She said her husband told her that morale among some sailors was low, and that they had been unable to receive packages from home for some time, but she believes the sailors are reluctant to speak out because they fear the consequences for their careers.“It’s not the sailors that are complaining. It’s their family members who are saying: ‘Whoa, whoa, whoa.’ They are the ones putting their foot down,” she said.Carl Otis Schuster, a retired US navy captain, said he thought more attention should be paid to the “human element” of these deployments, adding that “until we do that, you’re going to have repeats” of the kinds of problems that have emerged.“Unfortunately, we’ve made a habit of placing the sacrifices on the crewmen,” Schuster said. “Every generation says that this generation is soft, but I would argue the guys serving on the Abraham Lincoln have undergone stresses and strains that my generation rarely faced, and certainly I never faced.” Schuster served for26 yearson various US and allied warships.The Lincoln’s crew, he said, had “shown really strong resilience”. During his own service, he said, he never spent more than 90 days at sea, and warned: “All of us have a breaking point.”He said that typically about 70% of the crew on a ship like the Lincoln are age 26 or younger, living and working together in a confined space.“We have one carrier fulfilling the mission that would normally be done by two, so there’s nowhere to rotate them out, and so the tension and stress on the crew grows,” he said.Asked about Donald Trump’s comments last Friday that the Lincoln’s deployment was “not nearly long enough”, Schuster said that the US president may be correct strategically that the US needs a carrier in the region for longer, but that the statement “ignores the human element”, which he said was “everything”.Lory Manning, who served more than 25 years in the navy, said that sailors typically leave for deployments with a sense of when they will be returning and that “every time that is changed, it’s demoralizing”.Aircraft carriers, she said, were noisy, crowded and constantly operating. Sailors often work long hours, some in warm areas of the ship such as the engine room, where “you might not get much daylight”, and shortages of basic supplies can make prolonged deployments even harder.“There’s no privacy,” she said. “In a sense, [it can ultimately feel like] you’re in a jail because you’re on this ship and you can’t get off.”Yet Manning, who after retiring from the navy got involved with work centered on female veterans and women in the military, said that sailors continued to do their jobs despite the strains.“The work is getting done, the people are doing what they’re supposed to do,” she said.Still, she wonders what the long-term consequences may be.“How many of them will re-enlist someday?” she said.Explore more on these topicsUS militaryTrump administrationDonald TrumpUS-Israel war on IranUS politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Why is the Trump administration causing turmoil in the bond markets? | US Government borrowing | The Guardian
description: As yields are dragged higher in the UK, Europe and Japan, the impact for consumers and businesses will be far-reaching
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: As yields are dragged higher in the UK, Europe and Japan, the impact for consumers and businesses will be far-reaching
Content: Some analysts have highlighted parallels to the conditions preceding the 2008 global stock market crash.Photograph: Yuki Iwamura/APView image in fullscreenSome analysts have highlighted parallels to the conditions preceding the 2008 global stock market crash.Photograph: Yuki Iwamura/APUS Government borrowingExplainerWhy is the Trump administration causing turmoil in the bond markets?As yields are dragged higher in the UK, Europe and Japan, the impact for consumers and businesses will be far-reaching‘Starve the beast’? The $40tn cost of Republicans’ false promises to cut spendingRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentThu 20 Aug 2026 12.14 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGovernment borrowing costs around the world have surged to the highest levels in decades amid growing fears over US bond market turmoil.Anxiety about Donald Trump’s handling of the US economy, and concern that the US president’s war with Iran is driving up inflation, are causing a sell-off in the US bond market.Highlighting the world economy’s dependence on US stability, the yield – in effect the interest rate – onUK, French, German and Japanese government debthas been dragged higher.Here we look at the factors driving the bond market, and the likely consequences.What is happening in the bond market sell-off?Long-term US government borrowing costs have risen to the highest level since 2007, with the 30-year Treasury bond yield trading above 5%.Abondis a form of loan that investors make to a borrower, or bond issuer. The yield represents the money an investor receives for owning the debt as a percentage of its current price. Prices fall when investor demand wobbles, which pushes up yields.Against this backdrop, the US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent said this week thatWashington would at least double its purchasesof long-term US bonds in an attempt to assuage investor concerns. Washington also staged a joint intervention this month with Tokyo to prop up the value of theJapanese yen.Bessent’s intervention on Wednesday helped to push down yields, but the impact was only temporary: they were rising again on Thursday, reversing most of that early move.With US Treasury bonds a lynchpin in global financial markets, the rise in US borrowing costs has dragged yields higher for other countries. G7 nations have faced among the sharpest increases: UK 10-year bond rates are close to the highest since 2008 and 30-year rates are near 1998 levels; Germany’s are at 2011 levels and France at a 16-year peak. Japanese borrowing costs have also hit the highest level since 1996.Why are bond investors rushing for the exits?The breakdown of negotiations in the US-Israel war on Iran is the main source of investor unease. The US national debthitting $40tn(£29.3tn) for the first time – after having doubled over the past decade – is also stoking fear that Trump’s tax and spending plans are unsustainable.The stop-start fighting in the Middle East has pumped up the oil price, adding to worries over inflation and the hit to economic growth worldwide.Inflation is bad news for bond investors. This is because it undercuts the future value of money received for owning the debt, so investors demand a higher yield to compensate for the risk.In response to the inflation shock, the world’s most powerful central banks are also increasingly expected to raise interest rates. However, the unpredictable nature of the Iran war, and of the Trump administration, are making the challenge tougher.Albert Edwards, a senior analyst at Société Générale, said: “Many also believe US bonds are having a tantrum because new Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, refuses to spoon-feed investors with the forward guidance they had become accustomed to.”Investors are also worried by political risk: in the US, the fear is that Trump has little appetite to curtail soaring borrowing and debt levels. Investors have asked similar questions of Britain’s prime minister, Andy Burnham, and France is preparing for an election year in 2027 amid mounting political schisms. Japan also faces challenges as itpumps up government spendingdespite elevated debt levels and with itscurrency under pressure.Some analysts have also suggested Washington’s yen intervention was driven by worries about falling Japanese demand for US treasuries. Before the joint action, Tokyo had been attempting to prop up the currency by selling holdings of US treasuries to free up money to buy yen, which pushed down bond prices and lifted yields.The AI boom is another factor. Silicon Valley companies are borrowing heavily to fund their rollout of datacentres, which means bond investors are being asked to swallow sizeable amounts of debt.What are the consequences?The impact is far-reaching. Higher yields will push up the costs for consumers and businesses for their mortgages, loans and corporate bonds – hitting their capacity to spend elsewhere, and weighing on the economy more broadly.Governments worldwide, already awash with debt after the economic shocks of recent decades, are being squeezed. The rise in interest costs will not only add to Washington’s debt pile, complicating Trump’s tax and spending plans, but also make life harder elsewhere – including the UK and France ahead of tough budgets.Some experts predict a doom loop whereby higher debt costs crowd out room for governments to spend on growth-enhancing measures, locking in weak economic growth and tax revenues and making budget deficits and rising debt levels more likely.For the UK chancellor, John Healey, analysts at Société Générale expect the rise in borrowing costs could erase about half of the £23.6bn headroom left in reserve in the spring against the government’s self-imposed fiscal rules.What happens next?Much will depend on how the Iran war unfolds; and on whether the Trump administration changes course on tax and spending, or intervenes again in markets to support bond prices. The response from the world’s most powerful central banks will also be key.The US has historically held an “exorbitant privilege” given the US dollar’s status as the global reserve currency, ensuring demand for dollar assets and enabling it to run persistently high trade and budget deficits. However, some analysts warn that the Trump administration isputting this at riskthrough the president’s trade policies and eye-wateringly expansive tax and spending plans.The uncertainty comes as pressure is likely to mount on Trump in the run-up to the midterm elections in November.Most investors will be looking for an easing in geopolitical tensions, further market intervention, or a shift in tax and spending policy from Washington. Central banks offering reassurance could also help.However, some analysts warn that the ingredients are there for a market accident. Société Générale’s Edwards, who isfamous for his gloomy predictions, said the conditions could be coming together for a US financial crisis.Highlighting parallels to the conditions preceding the 2008 global stock market crash, started by theUS sub-prime debt crisis, and the1997 Asian financial crisis, Edwards said: “Just as well I have a long memory, for I can remember exactly what was happening in financial markets the last time French and US long bond yields were at these levels – c2007 and even further back to c1997 for Japanese and UK yields.”Explore more on these topicsUS Government borrowingBondsTrump administrationGiltsInflationUS interest ratesEconomicsexplainersShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was a damn unicorn’: the pioneering, divisive power of Paul Simon’s Graceland at 40 | Paul Simon | The Guardian
description: On its anniversary, the author of a new book about the album explains the complex legacy and masterful musicianship of the 1986 classic
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: On its anniversary, the author of a new book about the album explains the complex legacy and masterful musicianship of the 1986 classic
Content: Paul Simon performs with guitarist Ray Phiri on the Graceland tour.Photograph: Penny Tweedie/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPaul Simon performs with guitarist Ray Phiri on the Graceland tour.Photograph: Penny Tweedie/Corbis/Getty ImagesPaul Simon‘It was a damn unicorn’: the pioneering, divisive power of Paul Simon’s Graceland at 40On its anniversary, the author of a new book about the album explains the complex legacy and masterful musicianship of the 1986 classicEthan BeckThu 20 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 12.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was the summer of 1984 and things weren’t going well forPaul Simon. The year prior, a blockbusterSimon and Garfunkeltour ended in bickering. Meanwhile, even though the 1980 single Late in the Evening reached the US Top 10, Simon’s last two albums had not sold very well, and his marriage to Carrie Fisher was starting to unravel. In the midst of all that the 43-year-old folk icon was steadily working on building a beach home out on the far end of Long Island.‘I never said I was going to retire ...’ Paul Simon on disability, drive and the mystery behind his greatest songsRead moreMany of Simon’s pilgrimages from Manhattan out to Montauk were soundtracked by a bootleg tape of accordion-heavy mbaqanga, a South African music style with jazz rhythms and bright guitar chords, he had received from a friend. It was on those drives that the seeds of Graceland, the crown jewel of Simon’s discography, were planted. “Many of us, in that day and age, found a moment of self-reflection – of being able to go deep inside ourselves – when we were in the car on these road trips,” said Ashley Kahn, whose new book,Days of Miracle and Wonder, follows the gestation process of Graceland. “If it wasn’t the radio, it was cassettes.”Forty years on, Graceland remains the most nimble, ecstatic album that Simon’s hands have touched. It’s constructed around contributions from South African musicians whose “township jive” reminded Simon of the early rock and doowop records he heard as a kid in Queens. There’s musical detours of all kinds – a trip to Louisiana inspired Simon to record with zydeco group Rockin’ Dopsie and the Zydeco Twisters, while the song All Around the World or the Myth of Fingerprints features Los Lobos’ fusion of norteño and rock. Simon is at his best when among resonant rhythms from Johannesburg.Inspired by the bootleg, Simon booked jam sessions in Johannesburg with different bands – General MD Shirinda and the Gaza Sisters, Tao Ea Matsekha, the Boyoyo Boys – where he developed melodies and scribbled down lyrics as engineer Roy Halee tracked the groups’ grooves. Some of the songs that ended up on Graceland were assembled on top of these groups’ already-finished songs, such as Gumboots, a thrilling pop confection that Simon initially heard as an instrumental on that tape. For Simon, whose process often started with an acoustic guitar, it was a profound shift in how he approached his craft. “He’s finding a way of building from the rhythm up; that, for him, was profoundly new,” said Kahn, who compared Simon’s then-newfound process with hip-hop: “Start with the beat and match the words to the beat.”In these February 1985 sessions, Simon had found a surge of inspiration, but the harsh realities of South African apartheid loomed outside the studio doors. After dark, the Black musicians weren’t allowed on the streets of Johannesburg, nor were they allowed to use public transportation. As a result, a day of recording would reach an “uncomfortable time when the players couldn’t concentrate until they knew there might be a car to take them home”, Simontold Rolling Stone in 1986. In a foreshadowing of the backlash Graceland would go on to receive, the manager of the Soul Brothers told Simon he believed recording in South Africa constituted a violation of the United Nations’ 1980 boycott, which was passed to prevent the South African government from using culture as propaganda for apartheid.Kahn believes that Simon had the musicians’ labor rights in mind. “He wanted to have them participate, he wanted them to be credited and he wanted them to be compensated,” said Kahn, emphatically noting that Simon paid the South African musicians triple the daily rate of musicians in American unions. “Did he do it perfectly? No. But there wasn’t a set formula of how to approach this.” Simon has still faced backlash over the years about Graceland’s songwriting credits from several musicians who appeared on the album, including Los Lobos, Rockin’ Dopsie and the Zydeco Twisters, and even guitarist Ray Phiri, who helped construct the album’s title track. Against charges of cultural appropriation, Graceland advocates have suggested that Simon’s work in South Africa helped bring these bands, such as Ladysmith Black Mambazo, who round out the starry-eyed Diamonds on the Soles of Her Shoes, to a larger audience.View image in fullscreenPaul Simon with author Ashley Khan in 1988.Photograph: Courtesy of Ashley KhanBefore the first sessions at Ovation Studios in Johannesburg, Simon spoke with calypso legend Harry Belafonte, who had suggested that he reach out to the African National Congress. Believing that the power of art trumped laws, Simon resisted Belafonte’s recommendation. Months after the release of Graceland, the UN’s special committee against apartheid censured Simon and planned to add him to the list of performers who violated the boycott. “They were looking for a coordinated message, coordinated push, hence the issue with the boycott,” Kahn added. The UN’s decision was reversed months later when Simon wrote a letter to the committee noting that he had understood the ban focused on performing, not recording, and he had no intentions of performing in South Africa.Paul Simon review – at 84, back on stage after hearing loss, his resolute artistry is inspiringRead moreA career-long tug-of-war between Simon’s cerebral and conversational language courses through Graceland. He eschewed overt anti-apartheid protest songs, but the anxieties of his experience in South Africa seep into Homeless and The Boy in the Bubble, which opens on an image of “the soldiers by the side of the road” while the interplay between famo-style accordion and bass suggests something threatening up ahead. But Simon’s qualms – his failed marriage, his feelings about being washed up, his worries related to the information age – are what he fleshes out on Graceland, often through dizzying images (“lasers in the jungle”) or larger-then-life characters (“Fat Charlie the Archangel”).“One of the images that always comes to me is Paul in a room with a rubber ball – bouncing it, bouncing it, bouncing it – to get into a Zen-like state where lyrics start to come,” Kahn said. “He’s already thinking about songwriting. The lyrics are there. He just needs to silence all the other shit that’s in one’s mind.”Graceland’s steady stream of longing, sometimes offered through simple lines such as “You don’t feel you could love me but I feel you could,” contained unexpected emotional wallops. On the album’s very best songs, there’s an impressionistic flow of feeling in Simon’s lyrics. Nowhere is that clearer than in the title track, where the word Graceland had initially been written down as a placeholder. It eventually evolved into a figurative destination for Simon as he tried to mend his broken heart after his marriage to Fisher. “If I miss in the direction of head, I risk being obscure or pretentious,” Simonsaid in 1986. “If I miss in the direction of heart, I risk being sentimental. I dread both. I dance in the penumbra. That’s the thrill. When it’s right, I can feel it.”View image in fullscreenPaul Simon with Miriam Makeba and Ladysmith Black Mambazo during the African Graceland tour in 1987.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyMany revisions and additions happened stateside, including the guitar-synth textures from Adrian Belew and Steve Gadd’s AMS reverb-drenched drums on All Around the World. For another set of sessions, including the one in which they rerecorded You Can Call Me Al, Simon flew Phiri, Bakithi Kumalo – whose restless fretless bass is now synonymous with the Graceland album – and drummer Isaac Mtshali to New York, where Simon also shared his progress with David Byrne, Cyndi Lauper and Philip Glass. He would turn on a tape of an instrument track, get close to their ears and sing the melodies or lyrics he’d crafted. “The fact that Paul was open to sharing the process with a lot of people goes to show a certain strength, as well as an openness to saying, ‘I could be wrong,’ or, ‘I could be better,’” Kahn says.Graceland’s influence as a genre-defying, cross-pollinated album has spread far and wide, informing brilliant artists such asVampire WeekendandLorde, plus with one particularviral parodyof Simon’s approach. For almost as long as the album has been in stores, a healthy dose of criticism has followed: two decades before he would produce for Beyoncé and Eminem, a young Mark Batsonasked Simonhow he could justify “taking over this music”, before discussing how Black art has been “stolen” by white artists time and time again during a Q&A at Howard University. It’s a testament to the life-affirming melodies and jubilant grooves of Graceland that it hasn’t been consigned to the dust bin of history as an embarrassment – and that these conversations endure. “All these questions about appropriation, about systemic racist, about the entitled versus the non-entitled – that’s never going away,” Kahn says. “What Graceland did was show us a way to talk about it.”It’s hard to imagine when Graceland arrived in stores towards the end of August 1986 that it wasn’t an overnight sensation. Support from music critics, performances on Saturday Night Live and eventually Grammy wins helped it find an audience. (It entered the Billboard 200 album chart at No 94 in September 1986, before eventually peaking at No 3 next April, just over a month after the Grammys ceremony.) The final piece of the puzzle was pop radio programmers, who didn’t understand the stylistic jumps taking place across Graceland. The spring after the album’s release, radio honchos latched onto its lead single, You Can Call Me Al, with its attempts to find salvation in the “angels in the architectures”. It was a classic case of better late than never: “It was a damn unicorn,” Kahn says. “In the zoo of music, they had no idea which cage to put it in.”Days of Miracle and Wonder:Paul Simonand the Trials and Triumphs of Graceland by Ashley Kahn is out nowExplore more on these topicsPaul SimonSimon and GarfunkelPop and rockSouth AfricafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Amy Lee of Evanescence: ‘I could happily do an entire album of nothing but Portishead covers’ | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: As her band hits the road, the metal trailblazer answers your questions on sexualisation in show business, finding inspiration in dreams and Spinal Tap moments on tour
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: As her band hits the road, the metal trailblazer answers your questions on sexualisation in show business, finding inspiration in dreams and Spinal Tap moments on tour
Content: ‘I’m done with letting people make me feel I should be quiet’ … Amy Lee.Photograph: Chapman BaehlerView image in fullscreen‘I’m done with letting people make me feel I should be quiet’ … Amy Lee.Photograph: Chapman BaehlerFilm & Music reader interviewPop and rockInterviewAmy Lee of Evanescence: ‘I could happily do an entire album of nothing but Portishead covers’As told toDave SimpsonAs her band hits the road, the metal trailblazer answers your questions on sexualisation in show business, finding inspiration in dreams and Spinal Tap moments on tourThu 20 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 12.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou wrote Bring Me to Lifewhen you were 19. When you perform it now, how do you relate to the younger you?becgoldsmithI was in an abusive relationship, so Bring Me to Life was partly about processing the reality of that abuse and asking myself, what are you gonna do about it? Like, pick yourself up. I wrote it when I was crushing on my [now] husband, but the theme is about a quest for something bigger: opening your heart, finding more depth. It’s very empowering to perform it now in huge places; I’m very proud of the 19-year-old me that wrote it.Artists often reveal their influences through the songs they choose to cover. You’ve performed bothIt’s a Fire and Glory Box by Portishead. What drew you to those songs?VerulamiumParkRangerBeth Gibbons was one of my greatest vocal and musical inspirations. In the 90s when I was a young teen really feeling music I lovedPortishead, Massive Attack and the whole trip-hop vibe. It was dark and cool, really different. Beth’s vocals have a way of teetering on an emotional crack, on the edge of wild, barely restrained emotion but never belting, which I always thought was so cool and enticing. I could happily do an entire album of nothing but Portishead covers.View image in fullscreen‘Music has always been an outlet for whatever’s in my heart’ … Lee with Evanescence in 2025.Photograph: Chapman BaehlerYour new album,Sanctuary, feels delicately balanced between healing and reflection, but also anger about what is going on in the world right now. How did you manage that balance and how do you feel about using your voice to stand up against what’s wrong?Amlou7I hate politics, but our existence is political. Most of us don’t want anything to do with the atrocities that are going on today, but as human beings with hearts and souls we must rise to the occasion. I’m done with letting people make me feel I should be quiet or making me feel uncomfortable speaking about what we’re now calling politics, which is life and death, rape, genocide, stealing from people. Music has always been an outlet for whatever’s in my heart, so now the music is an outlet for those big things. I meet so many people around the world with different beliefs, and we’re not that different. Most people are good human beings who would help you if you were injured, and that goodness is precious and worth fighting for. We have to be strong and keep calling things out and not back down to fascism.View image in fullscreenLee and the band’s then guitarist, Ben Moody, at the MTV awards in 2003.Photograph: Dave Allocca/Starpix/ShutterstockCan you share any funny stories of things that have happened during the current Sanctuary tour?Andrew_ClevelandThere’s so many, we could make a blooper reel of all the mistakes. When you put yourself out there with a big production inevitably there’s more potential for things to go wrong. We have a moment where a kabuki [Japanese theatre] curtain drops down dramatically behind me. It’s beautiful, but in windy amphitheatres there’s been a couple of funny moments where it’s come down in the wrong place and dropped right on my head. It’s been great touring with Spiritbox and Nova Twins and we do a song together, Fight Like a Girl. One night, I sang entirely the wrong thing. Spinal Tap is totally like reality. I’ve experienced that scene of walking round in circles not being able to find the stage more times than I can count.What are your thoughts onNathan Fielder’s use of Bring Me to Life in The Rehearsal season two[he speculates thatCaptain Chesley ‘Sully’ Sullenbergerlistened to the song before successfully landing a passenger plane on the Hudson River]?thunderponceIt’s amazing to me that the song has reached so far, but that was just one of those surreal moments where you really think, “Wow, this is wild.” I thought it was strange and brilliant, like Nathan Fielder is. I had tears in my eyes by the end. It was so beautiful. I’m not saying Bring Me to Life helped land the plane, but it’s a cool way to demonstrate how music inspires people in stressful or big moments. Bring Me to Life has been used in all sorts of things and it took me a long time to get past the cynicism of “I don’t know about this … ” but I feel safe in it now.Watch the video for Who Will You Follow.I recently lost my 14-year-old dog and five-year-old cat, and listening to theSecret Doorhas been one of the only things helping me lately. The lyrics are beautiful and eerie, the background melodies reminiscent of a dream. What inspired those words?Feistj1I’m sorry for your loss. I had my amazing Maine Coon [cat] for 18 years before he passed away a couple of years ago. They became part of your life so it’s like letting go of a whole chapter. It’s interesting that you’ve mentioned dreams. I’m a very vivid dreamer and I have recurring places that only exist in my dreams. Sometimes music comes at me in dreams and it feels as if I’m tuned into some other channel. Once in a while I wake and think, “I’ve got to write this down”, or record it on my phone. Secret Door was one of those. I had a recurring dream where I’d go through a secret door in the woods and experience a feeling of beautiful love. The vibe came from the dream, the 3/4 time was in my head, and the bridge section came out as soon as I woke up and ran straight upstairs to work on it. A lot happens in those last moments of sleep when your mind is functional but you’re not yet in reality. It feels like a gift when that happens.View image in fullscreenEvanescence performing in Madrid, Spain, in 2022.Photograph: Javier Bragado/RedfernsI’ve been listening to you since the beginning of your career. I wanted to be a rock singer, too, but I’ve always been told I am ugly. Show business’s obsession with beauty and sexualization to boost sales horrifies me. You make amazing music and don’t try to sell it using sexual gimmicks. Is there even the slightest chance for an unattractive woman to be a rock singer?SerbianPersonThat question makes me so sad. First of all, I would hope that whoever told you that you are ugly is not anyone you would call a friend. Don’t think of yourself that way and don’t listen to those people. They’re probably just jealous. Beauty is the deep stuff: being an artist, making music. That’s where the gold is, and beauty comes out through the inside, so focus on the inside and making something great for people to experience. Selling your product and being an Instagram star is not the important part. Anybody can make great music if it’s in your soul: that’s the most beautiful thing about you.‘I couldn’t see, breathe or sing. I blacked out twice’: why are so many metal bands wearing masks?Read moreWhat is the coolest or most thoughtful gift that you have received from a fan?EvCollector87There’s been so many, but one is really special. In 2005 or so I saw this beautiful art that someone had done on the internet, a picture based on our song Imaginary. It took the lyric “in my field of paper flowers” and created a visual depiction of the song, with me laying in a field. It was just so beautiful. I managed to get in touch with them and asked if I could buy it. They told me it was a digital rendering, not a painting, but I commissioned them to paint it for me – a big version, 5ft tall or something – and it’s gorgeous. It still hangs in my space.With the likes of Elton John, Stevie Nicks and Bruce Springsteen in mind, do you think you’ll still be recording and performing live in your 60s and 70s?ChrisDLordIf you had asked me that when we were starting out and I was in my early 20s, I would have said, hell, no. I wouldn’t have predicted we’d be here this long, but now I turn 45 in December, and 44 definitely doesn’t feel like I’d imagined – it’s better. Turning 60 is only 15 years away, which doesn’t feel that long. I don’t know if we’ll be touring hard then, but they say use it or lose it, so I’m not ruling it out. It gives you so much life to be able to bring people together and share music, so it breaks my heart to imagine that we can’t do that any more for whatever reason. I’d have to be still making music or creating in some way. It doesn’t make sense to stop.The vinyl version of Sanctuary is released via Sony on 4 September. title: Abigail’s Party review – Tamzin Outhwaite’s Bev is Madame Bovary with a Cinzano  | Stage | The Guardian
description: Outhwaite’s performance as Beverly, a precision-tooled showcase in hidden anger and longing, is a triumph in this eternally resonant suburban drama
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Outhwaite’s performance as Beverly, a precision-tooled showcase in hidden anger and longing, is a triumph in this eternally resonant suburban drama
Content: Simultaneously funny and deadly serious … Tamzin Outhwaite as Beverly in Abigail's Party.Photograph: Anthony Harvey/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSimultaneously funny and deadly serious … Tamzin Outhwaite as Beverly in Abigail's Party.Photograph: Anthony Harvey/ShutterstockStageReviewAbigail’s Party review – Tamzin Outhwaite’s Bev is Madame Bovary with a CinzanoHarold Pinter theatre, LondonOuthwaite’s performance as Beverly, a precision-tooled showcase in hidden anger and longing, is a triumph in this eternally resonant suburban dramaArifa AkbarThu 20 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 13.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlison Steadman has cast a long shadow over the suburban gargoyle-cum-bored-housewife in Mike Leigh’s social satire about 1970s social mobility. So much so that her name is almost always invoked in relation to Beverly. Tamzin Outhwaite’s incredible achievement is that she banishes Steadman’s original portrayal of Bev as the definitive one.Having first assumed the role inNadia Fall’s 2024 production, that history shows in her polish and command of the character. The setting is a cocktail party in Essex and Outhwaite’s Bev (glittering dress, Farrah Fawcett flicks) is full of lady-of-the-manor pretensions as she serves up her officious rounds of drink. But there is a hard, calculating edge to her marital digs at estate agent husband, Laurence (Kevin Bishop) and her crude flirtation with guest Tony (Omar Malik, fantastically laconic), which she conducts with flamboyant disregard for his wife, Angela (Lauren Patel).This seeps out early on, even before she has started to knock back the gin. She is simultaneously funny in her physical comedy and deadly serious in her put-downs of the workaholic husband who is not giving her the attention she craves, as well as her manipulations of others. Beneath her patter as party hostess is rage, hurt and an almost Madame Bovary boredom.View image in fullscreenOutside Bev’s doorstep it could be Reform Britain … L to r, Lauren Patel as Angela, Omar Malik as Tony, Kevin Bishop as Laurence, Tamzin Outhwaite as Beverly and Pandora Colin as Sue in Abigail’s Party.Photograph: Anthony Harvey/ShutterstockHer performance, and Fall’s production as a whole, proves that this period comedy of manners is eternally resonant. That is partly down to the genius of the play but Fall adds an ingenious tweak in the suggestion that Tony and Ange are of “Pakistani” origin. This transforms its meanings in a subtle but deft way: the area, we hear, is being taken over by different kinds of people and you imagine this not only being a comment on working-class mobility but racial diversity here in the “white flight” heartland of Essex. Outside Bev’s doorstep, it could be Reform Britain.What does not work as well is the chemistry between Bev and Laurence, which lacks bite in the first act. Laurence is rather passive, and expressionless, the tension between them uncharged. The marital conflict does not seem ferocious enough for too long so you do not feel the truth of the friction between them when it bursts to the surface. They could just be George and Mildred on a bad night. In contrast, the fault-lines in Ange and Tony’s marriage are savagely revealed in his disdain of her, as much as she tries to cover it up with fake cheeriness.It is still hugely enjoyable to see Bev flirt with the monosyllabic Tony, and to hear Ange’s inappropriate reflections on divorce in front of recently divorced neighbour, Sue (Pandora Colin).She is the other guest at this cocktail party and the mother of eponymous punk-teen, Abigail, whose off-stage party can be heard in the background. For those who charge Leigh with othering the aspirational working-classes, not only through Bev but Laurence’s cultural snobberies, acquired in his ascension up the ladder (the framed Vincent van Gogh poster on Peter McKintosh’s orange-and-brown period set says it all), the middle-class Sue is key to Leigh’s satire. She is brilliantly portrayed as the socially-awkward, plummy ex-wife of an architect who tries to evade Laurence’s questions on the area and the class antagonisms underlying them.He insists they listen to Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony amid the rising hysteria and the record-player is truly weaponised, Demis Roussos used to needle Laurence to the point of near-violence. Bev is a such a glorious creation that you feel her disappointments in marriage even as you gasp at her comic monstrousness. But the darkness of the ending does not land. It is partly because there are unanswered questions around their marriage but also because it has all been so enjoyably comical that this switch to tragedy leaves Bev speechless and at sea, for once.AtHarold Pinter theatre, London, until 19 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreMike LeighreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The best hair oils for glossy, healthy looking locks | Hair care | The Guardian
description: They’re all the rage, but which scalp serums, oils and capsules can be counted on for nourishment and serious shine?
Author: Sarah Matthews
Headline: They’re all the rage, but which scalp serums, oils and capsules can be counted on for nourishment and serious shine?
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterHair careReviewThe best hair oils for glossy, healthy looking locksThey’re all the rage, but which scalp serums, oils and capsules can be counted on for nourishment and serious shine?The best hair masks for every budget, testedSarah MatthewsThu 20 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHair oil has become increasingly popular, with countless celebrities and influencers lauding its ability to smooth, protect and support hair growth. Some apply hair oil to their scalp, others to their strands; some apply oil to wet hair before styling, others use it on a finished style. With so many uses, it’s worth thinking about your goals before buying.I’ve worked my way through 11 bottles, from a cheap-and-cheerful £9.99 to a steeper £65, to bring you this list of the best hair oils. Whether you’re looking for thick, nourishing oils to help nurse damaged hair to life or a featherlight option to add shine and scent to your strands, there’s something on this list for you.Besides testing on my own locks, I spoke with trichologistHannah Gaboardito find out if and how hair oils can actually support hair growth. Read on for her comments and my nine favourite hair oils.At a glanceBest hair oil overallGisouHoney infused hair oil, 50ml£37 at Cult BeautyBest budget hair oilHaskRepair Series hair oil mist, 120ml£9.99 at SuperdrugBest hair oil for damaged hairK18Molecular Repair hair oil, 30ml£65 at Cult BeautyBest lightweight hair oilGoldwellSmooth Weightless Shine oil, 100ml£17 at LookfantasticBest smoothing hair oilArkiveThe Good Habit hybrid oil, 50ml£14.68 at AmazonWhy you should trust meHair oils have been a staple of my hair care routine for the past few years. I’ve tried thicker oils that weigh hair down, and thinner oils that barely touch the sides of my dry ends. My hair has always been long, and for most of this testing process, I had waist-length hair that hadn’t been cut for a year. If an oil could nurse my ratty old ends back to health, it was a winner.I’m also a beauty journalist, so I spend my life learning about advancements in hair care, from keratin bond fixers that “repair” hair strands to scalp-soothing formulas that support hair growth. A cosmetic science course has given me a background knowledge of all things hair health, from the scalp, right down to the cellular structure of hair.How I testedView image in fullscreenOiled up: each product was tested for shine, smoothing, texture and how it felt on the hair.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianI tested 11 hair oils from the most popular brands, noting how each product affected the finish of my hair, mainly focusing on how hydrated it felt. As part of the testing process, I also assessed the consistency and greasiness of each one. If it was scented, I also checked to see how well the scent lingered on my hair.In terms of ingredients, I looked for nutrients and vitamins that help to seal the cuticle and protect each strand from environmental stress. As always, price was a factor: you can forgive a lot more from a cheap hair oil than an expensive one.The best hair oils of 2026Best hair oil overall:Gisou honey infused hair oilGisouHoney infused hair oil, 50mlfrom£37£37 at Cult Beauty£37 at SephoraWhat we loveProvides a glossy shine and a divine honey scentWhat we don’t loveThe thicker consistency won’t work for everyoneView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£37 for 50ml at Cult Beauty£37 for 50ml at SephoraGisou’s honey-infused hair oil has been my go-to for more than a year now. Its thicker texture is perfect for nourishing the dry ends of my hair, adding a dose of hydration and shine where it needs it most.Why we love itGisou is known for its honey-powered hair care, and the hair oil is a hero product. The Mirsalehi honey included in this formula is rich in protective antioxidants and minerals, but also has humectant properties to hydrate each hair strand. It also works beautifully alongside the emollient coconut and sweet almond oils in the formula to smooth out hair.In my experience, a small amount of this hair oil goes a long way. I found it easy to disperse through my long hair after warming it in my hands and loved the glossy shine it gave, while making my hair strands feel stronger and preventing breakage. As with all the Gisou honey products, it also smells divine.It’s a shame that …its slightly thicker texture won’t be for everyone. If you don’t have issues with dryness or have very fine hair that can’t handle richer products, opt for something else.Size:50mlPrice per ml:74pKey ingredients:Mirsalehi honey, coconut oil, sweet almond oilVegan?NoCertified cruelty-free?NoSuitable for:wet and dry hairGisouHoney infused hair oil, 50mlfrom£37£37 at Cult Beauty£37 at SephoraWhat we loveProvides a glossy shine and a divine honey scentWhat we don’t loveThe thicker consistency won’t work for everyoneBest budget hair oil:Hask Repair Series hair oil mistHaskRepair Series hair oil mist, 120mlfrom£9.99£9.99 at Superdrug£9.99 at AmazonWhat we loveExtremely good value; adds shine without greaseWhat we don’t loveContains silicones that could lead to brittle hairView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£9.99 for 120ml at Superdrug£9.99 for 120ml at AmazonIf you want to avoid greasy hands, this lightweight hair oil mist from Hask is ideal. Simply spritz over your hair to evenly disperse a fine layer of oil, leaving smooth, shiny and lightly scented locks. It shone in my tests, despite its low cost, demonstrating brilliant value for money.Why we love itOther than its bargain price and clean application, I found this oil added shine without weighing my hair down or making it feel greasy. Its atomiser consistently produced a fine mist, giving a lovely, even coating of fresh floral-scented oil on my locks.The spray contains hydrating argan oil, as well as Hask’s trademarked RepairPro, which it claims can “repair” bleach-damaged hair by up to 98%. I couldn’t test this claim at home, but I can attest that my hair felt noticeably smoother after use. The silicones in the formula help to seal and smooth the hair cuticle, preventing snagging and further damage.It’s a shame that …these silicones can build up over time if they aren’t washed off correctly, or if they’re overused, which leads to more brittle hair in the long term.Size:120mlPrice per ml:from about 8pKey ingredients:argan oil, RepairProVegan?YesCertified cruelty-free?YesSuitable for:wet and dry hairHaskRepair Series hair oil mist, 120mlfrom£9.99£9.99 at Superdrug£9.99 at AmazonWhat we loveExtremely good value; adds shine without greaseWhat we don’t loveContains silicones that could lead to brittle hairBest hair oil for damaged hair:K18 Molecular Repair hair oilK18Molecular Repair hair oil, 30mlfrom£65£65 at Cult Beauty£65 at SephoraWhat we loveMakes hair feel stronger; a little goes a long wayWhat we don’t loveIt’s very expensiveView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£65 for 30ml at Cult Beauty£65 for 30ml at SephoraIf you’re looking to include hair oil in your routine, chances are you’re hoping to counteract the signs of damaged hair – dryness, frizz and dullness. While no hair product can fuse split ends back together, the “molecular repair” element of this hair oil refers to an increase in hair strength and elasticity observed on bleach-damaged hair strands in the brand’s testing. After use, bleach-damaged hair should be less prone to breakage and more resilient to daily stressors, such as brushing, sun exposure and heat styling. This is easily the hardest-working hair oil you can buy, justifying its high cost – and it’s my favourite oil on test if you don’t take price into consideration.Why we love itThis hair oil works to help hair strands look and feel stronger using K18’s patented peptides. The formula mimics the natural peptides that give healthy hair its structural integrity, which are diminished when hair is bleached, dyed or styled with heat. Packed in, you’ll also find antioxidant avocado and sunflower oils to condition the hair. Meanwhile, squalane and hemisqualane soften the hair and smooth the cuticle, locking in that goodnesswithout the need for heavy silicones.This oil can be used either on damp hair before heat styling or as a finishing flourish to add shine to styled hair. Thankfully, and perhaps counterintuitively when applying an oil to your hair, it offers heat protection up to 232C – so you don’t have to worry about it frying your locks. It’s a concentrated oil, giving a lightweight, even coating, and just a few drops left my locks looking instantly shiny and healthy.It’s a shame that …it’s expensive. If you already have healthy-looking hair, you really don’t need to spend this much.Size:30mlPrice per ml:about £2.17Key ingredients:squalane, avocado oil, sunflower oil, sh-Oligopeptide-78Vegan?yesCertified cruelty-free?YesSuitable for:wet and dry hairK18Molecular Repair hair oil, 30mlfrom£65£65 at Cult Beauty£65 at SephoraWhat we loveMakes hair feel stronger; a little goes a long wayWhat we don’t loveIt’s very expensiveBest lightweight hair oil:Goldwell Smooth Weightless Shine oilGoldwellSmooth Weightless Shine oil, 100mlfrom£13.56£17 at Lookfantastic£13.56 at AmazonWhat we loveWeightless and ideal for fine hair and oily scalpsWhat we don’t loveSilicone can build up on hair if not washed out oftenView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£17 for 100ml at Lookfantastic£13.56 for 100ml at AmazonEven the best hair oils can be too thick and goopy for some people, especially those with fine locks and oily scalps. This lightweight and affordable oil from Goldwell is perfect for adding a touch of glossy shine without weighing down the hair.Why we love itThis oil has an incredibly thin texture that feels completely weightless when applied. I used it to top off a bouncy blow-dry and it added a lovely shine while keeping the movement and volume I wanted. I was also impressed by how it handled frizz – Goldwell claims it can tame frizz for up to 72 hours, and I can confirm my hair stayed silky smooth on a particularly humid day in central London.Inside the formula, you’ll findHimanthalia elongataextract (or sea spaghetti), which helps to moisturise hair. This is another oil that can be used on damp or dry hair, and I loved its uplifting, sweet, fruity scent. I simply rubbed any left over into my skin after use, and it didn’t leave my hands feeling sticky or greasy.It’s a shame that …like many hair oils, it uses dimethicone, a silicone that could build up on the hair if overused and not cleaned out properly. It also doesn’t have as many oils blended in as other options, so it doesn’t feel quite as nourishing as heavier, oilier formulas.Size:100mlPrice per ml:17pKey ingredients:dimethicone, isoamyl laurate,Himanthalia elongataextractVegan?YesCertified cruelty-free?YesSuitable for:wet and dry hairGoldwellSmooth Weightless Shine oil, 100mlfrom£13.56£17 at Lookfantastic£13.56 at AmazonWhat we loveWeightless and ideal for fine hair and oily scalpsWhat we don’t loveSilicone can build up on hair if not washed out oftenBest smoothing hair oil:Arkive the Good Habit hybrid oilArkiveThe Good Habit hybrid oil, 50mlfrom£14.68£15 at Boots£14.68 at AmazonWhat we loveBrilliant at tackling frizz, and smells delightfulWhat we don’t loveContains silicones that build up if not washed outView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£15 for 50ml at Boots£14.68 for 50ml at AmazonIf you have thick, frizzy hair that takes a lot of taming, this affordable hair serum-oil hybrid could be the fix you need. Simply add a pump or two to damp, clean hair after washing and conditioning, style your hair as usual and watch it work its magic.Why we love itThis hybrid oil contains baobab and jojoba oils, which add shine and moisture to the hair. Jojoba oil is also an emollient that forms a protective layer to lock in the hair’s moistureand to give super sleek, smooth results. Used before styling, the oil helps protect your hair from heated tools, creating a shiny finish that was humidity-proof in my tests.I loved this oil’s delicate scent, with slightly fruity top notes, a light floral heart and a musky vanilla base. I was also pleased to learn that this fragrance stuck around after application.The next thing I noticed was its very thick, gel-like consistency. Even after warming the oil in my hands, it had a sumptuous, thick texture that properly coated each strand. This coated feeling vanished as soon as I styled my hair using ahot brush, leaving my strands looking hydrated, healthy and frizz-free.It’s a shame that …it uses the silicone dimethiconol to smooth the hair, which is effective at smoothing and preventing frizz, but can cause buildup when not washed out properly.Size:50mlPrice per ml:27pKey ingredients:baobab oil, jojoba oil, dimethiconolVegan?YesCertified cruelty-free?YesSuitable for:wet and dry hairArkiveThe Good Habit hybrid oil, 50mlfrom£14.68£15 at Boots£14.68 at AmazonWhat we loveBrilliant at tackling frizz, and smells delightfulWhat we don’t loveContains silicones that build up if not washed outThe best of the restDyson Omega hydrating hair oilDysonOmega hydrating hair oil, 30mlfrom£45.99£45.99 at Sephora£49.99 at Cult BeautyWhat we loveFree from silicones; great hydrationWhat we don’t loveMiddling smoothing; expensive; iffy bottle designView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£45.99 for 30ml at Sephora£49.99 for 30ml at Cult BeautyBest for:natural ingredients and heat protectionYou’ve no doubt heard of Dyson’shair dryersand stylers, but fewer people know about the brand’s recent expansion into hair care. Among Dyson Beauty’s latest launches is the Omega hydrating hair oil, which uses sunflower seed oil grown on Dyson farms to hydrate and nourish hair.More specifically, the Omega oil combines seven oils, each rich in omega fatty acids. These are sunflower, macadamia, avocado, olive, abyssinian, sesame and corn, and they work together to boost moisture, reduce frizz and protect hair against breakage. The Dyson hair oil also provides heat protection up to 230C, so you can style without damage.In my tests, I loved how lightweight this oil was and enjoyed its uplifting, subtle fragrance. I found it easy and comfortable to apply to my strands, and my dry ends felt far healthier after application. Its smoothing performance was middling, but this was a compromise I was willing to accept, considering the formula is free from silicones.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s expensive and its lid likes to slowly open itself over time. I certainly wouldn’t want to store this hair oil lying down.
