Luckily, it looks lovely and sculptural on a vanity table.Size:30ml;price per ml:from about £1.53;key ingredients:sunflower oil, macadamia oil, avocado oil, olive oil, abyssinian oil, sesame oil and corn oil;vegan?Yes;certified cruelty-free?No;suitable for:wet and dry hairDysonOmega hydrating hair oil, 30mlfrom£45.99£45.99 at Sephora£49.99 at Cult BeautyWhat we loveFree from silicones; great hydrationWhat we don’t loveMiddling smoothing; expensive; iffy bottle designHair by Sam McKnight Love Me Do hair oilHair by Sam McKnightLove Me Do hair oilfrom£34£34 at Space NK£34 at Cult BeautyWhat we loveSmall bottle is secure and perfect for travelWhat we don’t loveToo light for thick hair; tricky pouring dispenserView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£34 for 50ml at Space NK£34 for 50ml at Cult BeautyBest for:fine hairThis lightweight hair oil smooths frizz using a blend of argan, sunflower seed and camellia seed oils. It’s the perfect consistency for fine hair, for which thicker oils are too heavy. It absorbed quickly, without leaving an over-greasy feeling on my hands. Once applied, I noticed my hair had a lovely shine to it and felt smooth and well-conditioned, with frizz and flyaways staying away even in high humidity.The brand claims that this hair oil helps protect against UV-induced colour fading, so it could be a good option for those with dyed hair. And, if you travel often, the small lightweight bottle is far more secure than others I’ve tested.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s too lightweight to benefit those with very thick, dense hair. Its pouring dispenser is also difficult to control.Size:50ml;price per ml:68p;key ingredients:argan oil, sunflower seed oil, camellia seed oil;vegan?Yes;certified cruelty-free?Yes;suitable for:wet and dry hairHair by Sam McKnightLove Me Do hair oilfrom£34£34 at Space NK£34 at Cult BeautyWhat we loveSmall bottle is secure and perfect for travelWhat we don’t loveToo light for thick hair; tricky pouring dispenserRemi Density Drop overnight scalp serumRemiDensity Drop overnight scalp serum, 100ml£47£47 at RemiWhat we loveSupports hair growth; incredibly lightweight formulaWhat we don’t loveA little on the pricey sideView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£47 for 100ml at RemiBest for:scalp care and supporting hair growthPut down the rosemary oil. To best support hair growth, you want something water-basedthat can quickly and weightlessly penetrate the scalp, not just sit on top of it and cause buildup, like an oil. This lightweight, water-based serum from Ireland-based scalp-care brand Remi is what you need.This serum is formulated with rosemary extract and vitamin E. Both of these are antioxidants that help calm the scalp and protect it from environmental stress, while the multitasking rosemary extract helps promote microcirculation. This helps to keep the scalp feeling healthy and calm while the microcirculation increases blood flow, which feeds the hair follicle, creating the perfect environment for healthy hair growth. Hair loss can be caused by multiple factors, from hormones to genetics, so no hair oil or serum will fix that. However, hair grows best from a healthy scalp, so it makes sense to take care of it.In my tests, I was amazed by how lightweight this serum was. With a quick massage, my scalp instantly drank it up and was left feeling just as clean as when I started. I could apply this four or five times before it started to weigh down my hair.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s not exactly a hair oil. But if you want to apply something to your scalp that will support its health and, in turn, support hair density, pick this lightweight serum instead.Size:100ml;price per ml:47p;key ingredients:rosemary extract, glycerine, vitamin E, peptides;vegan?Yes;certified cruelty-free?No;suitable for:damp and dry scalpRemiDensity Drop overnight scalp serum, 100ml£47£47 at RemiWhat we loveSupports hair growth; incredibly lightweight formulaWhat we don’t loveA little on the pricey sideRehab Dose 1.0 hair oilRehabDose 1.0 hair oil, 30mlfrom£26£26 at Boots£26 at RehabWhat we loveWeekly capsules to streamline hair care routineWhat we don’t loveCapsules fiddly and smelly, but the oil is niceView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Sarah Matthews/The Guardian£26 for 30ml at Boots£26 for 30ml at RehabBest for:intense treatmentThis hair oil is incredibly rich and covers everything your hair needs to thrive. It includes omega fatty acid-rich Moroccan oil to add shine, while jojoba oil helps reduce breakage. You’ll also find moisturising vitamins A, C and E and moisture-locking vitamin B5. This oil smoothed my hair and enhanced shine, and, despite its thicker texture, didn’t weigh it down.The oil comes encased in capsules, each containing one application. It’s intended to be used as an intensive treatment weekly after washing and before styling, which means you only need to get your hands oily once a week, rather than daily. I thought the biodegradable capsules stank a bit, but the oil itself smells nice and fresh once out of the capsule.It didn’t make the final cut because …I found the hair oil capsules tricky to open without scissors, and messy to use when I eventually managed it.Size:30ml;price per ml:from about 58p;key ingredients:Moroccan oil, jojoba oil, aloe vera oil, vitamin A, vitamin C, vitamin E;vegan?Yes;certified cruelty-free?No;suitable for:wet and dry hairRehabDose 1.0 hair oil, 30mlfrom£26£26 at Boots£26 at RehabWhat we loveWeekly capsules to streamline hair care routineWhat we don’t loveCapsules fiddly and smelly, but the oil is niceWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenSmooth moves … hair oil can help nourish dry strands, tame frizz and add shine when used correctly.Photograph: Sarah Matthews/The GuardianWhat is hair oil and what is it used for?“Hair oils are a more natural way of moisturising the hair shaft,” says trichologistHannah Gaboardi. “They penetrate into the cuticles and provide them with the vitamins, nutrients and fatty acids needed for healthier hair.” Hair oils can add moisture to support dry, brittle hair, she adds, and when applied regularly, they can add shine and tame frizz.Some people apply hair oil to their scalp. This “can help promote hair growth by improving the circulation”, Gaboardi says. “More blood flow to the scalp allows the follicles to receive more nutrients.” Just always make sure you cleanse your scalp thoroughly afterwards to prevent clogging.Can hair oil help with hair growth?Not exactly. Hair growth rate is determined by many factors, including age, hormones and scalp health. Hair oils can only help with scalp health, and they need to be used correctly to make a big difference.“Hair oil won’t directly grow your hair, especially when your hair loss is caused by genetic factors or health conditions,” says Gaboardi. The good news is that the nutrients, vitamins and fatty acids that make for healthier hair also benefit the hair follicles. “Hair oil also helps moisturise the scalp to create a healthy environment,” she says.But it’s not all sunshine and roses. “When hair oil is used incorrectly, it can damage scalp health and can clog the pores in your scalp,” Gaboardi cautions. “This can cause a delay in the natural hair cycle and slow down growth if [the oils are] not washed out. It can also lead to sebum buildup and cause seborrheic dermatitis.”Can hair oil protect my hair from heat styling damage?This question has confused me for years. Some hair oils are designed to be used on freshly washed, damp hair before styling. Others are better suited to adding shine to finished styles. But surely adding a hair oil before using heat styling tools is a recipe for disaster that can only result in damaged locks?The answer to my fears lies in an oil’s smoke point. Smoke point is the temperature at which oils begin to smoke and break down. “Oils that have a lower smoke point can cause the hair further heat damage when combined with high heat tools,” says Gaboardi.Avoid using hair oils containing oils with a smoke point of below 177C, such as flaxseed oil or extra virgin olive oil, before heat styling. Luckily, few hair oils contain these.Instead, “oils that have a high smoke point can be used after hair washing to help retain moisture and defend against heat”, says Gaboardi. These include grapeseed oil, safflower seed oil, argan oil and avocado oil. If you’re in doubt, she recommends “using serums and oils designed for heat styling to ensure you’re safely treating your hair”.Can hair oil protect my hair from sun damage?“Certain oil types have antioxidant properties that are used as a shield against UV rays,” says Gaboardi. At the same time, some oils provide natural, albeit low, protection against UV rays.If you notice your hair getting drier and frizzier when exposed to the sun, using a hair oil can help keep your hair smooth and nourished. That’s because hair oil helps lock moisture into the hair strand that could otherwise dry out in the heat.For more, read the Filter’s guideto thebest hair masksSarah Matthews is a health and beauty consumer journalist who’s tested everything from hi-tech skincare gadgets to hair styling tools. With four years of hands-on experience, she’s built a reputation for honest, detailed reviews across hair removal, light therapy, and more. As someone with waist-length hair, she’s developed strong opinions on everything from heat protection sprays to detangling brushesExplore more on these topicsHair careThe FilterWomen's hairSkincareBeautyMen's hairfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘All the watering places are crammed with hot people’: on holiday with Dickens | Charles Dickens | The Guardian
description: Exhibition at Charles Dickens Museum in London looks at writer’s holiday pursuits, from Kent to the Isle of Wight
Author: Caroline Davies
Headline: Exhibition at Charles Dickens Museum in London looks at writer’s holiday pursuits, from Kent to the Isle of Wight
Content: Dickens’ former holiday home, now known as Bleak House, overlooking Broadstairs beach in Kent.Photograph: Ian Pilbeam/AlamyView image in fullscreenDickens’ former holiday home, now known as Bleak House, overlooking Broadstairs beach in Kent.Photograph: Ian Pilbeam/AlamyCharles Dickens‘All the watering places are crammed with hot people’: on holiday with DickensExhibition at Charles Dickens Museum in London looks at writer’s holiday pursuits, from Kent to the Isle of WightCaroline DaviesThu 20 Aug 2026 08.20 EDTFirst published on Thu 20 Aug 2026 04.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s summer in the city, the pubs are crowded, and the coast beckons. In a year that has so far broughtfive significant heatwaves, it is a fair description of the current holiday season.But the same was true, too, of the much less frequent hot, dry summers of the past, including 186 years ago whenCharles Dickensput pen to paper in anticipation of escaping London for the sea breeze in Broadstairs, Kent.“There is no news inLondon– everybody is hurrying out of town – the two great theatres are shut up – and all the watering places are crammed with hot people,” he writes to his brother Alfred on 12 August 1840.View image in fullscreenA bust of Charles Dickens looks out of a window of the Dickens House Museum in Broadstairs.Photograph: UrbanImages/AlamyHis letter, which is to go on public display for the first time, is one of several items of correspondence shedding light on Dickens and his holiday pursuits, from picnics on the Thames, beach showering on theIsle of Wight, and being ravaged by mosquitoes, bugs and other insects“While Dickens rarely slowed down, he made sure to find time for holidays and days off, packing up plenty of his belongings and heading to the Kent coast or the West Country with his family,” said Emma Harper, deputy director at London’sCharles Dickens Museum, where the letters will go on display in the study where he wrote Oliver Twist, Nicholas Nickleby and The Pickwick Papers.“While Dickens loved London, he was very happy to escape its crowded hot pubs for the cooler climes of the coast, or if he decided to break his routine by taking a spur of the moment day off, he would consider this a holiday. He would take his work on holiday with him and sometimes even brought his favourite pieces of furniture along so he could write from the chair and desk that suited him best.”View image in fullscreenCharles Dickens blue plaque in Bonchurch, Isle of Wight.Photograph: Angela Hampton Picture Library/AlamyHe positively gloated about his successful mission to construct an outdoor shower cubicle near his “very pretty” holiday cottage in Bonchurch on the Isle of Wight in 1849, expressing no qualms about spoiling the view for others. He writes to the printer William Bradbury: “We have made all visitors in search of the picturesque, mad, by putting up an immense wooden caravan on the beach, to shut in a noble waterfall and convert it into a shower bath! With some five hundred feet of fall. Which we take, every morning, to the unbounded astonishment of the aboriginal inhabitants.”Of an 1851 trip on the Thames with his son Charley “and three other young Eton Shavers”, he promises that if his friend Thomas Beard joins them, he will be “armed with a hamper from Fortnum & Mason’s”. They can dine on a bank, “and if you can come, you and I will console ourselves for our antiquity, after dinner, with a trifle of tobacco and champagne”.Dickens “relaxed energetically”, said Harper, and he loved to travel. To his biographer John Forster he writes of a 1842 trip to Italy: “I see myself in a striped shirt, moustache, blouse, red sash, straw hat, and white trousers, sitting astride a mule, and not caring for the clock, the day of the month, or the day of the week.”Reflecting on one long excursion, he tells Beard in 1845 of “the gentlemanly vagabond I have been, for the last six or eight months – the extraordinary beds I have slept in – and the bewildering amount of fleas, mosquitoes, bugs, and other insects I have unwillingly bepastured – these things have hardly left me any leisure in my holiday, until within the last four or five weeks. During the whole of which time I have been employed, chiefly, in lying on my back on sofas, and leaning out of windows and over balconies, in a sort of mild intoxication.”Summer in the City with Charles Dickens runs from 26 August to 27 September at the Charles Dickens Museum in LondonExplore more on these topicsCharles DickensExhibitionsLondonKentIsle of WightnewsShareReuse this content

title: Winner of Invertebrate of the Year 2026 crowned – and it is the size of a grain of rice | Environment | The Guardian
description: The leaf sheep, a neon green solar-powered slug, has inspired at least one Pokémon character and triumphs in global ballot
Author: Patrick Barkham
Headline: The leaf sheep, a neon green solar-powered slug, has inspired at least one Pokémon character and triumphs in global ballot
Content: Graphic with images of varied invertebrates including a sea slug, a bumblebee, a dragonfly, a woodlouse, a worm and others.Illustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGraphic with images of varied invertebrates including a sea slug, a bumblebee, a dragonfly, a woodlouse, a worm and others.Illustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianInvertebrate of the year 2026EnvironmentWinner of Invertebrate of the Year 2026 crowned – and it is the size of a grain of riceThe leaf sheep, a neon green solar-powered slug, has inspired at least one Pokémon character and triumphs in global ballotSee the top 10 shortlist hereChris Packham: ‘Life as we know it hinges on invertebrates’Patrick BarkhamThu 20 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘You’d want one as a pet’: the irresistibly cute solar-powered sea slugRead moreA neon green solar-powered slug that lives underwater is the winner of the increasingly popularInvertebrate of the Year competitionrun by the Guardian.Theleaf sheep,Costasiella kuroshimae, triumphed in the global ballot after hundreds of thousands of readers around the world read about and shared their appreciation for the spineless creatures who make up the majority of animal life on Earth.View image in fullscreenThe leaf sheep, which lives in tropical waters around Japan, Indonesia and the Philippines, was only first described by science in 1993.Photograph: Marli Wakeling/AlamyAnnouncing the winner, the broadcaster and environmental campaigner Chris Packham said: “It’s very, very beautiful but also very smart too. It harvests photosynthetic material from the algae it feeds upon and builds its own solar panels.”In a much closer contest than previous years – when thetardigradeand thecommon earthwormwon with popular landslides – the beady-eyed, charming leaf sheep fought off strong competition from the world’s largest bumblebee, themoscardón,Bombus dahlbomii, which finished second. This giant ginger bumblebee isincreasingly threatenedin its native Patagonia because of invasive bumblebee species introduced by humans in recent decades.In third place was thehorseshoe crab, a remarkable arthropod that pre-dates the dinosaurs and contains blue blood, closely followed by thecommon woodlouse.The winner of the Guardian's Invertebrate of the year 2026 revealedAlthough worms have historically polled very strongly in the competition, bringing up the rear in 10th place on this year’s shortlist was the astonishingbootlace worm, one of the longest animals in the world.The competition was launched three years ago to celebrate overlooked and often derided invertebrates, who number at least 1.7m species – about 97% of all animals – with probably millions more still to be discovered and described by science. Without the unpaid labour of wild invertebrates who pollinate crucial crops, filter water, recycle waste, clean up pollution and add fertility to soils, human life on Earth would quickly perish.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenThe leaf sheep feeds on algae that grows in fine silts around shallow reefs.Photograph: Westend61 GmbH/AlamyThis year, several thousand spineless candidates nominated by Guardian readers, including everyone from scientists to children, were whittled down to a shortlist of 10.As each candidate was announced during a two-week fiesta of invertebrate appreciation, experts offered their perspectives with Erica McAlisterextolling the importance – and beauty – of flies, the wildlife photographer Dara Ojo revealingthe joys of macro photography, and Connor Butler pointing out howthere is no “other” in the natural world:we are all part of the same living systems.The leaf sheep, which lives in tropical waters around Japan, Indonesia and the Philippines, was only first described by science in 1993. Since then, it has become increasingly celebrated in human culture thanks to advances in underwater macro photography that have revealed its remarkably cute appearance, which has inspired at least one Pokémon character.Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentInvertebrate of the year 2026InvertebratesMarine lifeWildlifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The long shadow of Argentina’s dictatorship: she wasn’t who she thought she was – neither was her father | Argentina | The Guardian
description: The long read: The political rift between them was profound. Then one evening, a kiss goodbye sent her on a remarkable journey that continues today
Author: Meaghan Beatley
Headline: The long read: The political rift between them was profound. Then one evening, a kiss goodbye sent her on a remarkable journey that continues today
Content: Pictured in front of the Monument to the Victims of State Terrorism, Buenos Aires, August 2026. Photograph: Anita Pouchard Serra/The GuardianA young activist thought her father’s disapproval of her leftwing views was purely political. Then one evening, a kiss goodbye sent her on a remarkable journey that continues todayLast chance to buy the summer issue of The Long Read magazine, now with 15% off.Click hereto orderByMeaghan BeatleyThu 20 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 11.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs a child, Analía Azic used to pretend she was secretly a princess, the heiress to a magical distant kingdom. In real life, she was the daughter of a greengrocer named Juan Antonio Azic and a demure housewife named Esther Abrego. The family lived in the province of Buenos Aires, which, as anyone from the area will tell you with a dash of pride, is not the city of Buenos Aires but its rougher neighbour. Analía was not royalty, but she had an iron will and audacity out of proportion to her small stature.Analía cared little for grades at the Ladies Institute of the Sacred Heart, where she rolled with thedominantes, girls who hiked their school skirts up so high they served as little more than belts, and dreamed of the weekend when they could finally trade in their school uniforms for designer jeans and tight tank tops and sashay into Electric Circus, the one local club that allowed in minors. There, Analía would climb atop the speakers and dance, then leap back down to toy with the boys from the Argentine air force’s technical trade school.It was the 1990s and she and her friends were middle-class kids from families with ties to the armed forces. Their understanding of recent events was that the nation had emerged, in the previous decade, from a “dirty war” between two opposing forces of equal strength. On the one side, a national army fighting for the preservation of Christian values and the fatherland; on the other, unscrupulous Marxist guerrillas advocating their overthrow. Both sides had committed crimes, that was true – but it was war, and thankfully the army had won and reinstated order. Analía absorbed this narrative both at school and at home, where her father, Juan Antonio, railed against what he called the “atheist, unpatriotic left”.From the age of nine, Analía had taken to reading the newspaper after her father had finished with it, and at night would sidle up beside him to watch his political programmes on TV. This bonded her to her father, as surely as it unsettled her mother. Esther believed that politics, like climbing trees, was not becoming of the female sex. Analía – who, by her own admission, possessed a “rebellious, contentious nature” – ignored her. But it was precisely this defiant streak that soon led her to question her parents’ politics. When Analía turned 15, she got her hands on Che Guevara’s complete works. She started to become curious about leftwing ideas.This was a period of relative calm and prosperity in Argentina, following decades marred by chaos and military dictatorships.Carlos Menem, the nation’s president for most of the 1990s, was a flashy, spray-tanned bon vivant with a penchant for posing by his Ferrari for magazine spreads. Though a Peronist – a member of the dominant leftist party in Argentina, named after its founder, Juan Domingo Perón – he ushered in a Washington-approved, free-market liberalisation programme that included privatising more than 400 state-run companies and effectively dismantling the welfare state. In the short term, his programme seemed to offer relief, especially to middle-class Argentines, who splurged on imported goods and holidays in Miami. But in the long term, it devastated many domestic industries and helped set the country careening toward a debt crisis.Analía had seen spiralling poverty first-hand through volunteer work with church groups. After she read Guevara, these impressions took on a new political dimension in her mind. He embodied the Latin American guerrillas of the 1960s and 70s she had been taught to revile. But now she wondered: if they’d been fighting to ease inequality in one of the most unequal regions in the world, hadn’t they been right?After finishing the book, Analía promptly bought a beret; from then on she took it off only to sleep and shower. She tacked a poster of Guevara’s face to her bedroom door. Her father did not tear it down, as she expected, but, with patient resignation, asked her to put it on the inside of the door.“As I continued to oppose the rightwing discourse of my family, an ideological rift opened up between us that grew even wider,” she later reflected. At the time, she saw it as “simply the result of the fact that he was old and I was young”. Later, she would come to see it very differently.If Analía’s politics began as teenage rebellion, by the time she went to university they solidified into conviction. She agreed to study law at the University of Buenos Aires after Juan Antonio shot down her first choice, sociology. (The department was a “nest of leftists”, he told her.) But it was at university that she joined the political organisation that would define her life.Venceremos (We will overcome) was the student arm of a self-styled nationalist and revolutionary movement called Patria Libre, which opposed the government’s free-market reforms. As the century ended andArgentinaslid deeper into an economic crisis, the government implemented harsh austerity measures. Analía, who was still living at home, threw herself into increasingly rowdy protests with Venceremos, while telling her parents that she was going to the movies or volunteering with church groups.The lies weighed on her. One night in 1999, while watching the evening news with her parents, Analía saw one of her fellow activists on screen, hurling a rock through a shop window. “I’m involved with that group,” she blurted out. “That’s where I spend my days. Not in church.” Esther froze. Juan Antonio just stared at her, with what Analía would later think looked more like fear than anger. “My relationship with my parents, and [Juan Antonio] especially, deteriorated from the moment I stopped lying,” she later wrote.View image in fullscreenAn anti-government rally in Buenos Aires during Argentina’s ‘dirty war’ in March 1982.Photograph: Horacio Villalobos/Corbis/Getty ImagesOn 1 December 2001, the government imposed a freeze on bank accounts, blocking Argentines’ access to their savings. People started rioting. Analía dodged blows from the police as she fled the centre of the capital after a protest, her high heels clacking against the pavement (she’d planned on going dancing afterwards). The riots raged on for weeks, peaking on 19 and 20 December, when police opened fire on protesters, killing 39.The months immediately after the December 2001 financial collapse were some of the darkest in recent Argentine history. Unemployment soared, and half the populationfell below the poverty line. Analía helped set up soup kitchens and communal vegetable gardens to feed the homeless and unemployed, and offered literacy classes and legal advice. She lived in an abandoned bank that had been converted into a cultural centre, with no hot water. Concerned about her health, her parents insisted she come home at least once a week for a home-cooked meal.It was at one of these weekly dinners, one Thursday night in July 2003, that Analía’s life was upended.After the fall of Argentina’slast military dictatorship in 1983, the country initially seemed to offer the world a rare model of effective transitional justice. In 1985, nine junta commanders were tried in what became the first major war crimes trial since Nuremberg. The prosecution drew heavily from Nunca Más (Never again), a 1984 report compiled by Argentina’s National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons, which documented 8,960 cases of forced disappearance, as well as other atrocities. The court convicted five of the nine defendants for “implementing a criminal plan” that included torturing and murdering Argentines. But just two years later, as a new wave of trials targeting middle-ranking officers approached, a faction of the military launched a mutiny, demanding an end to prosecutions for crimes committed during the dictatorship.To quell the unrest, President Raúl Alfonsín passed two laws. The first, known as the Full Stop law, set a deadline of 60 days for any new prosecutions for political violence. The second, the Due Obedience law, granted immunity to lower-ranking officers on the grounds that they were following orders when they committed crimes. Many Argentines simply called them the “impunity laws”. They meant that a decade after the dictatorship had ended, you could find yourself standing in line at the grocery store behind the very man who had tortured you.Following the 2001 financial crisis, many leftwing organisations demanded the repeal of the impunity laws, and for official recognition of 30,000 as the number of disappeared – far above the 8,960 cases documented in the 1984 Nunca Más report, which counted only those confirmed missing at the time. In the absence of legal mechanisms by which to hold people suspected of war crimes accountable, protesters would stand in front of their homes or workplaces and call them out for their alleged crimes, in a kind of public shaming. Analía was one of the participants in these protests, which were known asescraches.About 10pm on 24 July 2003, Analía was at her parents’ house for one of their weekly dinners when her father emerged from his bedroom impeccably dressed. He asked Analía to stay at home that evening and then left, “without any explanation, although he kissed … us goodbye”, Analía recalled, adding that it was “a surprising display of affection”.A few hours later, the phone rang. Analía picked up. It was her father, sounding odd. He dictated a number for Analía to take down and instructed her to call it in an hour. When she did so, a male voice answered. “Analía, is that you?” the man said. “Your father’s in the hospital. He just shot himself.”At the hospital, Analía found her father “unconscious and without a face”. The bullet hadn’t damaged his brain but it had completely disfigured him. Reeling, she stepped out of his room and walked down to the waiting area. That’s when she saw a list of names in bright red letters scrolling across a TV screen. They belonged to about 40 members of the Argentine military who had served under the junta and who were facing extradition to Spain to stand trial for dictatorship-era crimes. Juan Antonio Azic, her father, was on the list. (The trials were due to take place in Spain thanks to the efforts of the crusading judge Baltasar Garzón acting under the doctrine of universal jurisdiction, which allowed courts of one country to prosecute grave human rights crimes committed outside that country.)Analía had known her father had been in the military, but she’d always assumed he’d simply done his service as required by law. Now she learned he had belonged to a taskforce that kidnapped, tortured and disappeared people in the Esma, a navy mechanics’ school that had been converted into one of the largest and deadliest clandestine detention centres right in the heart of Buenos Aires. An estimated 5,000 people were held there throughout the dictatorship. The man who raised her, she discovered, had wielded an electric cattle prod against prisoners to get them to speak. “My father had suddenly ceased to be an innocent fruit-and-vegetable merchant and had become one of the people whose imprisonment I had been demanding for years,” she said.View image in fullscreenA mural featuring the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo in Buenos Aires, Argentina, December 2023.Photograph: Víctor R Caivano/APShe contacted theGrandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo, a celebrated human rights group fighting dictatorship-era impunity, with whom Analía had campaigned. She asked to speak to their head, Estela de Carlotto, an elegant matriarch with a halo of white hair. “I told her that I needed to apologise, because I had found out my father was a torturer, but that I also needed to hear that I still had the right to be politically active, that my genetic heredity did not automatically make me ineligible to keep fighting for the causes I believed in.” Estela arranged for them to meet. It was only later that Analía, who had been sobbing on the call, would think Estela had sounded strangely serene.A few days later, Analía walked into a bar to meet Estela and several other members of human rights organisations. They informed her they had reason to believe she was not Juan Antonio and Esther’s natural daughter, and suggested she have a DNA test. Rather than being the child of a war criminal, they had strong evidence that Analía might be the daughter of a couple of leftist dissidents disappeared by the junta.Across Latin America, just as elsewhere, the 1960s was a decade of revolution. In Argentina, a string of coups and one general’s prohibition of Peronism – more than a political party, the working man’s creed – contributed to the rapid radicalisation of Argentine youth. Some turned to armed struggle.The two most prominent guerrilla organisations were the People’s Revolutionary Army, a Marxist-Leninist outfit, and the Peronist Montoneros. These groups raided police stations and army barracks for weapons, robbed banks to fund their operations, and kidnapped military officers and business executives, sometimes for ransom, sometimes to execute them.On 24 March 1976, a military junta seized power in a coup and began dismantling any leftist opposition. By then, the Montoneros were weak, but they were labelled terrorists and targeted by the new regime, along with students, labour and trade unionists, intellectuals and anyone suspected of leftwing opposition.The guerrillas went underground. Among them were a couple in the Montoneros, María Hilda Pérez, known as Cori, and José María Donda, known as El Cabo, or Captain. Cori was passionate and impulsive. When her father told her to remove a cache of weapons she’d stashed in his house, she shoved them into an enormous duffel bag and hauled it down the street yelling, “Cowards!” back at her gawking sisters. José was quiet and commanding. He quickly ascended to a key position within the Montoneros.Cori and José’s love for Peronism, which they saw as a liberating force in Argentina, was matched only by their love for each other, and they married in a small ceremony in 1973 when she was 22 and he 19. Their witness was José’s older brother, Adolfo Donda, a career navy officer 10 years his senior whom José had idolised as a kid, even as their divergent politics opened a rift between them.It was Adolfo who, as a senior intelligence officer inside the junta, laid a trap for Cori and had her arrested in March 1977, when she was five months pregnant. When José learned of it, he told a neighbour he believed Adolfo had set her up to get to him. José himself was captured that May. Years later, a man who’d survived imprisonment in the Esma and crossed paths with Adolfo there testified to overhearing him say: “This is a war. And in a war you can’t show mercy to your enemy. I didn’t show mercy to my own brother, who was a Montonero. And I didn’t show mercy to my sister-in-law.”To avoid the bad press that had haunted Franco’s Spain and Pinochet’s Chile with their firing squads – loud and flashy affairs that received international condemnation – the junta turned to another mode of extermination, the “death flight”. This consisted of injecting prisoners with a sleep-inducing narcotic, tying rocks to their feet, loading them into a small plane, and tossing them out, midair, into the River Plate or the Atlantic.In April 1977, a group of 14 women gathered on the Plaza de Mayo before the Casa Rosada, the squat, rose-coloured presidential palace, demanding information on their missing children. Within weeks, the ranks of what became known as the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo had swelled to more than 100. Six months later, a few, soon to be called the Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo, asked another question. Where were the children of their missing pregnant daughters? Rumours churned that pregnant women who had been captured were kept alive long enough to deliver their children, only to have them taken away and handed off for adoption, often to regime sympathisers.After she was arrested in March 1977, Cori was held prisoner in the Esma. She gave birth on a wooden table in a small room in the attic sometime between July and September 1977. The baby was her second child; the first, a two-year-old girl, was in her grandmother’s care at the time. Cori was told to write a letter to her family asking them to take care of this new baby, too. Suspecting neither the letter nor the child would ever actually reach them, she hatched a plan with her cellmate, a 19-year-old woman named Lidia Vieyra who’d been pulled in to act as midwife, despite having never done so before. With a needle and bits of blue surgical thread left over from the birth, they sewed tiny blue loops around the baby’s earlobes. Cori hoped that one day, if she were freed, somebody would remember the baby with little blue hoops in her ears, and the sign would help her trace the child.Fifteen days after giving birth, the baby was taken from her, and according to testimony from survivors of the Esma, Cori was “transferred”. “Transfer” was the euphemism the military used to refer to the death flight. Her brother-in-law, Adolfo, was part of the detention centre’s leadership that decided on each week’s “transfers”. The circumstances around José’s disappearance are unclear.Lidia Vieyra, Cori’s former cellmate, survived. After she got out in July 1978, she sought out the Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo to tell them about Cori’s missing baby. Over the next few decades, a series of tips slowly brought them closer to finding the child’s new identity and whereabouts. One came from someone who questioned whether their previously childless neighbours, Juan Antonio Azic and Esther Abrego, were really the parents of the baby who had suddenly appeared in their home. And another came from the wife of a junior coast guard officer who said that in 1977, shortly after she’d given birth to a son of her own, a commanding officer from the Esma handed her a baby girl, less than a month old, asking her to nurse her. When she took the baby, she noticed something unusual. Bits of blue thread sewn through her ears, like tiny blue hoops.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe Long ReadLose yourself in a great story: from politics to psychology, food to technology, culture to crimeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionVieyra had one final piece of information. Before she died, Cori had given the baby a name. She’d called her Victoria.An estimated 500 babies were stolen during the dictatorship and, as part of a systematic plan, handed to military families or junta sympathisers who passed them off as their own. Couples who wanted a child joined waiting lists at military hospitals. Now Analía Azic had reason to believe that she was one of the stolen children.On top of her grief and confusion, she was saddled with an enormous responsibility. Taking the DNA test and confirming Juan Antonio Azic and Esther Abrego were not her biological parents might mean putting them behind bars. She was convinced that Juan Antonio, who had been working at the Esma when Cori gave birth in custody, had kept his wife in the dark about their new baby’s origins, and that Esther, an obedient and timid wife, had simply never asked. Harder still was reconciling her feelings for Juan Antonio himself. She described him as a stern but loving father, and “the most important man in my life”.It wasn’t until nearly a year later, on 24 March 2004, that Analía finally decided to take the test. She got her results in October. There was a 99.99% chance she was related to Cori and José María Donda. By this point, she can’t have been surprised. She had been shown a passport-sized photo of Cori. With the hooded eyes that conveyed both defiance and teenage ennui, jet-black hair falling at her temple, full lips and a strong chin – Cori was her spitting image.Analía changed her name to Victoria Donda, the name her mother gave her at birth, and her father’s surname. This was shortly after the election of a Peronist candidate named Néstor Kirchner, whose presidency inaugurated a new era of accountability for dictatorship-era crimes. He struck down the Full Stop and Due Obedience laws, putting an end to protection for those guilty of human rights abuses, and annulled a decree prohibiting the extradition of Argentines accused of torture and murder during the dictatorship.In this new climate, Victoria became well known in Argentina as a child found by the Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo. She wasn’t comfortable with the attention at first, though she later came to see it in a more positive light. “It’s a good thing for society to know what happened,” she said. “Argentina was a country where the dictatorship was not talked about.”The one person who knew the most about her origins – her biological uncle, Adolfo Donda, the naval officer who had been in the leadership group that ordered her mother Cori’s “transfer” – had still not spoken.Adolfo Donda had been first arrested in 1987 but was released after just four months. It was around the time the impunity laws were passed. For more than a decade, he faced no further legal consequences. That changed in 2003, when the impunity laws were repealed and he was arrested again. In 2011 and 2017, he would finally be convicted and sentenced to life in prison for a battery of crimes including kidnapping, torture and murder. But not Victoria’s abduction.Victoria’s new identity deepened her commitment to leftist politics. “I’d always been a woman of the left, but to find out that this was in line with my parents, that it was the first thing I’d shared with them, that gave me another impetus.”In 2007, members of Kirchner’s coalition encouraged Victoria to run for a congressional seat representing Buenos Aires Province. She was unsure whether she was ready to trade activism for a role in formal politics. But after some persuasion, she agreed. At 30, she became the youngest person ever elected to Argentina’s Congress, and the first stolen child of the dictatorship. She committed herself fully to the defence of human rights. “I owe this to my parents,” she later wrote, “who gave their lives to build a more just world for their daughters.”On 18 October 2014, Victoria gave birth to a baby girl of her own. She named her daughter Trilce, after a book of poems by César Vallejo, a portmanteau oftristeanddulce, sad and sweet. Two weeks later, she was in bed recovering from her C-section when she learned that there was to be a vote in the congressional committee on which she served on an abortion bill – an early step before a bill made it to Congress’ floor. She grabbed a bandage, wound it tight around her abdomen, swaddled Trilce, and lurched over to Congress. “I didn’t want my daughter to go through what I had,” Victoria said.View image in fullscreenVictoria Donda (centre) at a session in the Chamber of Deputies of Congress in Buenos Aires, 9 May 2017.Photograph: ZUMA Press, Inc./AlamyMany years earlier, when Victoria was 19, she had used her savings to get a clandestine abortion in a “more or less acceptable place”. Later, when she’d accompanied other women forced to have abortions under worse circumstances, she’d realised she’d been lucky.Abortion was a criminal act in Argentina, strictly prohibited by the nation’s 1921 penal code unless the pregnancy presented a threat to the woman’s life or health, or in cases of rape. Fearing legal repercussions, doctors were often unwilling to proceed even in permitted cases.When the 2014 abortion bill did not go forward, owing to a technicality, Victoria realised the campaign needed a new approach. Between the end of the dictatorship in 1983 and 2016, at least 3,040 women died of complications from abortion in Argentina. The true number was likely much higher since hospitals often logged the cause of death after abortions went wrong as “sepsis”. Hundreds of thousands of clandestine abortions were carried out each year, of which more than 50,000 ended up in public hospitals after developing complications. It was an unspoken healthcare crisis. Yet even progressive parties did not want to touch it. Just as silence had smothered the dictatorship’s crimes for two decades of democracy, it hung over this issue too. Victoria wanted abortion dragged out into the open.In 2016, while traveling through Tucumán, one of Argentina’s poorest provinces, Victoria learned of a young woman serving an eight-year sentence for homicide after having had what appeared to be a miscarriage. Belén, the pseudonym by which the woman came to be known, had checked into a hospital in 2014 for severe stomach pain. Unaware she was pregnant, she was arrested on the spot after staff claimed to have found a foetus in a toilet she had used. Police handcuffed her to her hospital bed, then transferred her to a prison.Victoria knew that a poor woman from a poor province imprisoned over a suspected abortion wouldn’t make national headlines – unless there was outrage outside the country. She arranged a visit from the United Nations special rapporteur on torture, who, after hearing Belén’s story, publicly condemned Argentina in the nation’s Congress in May 2016. The next day, his words, and the case, dominated national news.After more than two years in prison, Belén was released in August 2016 and acquitted in March 2017. The case helped “show what the consequences of abortion were”, Victoria said. “And the consequences were that if you were poor, you ended up dead or in prison. The rich could always pay for them. But not the poor.”Over the next few years, Argentina’s increasingly powerful feminist movement trained its attention on reproductive rights. In early 2018, President Mauricio Macri allowed a congressional debate on abortion for the first time in the nation’s history. On 6 March 2018, Victoria was one of four deputies who sponsoreda bill proposing to legalise abortionup to 14 weeks.As lawmakers and civilians made their cases for or against the bill over the next few months (in a rare set of proceedings, civilians were invited to speak before Congress), opponents repurposed the language of a crime Argentines were now all too familiar with, claiming that abortion was “the real forced disappearance of people”. In this way, many of the same people who denied that 30,000 people had been disappeared under the dictatorship now accused progressives – feminists in particular – of being the real killers in Argentina.At the urging of a friend, Victoria read Margaret Atwood’s The Handmaid’s Tale during those heady weeks of debate. Atwood has said she took inspiration from Argentina for the idea of giving babies from the lower classes to the ruling class. “It was hard,” Victoria recalled of reading the book. “I thought a lot about my mum. Locked up. With no possibility to choose,” she said.On 13 June 2018, Congress’s Chamber of Deputies voted on the bill. Victoria leaned into a microphone planted on her desk. “How can Argentines look at the world, this developed world we strive to resemble, when we have an authoritarian gene in us that makes us lock up women to have children? What kind of perverse project led us to have women kidnapped and disappeared and forced to give birth, as if their uteruses were spoils of war, and the results of those uteruses, those babies, were also spoils of war?” Her voice boomed as lawmakers around her rose to their feet, their applause echoing through the chamber.Aftera million women gathered to demonstrate, the bill passed the Chamber of Deputies with the smallest of margins. Two months later, it was struck down by the Senate. But on 30 December 2020, Argentina’s Congress approved a law allowing abortion up to 14 weeks. A few months later, an eccentric economist named Javier Milei launched a political campaign that combined dictatorship denialism and promises to repeal the abortion law. He was elected Argentina’s president in November 2023.Imet Victoria Donda in 2024 in a cafe in Boedo, a bohemian neighbourhood of Buenos Aires. Outside, a torrential downpour pelted the streets. The previous week, Victoria had sat in a small courtroom, chapel-like in its intimacy, as a judge handed her uncle, Adolfo Donda, a 15-year sentence for his role in her abduction and for concealing her identity. After having refused to see her years earlier in prison, because he said she was not a “recognised” family member, during the trial Adolfo had scolded her for going against her own “blood”. “Family is sacred, Victoria,” he had said. In their ruling, the judges described what happened to Cori during labour as “dehumanised childbirth”. It was the first time a ruling in one of Argentina’s stolen-baby cases used those words.Victoria did not forgive Adolfo. But she did forgive Juan Antonio Azic, the man she had once called her father and now referred to as “my appropriator”. After emerging from a coma after his suicide attempt in 2003, he had encouraged Victoria to take the DNA test that confirmed her identity as a daughter of the disappeared – which, in 2015, helped secure his own conviction for her kidnapping. Far from the glare of any camera, Victoria, over the years, regularly visited him in prison, bringing him small honey-glazed croissants calledmedialunas. He is now serving the remainder of his sentence under house arrest and Victoria continues to visit him. “I still love him,” she said quietly, gazing out the window as thick raindrops hit the pane.Later she pulled out her phone and scrolled through pictures of Trilce flashing bucktoothed grins at abortion protests. “We fought so hard for that law, and my daughter was right there with us,” she said, smiling at her child. With her dark, disheveled locks, hooded eyes and broad grin, Trilce looked unmistakably like Victoria. She also looked a lot like Cori.Adapted fromSex and Dissent: Stories of Feminist Resistance in Argentina, Chile, Mexico, and Spain, published by PenguinListen to our podcastshereand sign up to the long read weekly emailhere.Explore more on these topicsThe long readArgentinaAmericasActivismProtestSocial historyFamilyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Zomi Frankcom did not deserve to die. Israel’s refusal to investigate her death and its failure to apologise is despicable  | Geoffrey Robertson | The Guardian
description: The Israeli ambassador has claimed ‘a court came to a decision that there’s no criminal liability’ but there is no evidence that any court has been involved
Author: Geoffrey Robertson
Headline: The Israeli ambassador has claimed ‘a court came to a decision that there’s no criminal liability’ but there is no evidence that any court has been involved
Content: A protester in Melbourne holds a picture of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom, who was killed in an Israeli air strike while delivering food in Gaza.Photograph: AAP/ReutersView image in fullscreenA protester in Melbourne holds a picture of Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom, who was killed in an Israeli air strike while delivering food in Gaza.Photograph: AAP/ReutersOpinionIsraelZomi Frankcom did not deserve to die. Israel’s refusal to investigate her death and its failure to apologise is despicableGeoffrey RobertsonThe Israeli ambassador has claimed ‘a court came to a decision that there’s no criminal liability’ but there is no evidence that any court has been involvedThu 20 Aug 2026 19.29 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 19.34 EDTShareZomi Frankcom did not deserve to die. She and her six colleagues were traveling in a clearly marked humanitarian convoy to distribute food to starving Palestinians on a route that had been communicated well in advance to the Israel Defense Forces (IDF). It bombed them deliberately and repeatedly. Israel’s prime minister,Benjamin Netanyahu, announced the next day that the attack was a “mistake” and a few days later its two commanders were forced to retire, and three others were disciplined. An internal inquiry followed, but this week – well over two years later – the IDF announced that there would be no further investigation because there could be no suspicion that any crime had been committed: it was merely a mistake. This is a serious misunderstanding of the law of war.‘An insult’: Zomi Frankcom’s family issues strongly-worded statement as Israel rejects criminal investigation into her killingRead moreMistakes may have fatal consequences and, if they are the result of gross negligence or reckless or irresponsible conduct, they are culpable and deserving of punishment. The crime of manslaughter in Australian and English law reflects this grave level of criminality. In war law, under article 8 of the statute of the international criminal court (ICC) “intentionally launching an attack in the knowledge that such an attack will cause loss of life to civilians” and “directing attacks against personnel or vehicles involved in humanitarian assistance” are serious war crimes which may be committed by mistakes made through negligence or blind eyes turned to their foreseeable consequences. The IDF decision not to investigate Zomi’s killing on the grounds that it was merely a “mistake” is not a legitimate reason and the Israeli government’s refusal even now to apologise is despicable.Not that an investigation by the IDF is likely to lead to an indictment of those who ordered the attack. According to statistics provided by a UN inquiry into “Operation Cast Lead”, the 22-day war in 2009, more than 1,000 Palestinians were killed, but no indictments were brought against those responsible for this exercise in urban military aggression (provoked by Hamas rocket attacks). There were many war crime allegations including attacks on hospitals and mosques, and the IDF commenced 400 investigations against individual soldiers but only two were ever brought to trial and the only prison sentence – of seven months – was imposed on a soldier for stealing a credit card.The refusal to act over Zomi’s case and on two other atrocities involving the killing of workers for Médecins Sans Frontières was seemingly balanced by the decision to allow investigations into two other killings to go ahead – the murder of two doctors in a Red Crescent ambulance while they were tending to victims of an IDF strike, including five-year-old Hind Rajab, and another attack on ambulances that killed 15 medics. What was the difference that required an investigation in these two cases but not in the others? There is one simple explanation: the lies told by the IDF (that the ambulances were advancing without lights or markings) had been authoritatively refuted by phone footage and the evidence of survivors. Since there was unequivocal evidence that these were war crimes, the IDF was forced to agree that the inquiries would continue – but not necessarily to a court.Zomi Frankcom: Penny Wong condemns ‘insulting’ decision to clear IDF over Gaza strikes that killed Australian aid workerRead moreSo what can Australia do to vindicate the memory of the murder of a good citizen? It could fund her family to hire lawyers in Israel to sue the IDF in courts with judges who are not biased in favour of the Israeli government, but they are likely to find that access to justice against the IDF is too difficult because of time bars (hence the delays) and immunities. It could ask the ICC to investigate – although Israel is not a member,Palestineis and this court has held that it has jurisdiction over war crimes committed in Gaza (since the current proceedings against Netanyahu and his war minister for actions that have led to starvation and attacks on civilian residences).But invoking international justice for Zomi and her colleagues will be opposed by our major ally, the United States. Only last month the state department announced a campaign to “disable the court’s ability to operate” by putting pressure on its 125 national members to withdraw. Marco Rubio has falsely accused it of “maliciously abusing its authority” and has authorised sanctions against its chief justice and those of its judges to have ruled on Netanyahu’s case. Australia, like many other decent democracies, has been a stalwart supporter of the ICC but has vulnerabilities (especially over Aukus) if these irresponsible threats were carried out.The government has called for disclosure by Israel of the evidence on which the IDF has decided not to proceed, but this is unlikely to be forthcoming. The Israeli ambassador has been quoted as claiming that “a court came to a decision that there’s no criminal liability” but there is no evidence that any court – certainly not a court that is open and independent – has ever been involved. The secretly and illegally mistaken way in which her arbitrary killing has been covered up will have to be commemorated here, in a tribute to her compassion and her work for a better world.Geoffrey Robertson AO KC is a former UN war crimes judge and author of World of War Crimes – Eyeless in Gaza and Beyond (Penguin)Explore more on these topicsIsraelOpinionPalestineBenjamin NetanyahuAustralian politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: There is nothing scientific about The Great ADHD Myth? ‘documentary’ | Gina Rippon | The Guardian
description: Channel 4’s programme wastes a chance to ask important questions about how ADHD is diagnosed and treated, instead indulging in unscientific methods and conspiracy theories, says author Gina Rippon
Author: Gina Rippon
Headline: Channel 4’s programme wastes a chance to ask important questions about how ADHD is diagnosed and treated, instead indulging in unscientific methods and conspiracy theories, says author Gina Rippon
Content: Illustration: Jess Clark/The Guardian/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Jess Clark/The Guardian/Getty ImagesOpinionAttention deficit hyperactivity disorderThere is nothing scientific about The Great ADHD Myth? ‘documentary’Gina RipponChannel 4’s programme wastes a chance to ask important questions about how ADHD is diagnosed and treated, instead indulging in unscientific methods and conspiracy theoriesProf Gina Rippon is emeritus professor of cognitive neuroimaging at the Aston Brain Centre, Aston UniversityThu 20 Aug 2026 08.18 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.31 EDTShareWhenChannel 4announced that it would air a documentary titled The Great ADHD Myth?, an outpouring of fury followed. Despite this, I set out to approach it as a scientist – not just as a scientist whose own work has dealt with developmental disorders, but as someone who has enormous respect for the scientific process and for the importance of evidence-led debate.Channel 4’s press release claimed the documentary sought to determine whether attention deficit hyperactivity disorder was a “genuine neurodevelopmental disorder, or a social construct”. At one level this is a brave enterprise. ADHD is recognised worldwide as a disorder,by the World Health Organizationandour own NHSamong others. Estimates suggest ADHD affectsroughly 8% of children and adolescentsandabout 3% of adultsworldwide. To overturn this consensus would require robust, reproducible findings capable of explaining away decades of genetic, developmental and clinical research. The press release described the documentary as “science-led”, which hinted at just such an enterprise. Was it really science-led?The answer is a resounding “no”. It bore little relation to a genuine scientific debate; in fact, there was no evidence of a debate at all.One thing science tries to do is eliminate bias – not always successfully, but the intention should be there. The documentary does not start out well on this front. Max Pemberton, the presenter, has published widely about his ADHD scepticism: an article he wrote for the Daily Mail last year was headlined: “This is the REAL reason why there’s been an explosion in cases of ADHD – and why we should all be scared of the consequences.”The very title of this programme does not promise a balanced discussion (ADHD UK has saidits question mark does not serve as a “get-out-of-harm-free card”). Asking whether this is a “genuine” disorder or a “social construct” can all too easily be read as:“or made-up”.Asthe late physicist Richard Feynmanpointed out, good science should be as ruthless with the evidence that supports your thesis as it is with the evidence that contradicts it. This “documentary” (having seen it, I am deliberately putting this term in scare quotes) doesn’t report any evidence that might contradict the conclusion it has clearly reached at the outset. Not only that, the “evidence” (ditto) it does present mostly comprises a series of trenchant opinions from carefully selected talking heads, and focuses on a couple of so-called experiments that break just about every rule of genuine scientific inquiry.Is ADHD a “genuine developmental disorder”? Setting aside the support from the likes of the WHO and Nice, as well aspowerful genetic evidence unmentioned in the documentary, the presenter decided that if we could “see” ADHD in the brain, this might prove it to be genuine. He interrogated Prof Katya Rubia, a cognitive neuroscientist who does have a genuine track recordin ADHD research. She reported that key differences had been spotted at the group level and added that they were small. Alandmark study in 2017, combining MRI data from more than 3,000 people, reports just such findings. Pemberton missed the point she was making, and asked that perennially naive question that plagues brain imagers: can you “spot” ADHD in a single scan, or use it for a diagnosis? In response to her honest answer, no (which is exactly what you might expect, confronted with a single example from an enormously heterogeneous population), he appeared to conclude that if there was no brain-based marker that distinguished a brain with ADHD from one without, ADHD could not be a brain-based disorder. And, therefore it was not a genuine developmental disorder.Apparently, this means ADHD is a social construct – even if the evidence in favour of that conclusion is deeply flawed.Opinions about screen time and ultra-processed food and big pharma conspiracy theories were wheeled out in support of this claim, as well as scornful references to diagnostic manuals, this time without any attempt to offer supporting evidence. The presentation of “genuine” condition or “social construct” as a simple binary choice harked back to the old “nature or nurture” debates, with no acknowledgment of contemporary findings about the entanglement between the brain and its world. Just because you believe that something “out there” is responsible for certain kinds of behaviour, it doesn’t mean that the brain is not involved.At the heart of the programme were two so-called “carefully monitored experiments”. One involved a 10-year-old boy, Mason, being taken off his medication for six weeks. He was not randomly selected but “volunteered” by his mother, who felt that the medication was masking the real Mason. In addition to stopping the medication, a holistic practitioner removed items such as screens and mobile phones, ultra-processed food and chocolate, and suggested walks in nature, exercise and yoga. The consequencesof this were reported throughout the programme.View image in fullscreenMason, 10, who was taken off his ADHD medication for six weeks.Photograph: Minnow ProductionsThis was not a scientific experiment in any sense. Setting aside the fact that a case study such as this would not produce any kind of reliable evidence, you could point out that there were no “control” conditions. Was there a child taken off their meds but not offered holistic alternatives? Was there a child who stayed on their meds, but was also offered alternatives? One could go on. Mason’s story is powerful television because it is complicated, human and emotionally engaging. Those are not, unfortunately, the usual ingredients of a controlled experiment.Pemberton’s own contribution comprised a demonstration of the diagnostic process. After handing over £1,200 for a private online assessment, he triumphantly reported that he had (almost instantaneously) been diagnosed with ADHD. He seemed to conclude that ADHD therefore could not be a valid clinical construct. Setting aside, again, the non-contribution of an anecdote such as this to a genuinely science-led inquiry, his conclusion seems to be that if you can wrongly get an ADHD diagnosis, then ADHD can’t be real. It is worth noting that his foray into costly online clinics bears no resemblance to the immensely painstaking procedures behind an ADHD diagnostic procedure as laid outby Nice guidelines. Yet again, Pemberton displayed a warped non-scientific logic. A diagnostic process being flawed does not mean the construct it is trying to measure does not exist.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe frustrating thing about The Great ADHD Myth? is that buried inside it are several questions that science really does need to ask. Are diagnostic thresholds becoming too broad? Are all private assessments rigorous enough? Are drugs sometimes used where environmental changes would be better? Do schools demand an unnecessarily narrow range of behaviour from children? And do we know enough about the long-term effects of stimulant medication? These are important questions. But none require us to pretend that decades of genetic, developmental, clinical and neuroscientific evidence simply disappear.There is nothing unscientific about questioning ADHD. Science progresses by questioning accepted wisdom. But genuine scientific scepticism means subjecting your preferred explanation to the strongest evidence against it. It does not mean assembling a procession of experts and anecdotes that point in the same direction and calling the result “science-led”.Prof Gina Rippon is emeritus professor of cognitive neuroimaging at the Aston Brain Centre, Aston University, and the author of The Gendered BrainDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
