title: JD Sports boss is still struggling to turn up the heat on a tepid trainer market | Nils Pratley | The Guardian
description: Latest profit warning is particularly disappointing in a World Cup year, which should have given the global business a sporty buzz
Author: Nils Pratley
Headline: Latest profit warning is particularly disappointing in a World Cup year, which should have given the global business a sporty buzz
Content: Did Nike and Adidas push prices too far? Have they been outflanked by the likes of Hoka and On? Or have consumer tastes just changed? Probably all of the above.Photograph: Sneakers/AlamyView image in fullscreenDid Nike and Adidas push prices too far? Have they been outflanked by the likes of Hoka and On? Or have consumer tastes just changed? Probably all of the above.Photograph: Sneakers/AlamyNils Pratley on financeJD Sports FashionJD Sports boss is still struggling to turn up the heat on a tepid trainer marketNils PratleyLatest profit warning is particularly disappointing in a World Cup year, which should have given the global business a sporty buzzJD Sports cuts £50m from profit forecast as cost of living pressures hit trainer salesThu 20 Aug 2026 13.14 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareIt was a slower quarter for “high-heat footwear product”,said JD Sports. It didn’t mean it was struggling to shift sandals during a heatwave. Rather, it was referring coyly to the big global trainer brands’ failure to come up with hot new designs. When Nike and Adidas, reckoned by City analysts to account for slightly more than half JD’s sales, are on tepid form, the self-styled “king of trainers” retailer usually is as well.The low-heat grumble will be familiar to JD’s shareholders. So, too, the one about “incremental cost of living pressures”, especially in the US. And the phrase “a promotional market” has appeared so often in the company’s updates in the past couple of years that it would be easier to tell us when discounting isn’t dominant.The result wasanother warning on profitsand a 14% slump in the share price. JD now thinks it’ll make between £700m and £800m at an underlying pre-tax level this financial year. The difference from the previous estimate of £750m-£850m isn’t huge, but they all count. This wasthe third warning since early 2024. The particular disappointment this time is that it was a men’s football World Cup year, which ought to have been good for generating a general sporty buzz for a global business.The market clearly is genuinely weak. Nike’s share price is down a third this year even after a miserable performance in the last two. Or look at Adidas’s own recent warning that its big marketing bet on the World Cup didn’t pay off. Or at the sluggish spending among US consumers in response to higher energy prices: Walmart, the largest US retailer, this week reported its slowest sales growth in six years.Even so, the deeper worry at JD is that the whole “athleisure” trend isn’t coming back – or, if it does, at nothing like the level of the old days. The Covid pandemic created a mini-boom for joggers and trainers but since then the direction has only been one way. Did Nike and Adidas push prices too far? Have they been outflanked by the likes of Hoka and On? Or have consumer tastes just changed? Probably all of the above to an extent – and none is good news for JD.The cashflow forecast, for £460m-£520m, didn’t change, which is evidence to support JD’s boasts about sharpening internal controls after its previous boom years of successful global expansion in the 2010s. All the same, waiting for an upturn, counting the cashflow and buying back a few shares makes for an uninspiring life.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDisagreements about strategy reportedly led to the exit of the chair, Andrew Higginson, last month, and it is easy to see why there would be tension. The share price is back at 2019 levels. If this were a conventionally owned public company, as opposed to one with a 55% shareholder in the form of the Pentland Group, the chief executive Régis Schultz might be under more pressure to generate some trading heat via self-help. Non-Pentland shareholders are surely frustrated.Explore more on these topicsJD Sports FashionNils Pratley on financeRetail industrycommentShareReuse this content

title: Relax, everyone: Elon Musk has a mantra to make the climate crisis go away | Emma Brockes | The Guardian
description: It’s simple, says the SpaceX boss – according to something called the ‘Kardashev scale’, we just have to move energy production ‘off-planet’, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Author: Emma Brockes
Headline: It’s simple, says the SpaceX boss – according to something called the ‘Kardashev scale’, we just have to move energy production ‘off-planet’, says Guardian columnist Emma Brockes
Content: Elon Musk in London, November 2023.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenElon Musk in London, November 2023.Photograph: ReutersOpinionElon MuskRelax, everyone: Elon Musk has a mantra to make the climate crisis go awayEmma BrockesIt’s simple, says the SpaceX boss – according to something called the ‘Kardashev scale’, we just have to move energy production ‘off-planet’Thu 20 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTShareNext time the weather gives the UK61 days without rainand we wonder idly if this is the end, there is a term we may whistle up to soothe us. Like murmuring the rosary, or putting our fingers in our ears and humming, this phrase is to be mumbled on repeat – “the Kardashev scale, the Kardashev scale” – a buzzy concept in tech, much favoured by Elon Musk, and precisely the thing we’ve been waiting for. The Kardashev scale is the answer both to our impending doom and our anxiety around it – and if we decide to believe in it, we won’t have to give the climate crisis a single thought until the last drip falls from the tap.This is the idea and it’s a familiar one to anyone who has watched tech billionaires take intractable, commonplace crises and decide that, among the measures and proposals in play, the vital missing ingredient so far has been them. Do you remember when Jeff Bezos, rather than doing something quotidian and loserish like funding public education by ensuring Amazon pays the same tax rate as regular Americans, decided instead toreinvent preschools?OrMark Zuckerbergand his wife, Priscilla Chan, who also set up some schools – no expertise required, just a reach-for-the-stars attitude and a passion for change. At the risk of sounding callous, one might even put Steve Jobs’s eschewing of traditional cancer treatment in this category; after he was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in 2003, the founder of Apple delayed surgery in favour of his own holistic and dietary remedies. None of these ventures has been successful.We know what this is: the default belief held by tech billionaires that their particular brilliance is a kind of skeleton key for all human knowledge, past, present and future, rocket-fuelled by innovation and untethered from the limitations that come with the dull, plodding alternative: that of actually knowing stuff about a specialist subject. If they offer a magic bullet for any number of problems, the appeal to the rest of us is powerful. Who among us, when booking a flight or glancing up at another cloudless sky, hasn’t thought guiltily, oh, well, at some point someone will, like, invent a shield or something, and everything will turn out OK.Which brings us to the Kardashev scale, named for the Soviet astronomer Nikolai Kardashev, who in 1964 invented a rubric to measure the success of any civilisation based on its ability to harness energy. Kardashev came up with a sliding scale of energy usage on which humanity had not reached even “type I” according to his measurements – because we can neither control the weather nor fully harness the energy of the sun. The highest level in this schema was a type III, which describes a civilisation that has harnessed the energy of the galaxy – and above that further theoretical levels, including a type IV (the energy of the universe) and type V (the multiverse) to hold up against our dimwit civilisation’s current reliance on fossil fuels.You can see why this appeals in Silicon Valley: the Kardashev scale has a kind of nostalgic futurism about it familiar to any student of the space race or the works of L Ron Hubbard, and leans on fun terms such as “galactic”, “space-time” and “moon bases”. If this isn’t blue-sky thinking, I don’t know what is, and Musk has launched into it. He has suggested that a natural implementation of Kardashev’s ideas is to develop space infrastructure – in effect moving energy production “off-planet”, along with orbital datacentres – by launching millions of units into orbit to better capture the energy of the sun.It sounds super cool. And while visionaries need vast ambition and an ability to withstand ridicule, these proposals demand a willing suspension of disbelief from us, too. If you don’t, for example, let your mind drift back to that time Musk had Tesla engineersdesign a tiny submarineto fetch those kids trapped in a cave, or to whatever it was he did at the US “department of government efficiency” (Doge) that everyone in the Republican party now seems keen to pretend never happened, you can persuade yourself that the creator of Starlink might be on to something. The Kardashev scale, the Kardashev scale – don’t you feel better already?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEmma Brockes is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsElon MuskOpinionClimate crisisEnergyThe super-richSilicon ValleyMark ZuckerbergSteve JobscommentShareReuse this content

title: Humans have learned to fear ‘bugs’, but we shouldn’t – life as we know it hinges on invertebrates | Chris Packham | The Guardian
description: At this point of the crisis in our relations with the natural world, we’ve got to protect these creatures – and we are running out of time, says naturalist Chris Packham
Author: Chris Packham
Headline: At this point of the crisis in our relations with the natural world, we’ve got to protect these creatures – and we are running out of time, says naturalist Chris Packham
Content: The leaf sheep – this year’s winner of the Guardian’s Invertebrate of the Year competition.Illustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe leaf sheep – this year’s winner of the Guardian’s Invertebrate of the Year competition.Illustration: Petra Korlević/The GuardianOpinionInvertebratesHumans have learned to fear ‘bugs’, but we shouldn’t – life as we know it hinges on invertebratesChris PackhamAt this point of the crisis in our relations with the natural world, we’ve got to protect these creatures – and we are running out of timeRead more from theGuardian’s invertebrate of the year 2026Thu 20 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 13.30 EDTShareToo many animals are regarded as “bugs”. And, if anything is a bug, it is a short step to it becoming a “pest”. Too many of us have a learned fear – it’s not innate – of anything with six legs or antennae.I’m a big fan of the invertebrates and I love the Guardian’sinvertebrate of the yearcompetition because it focuses people’s attention on the little things rather than the typical animal superstars – the pandas, tigers and orangutans. In their diversity and varied ecology, the million-plus invertebrates on our planet often lead far more intricate and interesting lives than large animals with spines, like us. We urgently need to generate a much broader awareness of their beauty and importance. All these small creatures are as integral a part of our ecosystems as the fluffy things that we may want to put on our calendars.View image in fullscreenThe leaf sheep lives in tropical waters around Japan, Indonesia and the Philippines.Photograph: Marli Wakeling/AlamyI’ve always tried to champion invertebrates on Springwatch. One of my greatest joys filming the series over the years was meeting a naturalist who knew about tree slugs. I’d spent my life looking at trees with slime trails going up their trunks but I’d never bothered to get a ladder and investigate. So the discovery that every night these slugs venture out and climb to the tops of oak trees and then slither back down again before dawn breaks is amazing. And it’s all happening just over the fence.I’m 65 and the other day I caught an insect in my kitchen that I’d never before thought to identify. It turned out to be a parasitic wasp, one of more than 330 species ofnetelia, a genus of ichneumonid wasps. It was a cinnamon colour, with huge eyes because it is nocturnal and parasitises large moth caterpillars. It actually packs a powerful sting for humans, which I had no idea about. We are constantly learning about the miraculous alternative worlds unfolding all around us. In this invertebrate universe, there is an enormous repository of fascination just waiting to be discovered.I have previously encountered the third-placed invertebrate in this year’s competition. I once visited a beach in Florida wherehorseshoe crabshad spawned and died. There were so many that you couldn’t walk on the beach. It was like some sort of Jurassic apocalypse. Absolutely extraordinary.View image in fullscreenA horseshoe crab on the seabed in Palawan, the Philippines.Photograph: Laurent Ballesta/Wildlife Photographer of the Year/PAI didn’t know much about this year’s winner, the leaf sheep, until it appeared on theGuardian shortlist. Then I read up on it a bit more. Physically, they are one of these animals that might as well come from another planet; they have an amazing structure and life cycle. Taking in algae and using it to power yourself – only four and a half billion years of evolution could come up with something that wacko. It’s absolutely brilliant.Learning about these animals and celebrating them is important, but we want to know what we can do to help them too. The tempting thing to say is plant nectar sources and allow your garden to go a bit wild, if you’re lucky enough to have a garden. We take joy in making spaces for these creatures in our local neighbourhoods and that’s a battle, but it’s not going to win the war.We are running out of time – and here in the UK, we’ve got to lobby for better pesticide regulations. They’ve done it in France and reduced pesticide use on farmland. We banned insect-killing neonicotinoids in 2018 and yet this year, they haveagain been approvedfor “emergency” use on sugar beet crops. This should be causing an outcry. We need the public to pressurise the government into reforming and reducing pesticide usage.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWe are at a point of absolute crisis in our relations with the natural world, and we’ve got to protect our invertebrates. We need a wider public awareness of them and their importance if we want invertebrate life and therefore the bats and birds and everything else – including us – to prosper. Awareness is good, but it’s not enough. We must take action.Chris Packham is a naturalist, broadcaster and campaignerExplore more on these topicsInvertebratesOpinionAnimalsWildlifecommentShareReuse this content

title: To Iran’s political prisoners, trapped ‘between two blades of a scissors’ | Open letter | The Guardian
description: On one side, you face the domination of the Islamic Republic; on the other, the imperialist forces that republic claims to stand against
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: On one side, you face the domination of the Islamic Republic; on the other, the imperialist forces that republic claims to stand against
Content: Evin prison in northern Tehran.Illustration: Guardian Design/Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEvin prison in northern Tehran.Illustration: Guardian Design/Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/Getty ImagesOpinionIranTo Iran’s political prisoners, trapped ‘between two blades of a scissors’On one side, you face the domination of the Islamic Republic; on the other, the imperialist forces that republic claims to stand againstOpen letterThu 20 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 18.05 EDTShareAugust marks the anniversary of the 1988 mass executions in Iran, a horror that echoes in the country’s current surge in death sentences. It also marks the 19 August anniversary of the UK- and US-orchestrated coup against the prime minister Mohammad Mosaddegh in 1953. Amid the current, indiscriminate waves of US-Israeli military assaults against Iran, this letter of solidarity denounces the repression of the Iranian people and their political prisoners by forces both at home and abroad.To our fellow activists, students, thinkers, workers, artists, and other prisoners of conscience held behind the walls of all detention centers across Iran:We write to you from a place of deep solidarity, our hearts heavy with the knowledge of the struggle you face within Iran’s prisons: the torture, the systematic neglect, the enforced silence, and the brutal reality of sham trials and executions. As former and current political prisoners, activists, and scholars committed to the global project of abolition, anti-authoritarianism and anti-imperialism, we see you across the distances of geography and the silence of censorship and internet blackouts. And we stand in solidarity with you, as you are at the intersection of two sources of oppression.On one side, you face the Islamic Republic that, from its inception, enforced absolute social and political control based on an exclusionary ideology. It is a system that claims to counter imperial power while using its very logic of domination and systems of carcerality, torture and execution. On the other side, you face the aggression and violence of the very imperialist and Zionist forces the Islamic Republic purports to stand against. The US and Israel instigate brutal wars, destroy civilian infrastructure, kill innocent schoolgirls, and treat you as collateral damage in their pursuit of regional dominance. We remember the horror of 23 June 2025, when Israel struck the Evin prison complex, flattening its hospital ward, transgender section, and visitor center. You best exposed this dual oppression when you voiced that you “feel stuck between the two blades of a scissors, the evil regime that imprisons and tortures [you] and a foreign force dropping bombs on [your] heads in the name of freedom”.In the past year, we witnessed both blades of the scissor sharpen. We see the arbitrary arrests and the horrific wave of state executions. We see the deepening criminalization of the working class and unemployed, the targeting of Kurds, Arabs, and Baloch, and the scapegoating of Afghan migrants: all desperate attempts to kill the spirit of people they cannot contain. This is the logic of carceral states everywhere: when they fail to address the crises people face, they simply attempt to criminalize or disappear the people themselves.We see the same logic of domination when Israel uses “administrative detention” to hold Palestinian political prisoners for years without charge. We see it when Israeli authorities celebrate a new law that allows them to execute the Palestinian political prisoners they cannot dominate. We see it in the ICE detention centers where the US government imprisons our people in the pursuit of a political agenda of racist exclusion or detains our political activists for daring to speak against the US-backed Israeli genocide. We see it in the history of the US targeting freedom fighters, particularly Black, Indigenous, Puerto Rican and other anticolonial organizers, locking them away for decades to crush movements for national liberation and sovereignty. And we see the connections between these carceral systems sharing intelligence and governance techniques, such as when the USP Marion prison in Illinois became a blueprint for prisons built in Iran and Israel in the 1960s. Whether it is a border wall or a prison gate, the goal is the same: to silence people through fear, domination, and isolation.Your struggle is as global as our collective dreams of freedom and dignity. We stand with you, and we reject the false binary of imperialism and hollow anti-imperialism. We invite global civil society and anti-imperialist activists and organizations to extend their unconditional support and solidarity to all incarcerated kin fighting for our collective liberation, to build relationships with Iranian political prisoners and uplift their voices, to put pressure on the Islamic Republic by challenging its narrative, and to call upon that government to immediately stop all the executions and free all political prisoners.The Iranian authorities must stop their inhumane practice of death and incarceration now. And the US and Israel must end their barbaric wars and brutal sanctions that knowingly devastate our communities.In solidarity and with love,Alberto Toscano, emeritus professor of critical theory, Goldsmiths, *University of LondonAngela Davis, former political prisoner, distinguished professor emerita, *University of California, Santa CruzBernardine Dohrn, retired professor of law, *Northwestern UniversityBill Ayers, professor, *College UnboundCherríe L Moraga, distinguished professor emerita, University of California, Santa Barbara, Chicana feminist writer, and activistDan Berger, professor of comparative ethnic studies, *University of Washington BothellHossam el-Hamalawy, Egyptian socialist, scholar and former political prisonerJairus Banaji, historian, research professor, SOAS, *University of LondonJason Stanley, professor of philosophy, *University of TorontoJudith Butler, distinguished professor in the Graduate School, *University of California, BerkeleyKeeanga-Yamahtta Taylor, author, From #BlackLivesMatter to Black Liberation, professor of African American studies, *Princeton UniversityMichael Löwy, emeritus research director of sociology at the* Centre National de la Recherche Scientifique, ParisMichael Mansfield, human rights and civil liberties BbarristerMumia Abu-Jamal, current political prisoner, educator, journalist and activistNadia Abu El-Haj, professor of anthropology, Barnard College, *Columbia UniversityNisrin Elamin, assistant professor of African studies and anthropology, *University of Toronto, co-founding member of the Sudan Solidarity CollectiveRashid Khalidi, Edward Said professor emeritus of modern Arab studies, department of history, *Columbia University. President of Institute of Palestinian StudiesRicardo Jiménez, social activist, former Puerto Rican political prisonerRobin DG Kelley, distinguished professor of history, *UCLARuha Benjamin, professor of African American studies, *Princeton UniversityRuth Wilson Gilmore, Graduate Center, *CUNYSinan Antoon, associate professor of Arabic literature, New York University, novelist, poetWalden F Bello, international adjunct professor of sociology, *State University of New York at BinghamtonYasin al-Haj Saleh, Syrian writer, political dissident, and former political prisoner in Syria* Organizations for identification purposes only** Signatories are sorted alphabetically

title: The Guardian view on GCSE results: much to celebrate, much to reform | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Another post-pandemic cohort has shown its resilience and talent. But growing inequalities of outcome must be addressed
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Another post-pandemic cohort has shown its resilience and talent. But growing inequalities of outcome must be addressed
Content: Pupils collect their GCSE results at the Ark Greenwich free school in Woolwich, south London.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAView image in fullscreenPupils collect their GCSE results at the Ark Greenwich free school in Woolwich, south London.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PAOpinionGCSEsThe Guardian view on GCSE results: much to celebrate, much to reformEditorialAnother post-pandemic cohort has shown its resilience and talent. But growing inequalities of outcome must be addressedThu 20 Aug 2026 13.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareMost pupils who received their GCSE results this week were in the penultimate year of primary school when Covid struck, disrupting their preparation for secondary education. As with other post-pandemic cohorts, their achievements are therefore a testament to their ability, resilience and determination. Astrongset of results, particularly in the core subjects of English and maths, should also be seen as a tribute to teachers dealing with ever expanding workloads.Overall the impression is one of a welcome return to stability, as the legacy of the years of cancelled exams and teacher assessments is left behind. The proportion of top grades awarded in England, Wales and Northern Ireland rose compared with last year, but only by a tenth of a percentage point, while theoverall pass rate fellby the same margin to 67.3% – the same as in 2019. Nevertheless, the latest results throw up familiar grounds for concern.The ongoing decline in language learning appears to beacceleratingto an alarming degree, with GCSE take-up in French and other modern languages falling sharply again. A culturally enriching part of the curriculum is in danger of becoming thepreserveof affluent state schools and the independent sector.More broadly, inequalities of outcome suggest a fundamental change in approach is required to address regional disparities that have become entrenched. London schools once again pulled away from those in the north and the Midlands when it came to the awarding of top grades. Recent research hasshownthat good GCSE grades have a disproportionately beneficial impact on the life chances of pupils from less privileged backgrounds. A levelling up strategy is urgently needed.While overall results in English and maths were impressive, a significant proportion of teenagers failed to achieve a grade 4 pass. The data also confirmed that the policy in England of imposing compulsory resits in those subjects is blighting lives rather than raising standards. Only 18.8% of those aged 17 and over achieved the requisite pass grade in English, down from last year, with an even smaller proportion achieving a grade 4 in maths. Far too many young people are becoming trapped in a demoralising and humiliating cycle of failure, which is blocking their progress into the world of work.The government plans to introduce a new “stepping stone” qualification to build confidence ahead of resits, but a more radical overhaul is needed. At a time when an estimated 1 million 16- to 24-year-olds are not in education, employment or training, developing a more nuanced approach, including alternative pathways, should be a priority.An overhaul is what Andy Burnham and his education secretary, Lucy Powell, are promising. From 2028, the educational landscape in England may change significantly for 14- to 16-year-olds. The prime minister appearscommittedto rebalancing the curriculum by expanding the number of technical education options available to students, in a reprise of his approach as the mayor of Greater Manchester.If a true parity of esteem is to be established between academic and vocational routes, as Mr Burnham desires, it will require a significant injection of resources. But the focus is the right one. Though there was much to celebrate as another post-Covid cohort came of age, the inequalities and failures revealed again by this year’s results are long overdue for attention.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The Guardian view on Trump’s MMR executive order: endangering the children he claims to care about | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The president’s empty advice that children should receive separate jabs against measles, mumps and rubella will only lead to less take-up by parents
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The president’s empty advice that children should receive separate jabs against measles, mumps and rubella will only lead to less take-up by parents
Content: The US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, testifying before Congress in April this year.Photograph: Raphael Liy/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenThe US health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, testifying before Congress in April this year.Photograph: Raphael Liy/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionMMRThe Guardian view on Trump’s MMR executive order: endangering the children he claims to care aboutEditorialThe president’s empty advice that children should receive separate jabs against measles, mumps and rubella will only lead to less take-up by parentsThu 20 Aug 2026 13.46 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareNobody wants to hurt a child. The howl of pain, the tears, the look of betrayed shock all make it very hard to deliver a cherished small person to the needle-wielding nurse. But that’s part of being a responsible parent. It becomes a lot tougher if mum or dad is being fed mixed and erroneous messages about the benefits and harms of vaccination.Parents have to make a lot of decisions about what’s right for their child, from the school they should go to and the food they should eat to the hours they should spend on the phone or watching TV. In the US, Donald Trump wants them to add another: do they choose to give their children separate jabs against measles, mumps and rubella, involving six visits to the clinic, or should they opt for the combined MMR vaccine, which does the job in two? For decades, the vast majority of families have been taking the advice of doctors, accepting their assurance that the MMR vaccine is safe and very effective. But what are they to think when a US president announces that the triple jab could be “quite lethal” andsignsan executive order advising states to offer separate vaccines?View image in fullscreenAndrew Wakefield, pictured in 2010.Photograph: Luke MacGregor/ReutersFor the moment, what Mr Trump is proposing is an empty choice. The individual vaccines are not available. They have not been widely used in decades. In the US and in the UK, they don’t have a licence, and to get one, pharma companies such as GSK and Merck & Co would probably have to run new clinical trials to prove that they work and are safe, which would take years. Both have already said that no published scientific evidence supports splitting theMMRvaccine into single shots. They are not rushing to invest in making them, for all the US president’s enthusiasm.But we are likely to see a rerun of the furore and distress in 1998 caused by Andrew Wakefield, the British gastroenterologist (not an infectious diseases specialist) whodeclaredthat the MMR vaccine was linked to the gut disorder Crohn’s disease and thence to autism. His evidence-free advice was for parents to seek separate vaccines. As now, they were not readily available, so many children went without. Measles vaccination levels dropped alarmingly and measles cases rose.Struck off as a doctor, Mr Wakefield now lives in Texas, hero-worshipped by vaccine sceptics, and his views are embraced by all those suspicious of or hostile to the medical and scientific establishment,includingthe president and his health secretary,Robert F Kennedy Jr. They fit an anti-science agenda that has recently seen the pursuit by a congressional committee of Dr Anthony Fauci, who led the US response to Covid-19 and is now beingaccusedof covering up its origins.Mr Trump and RFK Jr already aim to shrink the vaccine schedule in the US from 18 to 11 shots, citing Denmark, where fewer vaccines are given to young children. But Denmark offers universal high-quality healthcare and excellent screening programmes to pick up those at risk. The US does not, and children fall through the cracks.No other country recommends single measles, mumps and rubella vaccines. But such is the confusion that some parents are likely to take away the message that the combined jab is unsafe – and that no jab is a better choice. President Trump is putting at risk the very “beautiful, healthy, lovely, delicate little children” that he claims to care about.Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Lack of water storage is an urgent national security issue | Water | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to the crisis facing Britain caused by the lack of reservoir capacity and hotter summers
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to the crisis facing Britain caused by the lack of reservoir capacity and hotter summers
Content: The bed of Bottoms Reservoir in Macclesfield begins to crack during low water levels in August.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe bed of Bottoms Reservoir in Macclesfield begins to crack during low water levels in August.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesWaterLettersLack of water storage is an urgent national security issueReaders respond to the crisis facing Britain caused by the lack of reservoir capacity and hotter summersThu 20 Aug 2026 12.17 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 12.25 EDTShareYour reporters came up with a good list of urgent climate policies in response to Andy Burnham’s somewhat surreal statement focusing on the sale of disposable barbecues following aCobrameeting (From grey water to cool spaces: 10 climate crisis policies Britain needs right now, 12 August), but they missed out the No 1 issue: the UK’s water-storage capacity.It is blindingly obvious that we need to dramatically and rapidly increase water storage. The current plans to fast-track the building ofnine reservoirsby 2050 might be speedy by the standards of UK infrastructure delivery projects, but they may well have been overtaken by climate change trends.Indeed, if we had had forward-thinking governments and a functional water industry, some of them would have been built by now to match historic population growth. As it stands, only one reservoir is forecast to come online in the next 10 years.Similarly, the building of farm-level water storage, which must be far simpler to deliver, appears mired in bureaucracy and is not rolling out nearly fast enough. Cutting through the red tape and supporting the building of thousands of farm ponds and small reservoirs would surely result in better crop yields while reducing pressure on summer water supply and wildlife habitat.We urgently need to hear from the government on how it is going to address a national security issue that has moved from threat to living reality this summer.Simon DruryWandsworth, LondonYour report on low reservoir levels (14 August) notes that no new reservoir has been built in the UK since 1992. Yet only months ago England emerged from itseighth wettest wintersince records began, with rainfall 42% above the winter average. Now we are in drought.The Victorians understood that reliable water supplies required storage. Faced with rapidly growing cities, they built reservoirs, aqueducts and local water-storage infrastructure. There are ageing water towers still dotted around Britain as monuments to the simple principle that it is sensible to store water close to where it will be needed. Governments like large infrastructure projects, and we undoubtedly need new strategic, large-capacity reservoirs. But these cost billions and can take many years to plan and build.Why not also develop a national network of smaller modern distributed-storage reservoirs, either underground or covered, close to the communities they serve, capturing water during our wet winters? They would have the additional advantage of being installed incrementally rather than waiting years for huge projects to be completed.Pete FordSustainability lead, HealthTech Research Centre, ExeterFor the past 50 years we have lived in part of a large country house. We were lucky that a past owner was a forward-thinking architect who built a large underground tank to hold 20,000 gallons of rainwater gathered from the roof. He also installed a pump engine, now defunct, to bring water up 360 feet from an underground source to a reservoir, and we inherited a smaller underground tank not far from the vegetable garden.With these three receptacles we have been able to store and pump water to our vegetable plots during the last two summers. Surely similar underground water storage could be incorporated into housing estates to take advantage of the wet spring seasons we have been having.Sheila Carey-ThomasAlton, HampshireWe already are living with the reality of surge pricing for our water (Water companies in England and Wales explore ‘surge pricing’ during drought, 16 August). Anglian Water imposes a water tariff on Norwich that is around 2.5 times greater than the winter tariff. The outcome for two adults is a bill of £99.98 for 82 days between May and July 2026. We are low water users at 8 cubic metres, which is less than the typical usage for one person. We recycle water in the garden and apply the lessons of thesummer of 1976– except for sharing a bath, as we prefer showers. I can’t see what further reductions we can make.Maureen BegleyNorwichHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Ministers are in denial about the scale of the crises we face | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Letter: Having just 20 Defra staff working on climate adaptations show the government is not taking the challenges of heatwaves, wildfires and droughts seriously, writes Dr Amy McDonnell
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Having just 20 Defra staff working on climate adaptations show the government is not taking the challenges of heatwaves, wildfires and droughts seriously, writes Dr Amy McDonnell
Content: The aftermath of a wildfire in Stourbridge, West Midlands. ‘The government has repeatedly assured us it understands the risk of the breakdown of nature and climate. Clearly not.’Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/GettyView image in fullscreenThe aftermath of a wildfire in Stourbridge, West Midlands. ‘The government has repeatedly assured us it understands the risk of the breakdown of nature and climate. Clearly not.’Photograph: Ryan Jenkinson/GettyClimate crisisLettersMinisters are in denial about the scale of the crises we faceHaving just 20 Defra staff working on climate adaptations show the government is not taking the challenges of heatwaves, wildfires and droughts seriously, writesDr Amy McDonnellThu 20 Aug 2026 12.17 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 12.24 EDTShareThis (Just 20 of 6,600 Defra staff working on climate adaptation amid drought and wildfires, 12 August) is a shocking revelation from a government that has repeatedly assured us it understands the risk of the breakdown of nature and climate. Clearly not.Families forced to deal withschool closures, hospitals havingto cancel appointments,wildfirescontinuing to tear through the country, and, so far, more than2,700 deathsrecorded from extreme heat. And yet adaptation remains a tiny corner of one department.It’s not as though ministers haven’t been warned. TheClimate Change Committeeraises the alarm in every progress report it produces, urging the government to act. So what’s gone wrong? Have the impacts of ecosystem collapse and climate change become politically expendable to the government?From a war on thosepesky newts and batsto Andy Burnham’s endless game of ‘“will he, won’t he” over more oil and gas, this is Westminster fanning the flames of climate change. The communities facing firewaves, floods and extreme drought don’t want to hear what’s already taking place – they want to know what’s going to change. Saying that we’re “already acting” clearly does not match the scale of the crisis. Just ask the “UK’s first climate evacuees” on whom you reported in February.Climate adaptation is a whole-of-government problem, not just for one desk at Defra. Why is there an AI minister around the Cabinet table, but no resilience and adaptation minister? Why don’t we have a dedicated commissioner with the authority to ensure that departments prepare for the risks of climate and nature breakdown, and to make sure that there is a public face for these issues so that communities are protected? And, crucially, why is no one asking these questions in government?Dr Amy McDonnellCo-executive director, Zero HourHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Unite’s mixed message on global heating | Climate crisis | The Guardian
description: Letters: The Unite union’s support for new North Sea oil and gas extraction is questioned by Edward Jackson. Plus a letter from Alan Gray
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: The Unite union’s support for new North Sea oil and gas extraction is questioned by Edward Jackson. Plus a letter from Alan Gray
Content: A protester during a walkout over hot working conditions at Wood Green bus garage in north London.Photograph: Chris Radburn/ReutersView image in fullscreenA protester during a walkout over hot working conditions at Wood Green bus garage in north London.Photograph: Chris Radburn/ReutersClimate crisisLettersUnite’s mixed message on global heatingThe Unite union’s support for new North Sea oil and gas extraction is questioned byEdward Jackson. Plus a letter fromAlan GrayThu 20 Aug 2026 12.17 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 12.24 EDTShareOf the mass walkouts of transport drivers in parts of London where temperatures have hit 34C, John Harris says: “Everything is being led by the union Unite” (Andy Burnham has barely acknowledged the climate crisis. If only Britain’s workers had that luxury, 17 August).This action makes perfect sense, although it is addressing one of the symptoms of the climate crisis (heatwaves) rather than one of its primary causes (global heating due to burning of fossil fuels).The irony is that Unite is alsopressingthe Burnham government to license the Rosebank oilfield and Jackdaw gasfield. Maybe it’s time for both to join the dots between these two campaigns and realise they are incompatible.In the long-term interests of all of us, these North Sea hydrocarbons should stay where they are. Focus instead on the just transition of skills into the increasingly productive renewables economy.Edward JacksonCrediton, DevonExcellent to see John Harris raising the fact that workers in this country are given so little protection in extreme heat. The Guardian reported three years ago on air-conditioned jackets for workers in Japan (The fan jacket: the Japanese innovation keeping workers cool in extreme heat, 25 July 2023), whilethis summerthese jackets are being issued to street sweepers in Chinese cities.Europe is dragging its feet on recognising the reality of climate change and the mitigations needed.Alan GrayBrightonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: International students bring much more than money to the UK | Universities | The Guardian
description: Letters: Catriona McCarthy says enduring personal and professional connections should not be overlooked, while Graham Thompson says university leaders should shoulder some responsibility for their plight
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Catriona McCarthy says enduring personal and professional connections should not be overlooked, while Graham Thompson says university leaders should shoulder some responsibility for their plight
Content: ‘Studying in the UK can create enduring personal and professional connections.’Photograph: GettyView image in fullscreen‘Studying in the UK can create enduring personal and professional connections.’Photograph: GettyUniversitiesLettersInternational students bring much more than money to the UKCatriona McCarthysays enduring personal and professional connections should not be overlooked, whileGraham Thompsonsays university leaders should shoulder some responsibility for their plightThu 20 Aug 2026 12.17 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 12.19 EDTShareThe financial pressures described by university leaders (UK universities face ‘financial crisis’ amid collapse in international students, 14 August) are both clear and serious, yet there are wider consequences of declining international student numbers that deserve attention.While the immediate economic contribution that international students make is significant, so is their broader value in bringing international perspectives to our campuses, enriching the learning experience, and strengthening the UK’s relationships, reputation and influence around the world.At a time when relationships, trust and influence increasingly matter, British Council research shows that studying in the UK can create enduring personal and professional connections. International graduates take those relationships into their careers, institutions and networks, maintaining connections with the UK long after their studies have ended, strengthening relationships, understanding and trust between the UK and countries around the world. UK universities are fundamental to that, and without them, this simply would not happen.Catriona McCarthyInterim director education, British CouncilUniversity leaders are right to warn of the financial turmoil in British higher education.Universitiesare undoubtedly facing uncertain futures. But those leaders must also shoulder some collective responsibility rather than reflexively laying blame elsewhere. It is a familiar refrain that when anything goes wrong the cause is external factors beyond the university’s control: first Covid, then energy prices and inflation, then frozen fees, and now the international visa system.Any success, on the other hand, is claimed by university leaders as a sign of excellence. That excellence, however, is rarely managerial. Too many university leaders and senior managers have failed upwards from unexceptional academic careers to a gravy train of well-paid positions for which they lack the strategic foresight that would better serve their institutions.This is the untold scandal of the higher education sector over the last decade. Did not one vice-chancellor understand that fees would not automatically increase with inflation after 2017 and put a plan in place to mitigate the effect on university finances? Did not the most basic analysis show that institutions were overreliant on international fee income?The higher education workers at risk of redundancy are potentially losing their jobs not just because of external factors, but because of sector-wide mismanagement by university leaders too quick to shirk responsibility.Graham ThompsonEmeritus professor of American literature, University of NottinghamExplore more on these topicsUniversitiesInternational studentsTeachingHigher educationStudentslettersShareReuse this content

title: Jordan Cox reflects on missed opportunities despite England’s big lead against Pakistan | England cricket team | The Guardian
description: England had four half-centurions on day two at Headingley but there were a few regrets on their failure to reach three figures
Author: Taha Hashim
Headline: England had four half-centurions on day two at Headingley but there were a few regrets on their failure to reach three figures
Content: Jordan Cox scored 73 in England’s first innings against Pakistan at Headingley.Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenJordan Cox scored 73 in England’s first innings against Pakistan at Headingley.Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty ImagesEngland cricket teamJordan Cox reflects on missed opportunities despite England’s big lead against PakistanCox: ‘We were hoping one of us would have kicked on’Sam Curran will miss rest of the summer due to injuryTaha Hashimat HeadingleyThu 20 Aug 2026 17.09 EDTFirst published on Thu 20 Aug 2026 08.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEngland v Pakistan: first Test, day two start delayed by rain – liveRead moreJordan Cox was one of four half-centurions as England maintained control of the first Test against Pakistan – but there were a few regrets as no one reached three figures on day two in Leeds.“We were hoping one of us would have kicked on and instead of make it just a hundred, make it 150, 160, 170,” said Cox, who hit 73 in his first Test innings at No 3. “And then the game looks, not completely different, but it puts us in definitely a better position.”Nonetheless, England look primed to take a series lead. Harry Brook top-scored with 91 as Joe Root and Dan Lawrence hit 66 and 51, respectively, after rain delayed the start of play until 2.45pm. England closed on 366 for eight, extending their first-innings lead to 195.Ali Usman was the one positive on another tough day for Pakistan, with the left-arm spinner claiming five for 92. “Hopefully, the boys can get 50 runs tomorrow,” said Cox. “You never know, we’ve still got Jamie [Smith] at the crease there and Jofra [Archer], who can still give it a good whack. So hopefully 50-odd runs and then get to our work.”For Cox – who edged behind off Usman – there were mixed emotions as he missed out on a first international hundred, a score that would have been a serious statement while he fills in for the absent Jacob Bethell.“I let myself down a tiny bit, but at the end of the day, you take 70, don’t you? Once I got to 50, I got to about 60 quite quickly, and I was thinking, there’s a chance here – just keep being disciplined. I definitely had it in the back of my mind thinking, you know, you’ve worked so hard, don’t give this opportunity up.”Elsewhere, a Test comeback has been put on hold for Sam Curran after the all-rounder was ruled out of the rest of the English summer with a groin injury. Curran is an option England are considering as they figure out life after Ben Stokes.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSam Curran has not played Test cricket since August 2021.Photograph: Jacob King/PAThe left-armer was not included in the squad for the first two Tests against Pakistan as he was not considered fully fit, but has been namechecked by Marcus North, the men’s national selector, as an option to balance England’s XI. He will undergo surgery on Friday, ruling him out of the third Test against Pakistan, starting on 9 September at Edgbaston, and the white-ball series against Sri Lanka that month.While a regular member of the two limited-overs teams, Curran – who made his debut as a 19-year-old against Pakistan in 2018 – has not played Test cricket since August 2021.Explore more on these topicsEngland cricket teamEngland v Pakistan 2026CricketnewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League 2026-27 preview No 19: Sunderland | Premier League previews 2026-27 | The Guardian
description: Sunderland fans hope Régis Le Bris and his talented squad can continue to surprise the pundits and Opta
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: Sunderland fans hope Régis Le Bris and his talented squad can continue to surprise the pundits and Opta
Content: Reinildo celebrates with fans after victory over Chelsea on the last day of the season sealed European qualification. Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersSunderland fans hope Régis Le Bris and his talented squad can continue to surprise the pundits and OptaByLouise TaylorThu 20 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGuardian writers’ predicted position:14th (NB: this is not necessarily Louise Taylor’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)Last season’s position:7thProspectsAfter finishing seventh last season,Sunderlandgo into the new campaign engaged in continental combat for the first time since a brief adventure in the old Cup Winners’ Cup in 1973-74. Will their startling upward trajectory under Régis Le Bris continue or will they succumb to the dreaded second-season syndrome? No one is quite sure.While many like to highlight Sunderland’s relegation-level XG statistics last season, it is important to note that a steadily improving squad lost six players to the Africa Cup of Nations in the winter. Moreover, no key player has been sold this summer, team spirit is superb and pre-season performances have been reassuringly convincing. Le Bris accepts coping with Thursday night football will be a challenge for a club that played in League One as recently as 2022, but insists it is something to be enjoyed rather than feared.It helps that Sunderland still have their captain, Granit Xhaka, controlling midfield. If Xhaka’s decision to recommit to life at the Stadium of Light despite serious interest from Chelsea lifted the pre-season mood, further optimism is provided by the presence of high-calibre individuals, including the fans’ favourite Enzo Le Fée, Chris Rigg, Robin Roefs, Noah Sadiki and Nordi Mukiele, in a versatile squad containing several players comfortable in assorted positions. Brian Brobbey is the sort of robust centre-forward few defenders enjoy marking. “We are growing together,” says Le Bris. “We’ve shown the team is strong.”Graph showing how Sunderland finished in past five seasonsOff-field pictureSunderland are majority-owned by the 29-year-old Swiss-French businessman and trust fund billionaire Kyril Louis-Dreyfus. The son of the late former Marseille owner Robert Louis-Dreyfus has a 64%stake in the club while the remaining 36% is held by the Uruguayan businessman and politician Juan Sartori. The strong relationship between Le Bris and the director of football, Florent Ghisolfi, has helped ensure on-pitch stability, although the past year has brought considerable off-field change, with several key executives replaced as Sunderland’s commercial strategy pivots in a more international direction. While the team toured the United States this summer, other marketing efforts have been concentrated on Africa, with a lucrative, and controversial, front-of-shirt sponsorship with Visit Ghana close to being finalised. More locally, the regeneration of the area adjacent to the Stadium of Light is transforming a post-industrial landscape.Owner-fan relationshipIf Louis-Dreyfus initially attracted a degree of suspicion and scepticism on taking the helm in 2021, he has earned the trust of the fanbase. Supporters were particularly impressed that the owner contacted Xhaka and convinced the Switzerland captain to join from Bayer Leverkusen last summer. Less positively, a creep towards increased corporate hospitality, allied to a divisive new club membership scheme, has polarised season-ticket holders.The managerLe Bris enjoys a spot of close-season surfing on the beaches of his native Brittany, so it is perhaps appropriate that the 50-year-old rode a footballing wave last season. His 2025 Championship playoff winners hit the Premier League ground running and proved they could last the course. Along the way, Le Bris parked his tanks on Newcastle’s front lawn by choreographing two league wins over their rivals. Le Bris holds a doctorate in physiology and biomechanics and a diploma in the mental training of elite athletes. He spent a decade as a highly regarded youth coach at Lorient before taking charge of the first team in 2022, with his love of trigonometry underpinning a coaching philosophy that views football as fundamentally being about triangles.Star signingView image in fullscreenThomas Meunier, who has 83 caps for Belgium, has joined Sunderland on a two-year contract from Lille.Photograph: Jean Catuffe/Getty ImagesSunderland tried and failed to sign Thomas Meunier from Lille a year ago, but patience has been rewarded. At the time of writing, the 34-year-old free transfer is the sole summer signing – quite a contrast to the 14 new faces 12 months ago – but at least two more new recruits are expected before the window closes. Meunier, who has 83 Belgium caps and played at the World Cup, will compete with Mukiele and Trai Hume at right-back. The experience he has acquired throughout a career involving stints at Paris Saint-Germain and Borussia Dortmund should prove useful in the Europa League.Stat attackIf matches were decided by Opta’s expected points metric, Sunderland would have been relegated last season. Instead they are preparing for a Europa League campaign after finishing 11 places higher than the XG figures implied they deserved. It was a wider margin between statistical performance and outcome than any other team in Europe’s big five leagues experienced, for good or bad.How teams finished and their expected position from underlying dataSet for a breakthroughTom Proctor, the son of Sunderland’s first-team coach and former forward, Michael Proctor, is only 17 and starting his second year as an academy scholar.He was included in the first-team squad for the pre-season tour of the United States. Proctor has impressed with his technical ability, awareness and eye for goal. With the squad set to be stretched by Europa League involvement, it will be no surprise if a player who joined Sunderland’s academy at the age of six makes a competitive first-team debut this season.World Cup impactSunderland had 12 players at the World Cup, more than Real Madrid, and such visibility delighted executives charged with growing the club’s commercial revenue streams. Wilson Isidor scored Haiti’s first World Cup goal since 1974 while Brobbey struck three times for the Netherlands. The entire group has since been joined by Meunier, who represented Belgium in the United States.Explore more on these topicsPremier League previews 2026-27SunderlandfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Gianni Infantino eyes junior tournament in Dominican Republic as potential route out of crisis | Gianni Infantino | The Guardian
description: Fifa’s president Gianni Infantino may target meetings around the tournament as a chance to lobby for votes
Author: Matt Hughes
Headline: Fifa’s president Gianni Infantino may target meetings around the tournament as a chance to lobby for votes
Content: Gianni Infantino is eyeing the tournament as a way of splitting Concacaf votes.Photograph: Luisa González/ReutersView image in fullscreenGianni Infantino is eyeing the tournament as a way of splitting Concacaf votes.Photograph: Luisa González/ReutersGianni InfantinoGianni Infantino eyes junior tournament in Dominican Republic as potential route out of crisisMeetings around event seen as chance to lobby for votesFifa president may meet his most credible challengerMatt HughesandNick AmesThu 20 Aug 2026 15.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGianni Infantino wants to split the European and North American coalition that is seeking to oust him by attending a junior tournament in the Dominican Republic this weekend in another gamble to cling on to power from the Fifa president.The Guardian has learned that Infantino has made plans to attend the U14 Boys Challenge competition organised by the Caribbean Football Union (CFU), 21 of whose associations are voting members ofFifa, despite being urged to stay away from the event by senior figures within Concacaf – the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football – which is working with Uefa to remove him.‘He must resign’: Fans’ petition calls for Infantino to quit as Fifa presidentRead moreInfantino will come face-to-face with the man widely viewed as his most credible challenger, the Concacaf president, Victor Montagliani, if he follows through with his intention to travel to the Dominican Republic, whose FA invited him to attend before the World Cup sell-off plan emerged last month.The Dominican Republic has since backed the joint Uefa, Concacaf and Asian Football Confederation statement calling for Infantino to hold an independent review of the Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, as well as an emergency meeting of the Fifa council.Infantino has largely fallen back on the support of his most steadfast allies by spending time in Morocco and Qatar as the storm has raged over the last month, but is understood to view the CFU meetings as a good opportunity split the Concacaf block and lobby for votes from the region’s smaller nations before next March’s presidential election.Concacaf’s most successful nation, Mexico, is defying the confederation by backing Infantino, who has also received support from two CFU members, Grenada and St Kitts and Nevis.View image in fullscreenVictor Montagliani, the Concacaf president, will be at the tournament in the Dominican Republic.Photograph: Omar Vega/Getty ImagesThe Boys Challenge and CFU meetings are not Fifa events, so Infantino’s plan to attend has raised eyebrows. Fifa declined to comment when asked about the president’s movements.Uefa, Concacaf and the AFC are continuing to explore calling for a vote of no confidence in Infantino, which would bring the matter to a head before next year’s election.Under Fifa’s statutes, its council can convene an extraordinary congress at any time if 43 of Fifa’s 211 member associations submit a written request specifying the items they want on the agenda, which can include no-confidence votes.An extraordinary congress must then be convened within three months, although the governing body’s statutes contain no specific provision regarding a vote of no confidence in its president.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionInfantino came under renewed pressure on Thursday with worldwide fans’ groupslaunching a petition calling for his resignation.Fans are being encouraged to sign the petition, which already has support from all six Fifa confederations spanning continental and national fan groups.“The shameful attempt by one individual – the Fifa president himself – to sell off the World Cup to private investors exposed a betrayal football will never forget,” a statement on behalf of the fan organisations said. “Infantino’s plan was stitched together in secret. Negotiated behind closed doors. Hidden from Fifa’s own members and from the millions of people whose passion makes football what it is.“A president who repeatedly betrays football and makes a mockery of our game has lost the right to lead it,” the statement continued. “For the credibility of Fifa – and for the future of the game – he must resign.”Explore more on these topicsGianni InfantinoFifaFootball politicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Can Aryna Sabalenka find a way to repair her collapsed form? | Aryna Sabalenka | The Guardian
description: With one semi-final in her last seven tournaments, the coming months will define the next stage of her career
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: With one semi-final in her last seven tournaments, the coming months will define the next stage of her career
Content: Aryna Sabalenka suffered a fourth-round defeat at the hands of Sara Bejlek in the Cincinnati Open.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAryna Sabalenka suffered a fourth-round defeat at the hands of Sara Bejlek in the Cincinnati Open.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty ImagesAryna SabalenkaAnalysisCan Aryna Sabalenka find a way to repair her collapsed form?Tumaini Carayolin CincinnatiWith one semi-final in her last seven tournaments, the coming months will define the next stage of her careerThu 20 Aug 2026 17.11 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTShareTowards the end of a messy first set tie-break late on Wednesday,Aryna Sabalenkawildly sprayed another painfully nervous backhand before slamming her racket to the ground. As the racket connected with the acrylic floor, its vibration dampener detached from the strings and rolled off in the direction of the broadcast camera pit by the side of the court.With the diminutive 20-year‑old Czech player Sara Bejlek leading Sabalenka 6-5 in the tie-break, this slapstick sequence forced play to pause while the Belarusian and a couple of volunteers comically searched for the missing vibration damper underneath the cameras until she gave up and retrieved a new one. A few minutes later, Sabalenka trailed by a set.‘Here we go’: Carlos Alcaraz confirms US Open return after four-month injury absenceRead moreNothing in the world seemed to fall in the world No 1’s favour at the Cincinnati Open as Sabalenka was toppled 7-6 (7), 6-4 by Bejlek around midnight, and it has been some time since anything did. On this occasion, Sabalenka sprayed errors, she moved sluggishly and failed to maintain her composure throughout her time on the court.Bejlek is a cunning lefty capable of narrowing the court with her excellent defensive skills and keeping opponents guessing by intelligently mixing up the spin and trajectory in her strokes. Still, Sabalenka’s mental collapse in both sets made for a shocking sight. After leading 5-1 in the first set tie‑break and losing five points in a row, Sabalenka led 4-1 in the second set before conceding the final five games of the match.View image in fullscreenSara Bejlek is the latest player to get the better of Aryna Sabalenka.Photograph: Robert Prange/Getty ImagesNothing about the way the world No 1 started her 2026 season hinted at the struggles to come. Sabalenka won 26 of her first 27 matches of the season; her painfuldefeat in the Australian Open finalto Elena Rybakina was counterbalanced by a remarkable achievement in March as she won the Sunshine Double, consecutively triumphing at Indian Wells and Miami.Even at the height of her powers, Sabalenka has had plenty of mental demons to battle. However, most of those difficulties have been confined to grand slam finals or semi-finals, the most consequential and pressure-filled matches. Otherwise, this period of Sabalenka’s career has been underscored by her toughness, composure and how often she finds a way through.After Miami, Sabalenka’s level abruptly collapsed. She is 17-7 in wins and losses since the start of April, having reached one semi‑final and zero finals in her past seven tournaments. Some of these losses have been absolutely shocking, particularly hertotal collapse against Diana Shnaiderin the quarter-finals at the French Open, where she led 6-3, 4-1 with a double break before losing 12 of the subsequent 13 games.As a result of these struggles, the No 1 ranking will surely fall. Sabalenka’s fourth-round loss in Cincinnati meant Rybakina, the current Australian Open and WTA Finals champion, has narrowed the gap to just 434 points as of Thursday.While Sabalenka will have 2,000 points to defend at the US Open as the defending champion, Rybakina reached only the fourth round last year. Her own form had briefly faltered earlier in the summer, but Rybakina, a finalist last week in Toronto, is playing well again at just the right time. It would take another title from Sabalenka in New York and a few catastrophic results from Rybakina for her to miss the boat.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenAryna Sabalenka after her defeat by Elena Rybakina in the Australian Open final in January.Photograph: Phil Walter/Getty ImagesThere are times when such drastic form shifts are often tied to injuries or off-court turmoil, but Sabalenka has remained healthy this year and, from what she has publicly shared, she does not appear to be enduring any significant personal issues away from the court.Before her loss, Sabalenka tried to project a positive mindset as she addressed her recent difficulties: “I feel like time flies faster and faster the older I get,” she said, smiling. “It’s crazy. I would say that I’m super‑happy with the beginning of the season. Then I went a bit down the hill, but I feel like I’m building myself back and I feel like I had a lot of great matches, a lot of great wins, a lot of tough lessons, but it’s also my journey and I only get better from that.”Her recent form merely stands as a reminder of how difficult it is to remain on top for a lengthy period. When things start to go wrong, the gruelling, relentless nature of this sport means there are few opportunities for players to regroup until the end of the season. Meanwhile, the great depth of the modern game ensures there will always be quality players ready to pick off a vulnerable top player.In recent years, the achievements of all-time greats such as Serena Williams, Novak Djokovic, Roger Federer and Rafael Nadal have made sustained dominance look so easy. These legends are total outliers in the history of the sport. Sometimes, great players just reach their mental or physical limits, and they quickly find themselves down the hill again, unable to summon the same intensity, toughness and quality that came so naturally before. Their responses to such difficult periods usually reveal plenty about them. How Sabalenka manages herself after a few challenging months is what will define the next stage of her career.Explore more on these topicsAryna SabalenkaTennisUS Open Tennis 2026US Open tennisUS sportsanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Australian rider says she was nearly hit by car at Tour of Britain Women | Tour of Britain Women | The Guardian
description: The Australian rider Maeve Plouffe said she was nearly hit by a non-race car during the opening stage of the Tour of Britain Women
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: The Australian rider Maeve Plouffe said she was nearly hit by a non-race car during the opening stage of the Tour of Britain Women
Content: Maeve Plouffe, pictured at the Track World Cup in Perth in March, said ‘cars from the general public coming at me from all directions’.Photograph: Alex Whitehead/SWpix.com/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenMaeve Plouffe, pictured at the Track World Cup in Perth in March, said ‘cars from the general public coming at me from all directions’.Photograph: Alex Whitehead/SWpix.com/ShutterstockTour of Britain WomenAustralian rider says she was nearly hit by car at Tour of Britain WomenMaeve Plouffe says incident on Wednesday was ‘scary’Josh Tarling to ride in Vuelta in memory of brother FinGuardian sportThu 20 Aug 2026 12.47 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Australian rider Maeve Plouffe has said she was nearly hit by a non-race car during the opening stage of theTour of Britain Women.With cycling still coming to terms with the death at the Volta a Portugal of the19-year-old British rider Finlay Tarling, killed last week in a collision with a vehicle that had entered the course, Plouffe said the incident occurred as she was chasing the peloton after a puncture on Wednesday.“While the race convoy was still in sight, and I was less than two minutes down, there were cars from the general public coming at me from all directions, including one that nearly hit me on a roundabout,” said the 27-year-old, who rides for O’Shea Red Chilli Bikes.“Later on, the moto escort was wonderful and I felt much safer. But considering the recent devastating events in our cycling community, it’s scary to see situations like this, when we know that this can have horrific consequences, especially so soon after suffering such a tragedy.”Jonathan Day, the events director of British Cycling Ventures – which organises the Tour of Britain Women –issued a statement to the BBC. “We note Maeve Plouffe’s comments about her experience during yesterday’s race, and we’re taking these extremely seriously,” it read. “Rider safety is paramount and will always be treated as a priority in our planning and how we operate any race.“We’re reviewing what happened with Maeve and her team O’Shea Red Chilli Bikes with the seriousness and empathy these comments demand.”Lorena Wiebes sprinted to victory on a rain-affected second stage on Thursday, after the race was neutralised in the middle of the stage for nearly an hour following an unrelated road traffic accident ahead of the peloton. The Dutch rider alsowon the opening stageof the race.Meanwhile Josh Tarling, the older brother of Finlay, will ride in the Vuelta a España, which begins on Saturday. The 22-year-old, who also rode in the Tour de France this summer, was confirmed as a member of the team by Netcompany-Ineos on Thursday.His mother, Dawn, posted on Instagram: “He has chosen to do so in honour of his brother Fin, with the full support of his family, surrounded by a team who have been incredibly supportive of whatever decision he made. I could not have wished for two boys who were closer growing up and into adulthood we have watched with pride as Joshua has been the most loving and supportive big brother to Fin. Following this devastating news he has been an incredible strength for us all.“Finlay was so incredibly proud of his big brother, and would be watching nose to the TV and shouting as he competed. So it is right that Josh honours that love and pride by doing what Fin always loved watching him do.”Explore more on these topicsTour of Britain WomenCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Enzo is a Chelsea player,’ says Alonso but doesn’t guarantee Fernández’s future | Chelsea | The Guardian
description: Xabi Alonso has refused to offer any guarantee that Chelsea will hold firm if Manchester City try to sign Enzo Fernández
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Xabi Alonso has refused to offer any guarantee that Chelsea will hold firm if Manchester City try to sign Enzo Fernández
Content: Enzo Fernández could still leave Chelsea before the transfer window closes on 1 September.Photograph: Paul Dennis/TGS Photo/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenEnzo Fernández could still leave Chelsea before the transfer window closes on 1 September.Photograph: Paul Dennis/TGS Photo/ShutterstockChelsea‘Enzo is a Chelsea player,’ says Alonso but doesn’t guarantee Fernández’s futureMidfielder linked with £120m move to Manchester CityChelsea still interested in Bournemouth’s Alex ScottJacob SteinbergThu 20 Aug 2026 11.50 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleXabi Alonso has refused to offer any guarantee that Chelsea will hold firm ifManchester Citytry to sign Enzo Fernández.Fernández’s future remains up in the air and the prospect of him leaving Stamford Bridge has not gone away, even thoughChelsea’s unofficial deadlinefor clubs to make written bids of £120m for the 25-year-old Argentina midfielder has already passed. City,who are also tracking Roma’s Manu Koné, have targeted Fernández as part of their midfield rebuild after Rodri’s move to Barcelona and are weighing up whether to make a move before the transfer window shuts.Instant classics, odd inspirations and barcodes: 2026-27’s best and worst kitsRead moreChelsea, who have identified Bournemouth’s Alex Scott and Crystal Palace’s Adam Wharton as possible replacements for Fernández, know the situation is fluid. The player has made no secret of his desire to leave the club and Alonso was noncommittal when asked if he would still be part of his squad at the end of the transfer window.“Enzo is a Chelsea player,” the former Real Madrid manager said. “He’s a top player. He’s training really well since he started 10 days ago with the team. Very integrated, and we are happy with him. He’s getting ready for Monday.”Chelsea open their Premier League campaign with a trip to Fulham on Monday night. Fernández is expected to be in the squad but Alonso dodged another question about whether the £106.7m midfielder has told him he wants to stay. “He’s training really well. I see him with a good attitude. That’s what we want. Everyone is trying their best to prepare for the kick off of the Premier League.”Chelsea will want a new midfielder if Fernández goes. They are huge admirers of Scott but have already failed with one offer for the 22-year-old and have been told that Bournemouth will resist a sale this summer. Wharton is an alternative, although City have had an offer for the England midfielder rejected by Palace.Alonso is also looking to trim down his squad before the window shuts. Nicolas Jackson, Liam Delap and Marc Guiu have fallen down the pecking order up front and are likely to leave. Everton, Leeds, Ipswich and Nottingham Forest are tracking Delap. Chelsea also have interest in Pedro Neto and Malo Gusto while Palace want to bolster their defence by signing Axel Disasi on loan.It has been another busy summer at Chelsea and Alonso must also consider whether keeping Fernández would sit well with supporters. Some booed him during the friendly win over Real Sociedad at Stamford Bridge last week. “He was not just booed, they as well chanted his name,” Alonso said. “It’s not unusual, it can happen. We support him. We have a great player with Enzo, he’s a top player, he’s been so important.”There was a reminder of Fernández’s standing when he wore the captain’s armband after coming on against Sociedad. Alonso could continue to use him as Reece James’s deputy. “Reece is the first captain and we have other leaders, other personalities that share the same role,” the Spaniard added.Explore more on these topicsChelseaTransfer windowManchester CitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for as the new season kicks off | Soccer | The Guardian
description: Manchester United’s new-look midfield, Ipswich’s ambition is tested and Kevin Keegan tributes at Newcastle
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Manchester United’s new-look midfield, Ipswich’s ambition is tested and Kevin Keegan tributes at Newcastle
Content: Youri Tielemans faces Hull; Marcos Senesi can calm down Spurs; and Alexander Isak will get a hot reception at Newcastle.Composite: Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenYouri Tielemans faces Hull; Marcos Senesi can calm down Spurs; and Alexander Isak will get a hot reception at Newcastle.Composite: Getty ImagesTen things to look out for this weekendSoccerPremier League: 10 things to look out for as the new season kicks offManchester United’s new-look midfield, Ipswich’s ambition is tested and Kevin Keegan tributes at NewcastleGuardian sportThu 20 Aug 2026 19.01 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google1Nwaneri out of Arsenal pictureWhile Myles Lewis-Skelly lookslikely to remain at the Emirates, the same can’t be said for Ethan Nwaneri. The 19-year-old was outstanding in his breakthrough season for Arsenal in 2024-25 but barely featured last season and was sent on loan to Marseille. That didn’t really work out and Arsenal are now exploring another temporary move to ensure Nwaneri gets regular football this season. Milan, RB Leipzig, Dortmund and Fulham are all thought to be interested, with Nwaneri unlikely to feature on the bench for Friday’s opener against Coventry as a result. Whether Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus are available remains to be seen as Arsenal attempt to find suitors for the Brazil duo.Ed AaronsArsenal v Coventry City, Friday 8pm (all times BST)2New United pair down for Tigers testManchester United’s summer transfer business has focused on recruiting in central midfield.
