It will be interesting to see who Michael Carrick selects in two key roles for the first game of the season. Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans have been present for more of pre-season than Kobbie Mainoo, who did not play a minute for England at the World Cup and was a late returner to Carrington after a holiday. Carlos Baleba surely will not have arrived in time to start at Hull. Mainoo is in the best position in the long term but if Carrick decides to ease him into the season, it would be intriguing to see how Santos and Tielemans team up, the stress test for a new partnership that could provide the perfect balance of defensive awareness and ability to move the team up the pitch.Will UnwinHull City v Manchester United, Saturday 12.30pm3Can Ipswich copy Black Cats’ success?Ipswich clearly learned a lot from what Sunderland did a year ago, as they went out and bought a lot of players. The Black Cats quickly moulded their 19 acquisitions into a successful unit but at least they had the positive of a head coach in Régis Le Bris who had his feet under the table. Gary O’Neil is the new man at Portman Road and he has 12 signings – at time of writing – to potentially use for the opener. The record arrival, Emersonn, who has moved to Portman Road from Toulouse, is the most eye-catching of those who have been acquired. The Brazilian has an underwhelming career goalscoring record and a few question marks hanging over his head. Even though it is their first game, Ipswich need to pick up points at home, and to do so require a striker who can cause problems for defenders. How quickly Emersonn adapts will be critical for the Tractor Boys’ success this year.WUIpswich Town v Sunderland, Saturday 3pmView image in fullscreenEmersonn is one of a number of big-money signings made by promoted Ipswich this summer.Photograph: Keeran Marquis/NurPhoto/Shutterstock4Glasner’s tough Diomande ready for debutAugust is the season for debuts and no one will be more satisfied than Oliver Glasner when Ousmane Diomande steps over the white line at the City Ground. Glasner wanted the Ivorian centre-back to replace Marc Guéhi at Crystal Palace, six months before the England defender departed forManchester City. Diomande, a £34m buy from Sporting, is expected to line up in a back three for Nottingham Forest against Leeds, when the Austria midfielder Xaver Schlager, who played for Glasner at Wolfsburg, could also make his Forest bow. Diomande is a quick and physical defender but another aspect of his appeal is his aerial power at set pieces. “They’ve both played Champions League football and they are used to competing for titles,” said Glasner. “They can add this winning mentality.”Ben FisherNottingham Forest v Leeds, Saturday 3pm5Serene Senesi can bring calm to SpursCristian Romero has taken his maverick brand of defending to Atlético Madrid, upsetting neutralPremier Leaguewatchers. His compatriot Marcos Senesi has arrived to shore up things at the back as Roberto De Zerbi desperately tries to steer Spurs away from a third straight season of battling relegation. The all-action Romero had his qualities as a leader and defender but never felt dependable, which is what most want from a centre-back and captain. Senesi impressed during his time at Bournemouth, rarely making headlines but proving himself a calm presence at the back. The Argentinian is good on the ball and will be more adventurous in possession than his countryman. He is yet to be sent off in three seasons as a Premier League player – Romero was dismissed twice in 2025-26 alone, not to mention a one-match ban and a fine for his behaviour towards a referee. His calmness will improve Spurs.WUBrentford v Tottenham, Saturday 5.30pm6Villa head south besieged by problemsIt is surely not how Unai Emery envisaged the countdown to Aston Villa’s season-opener at Brighton on Sunday – and certainly not as he enjoyed the afterglow from the club’s Europa League triumph over Freiburg in May. The manager has an extraordinary number of problems. Take the midfield where the new signings João Gomes and Johan Manzambi are injury doubts. Note: Amadou Onana is a long-term casualty while Youri Tielemans has been sold. It goes on. Emery is about to lose Ezri Konsa to Arsenal – in a summer where Villa have also sold Morgan Rogers and Lucas Digne. They are trying to move on Emi Martínez, while the future of Ollie Watkins is uncertain, with Al-Hilal circling. For the cherry on top, the rampaging 17-year-old striker Brian Madjo is a fitness concern. Emery’s teamsheet will be very interesting. Will he pitch the new goalkeeper, Zion Suzuki, who only signed on Wednesday, straight in?David HytnerBrighton v Aston Villa, Sunday 2pm7Maresca must win to silence City noiseIs Enzo Maresca already under pressure afterManchester City’s 3-0 schooling by Arsenalin the Community Shield? Maybe not, but if the Italian’s new team go down at home to Bournemouth on Sunday, you do not have to be a soothsayer to picture the scrutiny that will follow. Maresca and City are enduring a difficult transfer window, with Rodri’s departure to Barcelona the headline, a dizzying blow that has to be shaken off. The new Bournemouth coach, Marco Rose, has faced City six times in the Champions League with Leipzig and Mönchengladbach, and is sure to order his visitors to go for the jugular at the Etihad. City are vulnerable but Maresca can remedy this with a win of any sort. This, after all, is the job many felt he was the obvious choice for.Jamie JacksonManchester City v Bournemouth, Sunday 2pmView image in fullscreenAnything but a win for Manchester City at home to Bournemouth will increase scrutiny on Enzo Maresca.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/EPA8King Kev remembered at NewcastleKevin Keegan was supposed to have been the guest of honour at St James’ Park on Sunday, but his death from cancer in July means this meeting of two of his old clubs will turn into a tribute toone of English football’s enduring heroes. Keegan’s family will be present to witness an outpouring of love for the former Liverpool and Newcastle forward and (twice) Magpies manager. Once the game kicks off, all eyes will be on Alexander Isak, a St James’ Park old boy whose decision to force a £125m move to Anfield last summer did not go down well on Tyneside. The Sweden striker, making his first return to Newcastle, has much to prove at Liverpool, and now has a new head coach to impress in Andoni Iraola. Newcastle too have a new face in the home dugout, where Matthias Jaissle will occupy the technical area for so long inhabited by Eddie Howe.Louise TaylorNewcastle vLiverpool, Sunday 4.30pm9Former Madrid managers meet in capitalReal Madrid’s two head coaches from last season meet at Craven Cottage, with the focus on Xabi Alonso, rather than Álvaro Arbeloa. TheFulhamman, however, may have more to prove in the Premier League. His managerial career has been less prominent than that of his Basque rival – and he has clearly insisted on snapping up talent from the Bernabéu. Gonzalo García and César Palacios have made the trip over from the Spanish capital with Arbeloa. It shows great faith from the former Liverpool defender but it does put extra pressure on the trio, their fates now permanently intertwined. All three need a positive start to show they merit being in the Premier League. Otherwise, it would be very easily to criticise them individually and collectively.WUFulham v Chelsea, Monday 8pmExplore more on these topicsFootballTen things to look out for this weekendPremier LeagueArsenalManchester UnitedIpswich TownTottenham HotspurManchester CityfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: European playoffs: Rangers scrape first-leg win as Brighton draw in Norway | European club football | The Guardian
description: Ryan Naderi gave Rangers a 1-0 Conference League playoff first leg win against Jablonec, while Brighton drew 0-0 at Tromsø
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ryan Naderi gave Rangers a 1-0 Conference League playoff first leg win against Jablonec, while Brighton drew 0-0 at Tromsø
Content: Ryan Naderi’s goal gave Rangers a slender advantage to take to Czechia next week.Photograph: Luke Nickerson/Rangers FC/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenRyan Naderi’s goal gave Rangers a slender advantage to take to Czechia next week.Photograph: Luke Nickerson/Rangers FC/ShutterstockEuropean club footballEuropean playoffs: Rangers scrape first-leg win as Brighton draw in Norway10-man Rangers hang on for 1-0 win against JablonecTromsø 0-0 Brighton; Hearts 2-2 Rapid ViennaPA MediaThu 20 Aug 2026 18.54 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 19.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRyan Naderi’s second-half strike gave an unconvincingRangersa narrow 1-0 win in the first leg of theirConference Leagueplayoff tie against Czech sideJablonecat Ibrox. Derek McInnes got his first win as Rangers manager at the fifth time of asking with a 5-1 thumping of St Mirren on Sunday but there was regression in the goalless first half which brought boos at the interval whistle.The Govan side pepped up after the break and Naderi opened the scoring from close range in the 50th minute but in the 78th minute the substitute Cammy Devlin was sent off – minutes after coming off the bench – for a high tackle on Jiri Slama to leaveRangersto see out the game with 10 men.Fabian Hürzeler, admitted: “It’s not the result we hoped for,” afterBrightonwere held to a frustrating goalless draw againstTromsøin Norway. The Seagulls, who open the new domestic campaign against Aston Villa on Sunday, created several good chances but could not find a way past the Tromsø keeper Jakob Haugaard.View image in fullscreenBrighton players applaud the fans after their draw at Tromsø.Photograph: Mike Hewitt/Getty ImagesThe winger Ibrahim Osman – making his Brighton debut after three loan spells away – looked particularly lively during the first half. Tromsø then almost snatched a late winner on the break, but the defender Isak Vadebu sent his shot wide as the tie went into next week’s second leg at the Amex Stadium all square.Hearts’ head coach, Wouter Vrancken, hopes James Wilson’s stunning goal in the 2-2 Conference League draw withRapid Viennais a sign of things to come from the youngster. He drilled in an unstoppable drive from 30 yards just moments after coming on as the hosts took the lead in the playoff first leg.“He’s a young lad so for sure it will be extra special. Let’s hope he can make the next steps,” Vrancken said.Wilson’s effort marked an impressive turnaround after Josh McPade cancelled out Serge-Philippe Raux-Yao’s first-half header. However, Rapid scrambled in a late equaliser through Nikolaus Wumbrand to ensure the tie remains on a knife edge ahead of next week’s return leg.David Gray, theHibernianhead coach, savoured “a massive performance and a massive result” as his side kept themselves on course to reach the main phase with a spirited 0-0 draw in Belgium againstGent.For the second Thursday night in a row, Hibs ground out a stalemate on foreign soil after they eliminated Shkendija in North Macedonia last week. It could have been even better for them if Owen Elding’s 15th-minute penalty had not been saved by Davy Roef.Motherwellmade a whirlwind start at home toFreiburg, with Regan Charles-Cook sidefooting in Emmanuel Longelo’s cutback after just 73 seconds. But Matthias Ginter headed Freiburg level on 27 minutes and netted a second from the spot, after Martin Moormann was shown a straight red card on 65 minutes via a video assistant referee review.The substitute Keisuke Goto added a third with a stoppage-time header to leave the Scottish side with a 3-1 deficit mountain to climb in Germany next Thursday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Northern Irish champions,Larne, took a big step towards the league phase after a 2-0 win at 10-manLincoln Red Imps.The match looked set to finish goalless in Gibraltar after Red Imps had held firm following Yussef Flalhi’s 29th-minute red card. However, visiting Larne made their pressure pay when Paul O’Neill struck with five minutes left before fellow substitute Kevin O’Hara’s stoppage-time breakaway goal ensured Gary Haveron’s side will have a cushion ahead of the second leg at Inver Park.Shamrockwere held to a 1-1 draw at home by the Finnish sideKuPSafter they conceded an 85th-minute equaliser. The former Sheffield United full-back Enda Stevens put the Irish side ahead after 49 minutes, but they were denied a precious victory when the one-time Charlton youngster Piotr Parzyszek levelled late on at Tallaght Stadium.View image in fullscreenMohamed Salah had a tricky night against Ferencvaros.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesIn theEuropa League, Mohamed Salah played all 90 minutes of his home debut asTrabzonsporhostedFerencvaros, but the Hungarian side won 1-0 and their Turkish opponents had Chibuike Nwaiwu sent off in added time.Explore more on these topicsEuropean club footballEuropa LeagueConference LeagueBrighton & Hove AlbionTromsoTrabzonsporFerencvarosnewsShareReuse this content

title: Maracanã to host opening game and final at next year’s Women’s World Cup | Women's World Cup 2027 | The Guardian
description: The schedule for next year’s Women’s World Cup in Brazil has been released with the opening game and final to played at Rio de Janeiro’s Maracanã
Author: Tom Garry
Headline: The schedule for next year’s Women’s World Cup in Brazil has been released with the opening game and final to played at Rio de Janeiro’s Maracanã
Content: The Maracanã hosted the men’s World Cup final in 1950 and 2014.Photograph: Chris Brunskill Ltd/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Maracanã hosted the men’s World Cup final in 1950 and 2014.Photograph: Chris Brunskill Ltd/Getty ImagesWomen's World Cup 2027Maracanã to host opening game and final at next year’s Women’s World CupStadium has hosted two men’s World Cup finalsArena Itaquera in São Paulo will host 10 matchesTom GarryThu 20 Aug 2026 11.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Maracanã in Rio de Janeiro will host the opening game and the final of next year’s Women’s World Cup. The 78,838-capacity stadium, which hosted the finals of the 1950 and 2014 men’s World Cups as well as the finals of the Olympic football competitions in 2016, will be the venue for Brazil’s opening Group A match on 24 June, before staging the final on 25 July.Fifa released the schedule for all 64 matches for the tournament, which features 32 teams. The draw will take place after more of the qualification playoffs have been contested.‘For future generations’: Brazil working hard to ensure successful 2027 Women’s World CupRead moreBrazil will also play group matches at the Arena Itaquera in São Paulo – which will host 10 matches at the finals, more than any other host city – and at the Estádio Nacional in Brasília. Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo have been selected to host the semi‑finals, with the latter also staging the third-fourth playoff. All eight of the stadiums involved in the finals staged matches at the men’s tournament in 2014.Belo Horizonte – the scene of Brazil’s humiliating7-1 semi-final loss to Germany12 years ago – has been chosen to host a quarter-final. The winners of Group A will play in that quarter-final if they progress that far. Fortaleza, Rio de Janeiro and São Paulo will host the three other quarter-finals.Porto Alegre and Recife are also staging matches in the 10th official edition of the Women’s World Cup and the second to include 32 teams, after the expanded tournament, cohosted by Australia and New Zealand, in 2023.Spain won the title for the first timein Sydney after victory over England.View image in fullscreenSpain beat England in the final of the 2023 Women’s World Cup to lift the trophy for the first time.Photograph: Catherine Ivill/Getty Images“We can’t wait to witness a new chapter of women’s football history unfold when the world’s best players, coaches, fans and local communities take centre stage in Brazil next year,” said Fifa’s president, Gianni Infantino. “I already have goosebumps thinking about the incredible passion, colour and energy that Brazilian fans will bring to the tournament.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe former Brazil captain Aline Pellegrino said: “Each host city will add its ​own unique flavour, making ​this a colourful, joyful ​and unforgettable celebration. The ​world’s best players ‌will feel that ​energy from ​the stands and they will give it back on the pitch through moments and performances that will inspire girls and boys around the world.”It is the first time the women’s event has been staged in South America and the Maracanã will join the now-demolished Råsunda Stadium in Solna, Sweden, and the Rose Bowl in Pasadena, California, as having hosted World Cup finals for both the men’s and women’s game.Explore more on these topicsWomen's World Cup 2027Women's World CupWomen's footballBrazilnewsShareReuse this content

title: Max Verstappen signs new Red Bull contract to stay in F1 until 2030 | Max Verstappen | The Guardian
description: Max Verstappen has ended speculation about his future in Formula One by signing a new contract with Red Bull that will extend to the end of 2030
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Max Verstappen has ended speculation about his future in Formula One by signing a new contract with Red Bull that will extend to the end of 2030
Content: Max Verstappen and Red Bull team principal, Laurent Mekies.Photograph: Mark Thompson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMax Verstappen and Red Bull team principal, Laurent Mekies.Photograph: Mark Thompson/Getty ImagesMax VerstappenMax Verstappen signs new Red Bull contract to stay in F1 until 2030Dutch driver was linked with Mercedes and McLarenVerstappen: ‘I never felt that desire or need to change’Giles Richardsin ZandvoortThu 20 Aug 2026 04.13 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 18.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMax Verstappen has ended speculation about his future in Formula One by signing a new contract with his Red Bull team that will extend to the end of 2030, after almost 18 months of uncertainty around the Dutchman.After being linked with moves to Mercedes and McLaren, Verstappen’s commitment toRed Bullensures that all the major seats in the leading F1 teams are now locked in for next year, just as the sport’s silly season in terms of transfer speculation is beginning.The four-time champion’s future had been a subject of intense debate and not just in reference to switching teams. He had also seriously intimated that he might call time on his F1 career because he was so unhappy with how the new regulations have affected his enjoyment of racing.When discussing the new contract going into his home race this weekend at the Dutch Grand Prix, the 28-year-old said he believed the chances of him leaving F1 had been greater than that of him leaving Red Bull. “I never felt that desire or need also to change [to another team] to try and win somewhere else,” he said in Zandvoort. “If I feel well within the team here, why should I? Because I know that they do everything for me, and they know that I do everything for them once I’m on the track and trying to get the results.”View image in fullscreenMax Verstappen has confidence in Red Bull to return to peak form despite his annoyance with new regulations.Photograph: Márton Mónus/ReutersLooking relaxed and in good humour as he faced the media alongside the team principal, Laurent Mekies, Verstappen expressed his confidence that his team would deliver despite their travails with the new regulations this season. “I think I was closer to retiring than changing team,” he said with a laugh.Verstappen’s previous contract was set to run until the end of 2028 but was understood to include performance-based break clauses, which would have allowed him to leave had he chosen to do so, and while Red Bull have struggled with the 2026 rule set, Mercedes have emerged with a dominant car. Verstappen is sixth in the world championship, 110 points behind the title leader, Mercedes’s Kimi Antonelli.Quick GuideHow do I sign up for sport breaking news alerts?ShowIn the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from theiOS App Storeon iPhone or theGoogle Play storeon Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The Mercedes team principal, Toto Wolff, had made no secret of his desire to work with Verstappen but with Antonelli having stepped up with extraordinary assurance in only his second season and with his teammate George Russell confirmed, Mercedes were out of the equation. Ferrari similarly locked in Charles Leclerc, while Lewis Hamilton, who has a multi-year deal with the Scuderia and is newly invigorated and successful this season, ensured they too had a set lineup.McLaren then became a potential destination, perhaps as much a negotiating tool for Verstappen’s management with Red Bull as anything else, with a purported switch between McLaren’s Oscar Piastri and Verstappen being floated and the McLaren CEO, Zak Brown, admitting any team would be remiss were they not to consider the possibility of signing Verstappen. However, these rumours were ultimately given short shrift by Brown, who insisted they were happy with their lineup of Lando Norris, the world champion, alongside Piastri.The Dutchman has long said he would like to see out his career with Red Bull, whom he joined as part of their driver programme in 2014, before joining their sister team, Toro Rosso, in 2015 and being promoted to Red Bull early in the 2016 season.While his options for a new team were limited, his dislike for the new regulations and the emphasis they place on energy management was painfully clear, but with F1 and the FIA adapting them already for next year and beyond, and the prospect of the FIA returning to V8 engines with minimal electrical input in 2030, he has been swayed, not least in his faith in his team to turn things round and return further titles.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |FortnightlySign up toThe HotspotA new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“First of all, you need to feel good where you’re at. Let’s say, this year, if you are in the fastest car, but you don’t feel well [happy], I don’t think that’s going to last very long,” he said. “So, I feel very good in this team. I have the belief in the people that we can get back to the top. That’s what we are targeting. I still want to win races. I’m hungry to win more.”View image in fullscreenMax Verstappen celebrates winning the 2016 Spanish Grand Prix, his first race as a fullly fledged Red Bull driver.Photograph: Dan Istitene/Getty ImagesFor Mekies, who took over from Christian Horner in July last year, Verstappen is absolutely key in steadying the ship, not least in the driver’s ability to bring the team on as well as wrestling the absolute maximum from the car, as the team principal acknowledged.“What a demonstration of trust Max has put in the team by making this decision,” he said. “We don’t take it lightly; with that trust comes a huge amount of responsibility in living up to being able to give him the best package for the years to come.“The role that Max has in the team, he’s a lot more than the fastest driver in the world for us, he’s the central point of the team.”Explore more on these topicsMax VerstappenRed BullFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Israel’s Ben-Gvir posts video of gallows site for hanging Palestinians | Israel | The Guardian
description: Far-right minister says those convicted in military courts of terror offences will be executed after passing of death penalty law that does not apply to Jewish extremists
Author: Peter Beaumont
Headline: Far-right minister says those convicted in military courts of terror offences will be executed after passing of death penalty law that does not apply to Jewish extremists
Content: A screengrab from social media of Itamar Ben-Gvir at a building site for gallows where Palestinian convicts will be executed.Photograph: XView image in fullscreenA screengrab from social media of Itamar Ben-Gvir at a building site for gallows where Palestinian convicts will be executed.Photograph: XIsraelIsrael’s Ben-Gvir posts video of gallows site for hanging PalestiniansFar-right minister says those convicted in military courts of terror offences will be executed after passing of death penalty law that does not apply to Jewish extremistsPeter BeaumontSenior international correspondentThu 20 Aug 2026 08.34 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsrael’s far-right national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, has posted a gloating video of the construction of a gallows complex where Palestinians convicted of terror offences – but not Jewish extremists accused of similar crimes – will be hanged.Ben-Givr, who has previously attracted international sanctions and condemnation for his activities, said the new execution site would be equipped with viewing booths for families of victims to watch the hangings.He posted the video on social media of a visit he had made to the unidentified location, where he can be seen pointing at foundations being laid and boasting it was where “terrorists will be executed”.View image in fullscreenItamar Ben-Gvir celebrated his 50th birthday with a noose-themed cake.Photograph: XPhotographs in the Israeli media showed a bulldozer and heavy construction work in a cordoned-off area, reportedly close to a prison.“I promised to worsen the conditions of terrorists in prisons – we kept it,” said Ben-Gvir in the video. “I promised topass the Death Penalty for Terrorists law– we did. And now the death row and hanging facility are also starting to take shape.”Reports of the construction of the gallows, which will execute only Palestinians convicted of terror offences in the military courts system, and not Jewish extremists, follows the passage of a new law earlier this year. The law requires military courts to apply the death penalty as the only available sentence, unless the court finds special circumstances allowing for life imprisonment.Jewish Israelis are in effect protected from the death penalty by a provision that applies the law only to murder committed with the “intent to deny the existence of the state of Israel”.Ben-Gvir, who himself has convictions for incitement to racism, interfering with a police officer performing his duty, and support for a terrorist organisation (Meir Kahane’s banned Kach movement), has served as Israel’s national security minister since 2022 except for a two-month gap last year.One of the main drivers of Israel’s new death penalty law, Ben-Gvir has a long history of extremist statements and provocations. He celebrated his 50th birthday in May with the gift of a birthday cake decorated with the iced image of a noose.The death penalty law, one of two passed by Israeli MPs this year, has drawn widespread international condemnation since it passed the Knesset by 62 votes to 48 over allegations that it is fundamentally discriminatory.“It also dismantles fundamental safeguards to prevent the arbitrary deprivation of life and protect the right to a fair trial, and further empowers Israel’s system of apartheid, which is maintained by scores of discriminatory laws against Palestinians,” said Erika Guevara-Rosas, a senior director at Amnesty International, when the law was passed.The death penalty returns to Israel - podcastRead moreBen-Gvir in recent months became the subject of sanctions by France and Ireland in addition to UK sanctions imposed on him last year, attracted widespread criticism only days ago for advocating a policy of punitive killings in Gaza of 30-40 people a night.“I think we should be doing 30 to 40 targeted assassinations per night,” Ben-Gvir said. “Not just those who pose an immediate threat. There are people there who don’t deserve to live  … They are not even people.”The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, on Wednesday called Ben-Gvir’s comments “unacceptable and inhuman”, while the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said he strongly condemned “the inhumane appeals made by minister Ben-Gvir, which violate international law”.The UN secretary general, António Guterres, ecalled Ben-Gvir’s comments “appalling”, “outrageous”, “dehumanising” and “dangerous”.The video emerged amid growing wider international condemnation of Israel’s behaviour, including the issuing of new tenders for the massive E1 settlement block outside Jerusalem, which was denounced by the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, as an “unacceptable and destructive act” that risked separating the West Bank from East Jerusalem. He summoned Israel’s charge d’affaires in protest.“The UK has been clear privately and publicly in our opposition to E1 and our support for a two-state solution as the only way to ensure long-term security and peace for both Palestinians and Israelis,” Miliband said. “All settlements damage that prospect and are a flagrant breach of international law.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Biased’ Channel 4 programme on ADHD misrepresented my views, says expert | Attention deficit hyperactivity disorder | The Guardian
description: Prof Katya Dubia withdraws support for The Great ADHD Myth? as other leading figures voice criticisms
Author: Amelia Hill
Headline: Prof Katya Dubia withdraws support for The Great ADHD Myth? as other leading figures voice criticisms
Content: The programme was presented by the NHS psychiatrist Dr Max Pemberton, who concluded that ADHD was a ‘social construct’ rather than a medical condition.Photograph: Minnow ProductionsView image in fullscreenThe programme was presented by the NHS psychiatrist Dr Max Pemberton, who concluded that ADHD was a ‘social construct’ rather than a medical condition.Photograph: Minnow ProductionsAttention deficit hyperactivity disorder‘Biased’ Channel 4 programme on ADHD misrepresented my views, says expertProf Katya Rubia withdraws support for The Great ADHD Myth? as other leading figures voice criticismsAmelia HillThu 20 Aug 2026 13.54 EDTFirst published on Thu 20 Aug 2026 13.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA contributor to acontroversial Channel 4 documentaryon attention deficit hyperactivity disorder has withdrawn her support for the programme, saying it was biased and could lead to an increased suicide risk by encouraging parents to take their children off medication.Katya Rubia, a professor of cognitive neuroscience at the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology and Neuroscience at King’s College London, also said The Great ADHD Myth? misrepresented her views.The Great ADHD Myth? review – the most controversial show of the year is hereRead more“I agreed to take part in this documentary because I knew it was aiming to show ADHD was a myth and I wanted to provide an alternative view,” she said. “But they cherrypicked, largely misrepresented, truncated and presented my comments out of context to make them fit into their narrative.“Biased programmes like this one that push their view of ADHD as a mythical entity are irresponsible and will have detrimental effects, in particular at a time in our society where mental health conditions are escalating and where there is an urgent need for early diagnosis and early treatment to prevent further damage down the line,” she said.Rubia said ADHD was largely underdiagnosed and undermedicated in the UK. “Parents of children with ADHD may take their children off medication as seen on the programme, which could potentially lead to an increase of the risk of longer-term adverse outcomes of untreated ADHD such as increased anxiety and depression, lower self-esteem, greater risk of substance abuse, suicide, more antisocial behaviour and poorer academic achievement … and reduced employment prospects later in life.”TheChannel 4programme was presented by the NHS psychiatrist Dr Max Pemberton, who concluded that ADHD was a “social construct” rather than a medical condition, and schools should adapt to better support a wider range of children rather than medicating them into fitting into a restrictive norm.A Channel 4 spokesperson disputed the claim that it denied the lived experience of those diagnosed with ADHD and instead sought to present the views of a range of senior medical experts who seek to question the conventional understanding of ADHD and if it is a neurodevelopmental condition.View image in fullscreenThe Great ADHD Myth? followed the experience of 10-year-old Mason as he was taken off his medication.Photograph: Minnow ProductionsRubia criticised the documentary for filming the experience of Mason, a 10-year-old boy, while he was taken off ADHD medication.“This ‘experiment’ provided nothing but anecdotical evidence confounded by a host of factors,” she said. “The child was not only taken off medication, but also off screens, off additives and junk food, subjected to more nature experience and by implication to more interaction with family, friends and parents.“This can lead to greater happiness and stronger family bonds (for every child, not just ADHD children). There was also the uncontrolled placebo effect of being treated on TV.”Rubia said research showed most children preferred to be on medication because they had better control over their emotions as a result and consequently more friends and better relationships with others.“Substantial research on the effects of nutrition, supplements, exercise, neurofeedback, cognitive training and nature exposure shows unfortunately mostly non-significant or very tiny effects in children with ADHD, very inferior to the effects of medications,” she added.Rubia also criticised the documentary for itsnegative portrayal of medication for children with ADHD. “There is substantial evidence that long-term use of medication in ADHD is associated with many benefits such as reduced rates of suicide, comorbidities, crime, traffic accidents and substance abuse.“The side-effects are relatively minor and benefits are very large compared to other drugs in psychiatry. No mention was made about the potential negative consequences of Mason’s dropping school performance on his self-esteem and academic future,” Rubia said.The Channel 4 spokesperson said: “We are satisfied that Katya Rubia’s contribution has been edited fairly, is an accurate representation of the interview she gave and that her consent was informed.”They added: “Whilst the film does not seek to provide answers from one family’s experience, their experiences have opened up discussion around whether today’s world is equipped to accommodate ADHD behaviours and the ethics of medicating these, particularly in children and particularly when the long-term effects remain unknown.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“The welfare of the boy and his family were of paramount importance before, during and after the production process. An independent doctor, his GP, and a health and safety company were consulted. Advice was also taken from three independent psychiatrists on the medication break.”View image in fullscreenMason and his mother, Shauna. ‘The welfare of the boy and his family were of paramount importance,’ said a Channel 4 spokesperson.Photograph: Minnow ProductionsProf Anita Thapar, a clinician scientist at Cardiff University’s school of medicine, who chaired NHS England’s independent ADHD taskforce, also criticised the documentary.“It’s not a helpful argument to say ADHD is a ‘social construct’,” she said. “The programme did not use experts in clinical research on ADHD or consider all the risks of ADHD that have been shown. It seemed one-sided and used sensational language, such as likening medication to corporal punishment.”A Channel 4 spokesperson said the channel had a remit to stimulate public debate and challenge the status quo. They added: “Not everyone will agree with everything included in the programme and we acknowledge the strength of feeling that this subject evokes, however there is considerable public debate in this area and testing conventional thinking and exploring different ideas.”Prof Subodh Dave, the president of the Royal College of Psychiatrists, also criticised the programme. “Invalidating the condition does a disservice to people with ADHD and professionals involved in their care,” he said.A survey launched by the charity ADHD UK after the documentary was screened on Tuesday has received more than 4,000 responses.More than 94% of respondents said the documentary had increased stigma about ADHD. The same proportion said it was not fair in its representation of ADHD as a condition.More than 85% said the programme “clearly suggested ADHD is not a real condition” and 88% said it did not make clear that the sceptical views featured were minority views within medicine.The Channel 4 spokesperson said: “This documentary hears from an extensive range of senior medical experts, with a variance of views on the topic, including, but not limited to, psychiatrists, psychologists, psychotherapists and neuroscientists. Many of these experts work or have worked with the NHS or have held presidential roles at professional membership bodies.“It is undeniable that there is considerable public debate on various aspects of ADHD, including in relation to the prescribing of medication and diagnostic procedures, and it is not misleading to suggest that these views exist. Channel 4 has a remit which includes offering a platform for alternative views, stimulating public debate and challenging the status quo.”Explore more on these topicsAttention deficit hyperactivity disorderChannel 4NeurodiversityMental healthChildrenDocumentaryTelevision industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: BBC’s Trevor Nelson recovering after brain tumour surgery | Radio 2 | The Guardian
description: Radio 2 DJ, who stepped back from work commitments in June, says operation went ‘incredibly well’
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Radio 2 DJ, who stepped back from work commitments in June, says operation went ‘incredibly well’
Content: Trevor Nelson says he is feeling almost back to himself and is ‘raring to go’.Photograph: Joseph Okpako/WireImageView image in fullscreenTrevor Nelson says he is feeling almost back to himself and is ‘raring to go’.Photograph: Joseph Okpako/WireImageRadio 2BBC’s Trevor Nelson recovering after brain tumour surgeryRadio 2 DJ, who stepped back from work commitments in June, says operation went ‘incredibly well’Nadeem BadshahThu 20 Aug 2026 13.41 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTrevor Nelson, the BBCRadio 2DJ, has revealed he had surgery after being diagnosed with a brain tumour and is now on the mend.The broadcaster, 62, said in June that he wastaking a break from work commitmentsto deal with health issues.In a post on Thursday, Nelson said his “world was turned upside down” when he found out he had a brain tumour.The radio host has spent the last month “recuperating, resting, and recovering” after surgery that went “incredibly well”, and said he hoped to return to work soon.Nelson, who has spent a 30-year career at theBBCchampioning Black British music, said in a video message: “A lot of you may have seen the post that I put up at the start of summer, saying that I was stepping back from all my work commitments due to illness.“There’s been a lot of speculation as to what’s wrong with me, I know that much.”About 13,000 people in the UK are diagnosed with a primary brain tumour every year, according to the Brain Tumour Charity.Nelson said: “I’m not going to go into it all now, and I will probably deep-dive into it at a later date so you can hear the whole crazy story.“But I’ll tell you this: I was minding my own business, and then it was discovered that I had a brain tumour. My world was turned upside down. It was a shock to myself, my close family, and friends. My head was all over the place.”The broadcaster said he underwent surgery a few weeks after his diagnosis. “Thankfully it went incredibly well, and the last month I’ve been at home recuperating, resting, recovering, and getting some post-op treatment.”He said he was feeling “almost back to myself”, adding: “I’ve had a really serious situation, but I’ve come out the other side at this point and I feel great. I feel raring to go, and I feel in good health.”Nelson presented weekdays 2-4pm onRadio 2, and BBC Radio 1Xtra each Sunday from 11am to 1pm before his break. He previously worked for Kiss FM, Radio 1 and MTV.Explore more on these topicsRadio 2BBCRadio industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Charity campaigner’s death after microlight crash was accidental, coroner rules | Leicestershire | The Guardian
description: Claire Lomas died of severe injuries five weeks after aircraft crashed into rocks off runway while filming Apple video in Jordan
Author: Raphael Boyd
Headline: Claire Lomas died of severe injuries five weeks after aircraft crashed into rocks off runway while filming Apple video in Jordan
Content: Claire Lomas, pictured in 2017 after winning the disabled sportsperson award at the Pride of Sport awards, died in 2024.Photograph: Ian West/PAView image in fullscreenClaire Lomas, pictured in 2017 after winning the disabled sportsperson award at the Pride of Sport awards, died in 2024.Photograph: Ian West/PALeicestershireCharity campaigner’s death after microlight crash was accidental, coroner rulesClaire Lomas died of severe injuries five weeks after aircraft crashed into rocks off runway while filming Apple video in JordanRaphael BoydThu 20 Aug 2026 12.49 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe death of a disability campaigner after a microlight crash while filming a TV programme forApplewas an accident, a coroner has concluded.An inquest heard on Thursday that Claire Lomas, 44,died of severe traumatic injurieson 22 August 2024, five weeks after a light aircraft she had been piloting whilefilming a series to promote Apple’s Vision Pro headset“veered off the runway” during a landing operation and crashed into a rock in Amman, Jordan.After becoming paralysed from the waist down in a horse-riding accident in 2007, Lomas, from Leicestershire, became a charity campaigner. She raised more than £900,000 for the Nicholls Spinal Injury Foundation and was the first person to finish a marathon with the aid of a “bionic” suit when shecompleted the 2012 London Marathon in 17 days.The inquest heard that the Royal Aero Sports Club of Jordan had concluded there was no violation of ground or air safety procedures, and that there was no evidence the 180-degree camera attached to the aircraft had adversely affected the flight.Concerns about Lomas’s confidence to fly the microlight were explored during the hearing. Ben Ashman, a microlight designer whose company built an adapted version of the aircraft to allow Lomas to fly without the use of her feet, said he believed Lomas may have been stressed before the flight because she posted on Facebook about putting her “brave pants” on, which he said was unusual for her.Louise Pinder, the senior coroner for Rutland and NorthLeicestershire, recorded Lomas’s death as accidental, telling the hearing she “was involved in the filming of an episode of Adventure which formed part of a series designed for a virtual reality headset”.Pinder added: “During the final approach to the roadway, where she was to land, it became apparent to her and to those on the ground that the aircraft was not perfectly aligned.“Claire made a split-second decision to abort the landing and go around but the aircraft touched down firmly, veered to the left, the left wheel leaving the road on to gravel causing her to further lose control. The aircraft collided with rocks approximately 10 metres from the metalled road surface, as a result of which she sustained multiple traumatic injuries.”Pinder added: “I have heard no evidence establishing a causal link between any deficiencies in the risk assessment and Claire’s death. I am reassured, as I hope the family will be, that there have been thorough investigations as far as possible into the circumstances of Claire’s death and some lessons have been learnt.”Pinder noted that Lomas’s family had raised concerns about the quality of care she received in hospital in Jordan, but said there was insufficient evidence to conclude whether there were any missed opportunities in her treatment.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionKatherine Allen, a lawyer speaking on behalf of the Lomas family, said the inquest’s conclusion marked “the end of a very difficult, emotional process” for them and that “the family continue to live with the devastating consequences of their loss”.“Claire was deeply loved and her death has left a profound and enduring void in their lives,” Allen said in a statement. “They will never be the same again following what happened to her.”Explore more on these topicsLeicestershireApple TVAppleTelevisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lobsters and acidic seas: can shellfish help neutralise one of the greatest threats to the ocean? | Oceans | The Guardian
description: Crustaceans are the subject of tests to see if alkalis added to seawater, so it absorbs more CO2, harm marine life. But Trump’s halt to funding threatens to scupper the research
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Crustaceans are the subject of tests to see if alkalis added to seawater, so it absorbs more CO2, harm marine life. But Trump’s halt to funding threatens to scupper the research
Content: A lobster in St George, Maine. The crustacean is a tricky test subject, disliking warm seawater and ‘unfortunately, they eat each other.’  Photograph: D Grill/TetraCrustaceans are the subject of tests to see if alkalis added to seawater, so it absorbs more CO2, harm marine life. But Trump’s halt to funding threatens to scupper the researchByAlexandra Talty in Cape Cod, MassachusettsSeascape: the state of our oceans is supported byAbout this contentThu 20 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 11.20 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor many in the US region of New England, the lobster roll is synonymous with summertime. Loaded into a toasted bun, chunks of the sweet meat are served hot and soaked in butter, or chilled and slathered in mayonnaise with celery and herbs.The only thing more debated than the recipe is the price: the once-humble roll now routinely fetches $30 (£22), or even $50, in a sign of the changing times – and seas.A third-generation lobster fisherman, Scott Lord spendshis days hauling traps on the Gulf of Maine, which iswarming faster than 99% of the world’s oceans. “Whether you agree with who says why it’s happening, it is happening,” he says.Bycatch that was once plentiful, such as sea urchins, sand dollars or starfish, are increasingly rare. And, most concerning, Lord has noticed the number of inshore lobsters dropping dramatically over the past 15 years, pushing fishers farther and farther offshore.Motivated to find a remedy, Lord joined a regional shellfish committee. “Why are there not clams where there used to be clams? Why are they not coming back, no matter what we do?” he asks.Hundreds of miles to the south inMassachusetts, on a sandy crook of land that spins out to form Cape Cod, Adam Subhas, a scientist at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution, is trying to find the answers.View image in fullscreenScott Lord brings in his catch of lobster to the wharf in Tenants Harbor, MaineView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenScott Lord brings in his catch of lobsters from traps off the coast; he has had to go out farther from shore to find the shellfish in recent years. Lobster rolls at the Lobster Trap Restaurant & Fish Market in Bourne, MassachusettsSubhas heads LOC-NESS (Locking Ocean Carbon in the North-east Shelf and Slope, an initiative researching how to decarbonise the ocean, also known as marine carbon dioxide removal (mCDR). Scientists working in this field are trying to discover whether the ocean, which is estimated to absorb about31% of atmospheric carbon, could be manipulated to soak up even more.Proponents say ocean carbon removal could help stop the world from passing the 2C (3.6F)tipping point outlined inthe 2016 Paris Agreement, if used in conjunction with the reduction of fossil fuels.What was once a small-scale idea is rapidly gaining traction. A database newly launched by the Pulitzer Center,Ocean Carbon Removal Watch, which tracks mCDR investments, field trials and research, shows that more than £370m has been invested in the sector over the past five years.This was initially driven by the private sector but, thanks to a spate of US federal investments in 2023 – totalling at least £44m, according to a Guardian analysis of the database – scientific field trials began to catch up. Until, that is, President Trumpannounced sweeping cutsto all federally funded ocean sciences.View image in fullscreenAdam Subhas, who is heading the LOC-NESS programme, among lobster larvae at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution laboratory in MassachusettsView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenAdam Subhas with a tiny lobster at Woods Hole, with food being prepared for the lobsters“The funding cuts are affecting everyone,” says Subhas.With federal science backing nearly dried up, LOC-NESS is the last “unicorn” for US ocean carbon removal.It is testing the technique that has garnered the most support in the past few years:ocean alkalinity enhancement (OAE). Its central tenet is to encourage seawater to absorb more atmospheric carbon by dispersing alkaline materials over a wide area of ocean.Working 40 miles offshore from Boston in the Gulf of Maine’s Wilkinson basin last summer,Subhas’s team put about 65,000 litres of sodium hydroxide into the sea. The highly alkaline material was mixed with a red dye to make it easier for sensors and satellites to track.View image in fullscreenSubhas, left, and Kate Morkeski prepare to cast a net to pick up plankton off their research vessel during ocean alkalinity enhancement field trials“The ocean is 70% of the Earth’s surface and, if this is really going to scale [up], we have to understand how this might work in the open ocean, too,” says Subhas, who has a Loch Ness monster soft toy perched on a shelf in his laboratory next to the scientists’ bible, the CRC Handbook of Chemistry and Physics.The team used a fleet of boats and monitored alkalinity and carbon uptake for four days via autonomous underwater vehicles that provided highly sensitive measurements.“For a while, there’s been scientific debate around if you could even measure some of these signals,” says Subhas, whopresented his findings at this year’s Ocean Sciences Meeting. He believes they can provide a roadmap for how alkalinity enhancement can be measured and modelled in the future.View image in fullscreenThree ships took part in the LOC-NESS Project’s successful OAE trial in the Gulf of Maine, which included observers from the US Environmental Protection Agency, the Massachusetts state fisheries body, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration and the fishing industryView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenAdam Subhas, right, and Jennie Rheuban take samples from a CTD probe, which collects samples allowing scientists to measure the temperature, salinity, oxygen and acidity of seawater at different depths. Right, an autonomous glider with sensors to measure the alkalinity of the sea“We need to be really clear about the need for large-scale emissions reductions, while at the same time figuring out the science behind some of these more novel approaches that might help supplement those large-scale reductions into the future,” says Subhas.Outside the Woods Hole laboratories, the thrum of alkaline water being pumped into machines analysing dissolved inorganic carbon plays in the background.Lobsters and alkalinityBased on data collected last summer, the team is examining two years of trials to understand how marine creatures respond to different levels of alkalinity. After initial biological studies on species at the base of the food web such as phytoplankton, the team is now focusing on lobsters.It is a species that generates the second-highest value of any seafood landed in the US, accounting forjust under $700m (about £550m) in 2023. Then they will move on to the tautog wrasse, a popular species for sports fishing.Designing the experiment came with its own challenges. Lobsters are very sensitive during moulting, do not like temperatures above 20C (68F) and “unfortunately, they eat each other, given the opportunity”, says Chris Murray, a marine biologist who built special floating mesh cups to avoid cannibalism.View image in fullscreenChloe Dean, a researcher, assesses the biological impacts of higher alkalinity. Preliminary lab results showed no increased mortality or behavioural changes after exposure to elevated pH and alkalinitySo far, Murray and his team have not seen any lethal effects with either low or high levels of alkalinity, but they will analyse the lobsters’ RNA, the molecular building block for all cellular functions, at the end of the trials to better understandtheir physiological response and, in particular, their ability to secrete waste.Describing these studies as the “tip of the iceberg”, Murray says the next step of this experimentation would involve creating a mini-ecosystem featuring many marine species.“We need to do this research,” he says. “It’s really important to weigh these impacts against what is predicted to occur in the ocean. We know that ocean warming is going to be a major disruptive force to marine food webs.”Can European funding save the day?Luckily for the researchers, there is still a glimmer of hope from across the Atlantic. Just as US funding was abruptly stopped, Europe began scaling up its academic grants to study removal of marine carbon dioxide.According to analysis of the Ocean Carbon Renewal Watch data, the European Union disbursed more than £8.5m in grants in the past two years, which has distributed funds to more than 20 universities across Britain and the rest of Europe.At the University of Gothenburg, Sam Dupont, a senior lecturer who studies the effects of ocean acidification and warming on marine ecosystems, was buoyed up by this newstream of funding.Studying alkalinity thresholds of sea urchins, mussels and fish eggs, he is beginning two years of experimentation in Sweden and Iceland, where he is working with the country’s Marine and Freshwater Research Institute to see how alkalinity affects the same species in different bodies of water.“We want to cover a bunch of different creatures,” he says. “We see that if you go too high in alkalinity, there’s something going wrong in their physiology and they develop abnormally and die.”View image in fullscreenAn underwater glider with Amanda Pinson, of the Woods Hole marine chemistry and geochemistry department, and Patrick Deane, an engineer in the physical oceanography departmentDupont is concerned that private industry is starting to attract finance for large-scale experiments by issuing oceancarbon removal credits. Commercial scale is “ready to jump, but we don’t understand how it [OAE] is going to impact biology yet”, he says.“The equivalent would be: you smoke a cigarette and you go to the doctor the next day and say, ‘There is no effect on cancer’,” says Dupont, who estimates that it will be about a decade before scientists can accurately state what the safe alkalinity thresholds are for marine life.Back at Woods Hole, a few buildings over from Subhas, Ken Buesseler, a professor emeritus of marine radiochemistry, has experienced the US science funding cliff first-hand. He has spent three decades studying iron fertilisation – which adds iron to the ocean to encourage plankton growth, thereby sequestering carbon. That is, until his US Department of Energy (DoE) grant was stopped halfway through last year with, he says, only about half of the $5m promised being paid out.How the ‘evil twin’ of the climate crisis is threatening our oceansRead moreResearchers were to hear about a new phase of funding last winter, but “none of those came through”, says Buesseler. “There is no pipeline in DoE for carbon management any more.”Buesseler also leads an ambitious project calledEx-OIS, which is in the early stages of seeking permission to study iron fertilisation across more than 400 miles offshore of Alaska’s coast. It would be the first venture ever to have gone through national and international regulatory processes.But with little to no funding opportunities in the US, it is hard to imagine it attracting the $30m needed to launch the experiment in 2028.“I feel like we are just kicking the can,” says Buesseler, who believes that these geoengineering techniques need to be used in conjunction with fossil fuel reduction.“The climate crisis isn’t going away because we stop funding research into ocean solutions, so the problem will be with us. It is getting harder and harder to address.”This story was produced in partnership with the Pulitzer Centerand with support fromanAlicia Patterson FellowshipExplore more on these topicsSeascape: the state of our oceansOceansGreenhouse gas emissionsCarbon offsettingClimate crisisOcean acidificationMarine lifefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How one American couple ditched their lawn and created a wildlife haven – and you could too | Environment | The Guardian
description: Novice gardeners James Reed McGuire and Crystal Fritz wanted to try something new when they moved out to the suburbs. Little did they know they were joining a nationwide movement
Author: Whitney Bauck
Headline: Novice gardeners James Reed McGuire and Crystal Fritz wanted to try something new when they moved out to the suburbs. Little did they know they were joining a nationwide movement
Content: Crystal Fritz and James Reed McGuire at home in the Chicago suburb of Highland Park, Illinois.  Photograph: Thalia Juarez/The GuardianNovice gardeners James Reed McGuire and Crystal Fritz wanted to try something new when they moved out to the suburbs. Little did they know they were joining a nationwide movementByWhitney BauckThe age of extinction is supported byAbout this contentThu 20 Aug 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 07.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen James Reed McGuire and Crystal Fritz first decided to replace their lawn with native plants, they did not really know what they were doing. As former city-dwellers who had moved fromChicagoout to the suburb of Highland Park, Illinois, they had never done much gardening together beyond growing some planters of herbs and flowers on their balcony.But for McGuire, an avid birder who did not want to live with a sea of turf that does “absolutely nothing for the environment”, figuring out an alternative to the suburban status quo was imperative.View image in fullscreenCrystal Fritz and James Reed McGuire’s Highland Park front garden before they transformed it with native plantsThe couple’s early attempts to rewild their lawn were full of what they now deem missteps. They bought mixed wildflower seed packets and sprinkled them about aimlessly, rather than identifying specific species native to their area and planning where they should go. They tried digging up the turf by hand with a shovel, labour so difficult that McGuire laughs when he thinks about it now.But with each mistake, they learned. Despite having no horticultural training – Fritz works as a personal assistant, while McGuire is a creative director and writer – they slowly figured out how to identify native plants for their region and experimented with the best ways to grow them from seed to keep the project economical.View image in fullscreenNow, Fritz and McGuire’s garden is a thriving native ecosystem in the middle of the suburbsThey designed layouts for their garden that would allow them to enjoy blooms for as much of the growing season as possible. Every year, they added a few more native plants and every year they watched as more pollinators and birds were drawn to the garden.Quick GuideHow to rewild your lawnShowHow to rewild your lawn• Start small. You do not have to dig up the whole lawn at once; you can just pick one corner to work on and remove a small piece of turf.•  Remove any invasive species.•  When researching which native plants and wildflowers to use, look for ones that attract pollinators. In the US, you can source your plants using the native plant resource directory atHomegrown National Park.•  While it might take some effort to establish the plants at the beginning, many gardeners find that less exotic plants actually take less maintenance in the long run because they have evolved to live in the same conditions in which you are  planting them.Photograph: David Kilpatrick/www.alamy.comWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Today, McGuire and Fritz’s lawn has been transformed from a monoculture of turf to a thriving native ecosystem in the suburbs. The abundance of native plants provides food and habitat for a plethora of wild critters: sightings of birds, butterflies, bees, rabbits, bats and foxes are now common occurrences.“It’s really a stunning environment,” says McGuire. “It brings us a lot of peace and tranquility in a very troubled world.”View image in fullscreenMcGuire and Fritz in their yard: ‘It’s so rewarding,’ says FritzAs the first in the neighbourhood to make this switch, McGuire and Fritz have received an “unbelievable amount of positive feedback” from passersby. Families go out of their way to walk by the house so their children can see the abundance of fireflies there. One couple nearby asked for McGuire’s help in converting their own yard into a native habitat.The house has been featured in a local garden walk for the past few years, and the city granted the couple permission to landscape the city-owned roadside verge in front of their home to extend the habitat they created.And it is not just McGuire and Fritz’s human neighbours who love what they’ve done with the place. In 2023, their garden was designated aCertified Wildlife Habitatby the National Wildlife Federation, proof that their landscaping is a boon to wildlife, too.“It’s so rewarding,” says Fritz. “We’ve done this little tiny thing with this little piece of property, but it’s made a huge impact, at least in our little corner of the world.”Fritz and McGuire might have been the first on their block to convert their lawn, but they are far from alone. All over the US, people are beginning to dig up pesticide- and fertiliser-hungry lawns in favour of planting that is more biodiverse and better suited to the local climate and needs of wildlife.View image in fullscreenThe abundance of native plants provides food and habitat for wildlife: birds, butterflies, bees, rabbits, bats and foxes are commonAccording toDoug Tallamy, an entomologistwho has become one of the country’s biggest advocates for what he calls “conservation landscaping”, lawns first came to the US from Europe.“We copied the aristocracy,” Tallamy says. “We wanted to show that we were rich and had high status, and back then the only way you could have a lawn is if you had enough property that you didn’t have to farm at all, and you had enough wealth that you could either have slaves or sheep to manage that lawn.”With the invention of the lawnmower, as well as the arrival of pesticides and fertiliser, lawn maintenance became accessible to a much wider range of people, and by the mid-20th century, turf had become an entrenched status symbol for suburbanites. Today,an estimated 160,000 sq km (40m acres)of the US are turf – including golf courses – withmore surface area given over to lawnsthan individual irrigated crops such as maize or wheat.View image in fullscreenButterflies are naturally attracted to the native plantsWhile it might seem better than concrete, for example, grass lawns are environmentally problematic, Tallamy says. First off, US lawns usually consist of European grass species with short roots, which do little to draw carbon and water deep into the soil. When it rains, water runs off the top of these lawns rather than being absorbed, taking pesticides and fertiliser with it and depositing the chemicals in nearby rivers and lakes, where they wreak havoc on watercourses. Second, non-native turf grasses do not support pollinators or a viable food web, which starts with insects.Tallamy says: “We’ve got parks and we’ve got reserves, but we are headed towards a sixth extinction event, because those are too small, they’re too isolated and there’s too few of them. And the way we landscape in between the parks and reserves does not sustain biodiversity.”The good news is that it does not take much to begin righting these environmental wrongs. From Tallamy’s perspective, it does not even necessarily mean eliminating lawns entirely – if short grass is useful in one part of your garden so your children can play, that’s great.View image in fullscreenA wide variety of native species thrive in Fritz and McGuire’s gardenFor him, it is about shifting the balance so native plants become the norm and lawns are created specifically to serve a purpose. If everybody in the country cut their lawn in half and planted the other half with native species, it would go a long way towards creating and connecting the kind of habitats that would allow wild species to survive today’s ecological crises, he says.That is the idea behindHomegrown National Parks, an American conservation initiative founded by Tallamy that advocates bringing the wilderness to your home by planting native.Camille Dungy, an American poet and academic, is also known in her neighbourhood in Fort Collins,Colorado, for her gorgeous garden. Dungy spent a decade converting her single-species lawn into a biodiverse haven of native plant species that supports birds and pollinators year-round and uses less water.View image in fullscreenPoet and academic Camille Dungy in her bird- and pollinator-friendly garden in Fort Collins, Colorado. Photograph: Ben Ward/The GuardianBut she has also left room for a few non-native (though still non-invasive) species such as irises, which remind her of a loved one, as well as some lawn space for her child to play on (although she swapped the Kentucky bluegrass for native grasses). Her garden is now about 70% native plants to 30% non-native.Even that has been enough to make a marked difference in her garden’s ability to support biodiversity, says Dungy, who wrote about the process in her 2023 bookSoil: The Story of a Black Mother’s Garden.Along the way, she has also seen the culture around lawns slowly change.Insects are dying: here are 25 easy and effective ways you can help protect themRead moreWhen she first moved to Fort Collins in 2013, a member of the Homeowners’ Association (organisations that manage and set rules for shared spaces in US residential areas) would walk around with a ruler, measuring whether residents had plants growing above a permitted height, which favoured lawns. By 2023, Colorado had passed legislation prohibiting the associations from banning “water-wise” landscaping, which often uses native plants to conserve water in the chronically drought-stricken state.“We started as the first house on the block, and now everybody has some elements of this kind of low-water, pollinator-supporting landscaping,” Dungy says.The change is also happening elsewhere. Some parts of California now offer rebates to homeowners for every square foot of lawn replaced with a “xeriscaped” (dry landscape) garden, which use drought-tolerant plants, more efficient watering techniques and mulching to use less water.Minnesota and Pennsylvania pay residents to replace lawns with native plants, and Virginia has banned the sale of invasive species (some of which used to be considered exotic ornamental plants). Marco Island in Florida implemented a successful programme to pay residents to let the endangered burrowing owl build a nest in their lawns.View image in fullscreenAttracting pollinators is one of the reasons people are choosing to plant native gardensNow, evidence is emerging that even if state governments do not reward the choice to plant native, homebuyers might – real estate agents are finding thatnative gardens can be a selling point.Once you get started, and see the flood of pollinators and new birds showing up at your door, you may never look back. This is one of the things that Tallamy finds most powerful about the movement: for all the very real good you can do by installing solar panels or switching to an electric vehicle, it can be hard to see the impact your good choices have had.But when you rewild your lawn, “you get to see the results, and that empowers you”, he says. “You see the biodiversity come back to your yard, and even though you’re not saving the whole planet, you are saving the piece of the planet that you ‘own’ in a very functional way.”The Guardian receives support for visual climate coverage from theOutrider Foundation.The Guardian’s coverage is editorially independentExplore more on these topicsThe age of extinctionConservationGardensWildlifeChicagoColoradofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lewes rail line to reopen in September as work under way to remove train | Rail transport | The Guardian
description: Derailed carriages lifted using two cranes as workers operate under ‘very challenging circumstances’
Author: Alex Daniel
Headline: Derailed carriages lifted using two cranes as workers operate under ‘very challenging circumstances’
Content: A crane lifts one of the carriages from the Southern train that derailed near Lewes, in an image newly released on Thursday.Photograph: Network Rail/PAView image in fullscreenA crane lifts one of the carriages from the Southern train that derailed near Lewes, in an image newly released on Thursday.Photograph: Network Rail/PARail transportLewes rail line to reopen in September as work under way to remove trainDerailed carriages lifted using two cranes as workers operate under ‘very challenging circumstances’Business live – latest updatesAlex DanielThu 20 Aug 2026 10.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe East Sussex railway line on whicha train derailedwill reopen in September as crews continue to remove the carriages that left the track.Rail bosses said they were prioritising reopening the route before the end of the school holidays, despite recovery workers operating under “very challenging circumstances”.Three carriages at the back of the train operated bySouthernderailed on 13 August, injuring 30 people and trapping passengers on board.An initial report by the Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) on Wednesdayfound a track defect on the approach to where the train derailed,which happened on the hottest day of the year so far.Twenty people were taken to hospital and two suffered serious injuries, which are not deemed to be life-threatening.View image in fullscreenAn aerial view of the derailed train in East Sussex.Photograph: Network Rail/PAThe stretch of railway between Lewes and Haywards Heath is scheduled to remain closed until 1 September. That will give time for the train to be recovered – a complex job involving the derailed carriages being lifted by crane – and for recovery teams to make sure evidence is preserved.Lewes derailment: images show track defect before incident on hottest dayRead moreLucy McAuliffe, the Sussex route director for Network Rail, said: “I can only apologise for the disruption that this incident is causing to people’s journeys, and I want to personally thank people for their patience and their understanding alongside the many rail industry colleagues supporting the recovery.“The location of the derailment, which happened in close proximity to the River Ouse, means that reinstatement of the site is particularly complex, with teams working round the clock to reopen the line for customers as soon and as safely as possible.“The recovery is being carried out with careful consideration for the area around the derailment site, ensuring the area’s ecology is protected and being mindful of residents living nearby.”View image in fullscreenWorkers plan the removal of the carriages on Wednesday in East Sussex.Photograph: Network Rail/PAImages released on Thursday showed a crane holding up one of the carriages as staff took luggage and bicycles off the vehicle.John Whitehurst, the chief executive of Greater Thameslink Railway, which owns Southern, said: “Getting the line open in time for the end of the school holidays is an absolute priority for us and we are working closely with Network Rail to achieve this despite very challenging circumstances.”The RAIB’s initial report included an image that appeared to show the track had buckled – something that can happen in high temperatures – before the train derailed.The train, which had about 150 people on board, came off the track at 3.54pm last Thursday, doing “significant damage” to the carriages and the rail infrastructure, the watchdog said.The report pointed to “a sustained period of hot and dry weather” and said the ambient air temperature at the time was about 27C, according to the nearest weather station to the site.Explore more on these topicsRail transportRail industryEast SussexTransportSouthernnewsShareReuse this content

title: Frustrated GP patients hang up as Yorkshire accent baffles AI receptionist  | GPs | The Guardian
description: ‘Emma’ the Rotherham chatbot has 17 languages says AI firm – but health watchdog says system struggling with local ‘twangs’
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: ‘Emma’ the Rotherham chatbot has 17 languages says AI firm – but health watchdog says system struggling with local ‘twangs’
Content: One patient said of the AI system: ‘I could never get it to understand me, I ended up just hanging up and not bothering to try and book an appointment.’Photograph: Julian Claxton/AlamyView image in fullscreenOne patient said of the AI system: ‘I could never get it to understand me, I ended up just hanging up and not bothering to try and book an appointment.’Photograph: Julian Claxton/AlamyGPsFrustrated GP patients hang up as Yorkshire accent baffles AI receptionist‘Emma’ the Rotherham chatbot has 17 languages says AI firm – but health watchdog says system struggling with local ‘twangs’Mark BrownNorth of England correspondentThu 20 Aug 2026 05.25 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePatients in a SouthYorkshiretown are frustrated by an AI GP receptionist not understanding their “broad accents”, a health watchdog has said.Healthwatch Rotherham, a local health and social care watchdog, said a number of practices in the area had introduced a new AI receptionist called Emma.It said it was hearing accounts of the AI not understanding local accents. Its manager, Kym Gleeson, told the BBC: “One of the issues is this system can’t always understand what people’s inquiry is about due to their broad Yorkshire accent.“Across South Yorkshire, accents do vary quite a lot. There are different twangs so there’s a lot of variation. It seems the system isn’t always able to understand, so that causes frustration.”The system, whichis being usedby an increasing number of GP surgeries across the UK, aims to answer every patient call “instantly”, eliminating the often long wait times patients experience in a phone queue, waiting to speak to a receptionist.Gleeson said Emma had the potential to be a good system, but one disgruntled patient told Healthwatch: “I could never get it to understand me, I ended up just hanging up and not bothering to try and book an appointment.”The feedback came after the watchdog contacted groups representing older people and veterans’ communities, Gleeson said. “What they were telling us was they were having issues navigating this system.“Some of the people were so frustrated at not being able to understand how to navigate this AI system, it was forcing them to travel back to their GP surgery in person. The usual route of using a telephone was no longer a comfortable process for them.”Healthwatch said concerns around Emma were heightened when considering people less confident about using digital technology, or people with disabilities. “It’s important to remember that GP practices still have a legal duty to make reasonable adjustments for patients who need them,”it said.“If using an AI receptionist is difficult for you, you can ask your practice what alternative ways are available to access services.”QuantumLoopAI, the company behind the Emma system, said it was designed to understand a range of dialects and patients could speak to a human at any time.A spokesperson told the BBC: “Emma does not make clinical decisions. She is designed and trained to understand a wide range of accents and dialects and supports 17 languages in addition to English. Where she is unable to understand or deal with a patient’s request the call is transferred to the reception team. No caller is required to continue speaking with Emma, and anyone can ask to speak to a member of staff at any time.“Emma is designed to improve access by answering calls instantly and removing telephone queues.”Explore more on these topicsGPsAI (artificial intelligence)DoctorsNHSHealthYorkshireRotherhamnewsShareReuse this content

title: Working in Keir Starmer’s No 10 ‘unbearable’, says Sue Gray | Sue Gray | The Guardian
description: Former chief of staff tells of fears her conversations were being recorded and leaked to media by colleagues
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Former chief of staff tells of fears her conversations were being recorded and leaked to media by colleagues
Content: Baroness Sue Gray is the second senior woman from Starmer’s administration in recent weeks to have expressed frustration at his leadership.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PAView image in fullscreenBaroness Sue Gray is the second senior woman from Starmer’s administration in recent weeks to have expressed frustration at his leadership.Photograph: Liam McBurney/PASue GrayWorking in Keir Starmer’s No 10 ‘unbearable’, says Sue GrayFormer chief of staff tells of fears her conversations were being recorded and leaked to media by colleaguesRowena MasonWhitehall editorThu 20 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKeir Starmer’s former chief of staff has lifted the lid on how “unbearable” it was working in No 10, revealing she feared her conversations were being recorded by
