colleagues seeking to leak her remarks to the media.Sue Gray, who was the most powerful adviser in Downing Street before her resignation in 2024, was highly critical of the working environment under Starmer, saying she was “disappointed” that he did not act on her concerns about staff briefing journalists against her.In an interview with thePolitical Currencypodcast, shared with the Guardian, she gave her first major analysis of the extreme tensions in the early days of Starmer’s operation, providing an insight into the culture of what has been called a “boys’ club” operating with Downing Street.In the weeks before Gray quit, Starmer was accused of having lost control of his senior team after aseries of acrimonious leaksto the media about his chief of staff’s pay being higher than that of the prime minister and her apparently difficult relationships with senior colleagues.In relation to a story that she had tried to get Starmer’s other closest aide, Morgan McSweeney,moved further away from the prime minister, Gray told the podcast’s interviewer Ed Balls: “I had always taken a view as a civil servant and actually as a special adviser that you should be able to speak freely in rooms … I couldn’t recall those sort of discussions being briefed out, and yet here I found myself.“Stories about supposedly trying to moveMorgan McSweeneyto the back of the building. Actually, that was a genuine … ‘I can’t believe so many of you are going to sit in this small room. Let’s find a better room for you.’ It just got to the point where you know everything you say, you feel somebody is recording it.”Asked whether Starmer acted on her concerns, Gray said: “I talked to him a couple of times about it, and I don’t really want to disclose individual conversations. But I was disappointed that not more was done because I think it could have been done.”She said the atmosphere in No 10 was “definitely unbearable, particularly for me”, adding: “I would say that none of that briefing came from me. I think it was very difficult, and it was just affecting me and my life … It was a very, very, very difficult period.”Gray is the second senior woman from Starmer’s administration in recent weeks to have expressed frustration at his leadership.Yvette Cooper, the health secretary under Burnham and the wife of Balls, gave an interview to the same podcast earlier this month accusing Keir Starmer’s No 10 ofsidelining herduring the launch of a key immigration policy when she was home secretary.During his two years in Downing Street, Starmer oversaw a huge churn in his staff within No 10, with Gray lasting just four months in the job after working for him in opposition to prepare for government. She was replaced by Morgan McSweeney, who subsequently had to resign over his role in having appointed Peter Mandelson as US ambassador.Starmer has not given a big interview since being forced out of office by his MPs but he has previously said he waswrong to have appointed Gray, a former ethics chief and senior civil servant who carried out the Partygate inquiry for Boris Johnson, despite not wanting to have taken on that task.Starmer allies have previously blamed Gray for failing to prepare adequately for government when she was put in charge of the first 100 days of power whileLabourwas still in opposition.Gray defended her preparations, saying there was “a lot done” from working to restore British-Irish relationships, working with the European Commission and the US administration, and suggesting media announcements should have been for the media team. It has previously been reported that the communications team was not confirmed in jobs until the day Labour entered power in July 2024, and that preparations for government were split between planning for the key events of the first 100 days and day-to-day media operations.Some of those who worked in Downing Street at the time say their recollections of the atmosphere differ from those of Gray. One senior female adviser from the time pushed back on the suggestion there was a culture of briefings against Gray, describing it as “precisely the kind of paranoia that, ironically, Sue herself brought into the building”.“She was literally clapped in with genuine excitement about her experience. But she quickly undermined herself. It didn’t need to be this way, she wrote her own story,” she said.Another former female adviser also disputed the idea there was a boys’ club: “Before Sue’s arrival there was no narrative about a ‘boys’ club’ and in my whole time in there, I never recognised it. There have been damaging implications from that divisiveness; two and a half years on, the new prime minister is being asked about it, costing him time and energy, and the Labour government’s reputation.”There had been speculation that Burnham couldbring Gray, now a Labour peer, back into governmentin an advisory role. Asked whether she could be enticed back into another high-profile job, Gray said she was enjoying herself outside government and was still “taking part in many aspects of public life”.Looking back on what she thought had gone wrong with Starmer’s government, Gray said: “I think government and opposition are very different, and I’m not sure I would say they shouldn’t have survived, but I do think that we needed bigger people, people with bigger experience to be heads of, whether it was comms or policy or strategy. Government is very, very different.”Explore more on these topicsSue GrayKeir StarmerMorgan McSweeneyLabourShareReuse this content

title: Ukrainian publishers call for support after Russian attacks destroy 10m books | Publishing | The Guardian
description: The country risks ‘the collapse of the entire book ecosystem’ following destruction of warehouses in July and August, say Ukrainian publishers
Author: Emma Loffhagen
Headline: The country risks ‘the collapse of the entire book ecosystem’ following destruction of warehouses in July and August, say Ukrainian publishers
Content: Firefighters in Kharkiv, Ukraine, after Russian drones struck a warehouse on 1 August, destroying 8m books.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFirefighters in Kharkiv, Ukraine, after Russian drones struck a warehouse on 1 August, destroying 8m books.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesPublishingUkrainian publishers call for support after Russian attacks destroy 10m booksThe country risks ‘the collapse of the entire book ecosystem’ following destruction of warehouses in July and August, say Ukrainian publishersEmma LoffhagenThu 20 Aug 2026 11.37 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 12.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Ukrainian Book Institute hascalled onthe international publishing community to support Ukrainian publishers after Russian attacks in July and early August destroyed about 10m books and a significant share of the country’s book production capacity.The institute said the attacks on publishing, printing and warehouse infrastructure had left some companies at risk of financial collapse.A major attack on 1 August hit warehouses belonging to the RNK-Ranok publishing group in Kharkiv, destroying approximately 8m books, following July attacks in Kyiv which led to the loss of more than 1.5m books. In all, the recent attacks have led to the destruction of approximately 30% of the volume of books produced annually inUkraine.The RNK-Ranok logistics centre, which stores books for the company’s many imprints, is also the distribution centre for the national bookselling chain KnyhoLand, which runs 51 shops and several websites.Along with the estimated 8m books lost, a further 600,000 school textbooks were destroyed. The total loss has been preliminarily estimated at almost 1bn hryvnias (£16.5m).“At this stage, we face the risk of the collapse of the entire book ecosystem,” said Oleksandra Koval, director of the Ukrainian Book Institute.The institute is askingfor donationsto support Ukrainian publishers, and is calling on the international publishing community to work with Ukrainian publishers and raise awareness about Russian attacks on Ukrainian culture.Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and now occupies about a fifth of Ukrainian territory.On 16 August, a Russian attack on Kyivled to a fire breaking out at the Pochaina book market,destroying several rows of stalls, books and vendors’ property. The Pochaina market, founded in 1997, was once one of Ukraine’s largest book markets, with hundreds of stalls and books from more than 120 publishers.The institute said the book industry was of “strategic importance” to Ukraine, preserving and promoting Ukrainian culture and giving the country’s voice a platform at home and abroad.The Ukrainian government is developing support programmes for affected publishers and printing companies, including grants to restore equipment and compensation for property damage. But the institute said publishers’ losses could not be fully covered by state assistance.“Against the backdrop of Russia’s ongoing attempts to destroy Ukrainian identity, culture and history, Ukrainian publishing has a special mission,” saidOlena Odynoka, deputy director for international cooperation of the Ukrainian Book Institute. “Supporting Ukrainian publishers today is not simply about preserving an industry. It is about defending Ukraine’s right to speak in its own voice and shape its own narrative in the world.”The institute also called for an end to cooperation with Russian publishers and literary agencies, saying that solidarity with Ukrainian publishers was crucial to preserving cultural heritage that Russia was “deliberately trying to destroy”.Explore more on these topicsPublishingUkraineEuropeRussianewsShareReuse this content

title: Lily Hooper’s family was told she’d been found alive. ‘She’s coming home,’ her father said – then tears of joy turned to grief | New South Wales | The Guardian
description: After eight days missing in the rugged NSW bush, word came through that the 18-year-old had been located. Her family were waiting with presents
Author: Ima Caldwell
Headline: After eight days missing in the rugged NSW bush, word came through that the 18-year-old had been located. Her family were waiting with presents
Content: The command post for the search operation for Lily Hooper in the NSW southern highlands.Photograph: Ima Caldwell/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe command post for the search operation for Lily Hooper in the NSW southern highlands.Photograph: Ima Caldwell/The GuardianNew South WalesLily Hooper’s family was told she’d been found alive. ‘She’s coming home,’ her father said – then tears of joy turned to griefAfter eight days missing in the rugged NSW bush, word came through that the 18-year-old had been located. Her family were waiting with presentsFollow our Australia news live blog for latest updatesGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastIma Caldwellin MittagongThu 20 Aug 2026 19.58 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 20.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe rugged landscape of theNew South Walessouthern highlands loomed large on Thursday evening. This country had just revived, then killed hope. A young woman was found “alive”, but then it was confirmed she was dead: desperation, confusion, tragedy reigned.Here, where the bitumen of Wombeyan Caves Road runs into unsealed dirt, rolling hills dotted with cattle give way to expansive mountains. The late-afternoon sun sends long, beaming rays past the edges of clouds, casting a warm glow on distant cliff faces.From ‘elation’ to ‘terrible news’ in 10 minutes: how the confusion over missing bushwalker Lily Hooper unfoldedRead moreA few hours earlier, after eight agonising days of searchers scouring the Nattai national park, 90km south-west of Sydney, for the missing 18-year-old hiker Lily Hooper, fears had abruptly turned to joy. Police told her family she had been found alive.Footage from Channel Seven showed the relief and elation. Family and friends embraced, in tears. Her father, Jim Hooper, said “they’re going to get her now by the sound of it … she might be going straight to hospital I’d say”.He showed off the guitar and packet of Tim Tams he’d brought to the site “because it might lure her out of the bush”.Her smiling mother, Kirrily, said she had washed her hair and “put my good sneakers on” in anticipation of good news.There was a toast in celebration.“I was never going to give up,” Jim said. “She’s a beautiful girl and she’s coming home.”View image in fullscreenThe mountains where Lily Hooper went missing.Photograph: Ima Caldwell/The GuardianThe NSW premier, Chris Minns, interrupted a grilling in an estimates hearing back in Sydney toannounce the discoveryabout midday, sharing a curious detail that Lily had been found “with half a bottle of water”.Hope was shattered barely 30 minutes later.Minns, who had believed he was sharing good news, now interrupted proceedings again.“I’ve got some terrible news,” he said. “I apologise …Lily’s body has been found.” The bottle of water reference may have been rescuer code – not proof of life.The SES commissioner, Mick Wassing, on Friday would explain “it’s very common that code words are given to search and rescue crews” to avoid details being overheard by others on radios.“My understanding is that that’s what has occurred in this situation,” Wassing said.View image in fullscreenThe bitumen of Wombeyan Caves Road runs into the unsealed dirt of Wanganderry Road.Photograph: Ima Caldwell/The GuardianOn Thursday in the mountains, TV cameras at the site backed away, showing the family embracing, now in grief.The police commissioner, Mal Lanyon, later told reporters in Goulburn that the devastating miscommunication was “born out of elation”.“Tragically, that miscommunication then led to a deflation, and obviously, we know now, an impact on her family,” Lanyon said.Lily, an experienced hiker, had been found dead off the trail, a “significant distance” from her car.The assistant commissioner Joseph Cassar told reporters in Moss Vale on Thursday afternoon that the searchers had carried handheld radios and faced communication challenges in the “thick, dense terrain”.Nattai national parkNightfallAs the sun set over the southern highlands command post, the temperature dipped to a bitter chill. By 5.30pm, the sun was gone and the landscape stripped of its warmth, leaving muted greys and browns.Police said Lily was last seen wearing a T-shirt and shorts, and it was unknown if she had any equipment with her.The command post, where the search was coordinated, was now still. About 100 Australian Defence Force personnel had joined the operation in the 24 hours before the teenager was located. Almost 1,000 searchers and volunteers had been involved overall.Missing teen hiker Lily Hooper found dead as NSW police apologise for miscommunication ‘born of elation’Read moreEmergency workers and volunteers were packing up and driving out on Thursday evening. A NSW Rural Fire Service vehicle slowly towed a trailer back down the dirt road, leaving the command post and passing police cars.Bonnum PicThe mourning quiet was broken intermittently by the evening calls of birds and the low hum of idling engines.A significant presence remained stationed at the operation base. Unmarked four-wheel drives sat alongside SES vehicles, police search and rescue vans, and a large police incident response unit.The procedures of death were under way. In the distance, a group of officers wearing white jumpsuits gathered.Hooper’s car had been parked near the trail head on Wanganderry Road at High Range, Cassar said.The assistant commissioner said it was not yet clear how she died or if she had sustained injuries.A report was to be prepared for the coroner, investigating the time, place and circumstances of Hooper’s death, in addition to the communications problems.View image in fullscreenA solitary helicopter sits near the dwindling, demobilised search party.Photograph: Ima Caldwell/The GuardianAs night closed in, a solitary helicopter sat grounded in a field of tall, brown grass, near the demobilised search party. The last traces of light vanished entirely from the sky.Then, the whir of a second helicopter overhead broke the silence, touching down at the command post, just as the landscape went dark.On Friday morning, police announced that Hooper’s body had been winched out of the bush overnight.Explore more on these topicsNew South WalesAustralian police and policingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Women rally in support of Lindsay Clancy: ‘Nobody takes us seriously’ | Massachusetts | The Guardian
description: Hundreds of supporters, many wearing pink clothing, gather outside court in Massachusetts as trial continues
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Hundreds of supporters, many wearing pink clothing, gather outside court in Massachusetts as trial continues
Content: Supporters of Lindsay Clancy stand outside Plymouth superior court on 20 August 2026. Clancy is on trial for the death of her three children in Massachusetts.Photograph: Josh Reynolds/APView image in fullscreenSupporters of Lindsay Clancy stand outside Plymouth superior court on 20 August 2026. Clancy is on trial for the death of her three children in Massachusetts.Photograph: Josh Reynolds/APMassachusettsWomen rally in support of Lindsay Clancy: ‘Nobody takes us seriously’Hundreds of supporters, many wearing pink clothing, gather outside court in Massachusetts as trial continuesAssociated PressThu 20 Aug 2026 15.31 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 19.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHundreds of Lindsay Clancy supporters, many wearing pink clothing emblazoned with phrases such as “Believe”, “She Needed Help” and “Peace For Lindsay”, gathered on Thursday outside the courthouse where she is on trial in the killings of her three children.Several of the 300 women, and a few men, said Clancy’s story resonated with them and that they wanted to raise awareness about how the mental health system treats women. Clancy’s lawyer does not dispute that she killed the children, but says she should not be held criminally responsible because she was mentally ill.The live-streamed trial in Plymouth,Massachusettshas sparked massive discussions online and has brought attention to postpartum psychosis. Clancy’s attorney, Kevin Reddington, says she suffered from this rare mental illness, which is linked to the stress, sleep deprivation and hormonal changes that follow childbirth. Reddington said she also has bipolar disorder and had repeatedly sought expert help. After strangling her children, Clancy jumped from a second-story window and remains paralyzed from the waist down.Prosecutors say the former labor and delivery nurse planned the 24 January 2023, killings and contrived to get her husband out of the house by sending him to pick up medicine for one of their children and dinner for the family.How ‘forensic fandom’ in Lindsay Clancy trial threaten postpartum psychosis awarenessRead moreThursday’s rally was the first time during the nearly month-long trial that supporters have come out in such large numbers.“Women are being dismissed, neglected and ignored when we speak up,” said April Vincent, a 52-year-old paralegal from Providence, Rhode Island. “We’re scared because nobody takes us seriously.”The women stood silently for more than an hour ahead of Thursday’s proceedings, where a chaplain called by the defense testified about visiting Clancy in the hospital after the killings.At the sight of Reddington outside the courthouse, the crowd broke into applause.Rally organizer Renee Kimball implored the crowd to trust that Reddington “has Lindsay’s fight”.Toward the end of their rally, supporters formed a circle, said the Lord’s Prayer, held up their arms and formed hearts with their hands. Some held flags from different countries to show that the support for Clancy was international.Clancy, 36, has pleaded not guilty to murder charges in the deaths of Callan, Dawson and Cora Clancy, who ranged from eight months to five years old. Researchers estimate that postpartum psychosis – which is more serious and less common than postpartum depression – afflicts one to two cases per 1,000 women after delivery.Jeanne Zaborski, a 72-year-old retired nurse from Rockland,Massachusetts, said she hopes the case raises awareness about postpartum health. She and many others at the rally said they had been following the trial almost daily.“It’s very sad,” Zaborski said. “I am a mother. I am a grandmother. I have a sister who had problems after birth and it’s just very sad. I hope Lindsay gets the care she needs and deserves and other women will come together like we did today.”In court, Sheila Cavanaugh, a chaplain at Brigham and Women’s Hospital in Boston, testified that when she first visited Clancy, she was unconscious. By 31 January 2023, Clancy was conscious and no longer connected to a ventilator, Cavanaugh said, but “her emotional state was very neutral – a flat affect.”Cavanaugh said she “vividly remembers” one of the first things Clancy said to her.“She said to me, as I held her hand to comfort her, ‘I’m so glad my children are safe,’” Cavanaugh said. “I replied theologically to Lindsay. I said, ‘Lindsay, your children are safe. They’re safe in heaven with God’.”“We prayed for them,” said Cavanaugh, who saw Clancy more than 200 times and has visited her at the state mental hospital where she resides.Cavanaugh told the court that Clancy “alluded to hearing a voice, and the voice, according to Lindsay, told her that if she did not follow the command, neither she nor her children would be safe”.Prosecutors questioned why Cavanaugh had not documented the disclosure about the voice in notes she made in Clancy’s hospital record.“I’m not there to evaluate the patient; I’m there to bear witness to their suffering,” Cavanaugh said, noting that she is not medically trained and her notes aren’t meant to be verbatim transcripts of conversations.Their last visit was right before the trial started. She said Clancy “talks frequently about her children”.“She loves them deeply,” Cavanaugh said. “She carries immense grief.”In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsMassachusettsUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Travelodge boss quits amid fallout over hotel chain’s security failings | Travel & leisure | The Guardian
description: Joanna Boydell steps down after widespread criticism over company’s handling of guest safety issues
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Joanna Boydell steps down after widespread criticism over company’s handling of guest safety issues
Content: Travelodge said Joanna Boydell had stepped down and been temporarily replaced by its finance chief, Ray Reidy.Photograph: Hollie Adams/Bloomberg/GettyView image in fullscreenTravelodge said Joanna Boydell had stepped down and been temporarily replaced by its finance chief, Ray Reidy.Photograph: Hollie Adams/Bloomberg/GettyTravel & leisureTravelodge boss quits amid fallout over hotel chain’s security failingsJoanna Boydell steps down after widespread criticism over company’s handling of guest safety issuesKalyeena MakortoffThu 20 Aug 2026 08.47 EDTFirst published on Thu 20 Aug 2026 03.27 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe boss of Travelodge has resigned after a backlash over security failings at the hotel chain, including a case where adomestic abuser was given a key to a woman’s roombefore assaulting her.In acompany statementon Thursday, Travelodge said Joanna Boydell had stepped down and been temporarily replaced by its finance chief, Ray Reidy. The company has launched a formal search for a permanent substitute.The Travelodge chair, Stephen Shurrock, said the announcement “does not change anything about our focus on safety and security”.In March, Keir Starmer, the then prime minister, wrote to Boydellwarning that she must “seriously engage with MPs” over concerns about women’s safety after a spate of security breaches had left guests at risk of attack.The letter was sent after a hotel guest in Berkshire was sexually assaulted by a man who had wrongly been given access to her room in 2022. He had falsely claimed he was her partner, before sexually assaulting her in her hotel bed. The victim was later offered what she described as an “insulting” £30 refund.Woman assaulted after Travelodge staff gave room key to her abuserRead moreEarlier this month, it emerged that in October another woman who had been staying in one of Travelodge’s London hotels to escape her domestic abuser had been attacked after the man was given a key to her room by reception staff.He had persuaded staff to give him access, saying his girlfriend was upstairs having a seizure. Staff did not check with the woman before giving him the card and pointed him to her room where he kicked in the door, assaulted her and tried to grab her phone.The woman, who wants to remain anonymous, said she had run “shaking, crying and begging for help”.“I thought someone would protect me,” she told the BBC. Staff then offered her another room in the hotel.Travelodge has previously defended itself, saying such instances were “very rare” and customer safety was a priority.View image in fullscreenTravelodge said it had conducted an ‘audit’ to ensure all of its UK rooms had a secondary deadbolt and was making changes to its room access security policy.Photograph: PA Thompson/GettyJo Mackie, an employment law partner at the law firm Michelmores, said there was a risk Travelodge would go into “freefall” if it failed to regain public trust. “Travelodge has been beset by awful stories involving sexual assault and poor security at hotels,” she said. “The CEO is likely to have been under great pressure to resign for some time to try and reset the brand by hiring a new leader who will overhaul the image and try to regain trust.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“That is going to be incredibly hard for the incoming CEO to do, as these stories continue to appear in the media. It’s difficult to see who Travelodge could bring in who would instil trust and confidence quickly and stop the business going into freefall.”Alongside the company’s latest financial results, released on Thursday, Travelodge said a leading barrister had conducted a review of its room access security policies and escalation procedures, and its own internal review was ongoing.The company added that it had also conducted an “audit” to ensure all of its UK rooms had a secondary deadbolt, and was making changes to its room access security policy.Travelodge said: “Any additional or replacement room key now requires explicit permission from the guest staying in the room. This builds on our existing policy to never confirm to any third party that a guest is staying at one of our hotels.”The company said 12,000 of its customer-facing staff across more than 600 of its UK sites were being trained in the new room access security policy, and a violence against women and girls expert had been brought in to train Travelodge’s senior bosses.“They have reviewed our existing policies and procedures and will assist with how we respond to the independent review and its recommendation,” the hotel chain said. “The safety and security of customers in our hotels is extremely important and we want everyone to be safe, and feel safe, in our hotels. We have acted quickly to make changes to improve safety and security across our operations.”Explore more on these topicsTravel & leisureCorporate governanceWomenDomestic violenceViolence against women and girlsSexual harassmentHotelsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Specsavers pays £12m dividend to parent company after jump in earnings | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: Pre-tax profits rose at high street opticians to £429.7m in the year to February while sales rose 7% to £4.3bn
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Pre-tax profits rose at high street opticians to £429.7m in the year to February while sales rose 7% to £4.3bn
Content: Specsavers shared out a payment of almost £258m to  its hundreds of independent partners.Photograph: PjrTravel/AlamyView image in fullscreenSpecsavers shared out a payment of almost £258m to  its hundreds of independent partners.Photograph: PjrTravel/AlamyRetail industrySpecsavers pays £12m dividend to parent company after jump in earningsPre-tax profits rose at high street opticians to £429.7m in the year to February while sales rose 7% to £4.3bnSarah ButlerThu 20 Aug 2026 11.55 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 15.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSpecsavers has paid £12m to its parent company controlled by its founders Doug andDame Mary Perkinsafter the high street optician’s profits increased by more than a quarter.The group operates nearly 3,000 optometry, audiology and ophthalmology businesses globally in at least eight countries, including more than 1,200 in the UK, through hundreds of independent partners.Specsavers shared out a payment of almost £258m to these shop owners, up from £239m in the previous year.It said it had revived paying a dividend to its Perkins-controlled parent, Specsavers International Healthcare Limited, after pre-tax profits rose to £429.7m in the year to this February, while sales increased 7% to £4.3bn.No dividend was paid to the Guernsey-based parent in the previous year, when Specsavers said it had “paused all dividends” as a one-off “due to economic and political uncertainty and their own significant expansion and investment”. In the two prior years dividends of about £15m were paid.“The resumption of dividend payments at a level in line with historic amounts reflects the strength of the business and confidence in its future performance,” a spokesperson said. “Importantly, this has been achieved while continuing to invest in the organisation’s long-term growth and their commitment to delivering value for customers.”Specsavers said sales had risen “as we continue to attract customers to the brand despite a challenging macro-economic landscape”.View image in fullscreenDame Mary Perkins, co-founder of Specsavers.Photograph: Graham Turner/The GuardianAccording to the accounts, profits rose as the company had strived to keep costs flat and reduced “non-value add activities”.They said inflation “will continue to present both challenges and opportunity and our regional plans are constantly being reviewed and updated to respond to changing market forces”. The company said it aimed to “absorb inflationary price increases where possible and to avoid passing increased costs on to our customers”.The group faced inflation on wages, utilities and from supplier costs, as well as increasing regulatory pressure. It is also investing in improving its website as customers increasingly want to mix in-store visits with interacting online.The Perkinses, whose combined fortune is now calculated at £1.4bn by the Sunday Times rich list, founded Specsavers in 1983. The business was devised at the family table tennis table in Guernsey, and the first stores opened on the island and in the UK the following year.The couple, now in their 80s, met on their first day at Cardiff University and set up their own opticians when they were in their early 20s.In the 1960s it was still rare for women to train as opticians, let alone start their own businesses. Mary Perkins was one of four women on her optometry course in a class of 30.Explore more on these topicsRetail industryAnnual resultsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Boohoo fined €2.3m by French watchdog over deceptive discounts | Boohoo | The Guardian
description: Fashion site also broke rules on labelling by using terms ‘leather’ or ‘suede’ for synthetic products
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: Fashion site also broke rules on labelling by using terms ‘leather’ or ‘suede’ for synthetic products
Content: The French fine follows a settlement in a $100m US lawsuit in which fake promotions were allegedly used to mislead shoppers.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/GettyView image in fullscreenThe French fine follows a settlement in a $100m US lawsuit in which fake promotions were allegedly used to mislead shoppers.Photograph: Justin Tallis/AFP/GettyBoohooBoohoo fined €2.3m by French watchdog over deceptive discountsFashion site also broke rules on labelling by using terms ‘leather’ or ‘suede’ for synthetic productsSarah ButlerThu 20 Aug 2026 08.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe British online fashion sellerBoohoohas been fined €2.3m (£2m) by France’s consumer watchdog ⁠for deceptive ⁠practices ​such as offering fake discounts.The Manchester-based firm, whose parent company renamed itself Debenhams Group last year, was found to have exaggerated the discounts it was offering, giving shoppers a false impression ⁠of the savings they were making, ​according to the directorate-general for competition, ‌consumer affairs and ‌fraud control.Of ‌the promotions examined by the watchdog, 40% were found not to be real price reductions, 7% were a lower reduction than advertised, and 48% were a price ‌increase.Boohoo also used terms such as “leather” or “suede” to sell synthetic products, ​contravening French rules on product labelling, the regulator said.The fine comes four years after Boohooreached a settlementin a $100m (£73m) US lawsuit that alleged the retailer used fake promotions to mislead shoppers.The settlement of the case, brought in California, was agreed “without admission of liability”, according to Boohoo, whose brands PrettyLittleThing and NastyGal were accused of running sham sales and promotions in the US for at least four to five years.The French fine comes after a rocky few years for the online seller, which has faced rising competition from cut-price rivals such as Shein, Temu and the secondhand site Vinted as well increased delivery costs and tariffs in the US.The group has been battling to revive sales after aboom during the Covid pandemic, when high street shops were closed. With profits under pressure from inflation on wages and new regulatory demands, such as packaging and European textile waste rules, more established UK online sellers are struggling to invest sufficiently to keep up with Shein’s digital innovation.Boohoo’s brand was also tarnished in 2020 after reports of poor working practices in Leicester factories used by the company were found to be“substantially true”in adamning independent report.Debenhams Group, which owns brands including Oasis, Warehouse and Karen Millen as well as its namesake brand and Boohoo, in February raised £35m from shareholders to cut debt and has faced criticisms of its strategy from its biggest shareholder, the Sports Direct founder Mike Ashley’s Frasers Group, which now owns more than a quarter of the company.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA spokesperson for Boohoo said the problems related to a period from October 2023 to February 2024, when the business was under its previous management, and were now resolved.“We have cooperated fully with the regulator, ​and continue to ​review how ⁠we price and label our products,” the spokesperson said.Explore more on these topicsBoohooDebenhamsRetail industryManchesterConsumer affairsFashion industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Founder of China’s Evergrande jailed for life after pleading guilty to fraud | Evergrande | The Guardian
description: Hui Ka Yan also forfeits all his personal property and the company he set up is given hefty fines
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: Hui Ka Yan also forfeits all his personal property and the company he set up is given hefty fines
Content: Hui Ka Yan, the founder of the property developer Evergrande, in court in Shenzhen. The court said he had ‘severely disrupted the order of the socialist market economy’.Photograph: Xinhua/APView image in fullscreenHui Ka Yan, the founder of the property developer Evergrande, in court in Shenzhen. The court said he had ‘severely disrupted the order of the socialist market economy’.Photograph: Xinhua/APEvergrandeFounder of China’s Evergrande jailed for life after pleading guilty to fraudHui Ka Yan also forfeits all his personal property and the company he set up is given hefty finesBusiness live – latest updatesAmy HawkinsSenior China correspondentThu 20 Aug 2026 08.03 EDTFirst published on Thu 20 Aug 2026 07.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe founder ofEvergrande, one of China’s largest property developers, has been sentenced to life in prison and had all of his personal property confiscated.Hui Ka Yan, 67 and once named by Forbes as China’s richest man, with a net worth of $42.5bn (£31.2bn) in 2017,pleaded guiltyin April to eight charges.These included misuse of funds, fundraising fraud, illegally taking public deposits, illegally extending loans, fraudulently issuing securities and bribery.The company Hui founded, Evergrande Group, was fined 8.8bn yuan (£950m), while its property arm was fined 7bn yuan, according to Chinese state media.Hui’s convictions relate to a debt crisis at Evergrande, which shookChinaat a time when the government had been trying to make the world’s second-largest economy less reliant on the real estate sector.Evergrande, whichdelisted from the Hong Kong stock exchangelast year, has defaulted on most of its $300bn ​in liabilities.Shenzhen intermediate people’s court in southern China said in its ruling that between 2016 and 2021, Hui “violated state laws by employing methods such as sustained, large-scale financial fraud to inflate assets and conceal liabilities”.It said Hui’s actions had “severely disrupted the order of the socialist market economy” and “caused exceptionally heavy economic losses”.More than 50 individuals linked to Evergrande were also sentenced on Thursday, with prison terms ranging from 20 months to 18 years.Evergrande’s troubles began in 2020 when the Chinese government introduced regulations limiting the amount of debt that property companies could hold. This torpedoed the debt-fuelled real estate sector, which has traditionally accounted for between one-quarter and one-third of China’s GDP.Construction stalled on hundreds of property developments as companies scrambled for cash and struggled to pay suppliers amid weak demand during the Covid-19 pandemic. Astudypublished this year estimated that the regulatory crackdown led to about $347bn in sunk costs across the Chinese economy.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHui’s company was at the centre of this crisis. Evergrande’s implosion has been seen as a symbol for the wider troubles in the property sector, which still weighs heavily on the Chinese economy.Born to a poor family in rural Henan province, Hui was raised by his grandmother before setting up Evergrande in 1996.In 2018 he thanked the Chinese Communist party for providing “everything that Evergrande and I have”.Explore more on these topicsEvergrandeChinaReal estateThe super-richAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: Lambchop: Punching the Clown review – spectral, spellbindingly ambiguous stirring of US history | Music | The Guardian
description: Sounding weathered but undimmed, Kurt Wagner feels as if he’s standing right in front of you as he sings these superb, choir-swathed songs that invite and unsettle
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Sounding weathered but undimmed, Kurt Wagner feels as if he’s standing right in front of you as he sings these superb, choir-swathed songs that invite and unsettle
Content: Pained ruminations … Kurt Wagner of Lambchop.Photograph: Graham TolbertView image in fullscreenPained ruminations … Kurt Wagner of Lambchop.Photograph: Graham TolbertAlexis Petridis's album of the weekMusicReviewLambchop: Punching the Clown review – spectral, spellbindingly ambiguous stirring of US history(City Slang)Sounding weathered but undimmed, Kurt Wagner feels as if he’s standing right in front of you as he sings superb, choir-swathed songs that invite and unsettleAlexis PetridisThu 20 Aug 2026 07.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 12.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThirty-two years on from their debut album – and 26 fromNixon, the gorgeous country/soul confection that brought “Nashville’s most fucked-up country band” to a wider audience – Lambchop find themselves in a curious position. Their sole continuous member Kurt Wagner has displayed an admirable disinclination to rest on his laurels. He followed up Nixon with the austere, piano-drivenIs a Womanand subsequently diverted into electronics, smothered his voice in Auto-Tune and distortion. Their last album, 2022’sThe Bible, threw up everything from house music to glitchy rhythms to ambient drift to accompany Wagner’s pained ruminations on mortality and faith.View image in fullscreenThe artwork for Punching the Clown.Throughout,Lambchophave kept up a remarkable level of quality control that’s meant they’ve ended up being slightly underrated or at least taken for granted. There’s been no career-defining crossover hit, no unexpected viral success, no foundation-shaking disaster followed by an attention-grabbing return to form; just a stream of really good albums and positive reviews. It’s the kind of steady success that’s hard to maintain but easy to overlook in an attention-deficit economy.So perhaps we should detect a certain sardonic note to the voice that unexpectedly disrupts Just West of Nicollet, the opening track of Lambchop’s 17th studio album. A rapper in braggadocious fairground-barker mode appears midway through, excitedly bellows “LAMBCHOP NEW SHIT!” then vanishes, never to be heard from again. It couldn’t sound more out of place with the music, which, like the rest of Punching the Clown, pares back Lambchop’s sound to bare essentials: acoustic guitar and banjo – the latter played by Bon Iver’s Justin Vernon – the very occasional deployment of bass or piano, the faintest smear of electronics on Weakened. Wagner’s voice appears stripped of Auto-Tune, distortion, even reverb: he sounds as if he’s singing directly in front of you.Lambchop: Weakened – videoIt would be spartan were it not for the backing vocals, provided by the London Choir and the Eau Claire Vocal Sextet, and inspired by Wagner encountering lined-out singing, a form of hymnody with roots in 17th century Britainthat’s still used in some southern Appalachian Baptist churches. You can trace the outline of its call-and-response structure in the way the title track and Cigar surge from Wagner’s voice – weathered, nicotine-stained, intimate – to choral stridency or lushness, although there are moments, as on Afterburner, when the backing vocals also seem to evoke the lovely, warm harmonies of starkly arranged pre-second world war pop singles by the Mills Brothers or the Ink Spots.An album this unvarnished needs strong tunes – not always a given with Lambchop’s work, which can lean into the spectral and the atmospheric, but they’re here in abundance. The rich swirl of harmonies at the centre of Andrew Jackson Asshat is breathtaking; Stella boasts a melody that, in the best possible way, could have been written at any point in the last 100 years; The New World Wave beautifully juxtaposes Wagner’s muttered vocal with a dreamy chorus carried by the choir. The lyrics are harder to button. Wagner tends to write obliquely, forcing the listener to latch on to odd, striking lines, like snatches of overheard conversation, and that’s certainly the case here: you might expect a song as stridently titled as Andrew Jackson Asshat to concern Donald Trump, who’s proved remarkably eager to compare himself to America’s controversial seventh president, but its subject is more implied than explicit: glancing references to Jesus and the parable of the rich man and Lazarus suggest someone posthumously suffering in hell.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toSleeve NotesGet music news, bold reviews and unexpected extras. Every genre, every era, every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘I don’t want to retreat any more’: William Tyler on grief, alcoholism and his healing new albumRead moreIt’s not the only moment where Punching the Clown feels informed by current events. White People borrows the chorus of Allan Toussaint’s late-70s funk track Night People, changes one word, and shifts its mood from eager to ominous, leaving it unclear as to whether the titular Caucasians “looking at each other, waiting for something to happen” are about to cause havoc, fearful about the future or stunned into inaction. The latter theme recurs in Afterburner: “America on mute … we’re so broke we can’t even pay attention / My God.” Its references to the past seem similarly ill-omened: Stella is studded with fragments of Wabash Cannonball, a folk song about a fictional train that carries the dead away; The New World Wave depicts a family, then adds “in 1929”, pitching them into the Great Depression.It’s an album that lures the listener in with the warmth and intimacy of its sound, but ultimately leaves you unsettled. An intermittent but unignorable sense of disquiet hangs around long after Punching the Clown is over, its haunting quality amplified by the fact that you can never be 100% certain exactly what Wagner is driving at. It’s strange and powerful, the kind of carefully balanced impact that clearly requires skill, developed over time, and time to develop is one thing that steady, unflashy success affords an artist. Kurt Wagner seems to be more than fine with that.This week Alexis listened toL’Rain – BorderlineL’Rain’s fourth albumFata Morganais every bit as seductive and strange as you might hope given her past form: Borderline marshals her scattered, dream-like sound into something almost anthemic.Explore more on these topicsMusicAlexis Petridis's album of the weekAmericanaLambchopIndiereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Little Animals review – Motherland milquetoast creates a clever climate plea | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Paul Ready’s playwriting debut expertly utilises his bumbling acting persona to examine what is enough in our response to climate emergency
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Paul Ready’s playwriting debut expertly utilises his bumbling acting persona to examine what is enough in our response to climate emergency
Content: A captivating performance … Paul Ready in Little Animals.Photograph: Jennifer Forward-HayterView image in fullscreenA captivating performance … Paul Ready in Little Animals.Photograph: Jennifer Forward-HayterEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewLittle Animals review – Motherland milquetoast creates a clever climate pleaTraverse at Royal Lyceum Studio, EdinburghPaul Ready’s playwriting debut expertly utilises his bumbling acting persona to examine what is enough in our response to climate emergencyMark FisherThu 20 Aug 2026 09.52 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNobody does self-effacement as well asPaul Ready. The Motherland/Ann Droid actor excels at playing the kind of man who apologises for his own existence, well-meaning, but insecure – often comically so. He hesitates, smiles sheepishly, backtracks and gabbles to fill the silence. He, he, he is forever launching, launching into sentences, sentences that never get all the way to the … We get the gist.It is the same now he is making his playwriting debut with Little Animals and it works to his advantage. Performing in the round to a small audience, he gives every impression of having interrupted us in the middle of something else. We are not here, he ascertains, to remember his good friend Richard, in fact, we did not even know him, but sorry, if it is all right, he will tell us about him anyway.Richard, it transpires, is the good guy in the story. He is the schoolboy disruptor with the courage to resist social pressure, the one who scoffed at their entitled classmate for the arrogance of writing an essay called How I Would Change the World. “We need to completely rewrite the story,” says Richard, committing his life to environmental activism in anera of global heating.If Richard is the good guy, what does that make our unnamed narrator? Surely this endearing man in suit and tie, circling the room, catching us in the eye, bonding with each nervous laugh, is too reasonable to be on the wrong side. Like any of us, he recycles his waste and boycotts the correct things. He works hard, loves his family and believes in introducing daughter Ellie to the cultures of the world.Sam Eley Is Basil Crumbwick review – cantankerous cult hit brings laugh after laughRead moreAnd because he is so reasonable, it makes Richard seem hysterical. His protests are surely the actions of an overgrown schoolboy, a man who knows nothing of responsibility, who is simply not realistic. Could he not have made the same modest compromises as the rest of us? Richard makes him defensive and indignant.Directed by Caroline Steinbeis for Pentabus andFern Culture, a company encouraging better storytelling about the climate, Ready performs in natural light with neither props nor set. In a captivating performance, his message is familiar, but his call to action no less urgent.At Traverse atRoyal Lyceum Studio, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: It Ends review – gripping micro-budget horror ranks among the year’s best  | Horror films | The Guardian
description: Led by a stellar cast of gen-Z newcomers, Alex Ullom’s directorial debut is an expertly crafted nightmare about a road trip gone wrong
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: Led by a stellar cast of gen-Z newcomers, Alex Ullom’s directorial debut is an expertly crafted nightmare about a road trip gone wrong
Content: Phinehas Yoon, Akira Jackson and Noah Toth in It Ends.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonView image in fullscreenPhinehas Yoon, Akira Jackson and Noah Toth in It Ends.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonHorror filmsReviewIt Ends review – gripping micro-budget horror ranks among the year’s bestLed by a stellar cast of gen-Z newcomers, Alex Ullom’s directorial debut is an expertly crafted nightmare about a road trip gone wrongOwen MyersThu 20 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTime loops often feel like the movies’ favorite zany stylistic trick: Bill Murrayplottingto win Andie MacDowell’s heart, a college student solving themysteryof her own grizzly murder, or as a ruse for Anne Hathaway toface off with a T rex. The excellent new indie horror film It Ends takes a different approach with its nightmarish depiction of a carful of friends stuck in an endlessly repeating day. It’s less of the moony japes ofGroundhog DayorPalm Springsthan an arthouse spin on the Prometheus myth, with the unfortunate souls of the film cursed not with death but with the torture of eternal life.Insidious: Out of the Further review – evil returns but so does boredomRead moreAfter helping their friend move into a new apartment, a crew of aimless twentysomethings take a late-night drive to get food, but after GPS leads them deeper and deeper into a desolate forest, it’s clear that they have lost their way. When they pull over, they are set upon by a group of people that look eerily similar to them – young people who are dressed like they stepped out to the corner store and couldn’t find their way back. “They look scared,” one character says with a pained expression. “Why are they scared?”As the group swarm their Jeep every time they pull over, the central quartet has no option but to keep driving deeper and deeper into the unknown forest on a road which seemingly has no end. It turns out that even stranger things are afoot: the car’s gas dial hasn’t moved, and they oddly aren’t craving any of their normal bodily needs. “I’m not tired, not hungry, and [have] no sexual arousal,” one character informs us, just in case we were starting to wonder why no one was getting frisky in the back seat.Made for just $50,000, there’s a palpable sense of dread to first-time director Alex Ullom’s film, mirrored by the perfectly creepy, creaky score that plays as the characters agonize over what led them to this wretched fate. Could it be a wormhole or an ancient curse? Karma for their past misdeeds? Is the doofy Tyler (Mitchell Cole) being punished for dumping a girl after she suggested a date at the local pumpkin patch, or, more gravely, is it something to do with the recent suicide attempt of Day (Akira Jackson)? In the absence of definitive answers, It Ends begins to feel oddly in sync with the kind of existentialist questions that might cross your mind on a daily basis. What’s really the difference between an endless road to nowhere and the everyday terror of hurtling towards a future where nothing is promised and everything will likely get worse?Running counter to the ennui is the cast’s warm chemistry. Naturalistic performances anchor some of the sweetest scenes as the foursome celebrate each other’s birthdays and play made-up road trip games. (In “Like or Dislike”, they debate the merits of windshield wipers or “the ocean”.) The hatchback they live in becomes the film’s chief setting as It Ends evolves into a kind of chamber piece on wheels, with the characters decorating the insides of the vehicle with a dry erase marker so that it looks somewhere between graffiti art and the scrawlings on the wall of a cheesy movie set in a psych ward. And while Fisher (Noah Toth) seems to find some sense of zen amid the endless asphalt, James (Phinehas Yoon) wails at the sky in a plea for mercy from a higher power, in a clash of attitudes that provokes friction as well as flashes of empathy.View image in fullscreenAkira Jackson and Noah Toth in It Ends.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonIt’s tempting to call It Ends something like a Blair Witch take on No Exit, the 1944Jean-Paul Sartrework where a group of strangers were trapped in a room for eternity and which declared that hell was other people. But in a statement to accompany the film, director Ullom says that the film is instead rooted in his own struggle with dissociative depression and attempts to find a framework to make life survivable. If Sartre famously said that hell is other people, It Ends seems to suggest that they might be able to save us too.Despite a few jokes that already feel dated (one character mourns that she didn’t have the foresight to download Subway Surfers), It Ends often reaches the quality of high-concept cult horror classics while also nodding to our uniquely modern malaise. “What if we’re supposed to suffer here,” says Fisher at one low moment. “What if that’s the point?” It’s unclear if he’s talking about their nightmarish road trip or what it can feel like to live on this mortal coil. It Ends is confident enough to leave the question unanswered.It Ends will be released in the US on 21 August and 3 September in Australia with a UK release to followExplore more on these topicsHorror filmsThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: David Mitchell’s crime-solving Ludwig returns  | Television | The Guardian
description: The popular cosy-crime drama is back – with a couple of changes. Plus: some late-starters get into the dating game. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: The popular cosy-crime drama is back – with a couple of changes. Plus: some late-starters get into the dating game. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: David Mitchell as John Ludwig.Photograph: PHOTOGRAPHER:/CREDIT LINE:BBC/Big TalkView image in fullscreenDavid Mitchell as John Ludwig.Photograph: PHOTOGRAPHER:/CREDIT LINE:BBC/Big TalkTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: David Mitchell’s crime-solving Ludwig returnsThe popular cosy-crime drama is back – with a couple of changes. Plus: some late-starters get into the dating game. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Hollie Richardson,Priya Elan,Jack SealeandSimon WardellThu 20 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLudwig9pm, BBC OneIs there a danger that, with John “Ludwig” Taylor’s true identity revealed, this cosy-crime drama will lose intrigue in its second series? Jeopardy is just about maintained: John is now a police employee but he’s still investigating his brother’s fate, while solving a case a week in his bumbling style. But chief constable Ziegler is on his case – he knows something’s up, he’s just not sure what. Undemanding fun, enlivened by Mitchell’s lead and Anna Maxwell Martin’s Lucy.Phil HarrisonDragons’ Den8pm, BBC OneA big first for the show in its 23rd season: with guest judges Susie Ma and Jenna Meek onboard, there are more female dragons than male. Pitches kick off with Kimberly and her eco-conscious haircare range Selkie, before mother and son Shashi and Sanjay fill the den with Spice Kitchen aromas.Hollie RichardsonThe Yorkshire Vet8pm, Channel 5Reality show featuring James Herriot’s former trainee Peter, his vet pals and a god-like voiceover from All Creatures Great and Small’s Christopher Timothy. Your enjoyment of the show depends on how much you like watching the surgical treatment of a recently pregnant cow with a prolapse.Priya ElanView image in fullscreenKate Lister and David Olusoga in A House Through Time.Photograph: BBC/Twenty Twenty Productions Ltd/Richard RankenA House Through Time9pm, BBC TwoBack to Edinburgh where David Olusoga is busy bringing more dusty census records to life. We’ve reached the Victorian era in the house on Calton Hill and the residential turnover is brisk. There’s Thomas Mains, a struggling shoe-maker; Thomas Glen, a renowned bagpiper; and, most intriguingly, Catherine Johnston, a brothel keeper.PHBetter Date Than Never9pm, BBC Three“Better late than never! Who would have thought?” This dating show is a cheerful treat, following daters who range in age, gender and identity but who have left it late to get into the dating game. This time it’s the turn of Charles, who is trying speed-dating, and Kento, who is excited about a second meeting.PHPossession9pm, Sky AtlanticKarla Crome’s rich, intelligent thriller about the echoing injustices of slavery comes to a mesmeric conclusion, which begins with British-Jamaican lawyer Claudia (Gugu Mbatha-Raw) trapped beneath the floorboards of a house that thrums with past pain. Violent confrontations, in the present day and the 18th century, resolve the narrative in stunning fashion.Jack SealeFilm choiceNovak Djokovic: The Wolf in Winter, Thursday, Prime VideoView image in fullscreenNovak Djokovic: The Wolf in Winter.Photograph: Amazon MGM Studios“He’s soft and gentle … but he’s also angry.” Jelena Djokovic’s assessment of her husband is the knotty thread that runs through Jason Hehir’s documentary about a giant of tennis who has yet to be forgiven for surpassing the achievements of crowd favourites Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer. His intensity and stubbornness (a Serbian national trait, we’re told) hasn’t endeared him to the public but, as we go behind the scenes at the 2025 Australian Open and meet an honest, engaging family man with a long history of tough choices, this film could go some way to changing minds.Simon WardellExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Aigul Akhmetshina: Mujer Fatal album review – classy and sensual in music from Bizet to Britten and Bernstein | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The mezzo-soprano lends supple and elegant voice to opera arias and musical numbers that explore womanhood
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: The mezzo-soprano lends supple and elegant voice to opera arias and musical numbers that explore womanhood
Content: Languid lines … Aigul Akhmetshina.Photograph: Paola KudackiView image in fullscreenLanguid lines … Aigul Akhmetshina.Photograph: Paola KudackiClassical musicReviewAigul Akhmetshina: Mujer Fatal album review – classy and sensual in music from Bizet to Britten and BernsteinAkhmetshina/Pappano(Decca)The mezzo-soprano lends supple and elegant voice to opera arias and musical numbers that explore womanhoodClive PagetThu 20 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 12.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAcclaimed for embodying opera’s femme fatales such as Carmen and Dalia, Aigul Akhmetshina explores womanhood more broadly on her second album, Mujer Fatal. Accompanied on piano byAntonio Pappano, the repertoire ranges from Spanish, French and Russian art song, to Broadway and beyond.View image in fullscreenCover art for Mujer FatalThe title track, written by Elena Roussanova especially for the Bashkortostan-born mezzo-soprano, sets the tone. Akhmetshina’s supple instrument wraps itself around the languid vocal lines while Pappano’s sensitive touch draws out the music’s delicate melismas. Two of Montsalvatge’s Canciones Negras find the singer spinning long-breathed melodies, dipping down elegantly into her burgundy lower register.She’s at her classiest inhabiting Bizet’s sultry Adieux de l’hôtesse arabe and Ravel’s hip-swaying Vocalise-étude en forme de habanera. She is, of course, entirely at home in Balakirev, Rimsky-Korsakov and especially in Tchaikovsky’s None but the Lonely Heart.On the whole, these are very fine, if perhaps a trifle restrained performances.When it comes to letting her hair down, Akhmetshina is suitably uninhibited in a sensual Bésame mucho. If Gershwin’s The Man I Love and Bernstein’s Lucky to be Me feel a tad strait-laced, she warms nicely into Weill’s Speak Low. The recital closes with Britten’s O Tell Me the Truth About Love, a delicious party piece where she finally allows herself to have some fun.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: All of Us Atoms by Holly Dawson audiobook review – an extraordinary self-portrait | Books | The Guardian
description: Helena Bonham Carter narrates the playwright’s impressionistic memoir, written as she was experiencing the loss of her memory
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: Helena Bonham Carter narrates the playwright’s impressionistic memoir, written as she was experiencing the loss of her memory
Content: Scattered recollections … Holly Dawson.Photograph: Silvia VarelaView image in fullscreenScattered recollections … Holly Dawson.Photograph: Silvia VarelaAudiobook of the weekBooksReviewAll of Us Atoms by Holly Dawson audiobook review – an extraordinary self-portraitHelena Bonham Carter narrates the playwright’s impressionistic memoir, written as she was experiencing the loss of her memoryFiona SturgesThu 20 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlaywright Holly Dawson’s memoir tells of memory lapses and a series of seizures that signal something isn’t right. Before visiting a doctor, she had been muddling up words, forgetting people’s names and flooding the bathroom.The book finds Dawson in conversation with her brain, which is both part of her and a separate entity. “Don’t be cross with me, my love. I am tired,” it tells her. “Between your ears hearing a word and your mouth repeating it, I am doing all this work you don’t see.” Dawson, who is approaching 40 and a single mum of two children, later learns she has epilepsy and a brain tumour, which may or may not be benign. A consultant explains she must wait several months to find out, and so she sets about preserving memories and words while she still has them. “Come. Sit. Take your notebook … write it down,” says her brain.What follows are scattered recollections of her life, which include childhood days spent at her grandmother’s house; school holidays playing with her siblings and pretending to dig a mine at the bottom of the garden; ballet training and an eating disorder that robs her of puberty. These snapshots, which shift in perspective and move between the second and third person, gradually build a picture of her past.The actor Helena Bonham Carter is the narrator, bringing fresh shape and clarity to Dawson’s deliberately fractured and impressionistic prose. What emerges is an original self-portrait and a compelling exploration of memory, identity and the self.Available via Canongate, 7hr 29minFurther listeningThe Rose FieldPhilip Pullman, Penguin and David Fickling Books, 22hr 36minMichael Sheen narrates the final instalment of the Book of Dust trilogy, in which Lyra and her daemon are given an epic farewell. Also features a bonus Q&A between Pullman and Sheen in which they discuss the legacy of the series.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories.
