title: ‘Are you ready for some filth?’ Julian Clary and more on comedy’s great smut explosion | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Clary’s back with Fully Dilated, a burlesque star called Entendre Entendre is doing lewd singalongs and there’s an A-Z of very dirty words. Our writer investigates Edinburgh’s smut outbreak – and ends up getting his own fantasies turned into erotica
Author: Tim Jonze
Headline: Clary’s back with Fully Dilated, a burlesque star called Entendre Entendre is doing lewd singalongs and there’s an A-Z of very dirty words. Our writer investigates Edinburgh’s smut outbreak – and ends up getting his own fantasies turned into erotica
Content: Shocked the elderly of Harrogate … Clary backstage at Assembly Rooms, Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenShocked the elderly of Harrogate … Clary backstage at Assembly Rooms, Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianEdinburgh festival 2026‘Are you ready for some filth?’ Julian Clary and more on comedy’s great smut explosionClary’s back with Fully Dilated, a burlesque star called Entendre Entendre is doing lewd singalongs and there’s an A-Z of very dirty words. Our writer investigates Edinburgh’s smut outbreak – and ends up getting his own fantasies turned into eroticaTim JonzeThu 20 Aug 2026 00.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a street in Edinburgh, a woman I’ve only just met is quizzing me on my sexual fantasies. “Do you want softcore or hardcore? What positions do you prefer?” asks Cameryn Moore, a former phone sex operator turned playwright from the US, along with other, less printable, questions.Her business plan is simple: for £20, punters can tell Moore what turns them on. She will then bash out a piece of bespoke erotic fiction for them on her typewriter. “I listen to their content then spit it out on paper – no punctuation, very stream of consciousness,” she says. “I also offer to read it out loud to them – and they walk away grinning from ear to ear because nobody’s ever asked them what they like when it comes to sex. So that’s what I do every day at the fringe: sit down for four or five hours a day and crank out dirty shit.” She calls the service Sidewalk Smut.double quotation markA common sex confession at Smut Slam involves people falling asleep during threesomesThat’s not all Moore is doing – her custom erotica stand is an innovative way of drumming up support for Smut Slam, her nightly session of dirty storytelling that has travelled the globe since she started it in a Boston Irish pub in 2011. There’s a segment in the show in which anonymous sex stories are dropped in a bucket and picked out to be read aloud. “One story that comes up a lot lately is someone finding out that their hook-up is radically rightwing.” Others have involved people falling asleep during threesomes or nipple rings going astray at sex clubs. “I am forever amazed at the variety that exists in the human sexual experience,” laughs Moore.View image in fullscreen‘What positions do you prefer?’ … Sidewalk Smut’s Cameryn Moore quizzes our writer.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianIt is Smut Slam’s first trip back to Edinburgh in seven years, and it’s not the only sex-laden show in this year’s lineup. So, are we currently simmering in a summer of smut? Californian performer, writer and director Bryn Woz has a show simply called Smut, while English TV star Tom Read Wilson’s An Alphabet of Me alights at some rather filthy pit stops.Most telling of all is an Edinburgh comeback forJulian Clary, after 17 years away, with a show called Fully Dilated. “That means I’mopening upto the public,” says Clary when we meet in a pub garden. “And once you have dilated, that’s when everything comes out.”Clary is well aware that he’s best known for a smutty joke: at the 1993 BritishComedyAwards he told the audience he had been “fisting Norman Lamont” (their shocked laughter drowned out the punchline – “talk about a red box”). The new show reflects on the run-up to this gag, in which Clary’s life was split into two wildly different sides – soaring to mainstream TV stardom on the one hand, tending to his friends who were dying of Aids on the other. “This isn’t going to sell me any tickets,” he says with a smile, “but I’m talking about loss. It’s uncharted territory for me, and something I could never have done at the time.”View image in fullscreenActually rather erudite … Tom Read Wilson limbering up for his bawdy A-Z.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianBawdy humour has been around since at least the ancient Greeks, but the kind we know so well in Britain is best associated with music hall and pantomime, where actors used innuendo and nudge-nudge wink-wink humour as a way of avoiding prosecution for obscenity. This style perhaps reached its zenith with Clary, who used smut as a way to slip the realities of gay sex into homes around the country. He has become something of a smut godfather, and you can certainly trace his disciples. Read Wilson describes Clary as a “huge hero” and namechecks a joke he once made at the London Palladium panto: “He came on dressed as an enormous bloom and said that he’d woken up with stamen all over him.”Read Wilson’s alphabetical tour may sound crude – W is for Willy, after all – but it’s actually rather erudite. His word-of-the-day series on social media sometimes incorporates smut and slang (fuck-a-doodle-do was once analysed, alongside less rude offerings such aspettifogging). What makes his love of words especially infectious, though, is his Honor Blackman-esque purr, not to mention a rather Wildean flourish. It lends itself to smut throughout his Edinburgh performance, from his opening line (“Thank you for your warm hand on my opening”) to his selection of penis jokes (describing one penis, he says sympathetically: “Its two neighbours are nuts and it has an arsehole living at the back”).We can’t even escape innuendo during our chat. “You know,” Read Wilson says at one point, “the trouble with the lexicon of smut is that it becomes indelibly seared on your mental retina and it doesn’t wipe off.” When our internet connection starts to glitch I find myself saying: “I’m just going to take you downstairs … do you think it’s your end or mine?”Smut can be fun and frivolous, but for Chelsea Birkby, a young comedian performing her third show at Edinburgh, filthy gags are more than just a way to get laughs. “As a teenager I used to hate standup because of the sexual humour,” she says. “But that’s because I grew up feeling ashamed about sex.”View image in fullscreen‘Now we’ve got new rules about consent, how can we have a laugh?’ … Chelsea Birkby at Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianAfter being persuaded to see live comedy while studying philosophy at university, she had an epiphany. “Simon Amstellwas the biggest influence,” she says. “Being so confessional, and so much about sex, I saw him and thought, ‘Yeah, this changes everything.’ And now, getting older and working through some of that shame, I find that being able to talk about these things is liberating! Sex is kind of confusing and it’s often private, so it’s fun when you bring it out into the spotlight.”Birkby’s show is about desiring total domination and control and is fuelled by self-help guides along with a sexually explicit PowerPoint presentation. She has an easy way with the audience, especially when quizzing two older comedy-goers about whether they know what “edging” means. But that doesn’t mean it’s all plain-sailing for her. Smut, when performed by a woman, brings drawbacks. “If you’re talking about mental health, people aren’t really assessing you, like, ‘How mad is she?’. But if you’re talking about sex, peoplearethinking about you in a sexual way. There is a judgment there, which can be exposing.On TikTok she noticed she had become the subject of the game Smash or Pass. “And it’s like, I’m just sharing a joke, I’m not asking to be rated. Having said that, the extra liberating thing about standup is that then you can just incorporate all that into more stuff that you talk about.”Bryn Woz has been trading in smut for some time. But while she used to have no trouble regaling audiences with her sexual stories, over time she started to find it more difficult, which is why her new show is delivered through filthy alter ego Entendre Entendre. “I realised I had been using some version of this persona my whole life to kind of fool myself from realising how vulnerable I was,” she says. “I used to be, like, ‘Yeah, I did it for the story, so what if I hooked up with my friends in the car park outside their wedding rehearsal?’” But, lately, she says of making a show about her sexual adventures, “I realised I wasn’t quite the person I thought I was, and that trying to say these things as myself didn’t feel honest. So the Entendre persona is like a personification of all the coping mechanisms I’ve used throughout my life and all the masks I’ve worn. She can tell these stories very easily because she doesn’t think of the consequences. She’s unfazed.”View image in fullscreen‘I realised I wasn’t the person I thought I was’ … Entendre Entendre at Assembly Roxy, Edinburgh.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianShe certainly is – as Woz peels off her emotional layers during her Edinburgh show, she also performs a burlesque striptease. While scarf, gloves and brassiere (there are strategically placed stars underneath) are discarded, Woz runs the full gamut of smut – we get songs with audience sing-alongs (“Call me when you learn how to use that dick”), and what Woz calls “beautiful poems, such as Stanky Dick and Balls”. But there’s also sadness, as Entendre considers the emptiness behind a life of “doing it for the story”. “We get to see the person underneath,” says Woz.Smut may have a therapeutic element for some of its practitioners, but when I put this to Clary he looks agog. “I’ve nothadany childhood trauma,” he says. “I don’tneedsex therapy. No, no, I’ve never thought down that line.”For Clary, smutty humour started at home – his mother would make the family laugh by dropping naughty words into conversation. At school with his friend Nick he would draw rude cartoons of his teachers having sex. After studying Greek drama and the war poets at university, he decided that the works of Wilfred Owen simply weren’t smutty enough and headed off in the opposite direction. “I like the way smut makes everyone a child again,” he says. “And there’s a different type of laugh you get with smut. A proper belly laugh, not a cerebral titter, which is of no use to me.”The first line of his Edinburgh show is, “Are you ready for some filth?”, and he thinks the reason gay comedians are adept at smutty humour is because: “There’s a lot of sex and immediate gratification that goes on, so we tend to cut to the chase.” Yet Clary’s own brand of smut thrives on its coyness. He recalls one of his favourite lines by Kenneth Williams, who once said: “Whenever I see innuendo in a script, I whip it out immediately.”Clary says that in the UK, the further north you travel the more likely an audience is to appreciate smut. “Although I remember talking about fisting in Harrogate and there were a lot of old ladies in the audience. I’d just been on Strictly so I think they were expecting charming anecdotes, but I did enjoy the gasp.” Australia and New Zealand are keen smut consumers, he says, but the US he always found tricky. “They never used to really understand the coyness of it,” he says.View image in fullscreen‘A cerebral titter is of no use to me’ … Julian Clary backstage at Assembly Rooms.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThis may be true. Smut Slam’s Moore was raised as a Mormon, yet despite (or possibly because of) this, she has always rejected “comedy that tiptoes around things or has euphemisms. That’s not funny or cute to me. I would much rather just say the thing.”Woz agrees: “I think you guys [the Brits] probably do it a little smarter than us because of all your repression.”Thanks to Smut Slam’s international success, Moore has a good knowledge of different nations’ appetite for smut. “When I apply for a German visa to perform I have to print off all these pieces of paper detailing what I do and they don’t even blink.”Some countries, on the other hand, need a little warming up. “Whenever I tell people I’m taking Smut Slam to Finland they say, ‘Oh my God, are you sure?’ Because Finnish and Estonian audiences are considered to be very stern. It takes time to open them up, but it’s satisfying when you do.” Moore’s favourite thing is to bring Smut Slam to places where it’s considered genuinely transgressive – the American south, Alberta, Canada, Ljubljana in Slovenia. As for British audiences, she says, we’re good listeners but need a bit of cajoling when it comes to contributing. That’s certainly the case for me as Moore attempts to interview me for her erotic story. “You’ll need to take off your sunglasses,” she says as, to do this properly, eye contact needs to be established. It’s not long before I’m telling her things I’ve never discussed with close friends.So why this gargantuan appetite for smut? And why now? “Smut is perhaps one of the great primary colours in the world of escapism,” says Read Wilson. “People in these difficult times need a good laugh,” adds Clary. “I’d much rather see something smutty and rude than some kind of highbrow analysis of Trumpism. That wouldn’t make me feel better at all.”Moore sees smut’s power entwined with the sexual politics of our age. “It’s a mistake to underestimate the power of raw, authentic language,” she says. “It’s very easy to write off smutty humour as just tits and giggles. But if you’re good at it, you will plant seeds that are going to have people thinking about their own stuff, perhaps about shame in their own life, or how they’re having these conversations with other people.”Both Birkby and Woz have noticed an uptick in women reading erotic fantasy novels. “There are more single women than ever who think: ‘I’m not gonna settle for less than what I deserve like my mother did, like my grandmother did’,” says Woz. “Consuming smuttier content is their way of getting that eroticism on their own terms, not expecting it from another person.”“I do think we are on an upswing at the moment,” says Birkby. “There’s been a lot of nervousness around sex and talking about sex for the last few years, which absolutely needed to happen. But now that we’ve had these valuable discussions about what consent is, perhaps we can say, ‘We’ve got these new rules, how can we have a laugh about things now?”She references the hemline index, a theory that whenever countries enter a recession, women’s hemlines lengthen. “Perhaps there’s a comedy equivalent,” she says, “that whenever the world gets worse, the jokes get smuttier.”My smut-filled tour of Edinburgh has sadly come to an end. And so, after learning the tricks of the trade from some of comedy’s lewdest practitioners, there’s only one thing left for me to do: unfurl the story Moore wrote with me and see if I have become a true smut convert. “The bedroom is already warm this late in the morning,” it begins, “but her –”Unfortunately, readers, we have just hit our word count. If you really want to know the rest, you’ll just have to use your (filthy) imagination.Smut Slamis at Banshee Labyrinth until 30 August.Bryn Woz: Smutis at Assembly Roxy until 31 August.Julian Clary: Fully Dilatedis at Assembly Rooms until 23 August.Tom Read Wilson: The A-Z of Meis touring from 6 September.Chelsea Birkby: is in Full Control The Entire Timeis at Pleasance Courtyard until 30 AugustExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreJulian ClaryComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)SexfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ref, I barely brushed him! The artist who’s painted all of Roy Keane’s red cards | Art | The Guardian
description: Before he was an irascible TV pundit, the Irish midfielder was equally feared on the pitch. Irish painter Seánie Harte has documented all the times Keane was sent off playing for Manchester United. ‘It’s a bit of fun,’ he says
Author: Larry Ryan
Headline: Before he was an irascible TV pundit, the Irish midfielder was equally feared on the pitch. Irish painter Seánie Harte has documented all the times Keane was sent off playing for Manchester United. ‘It’s a bit of fun,’ he says
Content: Red menace … David Elleray sends Keane off in the 1999 FA Cup semi final replay.Photograph: Seánie HarteView image in fullscreenRed menace … David Elleray sends Keane off in the 1999 FA Cup semi final replay.Photograph: Seánie HarteArtRef, I barely brushed him! The artist who’s painted all of Roy Keane’s red cardsBefore he was an irascible TV pundit, the Irish midfielder was equally feared on the pitch. Irish painter Seánie Harte has documented all the times Keane was sent off playing for Manchester United. ‘It’s a bit of fun,’ he saysLarry RyanThu 20 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAcross his career in the 1990s and early 2000s, Roy Keane, the Ireland andManchester Unitedfootballer, was a widely decorated midfielder with a relentless will to win. He also had his share of controversies, which included being famously sent off on several occasions.These have now been documented in Irish painter Seánie Harte’s Red Card series, which marks the 11 times Keane received his marching orders while playing for Manchester United.The colour-filled paintings, done in a loose, figurative style, somewhat resemble the work ofElizabeth Peyton– if she’d used Sky Sports’sPremier League Yearsfor inspiration rather than louche bohemians and Britpop luminaries. Although Harte’s oil pastel paintings often depict acts of aggression or their aftermath, their light look, with a hint of the absurd and nostalgia, gives a feel of visual one-liners.View image in fullscreenRoy Keane lands one on Alan Shearer … ‘People annoy me – and he still annoys me’.Photograph: Seánie HarteIn the years since Keane retired as a player and stepped away from management, he has become better known as a pundit and podcaster, with a no-nonsense approach to analysis and a sharp sense of humour. Some years ago, on the hugely popular Stick to Football podcast that he co-hosts with other former players,he recountedhis array of red cards with a typical bluntness and humour.Harte remembered the matter-of-fact manner in which Keane discussed getting sent off in 1995 for stamping on Crystal Palace’s Gareth Southgate. “Gareth deserved that. Gareth lunged at me,” Keane says on the podcast. “Gareth was nasty. Everyone thinks Gareth is a nice guy. I’ll tell you … he tried to break my leg!”View image in fullscreenOops, he did it again … Keane gets a second yellow for ‘diving’ against Blackburn in 1995.Photograph: Seánie HarteThis was when inspiration struck. “The way he talked about them was quite funny,” Harte says. “They didn’t seem as bad then, looking back, and I thought with my art style I could do something similar, where it can shift the mood from aggressive violence into something more colourful and playful.”He adds: “I was not planning to do all of them. I ended up doing one or two, and then I got a bit of traction and I thought: Oh I need to do them all now.” Each painting is paired with a one-liner from the footballer himself.“People annoy me – and he still annoys me,” accompanies a painting of Keane scuffling with Newcastle’s Alan Shearer. “Yeah it was reckless. I enjoyed it. You have to put down a marker,” features the aftermath of a challenge that leaves Gus Poyet of Chelsea writhing in pain during an FA Charity Shield match. “I don’t think that tackle was that bad,” shows him in the middle of a notoriousrevenge foulon Alf-Inge Haaland.Harte first posted the images on Instagram and sells prints online. His exhibition, Sent Off: Paintings of Every Roy Keane Red Card opens soon at theHen’s Teeth spacein Dublin. They’ve had a big response since he first put them out last year, though he admits: “I know Roy is doing a lot of the heavy lifting here.” Among those to get in touch with praise was one of the directors ofSaipan, the film inspired by Keane’s falling out with Ireland manager Mick McCarthy ahead of the 2002 World Cup.View image in fullscreenKeane stamps on Gareth Southgate in the FA Cup semi-final replay, 1995 … ‘Gareth deserved that’.Photograph: Seánie HarteHarte, 36, lives in Dublin where he trained as a graphic designer. He only returned to painting two years ago for some distraction. “I’m looking at screens the whole time and in quite a niche area as well, where I’m designing billing systems,” he says. “It’s not the most creative stuff. So I really felt like I needed something a bit more tactile and creative. When I started doing it I decided I’m just going to paint things that I want to do. Things that I enjoy. And football was one.”Being a lifelong Manchester United fan, and Ireland supporter, has provided fodder for his paintings. Keane was an obvious touchstone. Harte also paints other things that amuse him – he’s made a run of paintings based on scenes from Father Ted.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenKicking off … Keane lashes out at Alf-Inge Haaland in the Manchester derby, 2001.Photograph: Seánie HarteThough he has painted some recent football events, such as an Irish fan taunting Cristiano Ronaldo after he was sent off in a World Cup qualifier last November, and Troy Parrott’s dramatic winner for Ireland against Hungary, he usually prefers to look further into the past. “Thinking back to when I was younger and those memories around football,” he says.To create the paintings, Harte uses grainy TV footage and old photos of an incident as a guide for sketching. He has painted some images of Ireland’s past World Cup exploits andDavid Beckham’s infamous red cardat the 1998 tournament in France. There’s also a rendering of Eric Cantona’s 1995 lunge at a Crystal Palace fan. Also, given Keane’s considerable achievements as a player, Harte plans to expand his oeuvre in depicting the more positive aspects of his game.As for the red cards: Harte doesn’t know if Keane has ever seen the paintings. Recently, though, his girlfriend met a former teammate of Keane and showed him the images. Harte relays that the teammate said “He [Keane] would probably love them but say he doesn’t.” Keane’s representatives were contacted for comment on the art but no reply has been forthcoming.“It would be a real dream for Roy to harshly critique my artwork,” Harte concludes. “That would easily be the funniest outcome.”Sent Off: Paintings of Every Roy Keane Red Cardis at Hen’s Teeth, Dublin on 3 September.Explore more on these topicsArtRoy KeaneExhibitionsManchester UnitedfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Mary Heilmann obituary | Art | The Guardian
description: Playful American painter whose works were informed by her previous focus on ceramics and sculpture
Author: Charles Darwent
Headline: Playful American painter whose works were informed by her previous focus on ceramics and sculpture
Content: One of Heilmann’s 1979 paintings, Tehachapi #1. She described her pink and black artworks of this time as ‘playful and sarcastic’.Photograph: Genevieve Hanson/Mary Heilmann/Hauser & WirthView image in fullscreenOne of Heilmann’s 1979 paintings, Tehachapi #1. She described her pink and black artworks of this time as ‘playful and sarcastic’.Photograph: Genevieve Hanson/Mary Heilmann/Hauser & WirthArtObituaryMary Heilmann obituaryPlayful American painter whose works were informed by her previous focus on ceramics and sculptureCharles DarwentThu 20 Aug 2026 12.50 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 13.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVisitors to Mary Heilmann’s show at theWhitechapel Gallery in 2016were offered the novel experience of looking at art while scooting about on wheeled wooden chairs. These, too, turned out to be artworks. One,Sunny Chair for the Whitechapel, had been made by Heilmann for the occasion. Rough-hewn from plywood, backed in nylon webbing and painted bright yellow, it seemed happily untidy; as an object, but also as a type. This was true of all the works in Looking at Pictures, and was intentional.Heilmann, who has died aged 86, had an untidy past as a maker. It was while doing a BA at the University of California, Santa Barbara (1959-62), that she discovered ceramics, which were to occupy her first decade as an artist. The untidiness of her artistic history, however, was to be shaped by more than her choice of materials.Born in San Francisco, she was the daughter of John, a civil engineer, and Mary (nee Webb), a nurse. Her mother had insisted on continuing to work while raising her two children. She instilled the need for self-sufficiency into her daughter, who trained as a teacher before going to art school.When Heilmann was seven, her family moved south to Los Angeles. The city’s surf culture attracted her, particularly diving. “I became a fledgling competitive diver at 11,”she told the Guardianin an interview for her Whitechapel show. “A little girl could get a lot of attention diving off the tower at the Coliseum.” As she would discover, though, attention was harder to come by as a female artist.View image in fullscreenHeilmann in her San Francisco studio, 1979.Photograph: Mark Magill/Hauser & WirthIn 1965, she signed on to a ceramics and sculpture MA at Berkeley, taught by the celebrated ceramicistPeter Voulkos. “He was amazing,” Heilmann recalled. “A super-radical nut-job hippie.”Voulkos’s huge, abstract expressionist ceramics were on the scale of sculpture, although he had initially trained as a painter. His student would now go the other way, exchanging ceramics for sculpture and then, by the late 1960s, painting.For all that, Heilmann did not get the kind of attention she had had as a high-board diver, or that male friends such as Bruce Nauman andRichard Serrawere now getting as students. “It was the case that girls were very not noticed as artists,” she told an Archives of American Art interviewer in 2022. “There were a lot of really good young women artists, but only a few got any attention.”This, in part, is what drove her to untidiness. If teachers such as Voulkos overlooked her and her work, she would get their attention “not by being sexy and cute and flirty, but by being provocative and ornery, and then making art that was provocative and ornery”.In 1968, Heilmann left California for New York, intent on meeting the minimalist artistDonald Judd. (Judd too had made chairs, although his “were not very comfortable”, Heilmann told Vogue magazine. “Mine are.”) Moving into Serra’s former loft in Manhattan’s Tribeca, she was visited by Holly Solomon, a dealer whose eponymous gallery specialised in the work of Californian artists. From 1976, Solomon gave Heilmann a series of shows. The third, in 1979, was a flop.The problem was pink. In her desire to be ornery, Heilmann had made a series of paintings that defied the colour’s association with femininity – “fluffy dress pink”, as she called it. “Pink is a pretty colour,” Heilmann said, “but it was also a hip, culturally hip, naughty colour, or a rough, rough colour.”View image in fullscreenHeilmann’s 2016 exhibition, Looking at Pictures, at Whitechapel Gallery, London.Photograph: Stephen White/Hauser & WirthThe one she used for her paintings in the 1979 show was assertively naughty and rough – an acid, eye-popping pink offset in each canvas by black. The works, Heilmann said, may have been “playful and sarcastic”, but they were also “very, very serious, and formal, and colourist”, informed by the thinking of the Bauhaus colour theorist Josef Albers. This fact eluded the critic of the Village Voice, who sniffed that the canvases lacked “real muscle”, and that Heilmann “hadn’t been doing her push-ups”. What made this borderline misogynistic attack particularly painful was that the critic was a woman.Leaving Holly Solomon soon after, Heilmann went to the gallerist Pat Hearn, who gave her a series of exhibitions throughout the late 80s and 90s.Her life changed when, in 1997, she was taken up by the Swiss kingmakers, Hauser & Wirth. In that year, she had her first international one-woman exhibition in Zurich, at the Zürcher Stiftung für Konstruktive und Konkrete Kunst. A solo show at the CamdenArtCentre in London followed in 2001, and at the Museum Ludwig in Cologne in 2010.Through all of this, Heilmann and her art proved resistant to tidiness. The earliest pieces in her Whitechapel show, such asLittle 9 x 9 (1973), were finger paintings, a method Heilmann had learned when teaching children. She would have a longer career teaching adults, at Stony Brook University on Long Island and then at the School of Visual Arts in Manhattan. “I made the work by squeezing through the paint with my fingers,” she said.View image in fullscreenHeilmann’s 2005 painting Surfing on Acid. ‘Her paintings were sculptures, as were her chairs.’Photograph: Mary Heilmann/Hauser & WirthBlack Cracky (1990) showed a fascination with breakage, a relic of her life as a ceramicist. That she saw the canvas as an object rather than just a surface – sides and stretcher bars were also painted – she ascribed to having been a sculptor. Her paintings were sculptures, as were her chairs. The blobs that seemed to fly up the gallery wall from the double canvas of Good Vibrations Diptych, Remembering David (2012) recalled “a time in the 60s, the hippy era, when people saw spots flying around due to certain substances that were also flying around,” Heilmann cryptically said.That she had indulged in those substances herself was just one of her untidinesses. She had, she said, dried out in 1983, although titles of works such as Surfing on Acid (2005) suggested a lingering fascination with the beach and the counterculture it bred. Given all this, her attitude to Catholicism was perhaps even more surprising.Brought up in a devoutly Catholic household – her brother trained as a priest – she had been sent to schools with names such as the St Rose academy and American Martyrs. The experience never left her. “I loved the whole Catholic culture as a kid, and that’s carried on into my life, the way I make things up now,” she told thedocumentary channel Art21 in 2009. Her 1983 paintingRosebudwas a meditation on the martyrdom of St Sebastian. Another canvas was called Our Lady of the Flowers.Heilmann spent her last years in Bridgehampton, Long Island. Her brother, John, predeceased her. She is survived by his three children.Mary Anne Heilmann, artist, born 3 January 1940; died 14 August 2026Explore more on these topicsArtPaintingCeramicsSculptureobituariesShareReuse this content
