Content: Deeper chemistry … Beck.Photograph: Mikai KarlView image in fullscreenDeeper chemistry … Beck.Photograph: Mikai KarlFilm & Music reader interviewBeckPost your questions for BeckThe genre-hopping hitmaker’s new album fingerpicks the same melancholy heartstrings as Sea Change. You can ask him anything in our upcoming reader interviewThu 20 Aug 2026 06.42 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 07.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNews of a Beck album is always cause for celebration, especially when it’s seven years since the last one – 2019’sHyperspace– but even more so when it’s recorded with the same wrecking crew as the melancholy classicsSea ChangeandMorning Phase(having originally got together for 1998’s Mutations). That’s Smokey Hormel, Joey Waronker, Justin Meldal-Johnsen, Roger Joseph Manning Jr and Jason Falkner; Nigel Godrich also joined on mixing. Beck said: “This time it felt like the playing and the chemistry had evolved and deepened – a sound that’s come together over the decades of working together.”A first taste of their wares is already available in Ride Lonesome, a wise, almost cosmic ode to keepin’ on keepin’ on, and the serene, fingerpicked In the Night.You could ask Beck about his new record or anything else when he sits for the Guardian’s reader interview soon. Perhaps working withBeau Travailstar Denis Lavant onthe video for In the Night, his artistic childhood, love of blues, the strangeness of peak-MTV 90s success, working with the Dust Brothers on Odelay – or any of his esteemed collaborators, among them Paul McCartney, Phoenix, Edgar Wright, Philip Glass, the surviving members of Nirvana and many others.Post your questions in the comments by10am BST on 25 August 2026and the best answers will appear in a future edition of the reader interview.Ride Lonesome is released via Iliad/Capitol on 18 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsBeckFilm & Music reader interviewIndiePop and rockcalloutShareReuse this content

title: The Song of Hiawatha review – Rafael Payare reveals the riches of Coleridge-Taylor’s hit cantata | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Festival director Nicola Benedetti’s bold programming of these once-popular Victorian cantatas paid off with a crisp chorus and strong soloists tautly conducted
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Festival director Nicola Benedetti’s bold programming of these once-popular Victorian cantatas paid off with a crisp chorus and strong soloists tautly conducted
Content: Dramatic momentum … Rafael Payare conducts his Orchestre Symphonique de Montréal at the Usher Hall this week.Photograph: André GodinhoView image in fullscreenDramatic momentum … Rafael Payare conducts his Orchestre Symphonique de Montréal at the Usher Hall this week.Photograph: André GodinhoClassical musicReviewThe Song of Hiawatha review – Rafael Payare reveals the riches of Coleridge-Taylor’s hit cantataUsher Hall, EdinburghFestival director Nicola Benedetti’s bold programming of these once-popular Victorian cantatas paid off with a crisp chorus and strong soloists tautly conductedMichael DownesThu 20 Aug 2026 11.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Song of Hiawatha, Black British composerSamuel Coleridge-Taylor’s turn-of-the-century cantata trilogy,packed the Albert Hall for weeks on endbetween the wars, but it reallyshouldn’t work today. The unmistakably Victorian if charming score is the least of the difficulties. More problematic is the libretto: 800-plus lines of “Rum-ti Rum-ti Rum-ti Rum-ti” (trochaic tetrameter, to be technical) from Henry Wadsworth Longfellow. More challenging still is a story that shows the Native American Hiawatha endorsing his country’s colonisation by “people with white faces”.Rafael Payare did not know Hiawatha beforeNicola Benedettiinvited his Orchestre Symphonique de Montréal to give this Edinburgh international festival premiere, but he conducted with commitment and verve. Tightly coiled yet expansive of gesture, he never let the tension drop. The occasional drawbacks of his approach – soloists denied flexibility and space; chorus not guided towards longer phrases and quieter singing – were outweighed by the rewards. Payare highlighted the cantatas’ thematic and tonal connections and was alert to their dancelike character.View image in fullscreenApplause at the Usher Hall for The Song of Hiawatha.Photograph: André GodinhoHiawatha is demanding for the chorus, which sings a lot of notes and needs to conjure up the scenery – Longfellow tells rather than shows. The Edinburgh Festival Chorus, meticulously prepared by James Grossmith, produced clear textures and crisp diction, though tenors and basses dispatched lines with such aplomb that upper voices sometimes seemed underpowered by comparison.Only the third cantata, Hiawatha’s Departure, permits the soloists to embody genuine characters, and here the performance gained dramatic momentum. Soprano Francesca Chiejina displayed a radiant upper register and a steely core sound but remained score-bound. Baritone Christopher Maltman’s moving rendition of Hiawatha’s farewell harnessedthe weary authority of his Wotan. Tenor Nicky Spence injected proceedings with welcome theatricality – greeting the chorus like comrades before his bravura aria in Hiawatha’s Wedding Feast, enjoying the banter as he couldn’t convince them he’d seen a flood, conveying the sheer weirdness of his invocations of Jesus and Mary.So did it work? Almost. Hiawatha’s eccentric dramaturgy and questionable politics mean it will never return to the regular repertoire, but the musical riches unveiled by Payare more than justified Benedetti’s bold decision to programme it.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalOperareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Larry David says former friend Alan Dershowitz ‘made a deal with the devil’ as Trump’s lawyer | Larry David | The Guardian
description: The Seinfeld and Curb Your Enthusiasm creator says Dershowitz, who has also defended Jeffrey Epstein and Harvey Weinstein, ‘only has himself to blame’ for being ostracised
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: The Seinfeld and Curb Your Enthusiasm creator says Dershowitz, who has also defended Jeffrey Epstein and Harvey Weinstein, ‘only has himself to blame’ for being ostracised
Content: Larry David pictured in New York City in 2024. The Seinfeld and Curb Your Enthusiasm creator has spoken about his public falling out with former friend Alan Dershowitz.Photograph: Dave Allocca/StarPix/Rex/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenLarry David pictured in New York City in 2024. The Seinfeld and Curb Your Enthusiasm creator has spoken about his public falling out with former friend Alan Dershowitz.Photograph: Dave Allocca/StarPix/Rex/ShutterstockLarry DavidLarry David says former friend Alan Dershowitz ‘made a deal with the devil’ as Trump’s lawyerThe Seinfeld and Curb Your Enthusiasm creator says Dershowitz, who also defended Jeffrey Epstein and Harvey Weinstein, ‘only has himself to blame’ for being ostracisedSian CainThu 20 Aug 2026 00.06 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 00.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLarry David has opened up about the collapse of his friendship with Alan Dershowitz, saying that Dershowitz “made a deal with the devil” when he became Donald Trump’s lawyer.Dershowitz, a former Harvard University law professor, has been a member of legal teams for Trump, Jeffrey Epstein, OJ Simpson and Harvey Weinstein at various points in his career, andserved on Trump’s defense teamduring the president’s first impeachment trial in 2020.Reports emerged in 2021 that David and Dershowitz, who were friends and neighbours for years on Martha’s Vineyard, had a public argument during which the Curb Your Enthusiasm and Seinfeld creator was heard to call Dershowitz “disgusting”.Dershowitz later confirmed the account was accurate, telling the New Yorker in 2022: “Suddenly,Larry Davidwalks in to buy some groceries. I say, ‘Hey. Hi, Larry,’ and he turns away, and he just walks away. I say, ‘Larry, can’t we at least talk?’ He said, ‘No. You’re disgusting.’Life, Larry and the Pursuit of Unhappiness: only Larry David would have the titanium balls to pull this offRead more“He called me disgusting, and he said he could never talk to me,” he added. “Here’s a guy who used to come to our house to work out in the gym. He would come to our house for dinner two or three times a summer.”In a new profile of Dershowitz published bythe Atlanticthis week, David spoke about the incident for the first time. “I have lots of confrontations on my show but rarely in life. And then only if I think I can take them in a fight. Hence the Dershowitz dust-up,” he said.In the Atlantic, Dershowitz spoke of feeling hurt that David had not contacted him when his son Elon died from a stroke last year aged 64. In response, David said he was “starting to feel a little sorry” for Dershowitz, “certainly because of his son.”“I certainly regret not [reaching out],” David told the Atlantic. “As I said on Curb once, ‘I think of nice things. I just don’t act on them.’”But the next day David contacted the Atlantic again to add: “I’m loath to say anything mean because he’s been so ostracised. But he only has himself to blame. He made a deal with the devil. Literally. And I’d bet the devil hasn’t said a word to him since the impeachment.”In April, Dershowitz announced he was swapping to the Republican party after decades of supporting the Democratic party, which he labelled the “most anti-Israel party in US history”.In June the US supreme courtturned down a request by Dershowitzto revive a $300m defamation lawsuit he filed against CNN over the network’s coverage of remarks he made while defending Trump, which he claimed had been edited to make it falsely appear that he “had lost his mind”.Explore more on these topicsLarry DavidUS politicsDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: You be the judge: should my partner stop hogging my side of the bed? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Pádraig has a favourite side, whereas Dave likes to sleep farthest from the door. Help us put this argument to bed
Author: Georgina Lawton
Headline: Pádraig has a favourite side, whereas Dave likes to sleep farthest from the door. Help us put this argument to bed
Content: Illustration: Igor BastidasView image in fullscreenIllustration: Igor BastidasYou be the judgeLife and styleYou be the judge: should my partner stop hogging my side of the bed?Pádraig has a favourite side, whereas Dave likes to sleep farthest from the door. Help us put this argument to bedFind out how to get a disagreement settled or become a jurorInterviews byGeorgina LawtonThu 20 Aug 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 11.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTheprosecution: Pádraigdouble quotation markI sleep better on the left side of the bed. I shouldn’t have to swap just because we’ve moved to a new flatMy partner Dave and I are two stubborn boys who both adore a great night’s sleep. But we cannot settle a disagreement about which side of the bed belongs to whom. We’ve recently moved into a new flat and the orientation of our room and bed has shifted. Now, the side of the bed I assumed was mine has become Dave’s.We lived in our old flat for three and a half years. We slept like kings there: a humongous bed and individual duvets, which our Swedish friend had recommended for a good night’s sleep. I was on the left side (if you were standing at the foot of the bed facing it). I felt well rested and got into a great sleep routine.Due to the orientation of our new bedroom, Dave wants to be furthest from the door, so I’m now sleeping on the right side and he is on the left. He thinks the sides we sleep on should be interchangeable, depending on where the door is, but I say the left side is mine, no matter what. So I’ve been forced to sleep on what I deem to be the wrong side for the last few months. I find it challenging to fall asleep and can’t get used to it.double quotation markNow I’m tossing and turning, trying to sleep on a side of my body that feels unnaturalI commute further to work and get up before Dave, so he thinks I should be closer to the door so I don’t disrupt him. I pack all my stuff the night before and leave it outside the room to avoid waking him up, so I don’t feel it makes much difference.I’m a sensitive sleeper and it’s a big thing to retrain yourself to sleep on a different side of the bed. I slept so well before. Now I’m tossing and turning, trying to sleep on a side of my body that feels unnatural. In the night, Dave and I move closer and closer to our old sides and bump into each other in the middle. My sleep is disturbed. I want to swap back.Every time we go on holiday or sleep somewhere else for the night, we repeat this battle, depending on how the room is laid out. We are in between places at the moment and I don’t know what will happen when we move again. I want an opportunity to get my side back.You be the judge – send us your domestic disputesRead moreThe defence: Davedouble quotation markPádraig gets up early for work – if we switched sides, he’d wake me up at 4am every morningPádraig views the left-hand side of the bed as his, and the right-hand side as mine, but that’s not how life works. He says the side of the bed is absolute, like the left or right in a car, but I view the two sides of the bed as relative to where they sit in the room, and who wants to be closest to the door or window, not the actual side of a bed, because of course all rooms are different.We lived in one place for three and a half years and another place for two years before that; when we moved out of the first place, I said: “We need to flip sides – it isn’t working logistically.” We had a big argument about it then because I wasn’t happy. Pádraig is over 6ft tall and I’m fairly wide, so in the past, when we had a double bed, we argued. In our current place, we have a king bed but the room orientation has shifted.Pádraig tosses and turns all night, which is annoying, as it wakes me up. He gets up at 4am for work, so if he’s moving around the room, it’s disruptive to my sleep. But he also gets home late after a big night out, sometimes at 5am. I don’t mind, except for when it wakes me up. I like to stay on the side furthest from the door for this reason.double quotation markPádraig could learn to sleep on this new side, but I can’t learn to sleep through his noise in the morningsI disagree that we argue about this on holiday. To me, it doesn’t matter as much when we’re away. But right now, everything about our sleep is becoming an issue. We have a fan on all night and both of us move around a lot. I think Pádraig could learn to sleep on this new side, but I can’t learn to sleep through his noise in the mornings.It’s been suggested that we move the bed in our room: it is now opposite the door, against the wall where the window is. My side is closest to that window, which used to be Pádraig’s old side. But if we moved the bed to suit him, it would be bad feng shui as the door would be too close to the bed. I believe there are other considerations around sleeping, beyond just: “I like being on the left or right.” Pádraig needs to adjust.Names have been changedThe jury of Guardian readersDave should show Pádraig more consideration as he gets up at 4am (Dave, count yourself lucky you don’t have to), but I don’t think he needs to be nearest the door, as long as he exits the room quietly. Has Dave tried earplugs? Whatever happens, I hope they can put this argument to bed.Toby, 36skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionI’m sympathetic to both sides, but Dave’s insistence that “Pádraig needs to adjust”, while being totally unwilling to try other solutions puts him on the wrong side of this argument. Everyone needs to feel comfortable when they’re sleeping, so changing the position of the bed seems like the only fair compromise.Sarah, 40It’s the same mattress and bed as before, so the couple should keep the sides from prior sleeping arrangements. If the only complaint from Dave is the disturbance from the morning routine, then Pádraig can work on adjusting it.Angela, 44It is the BED that chooses the sides for us, not us who choose the sides. Dave, ignores this at his peril. Respect your bed and you will be given intimacy, harmony and rest. This also means not barrelling in at 5am after a night out – then you’re on the sofa, Pádraig.Simon, 48Sorry Dave, that is how life works! Throughout life’s challenges and living arrangements, you find comfort and constancy in your life partner – and the side of the bed that feels most like home to you. Window and door position have less bearing on this, in my opinion.Siu, 32Now you be the judgeIn our online poll, tell us: who needs to move over?The poll closes on Wednesday 26 August at 9am GMTLast week’s resultsWe asked ifJulie should stop scribbling notes on every book she reads35%of you said yes –Julie is guilty65%of you said no –Julie is not guiltyExplore more on these topicsLife and styleYou be the judgeRelationshipsSleepfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Where did all the XXL clothes go? Fashion brands are scrapping plus sizes in the GLP-1 era | Fashion | The Guardian
description: As weight-loss drugs gain popularity in the US, brands are scaling back their ranges – and frustrating customers
Author: Hannah Marriott
Headline: As weight-loss drugs gain popularity in the US, brands are scaling back their ranges – and frustrating customers
Content: ‘It just boils down to the fact that plus-size people are seen as less than,’ influencer Tess Holliday says of the shrinking plus-size ranges at mainstream retailers.Illustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘It just boils down to the fact that plus-size people are seen as less than,’ influencer Tess Holliday says of the shrinking plus-size ranges at mainstream retailers.Illustration: Guardian Design / Getty ImagesFashionWhere did all the XXL clothes go? Fashion brands are scrapping plus sizes in the GLP-1 eraAs weight-loss drugs gain popularity in the US, brands are scaling back their ranges – and frustrating customersHannah MarriottThu 20 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 13.00 EDTShareIn March 2023, the model, activist and writerTess Hollidayannounced that she had been working as a size and inclusivity consultant for H&M. The fruits of their partnership felt like “one of the most meaningful things that I’ve done in my career”, shetoldUS Vogue at the time. The fashion juggernaut had committed to an expansion of its sizes, from XL to 4XL, and to increased body diversity of its models.This bucked a trend, coming at an otherwise gloomy time for plus-sized fashion. By 2023, the fashion industry was in the grips of an Ozempic-fuelled celebration of skinny bodies, after its brief flirtation with curves during the body positivity movement of the late 2010s.But by 2026, just three years after the H&M partnership was announced, the fruits of the project had vanished. The research firm Edited, which tracks items as they launch on retailers’ websites, analysed H&M’s offerings for spring/summer 2026, recording all new women’s dresses landing on the site from January to May and compared it with the same period in 2025. Last year, 3XL and 4XL made up 2% of the new inventory. This year those sizes were entirely absent. Other large sizes fell too: XXL, which had accounted for 13.3% of inventory in 2025, was down 3 percentage points, while XL was down 2 percentage points, and smaller sizes, XS to large, rose by 3 percentage points on average.View image in fullscreenTess Holliday arrives at a special screening of film Sacramento on 7 April 2025 in Los Angeles, California.Photograph: Steve Granitz/FilmMagicHolliday no longer works with H&M. Even when she went into the collaboration she was, “a little pessimistic”, she says. “I’ve been plus-sized my entire life. I’ve worked in the industry for over 15 years, I’ve seen the rise and fall of a lot of brands. I’m always worried whether something is genuine.” Once she began working with the brand, though, “I became very optimistic because a lot of the changes that I wanted to implement were being implemented. Unfortunately, I don’t think that maybe it was as genuine as I hoped.”In a statement to the Guardian, H&M said that it continually monitors fit and sizing demand and confirmed that “we have chosen to discontinue sizes 3XL and 4XL, as we have seen lower demand for these sizes.”H&M is not the only brand scaling back plus-sized garments this season. Mango, too, reduced its inventory of new dresses in sizes 16 to 20, from 6.6% in spring/summer 2025 to 0.5% in spring/summer 2026, according to Edited. Meanwhile, an analysis of dresses for sale at Anthropology during July 2026 revealed a year-on-year reduction from 10.5% to 9% in plus-sized offerings. This latest size shrinkage comes after years of other rollbacks, from closures of extended sizes ranges (Loft closed its plus-size range in 2021 after three years; Old Navy scaled back its offerings in May 2022, only nine months after launching a new plus-sized initiative). Last year, 151 locations – nearly a third of all stores – closed at the plus-sized chain Torrid. The options are so limited for plus-sized people now, says influencerNikki Apostolou, that “I’ve given up entirely trying to go into a store or going into a mall hoping to find clothes.” Reddit is full of threads of plus-sized shoppers talking about their lack of options; some are so over it they have startedsewing their own garments.Holliday, who founded the #EffYourBeautyStandards campaign in 2013 seeking to foster self-love and acceptance of all body types, says she noticed the reduction first during Covid. Then, from 2022 on, she says: “There has been a rapid decline in plus-size offerings. Diversity, as a whole, is no longer a priority for a lot of brands.”‘Ozempic arrived and everything changed’: plus-size models on the body positivity backlashRead moreMany analysts, such as Impact Analytics’ CEO, Prashant Agrawal, pin the most recent changes in sizing to GLP-1s, which Agrawal describes as the “number one reason” apparel retailers are anxious about sizes at the moment.Mintel’s latest research says that 18% of US adults reported using GLP-1 drugs as of June 2025, up from 12% in 2024. The impact on the average American body size has already been significant: the rate of US adult obesity appeared to peak, after rising for decades, at 39.9% in 2022, and it dropped to 36.4% this year, according toGallup.“It’s like nothing that anybody’s ever experienced,” says Agrawal. Before now, “each year, over the last 50 years, the US has grown bigger. This is the first time the US has gone the other way.” His company’s data, which draws from sales figures from an undisclosed number of large US apparel retailers, shows two years of rising sales of small garments (size XS up 0.45% between 2023 and 2024 and 0.43% between 2024 and 2025), and minor declines in medium (down 0.05% and 0.02%), large (down 0.31% and 0.30%) and sizes XL and larger (down 0.38% and 0.39%). In brands that order billions of units of garments in advance of each season, such small percentage points could represent a big financial, and environmental, liability.Drill down into the figures, though, and the reasons for the abandonment of plus-sized shoppers by mainstream fashion brands are more complex. Even in the GLP-1 era, after all, the majority of Americans are still plus-sized, including those who have lost weight on GLP-1s. The latest research suggests that most GLP1 users lose between 10% and 20% of their body weight; last year Jack Plunkett, CEO of Plunkett Research, estimated that66% of US women still wear size 14 or above, which most brands classify as plus-sized. Even now – and despite all evidence to the contrary in visual culture – plus-sized shoppers are fashion’s vastly underserved majority.double quotation markGLP-1s are changing the size curve, but they’re not eliminating the need for size inclusivityBrittany SteigerMany plus-sized customers have given up on new clothes and are turning to the secondhand market. ThredUp, like many other used clothing platforms, reports a surge in donations of larger garments in recent years (listings were up 32% year over year in the first half of 2026, and have doubled since the first half of 2023.) But they have also seen a remarkable uptick in demand. So far this year, purchase volume for large, XL and plus-sized items in women’s apparel grew 17.4% – more than double the 6.8% growth rate for small and medium.“Demand for larger sizes isn’t fading, it’s one of the fastest-growing parts of our marketplace,” says Kristen Brophy, senior vice-president of marketing at ThredUp. The company has no data on whether this is related to GLP-1 usage, but Brophy says that resale has long played a part in shopping when people’s bodies are changing. “We’ve also heard from customers that many brick-and-mortar thrift stores don’t accept or stock plus-size items in the first place, which pushes even more of that shopping behavior online.”Brittany Steiger, associate principal of retail and e-commerce at Mintel, says that GLP-1s are affecting the market – but that impact should be kept in perspective. “GLP-1s are changing the size curve, but they’re not eliminating the need for size inclusivity. Sixty-nine per cent of shoppers say brands need to offer more size and length options. The bigger story isn’t shrinking bodies – it’s the ongoing challenge of fit.” In her view, the opportunity for brands is to concentrate on size flexibility and adjustability – and more brands are indeed incorporating elements such as hidden drawstrings, according to Edited – rather than offering fewer sizes.Edited’s senior retail analyst Krista Corrigan says that the flow of traffic isn’t all going the same way. Anthropology, for example, which typically serves an affluent customer base, “is showing a pronounced ‘GLP-1 effect” not only in pruning larger garments but in switching many of its garments from numeric to alpha sizes. Corrigan says it’s because alpha sizes – size medium rather than size 14, for example – are deemed more likely to “absorb minor body fluctuations better than tailored numeric fits”, making them less prone to fit issues “for consumers undergoing body transitions”. Anthropology customers, she says, “are probably the demographic that would be adopting these GLP-1 most”.Walmart, meanwhile, which typically serves budget-conscious shoppers, was a rare example of a brand adding inventory for larger customers this season. “That makes a lot of sense,” says Corrigan, “they’re doing something very smart and continuing to keep that thread of inclusion throughout most of their assortment, capitalizing on some of that white space.”double quotation markThey don’t see us as worthy customersTess HollidayWhat this suggests, though, is that plus-sized people are being ejected from the affluent and trend-led part of the market more quickly than elsewhere. A correlation which tracks with hundreds of years of celebrity culture (Wallis Simpson, who reportedly coined the phrase “you can never be too rich or too thin”, would have loved Mounjaro) and economic reality – the inverse association between economic advantage and body mass index within western societies has been established by multiplestudies. Semaglutide, which is unaffordable for many, only deepens this divide (one recent study of4.5 million adults in Denmarkshowed that the proportion of individuals with a redeemed semaglutide prescription increased with income, even though the proportion living with obesity decreased.)Despite that correlation, the US size 14-plus market is so substantial – literally tens of millions of people – that the assumption Holliday feels retailers make, all-too-readily, that all plus-sized people “can’t afford to shop anyway” is clearly untrue. For Holliday, it ties into other stereotypes she is sick of hearing. People “assume that we’re lazy or that we’re uneducated or a lot of other things”, she says. “There’s a really big disconnect, and it just boils down to the fact that plus-size people are seen as less than. Until we fix that issue in society we’re always going to keep having the same conversations over and over, because they don’t see us as worthy customers.”‘Please don’t lose another pound!’: Ozempic is upending the wedding dress industryRead moreSome cherished brands remain. Holliday recommends Lazy Oaf, a British brand she buys whenever she is in the UK, as well as Eloquii and Torrid, even if the latter can be frustrating on price, she says. Apostolou goes to Lane Bryant for bras and likes Target’s Wild Fable line for on-trend clothes, as well as Eloquii – though she feels they have gone downhill – for special occasion dresses. Steiger says plus-sized shoppers speak highly of Walmart at the budget end and praises Universal Standard as a higher-end brand “founded on size inclusivity”. Also at the higher end, Apostolou is into RCA Public Label, and says she wants to try to support small, plus-sized designers when she can, “designers who are working for themselves, not part of corporations who will swing wherever the wind blows them”.For Apostolou, it is a lack of care and investment that lead so many plus-sized ranges to fail. “So many of the brands that do exist are giving us versions of things they’ve been offering since 2010. They feel like, OK, you have to hide your stomach, wear these jeans that are gonna squish you in. Wear this cold shoulder top – it’s like the plus-sized uniform – because your shoulder is the only skin that you should be allowed to show. Or it’s the same dress – here’s the cleavage and the rest is a tent.”The narrative around Ozempic, she argues, is an excuse for fashion brands to cut back and not have to think about plus sizes. “They’ve been using every excuse that they possibly could think of for years now – ‘oh well, people aren’t shopping’ – when they’re offering the ugliest, most hideous styles ever.”

title: Ooni Koda 2 pizza oven review: serves up perfect pizzas in minutes | Pizza | The Guardian
description: Quick to fire up and compact enough to take camping, Ooni’s gas-powered model sets a high bar for outdoor dining
Author: Rachel Ogden
Headline: Quick to fire up and compact enough to take camping, Ooni’s gas-powered model sets a high bar for outdoor dining
Content: Slice of the action: the Koda 2 delivered evenly browned pizzas and reliable results.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSlice of the action: the Koda 2 delivered evenly browned pizzas and reliable results.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterPizzaReviewOoni Koda 2 pizza oven review: serves up perfect pizzas in minutesQuick to fire up and compact enough to take camping, Ooni’s gas-powered model sets a high bar for outdoor diningThe best pizza ovens – testedGozney Dome Gen 2 pizza oven reviewRachel OgdenThu 20 Aug 2026 05.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you’re looking for a gas-powered, compact, portablepizza oventhat’s easy to set up, yet still offers generous cooking space, the Ooni Koda 2 may be the pick for you.The second generation of the company’s award-winningKoda 12 ovenhas space for a 14in pizza compared with the original’s 12in one. There is also more room to manoeuvre inside, a wider temperature range (so you can cook seafood and steaks, too), and a flame designed for better heat distribution. Unlike the Koda 12, the Ooni Koda 2 is available with optional accessories, including the rotating stone bundle tested here (apricey upgrade of £229) and a smart temperature hub(the Connect, £89), which means you don’t have to constantly reach for an infrared (IR) thermometer.Essentially, the Ooni Koda 2 is a great all-round pizza oven, and my favourite gas-powered model. Folding legs and a weight of 16kg make it just light enough to transport; it’s relatively affordable at less than £400; and it’s pretty much plug-and-play, so you can be up and running in minutes.View at OoniView at John LewisHow I testedView image in fullscreenCooking on gas: the Ooni Koda 2 being temperature checked before being loaded with pizza.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianI tested the Ooni Koda 2 using the same methods as the otherpizza ovensI’ve reviewed for the Filter. As well as assessing the quality of the cook by making differently topped pizzas – cheese and tomato at about 430C; a veggie pizza with onion, pepper and tomato at a lower 350C to caramelise and soften the ingredients; and a salami-topped pizza at about 400C – I rated it for ease of assembly, overall use, lighting, temperature control and storage.I tested it with the static stone that comes as standard and the optional extra rotating stone to see if this made any difference to the cooking performance.What you need to knowView image in fullscreenGet ready to bundle: the Koda 2 is customisable with a large range of accessories.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianView at OoniView at John LewisMy favourite aspect of the Koda 2 is that it’s more customisable than most pizza ovens. You can pay a reasonable price and quite happily cook in it just as it is, without feeling like you’re missing out.Or, you can add a range of accessories to make it suit the way you want to cook. Therotating stone, for example, helps to reduce burnt crusts and does away with the need to manually shuffle your pizza around. Instead, a wave of the hand in front of an infrared sensor under the front of the oven starts and stops the rotation. Far more convenient when you’re holding apizza peel. However, it’s a pricey addition, and it reduces the Koda 2’s cooking capacity from 14 inches to 12. I also found the rotating stone less effective with the rectangular premade dough I was using, as the corners still tended to burn. If you use rounds, though, you’ll be fine.Similarly, the Connect digital temperature hub reduces the need to slavishly monitor the oven’s temperature with an IR thermometer. Instead, you can monitor it at a distance, or via your smartphone as you prepare food elsewhere. Note that it relies on Bluetooth, so connectivity can be spotty.Ooni Koda 2 specificationsDimensions:47.2 x 54.5 x 33.3cm (WDH), mouth 39.3 x 11cm (WH)Maximum capacity:35 x 39cm pizza stone (working capacity 14in, or 12in with the rotating stone)Features:folding legs, matchstick holder, optional rotating stone, optional digital temperature hubFuel:gasSpare parts:available from Ooni support direct (see below)Weight:16kgWhat we loveView image in fullscreenHow char-ming: the vegetables on the veggie pizza were perfectly soft and gently charred.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianOne of my biggest gripes about pizza ovens is poorly placed battery-powered ignition. Too often, the battery compartment is hard to reach or in a visually obtrusive spot. Ooni handles this well: the Koda 2’s batteries are neatly concealed inside one of the legs, making them easy to reach without being on display.The controls are similarly well thought out, positioned on the side of the oven. This makes them easier to adjust than rear-mounted controls and keeps them clean – which can be an issue with controls at the front.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markWith either the rotating or static stone, cooking performance was excellentThe Koda 2 always lit first time, and thanks to its tapered back burner, heated up in less than half an hour. Different spots on the stone often showed very different temperatures, but with either the rotating or static stone, cooking performance was excellent. Any scorches were largely down to me either not turning the pizza fast enough or not getting it out on time.I was especially impressed when cooking the veggie pizza on the rotating stone – the vegetables received equal heat, so they were soft and gently charred. All the pizzas I made rose well and browned evenly. A 2in stainless-steel ledge at the mouth is handy for resting the pizza and checking on progress, too.Storage is another strong point. Three folding legs make the Koda 2 easy to tuck away, even if you have limited room outdoors. This caused some issues when setting up the oven, though, as they tended to fold back in before all three were fully extended. Some kind of locking mechanism would be useful.What we don’t loveView image in fullscreenMind the gap: the relatively small mouth can be awkward for beginners.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianWhile I enjoyed the consistent cooking on the rotating stone, fitting it proved fiddly – it’s not a quick lift-in, lift-out fixture. Note, too, that once fitted, it prevents the legs from folding in unless you detach the stone’s motor. It’s also pricey, at£229.Once the oven reaches the highest temperatures, it can take a while for it to drop again for lower-heat cooking. With the static stone in place, I found it took almost as long for it to heat up as it did to drop back down to cook pizzas with veggies and meat.The Ooni Koda 2’s mouth is also more awkward than some models to get pizza in and out. It’s not as beginner-friendly as larger ovens or those designed with a slightly taller or wider mouth.Warranty, repairability and longevityOoni offers a five-year extended warranty for the Koda 2 if you register it, or one year as standard. The rotating stone is guaranteed for two years if you register, as is the Connect digital temperature hub(or one year if you haven’t). You can contact the company for spare parts, including the pizza stone, folding legs, leg fixing spares (foot and leg release button), propane regulator, Torx key, matchstick holder, battery cover set, FSD/sparker/thermocouple module and flamekeeper.Ooni Koda 2: should I buy it?View image in fullscreenHot stuff: reliable results and easy storage make the Koda 2 a strong all-rounder.Photograph: Rachel Ogden/The GuardianThis well-designed pizza oven will tick most boxes for most people, and it’s ideal for families. It’s easier to store than its bigger brethren (such as theKoda 2 Pro, which fits an 18in pizza, or theKoda 2 Max, which accommodates a 24in pizza), compact enough to take with you to a campsite, and reliable in terms of lighting and results.The capacity might be an issue if you’re throwing a big event. While the Koda 2 can churn out pizza after pizza in a matter of minutes, it doesn’t have the cooking area of larger ovens, especially with the rotating stone in place. For smaller alfresco get-togethers, though, the Ooni Koda 2 is a welcome party guest.View at OoniView at John LewisFor more, read thebest pizza ovens in the UK, thebest BBQs and grillsand thebest (and worst) chefs’ knivesRachel Ogden has worked as a consumer journalist for decades, becoming an expert unboxer before it was a thing, although she is less successful at assembling and repacking. Her home has hosted hundreds of appliances while her garden has seen a succession of pizza ovens, barbecues and heaters put through their paces. It takes a lot to impress her – many appliances have tried and failedExplore more on these topicsPizzaThe FilterFoodGardensHomesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ​My coastal road trip confirms that seaside ​food ​still ​beats ​fine ​dining | Food | The Guardian
description: ​A​ family holiday shaped by salt air, seagulls and unpredictable weather proves that the seaside serves a kind of joy no restaurant can engineer
Author: Georgina Hayden
Headline: ​A​ family holiday shaped by salt air, seagulls and unpredictable weather proves that the seaside serves a kind of joy no restaurant can engineer
Content: Best enjoyed by the seaside, classic fish and chips.Photograph: mtreasure/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenBest enjoyed by the seaside, classic fish and chips.Photograph: mtreasure/Getty Images/iStockphotoFeastFood​My coastal road trip confirms that seaside ​food ​still ​beats ​fine ​dining​A​ family holiday shaped by salt air, seagulls and unpredictable weather proves that the seaside serves a kind of joy no restaurant can engineerSign up here for our weekly food newsletter, FeastGeorgina HaydenThu 20 Aug 2026 07.40 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 07.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere are few things more powerful than the smell of salt, vinegar and hot oil carried on a sea breeze. Or sugar-coated doughnuts, still warm in a grease-stained paper bag. Such distinctly British perfumes are the smell of my summer, because my family and I are road-tripping through the UK and Ireland. We are embracing as much of coastline as we can, while battling seagulls and unpredictable weather along the way. And, unlike the carefully curated dining experiences we seek on holidays abroad, seaside food has always been wonderfully simple. It is rarely elegant, but it is pure comfort and nostalgia.First up,fish and chips, in my opinion, they remain the undisputed king of Britain’s coastal cuisine. Every seaside town insists that theirs is the best (so far, the finest I’ve tried were inYorkshire, but I am prepared for that to change on this holiday). If you are at home this summer, or not near a British seaside, you can, of course, have a go at making your own.Tim Hughes’sandFelicity Cloake’srecipes are as authentic as they come, along with a crisp beer batter for firm white fish. For a slight twist, Yotam Ottolenghi’sfish and spiced sweet potato chipsis an excellent, inspired dish. Either way, all options deliver.View image in fullscreenSquidgy with jam … Benjamina Ebuehi’s strawberry custard doughnuts.Photograph: Matthew Hague/The GuardianNext on my list of seaside classics is a paper bag of hot doughnuts and a99 Flake ice-cream. I quite enjoy making my own doughnuts – it’s a fun activity for a quiet afternoon – but the ones I make at home will never be in the same realm as the seaside ones. Mine are often fluffy, squidgy buns filled with a piped custard or seasonal jam; a bit like Benjamina Ebuehi’sstrawberry and custard doughnutsor Felicity Cloake’sperfect jam doughnuts. And, the chances are that you won’t be able to recreate a classic ice-cream to hold the Flake unless you havea snazzy machine. Still, there are excellent no-churn methods; consider Yotam’srecipeor thisstrawberry ice-creamfrom Tom Hunt. Other nostalgic ice-cream puds include: cherry sundaes and banana splits, andtheseby Helen Graves are perfect make-at-home versions that will make you feel like a kid again.And let’s not forget other notable seaside classics such as a simple, tender and sweetcrab sandwich, ideally eaten somewhere along the south-west coast. Polystyrene cups ofcocklesand whelks eaten with a toothpick. And treats such as fluorescent rock and sticks coated in a cloud oftooth-achingly sweet candyfloss. Not something you might eat day-to-day, but on a cold, windswept British beach? They’re a necessity. And, if you ask me, they all beat Michelin-starred meals.My week in foodView image in fullscreenMake it at home or move to Greece … Georgina Hayden’s one-pan moussaka.Photograph: Ola O Smit/The GuardianOdysea’s odyssey|While the world goes nuts for the blockbuster film, I’m excited finally to get my hands onGreek Odysea: Flavours of Greece from Pantry to Plate. Written by the family behind the much-loved food brand Odysea, this cookbook is a glimpse into founder Panayis’s childhood, recipes from his mother and family, and stories of the small-scale producers whose ingredients shape every dish. It will make you want to spend the day lovingly making a moussaka (or move to Greece).Heard it here first|Every parent knows that even the most restaurant-accustomed child has a time limit on how long they’ll sit still for – because delicious food and sticker books will get you only so far. But a recent visit toHeard, a small chain in London, proved a huge hit for all of us: incredible burgers from Michelin-starred chef Jordan Bailey for the adults, and the same excellent components for the kids. TheHeard mini makersset-up is a pick’n’mix burger, all lined up on a tray, complete with mini tongs, squeezy bottles of sauce and a little salt shaker filled with a tomato powder to sprinkle on chips (my girls’ favourite).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFeastRecipes from all our star cooks, seasonal eating ideas and restaurant reviews. Get our best food writing every weekEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNoodles, now|There are a few pantry staples that I swear by, and instant noodles are one of them. So, I was intrigued when I came acrossChilli Chan’sin a local deli, not least because the packaging is fresh and hopeful, as is the story behind them. Having tasted the XO mushroom knife cut noodles and spicy Mala varieties, I can confirm that they’re delicious.If you want to read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive Feast in your inbox every Thursday.Explore more on these topicsFoodFeastSummer food and drinkBritish food and drinkIce-cream and sorbetFishChips (french fries)BakingnewslettersShareReuse this content

title: When it comes to rosé, pink doesn’t have to mean Provence | Wine | The Guardian
description: From Morocco to Monmouth, there’s a whole world of blushing rosé wines to discover
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: From Morocco to Monmouth, there’s a whole world of blushing rosé wines to discover
Content: ‘Blushing like cheeks in a summer romance, pale rosé captures the easy and fun holiday spirit.’Photograph: flyparade/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘Blushing like cheeks in a summer romance, pale rosé captures the easy and fun holiday spirit.’Photograph: flyparade/Getty Images/iStockphotoGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.WineWhen it comes to rosé, pink doesn’t have to mean ProvenceFrom Morocco to Monmouth, there’s a whole world of blushing rosé wines to discoverMina HollandThu 20 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHello, from rosé season, the only time of year I order wine like a patriarchal septuagenarian. For this fleeting moment in the wine-drinking calendar, questions are out and assumptions are in; everyone’s happy to drink pink – specifically, pale, dry and berry-crisp Provence rosé. Blushing like cheeks in a summer romance, pale rosé captures something of the hazy holiday spirit: easy, fun, objectively delicious. The liquid equivalent of chips with ketchup, it’s a safe bet.Finding a wine that almost everyone approves of is close to the holy grail – and if Provence has cracked it so everyone’s happy, why deviate? But unless you’re in primary school, chances are you wouldn’t eat chips at every meal, and I’d apply the same logic here. We’re human! We’re omnivores! And even within the category of rosé, there is a world to discover beyond the Provençal style that dominates supermarket shelves. What’s more, the likes of Whispering Angel may make decision-making easy, but they also command some hefty prices (£22.50 on Ocadoat the time of writing).Rosé is defined by brief skin contact – a process less sexy than that sounds, involving a fleeting encounter between the juice of pressed red grapes with their skins, giving the wine its seductive hue. Said hue can range from almost imperceptibly peachy right through to deep cherry juice, where the line between “rosé” and “chilled red” becomes fuzzy. Sometimes rosé is made entirely with red grapes, as are several in today’s pick, or with a blend of red and white, which is typical of Provence, where big-hitting red varieties such as grenache and syrah are blended with a white, usually vermentino, for floral freshness.The wines here all hail from outside Europe and arguably offer something a bit more than a Provence rosé; most are better all-rounders to see you from aperitif through a meal, but often put some of the grape varieties most associated with Provence to work. They include Babylonstoren’s 100% mourvèdre from Simonsberg, a mountainous enclave of South Africa known for world-class reds; this – the official wine of the Chelsea Flower Show, no less! – is fresh, structured and hugely table-friendly. Meanwhile, the excellent Moroccan number, sometimes called avin gris(grey wine) due to its pallor, is made with a blend of cabernet sauvignon and grenache with heat-tolerant hybrid grapes, marselan and caladoc. Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley is making some delicious rosé, too, where surrounding mountains and a sea breeze bring cool nights to offset hot days. In Itata, Chile, granite soils and maritime climate produce En Cabeza, a cinsault rosé that’s juicy and mineral – and a good gateway to natural wine. I’d order that for the septuagenarian in my life, no questions asked.Five alternatives to a Provence roséEn Cabeza, Luca Hodgkinson, Chile£13 Forest Wines, 12.5%. A touch of aromatic moscatel joins cinsault for a gluggable and food-friendly summer go-to.Volubilia GrisLa Zouina, Morocco£14.95 Buon Vino, 13%. Blushing and eyelid-batting, a Provence-style bottle that will please fans of very dry rosé.Babylonstoren Mourvèdre Rosé, South Africa£18 Waitrose, 13%. Light yet robust, a rosé to see you from dawn till dusk, if you feel so inclined.Massaya Rosé 2024, Lebanon£16.50 Wine Society, 13.5%. Pretty 100% cinsault with a savoury, spiced note – a great companion to meze or piquant dishes.Cowboys Don’t Have Curls, Ain’t My First Rosé,UK£27 Wright’s Wine, 9.5%. By some standards, not European! A wild and wonderful field blend grown in Somerset and made in collaboration with Monmouth winemaker, Dave Morris, this will make you reassess rosé.Explore more on these topicsWineFoodNorth African food and drinkMiddle Eastern food and drinkBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for spaghetti with semi-dried tomatoes, garlic, herbs and breadcrumbs | Italian food and drink | The Guardian
description: Sun-drying tomatoes until they’re leathery on the outside and soft within is something of an art, but it’s more than worth it for this moreish pasta dish
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: Sun-drying tomatoes until they’re leathery on the outside and soft within is something of an art, but it’s more than worth it for this moreish pasta dish
Content: Rachel Roddy’s spaghetti with semi-dried tomatoes, garlic, herbs and breadcrumbs.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRachel Roddy’s spaghetti with semi-dried tomatoes, garlic, herbs and breadcrumbs.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianA kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkRachel Roddy’s recipe for spaghetti with semi-dried tomatoes, garlic, herbs and breadcrumbsSun-drying tomatoes until they’re leathery on the outside and soft within is something of an art, but it’s more than worth it for this moreish pasta dishRachel RoddyThu 20 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 12.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne set of guidelines I received in Sicily for sun-drying tomatoes was two to seven days, depending on temperature, humidity, wind and the size of the fruit. I might as well have been given a surfboard and told “go”, because that advice felt far too broad and general to be helpful to a complete beginner. So I asked someone else.For them, with an ideal temperatures of 35C and low humidity, trays of egg-sized tomato halves arranged on wire racks on wooden boards, sprinkled with salt and left in full sun during the day, and taken in at night, generally took three days to reach the desirable point: dry enough to store, but still with a flexibility and sweet chew. From broad to specific, this advice also felt overwhelming: What if the temperature changes or turns humid? What are the signs of humidity? What if my tomatoes are bigger than eggs? What happens if it rains? In the end, though, between these two extremes of advice and temperatures swinging between being in the pleasant 20Cs and burning 40Cs, too much humidity, rain (bring them inside) and not being particularly organised, I have managed to – relatively successfully – dry batches of tomatoes of all shapes and sizes.Experimenting has also taught me that I like a semi-dried tomato: the red, ear-like halves that are leathery and dry on the outside but soft and toffee-like in the middle – the sort that stir memories of those bought from Sainsbury’s in the late 1980s. Temperatures as they are this summer, I have made several batches of semi-dried cherry tomato halves arranged on wire racks outside and in direct sun for two days (coming in at night). I have also made several batches with the help of a little sugar in the oven at 130C for an hour for smaller tomatoes, longer if they are the size of a yolk or an egg, and, if necessary, turning off the oven and leaving the tray inside while it cools. The aim is wrinkled and a little dry on top, but still juicy and sweet within. Prepare at least 1kg, and ideally 2kg, with some packed in a jar and covered with olive oil, and the rest for this week’s recipe.Spaghetti with semi-dried tomatoes, garlic, herbs and breadcrumbsWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep2hrs or 2 daysCook20 minServes41kg cherry tomatoes,or golf-ball size vine tomatoesSaltOlive oilSugar2garlic cloves1 medium-size tomato,peeled and crushed (hands are best)1 small bunchflat-leaf parsley1 small bunch basil100g soft white breadcrumbs500g spaghetti, linguine or tagliatelleCut the cherry tomatoes in half, put them in a bowl with a pinch of salt and four tablespoons of olive oil, and toss well. Arrange the halves cut side up on a large baking tray, sprinkle with a little sugar and bake at 130C (110C fan)/250F/gas ½ for an hour for small tomatoes, longer if they are large; the aim is wrinkled and a little dry on top but still juicy and sweet within. Set aside to cool, then set half aside for this recipe and put the rest in a jar covered with olive oil.Peel the garlic and slice very thinly, cut the tomatoes you have set aside into quarters, and mince the herbs.In a frying pan, warm two tablespoons of olive oil and the breadcrumbs, along with a pinch of salt. Move the crumbs around with a spoon until they are lightly golden, then tip on to a plate.Bring a large pan of water to a boil, add salt, stir, then cook the pasta according to packet instructions.Meanwhile, back in the frying pan, gently warm three tablespoons of olive oil and the garlic, until it softens and becomes fragrant, then add the crushed tomato, stir for a few minutes, then add the semi-dried tomatoes.Once the pasta is ready, lift it directly into the saucepan and toss well. Add the herbs, toss again, then divide between between four plates, topping each with a handful of crumbs. Pass around the jar of oil-covered tomatoes, if anyone wants extra – also asking if they can guess whether they took two hours or two days to dry.Explore more on these topicsItalian food and drinkA kitchen in RomeFoodPastaMain courseTomatoesStarterrecipesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The only way is up’: cycling Norway’s mountainous ‘Milky Way’ | Norway holidays | The Guardian
description: The Mjølkevegen was once used to bring milk from high pastures to the towns below. Now cyclists are discovering the road’s breathtaking panoramas of peaks and lakes, dotted with cosy inns
Author: Ailsa Sheldon
Headline: The Mjølkevegen was once used to bring milk from high pastures to the towns below. Now cyclists are discovering the road’s breathtaking panoramas of peaks and lakes, dotted with cosy inns
Content: Ailsa Sheldon cycling Norway’s Mjølkewegen.Photograph: Markus StitzView image in fullscreenAilsa Sheldon cycling Norway’s Mjølkewegen.Photograph: Markus StitzNorway holidays‘The only way is up’: cycling Norway’s mountainous ‘Milky Way’The Mjølkevegen was once used to bring milk from high pastures to the towns below. Now cyclists are discovering the road’s breathtaking panoramas of peaks and lakes, dotted with cosy innsAilsa SheldonThu 20 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 07.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Norway is a hilly country,” shrugs Glenn Roar Berge. He’s not wrong, though he is fond of an understatement. I’m in Valdres in southern Norway to explore the cycle routes that skirt the edges of Jotunheimen national park. Glenn fromJotunheimen Travelis our guide, a born-and-bred local of these mountains.For most of our three-day ride, we’ll be following theMjølkevegen, or Milky Way, a 155-mile (250km) route from Vinstra in the north to Gol in the south. It was developed after the second world war, when increased demand for fresh milk meant connecting the mountain farms with the towns below. While farming continues, the road has been embraced in recent years by gravel cyclists, (typically riders on drop-bar bikes favouring unpaved roads and trails),looking for a multi-day adventure far from towns and cities.Ruten Fjellstueis a traditional inn, set up for cross-country skiing in winter, hiking and biking in summer. My trip starts here and it’s where I’ll meet my guide and group, and pick up my hired bike. It’s set high above the valley and paintedfalunred – the iron-oxide agricultural paint typical across Nordic countries. Berit and Arthur are the third-generation owners. I arrive late, so Arthur picks me up from Vinstra train station (about three hours north-west of Oslo) and Berit has kept a home-cooked meal warm: a generous plate of fish with potatoes, vegetables and cream sauce, followed by apple crumble.View image in fullscreenThe route passes along Lake Vangsmjøse near the village of Øye.Photograph: Markus StitzThese small inns are part of what makes cycling through the region work. At breakfast, there’s an expectation that you’ll make your own sandwiches from the buffet, with provisions laid out ready. We’re even given a reusable beeswax wrap. Cycling here is powered by sandwiches, waffles with sour cream and berry jam, and plenty of cinnamon buns – and that’s just to keep you going between meals.Our first morning begins with a cruisy downhill run before the road turns into a rough track. A temporary road closure has sent us on to a mountainous diversion. I’ve never used drop handlebars before and it takes me a while to figure out the gears.double quotation markFurther along the valley, our guide points out a steep triangular cave up high. We’re into troll territorySilje Wilson, who works to promote the mountain hotels in the area, is also joining our group of 12 riders from across Europe. She tells me she has never ridden a gravel bike either, so I’m hopeful I’ll have company at the back, but she leads every climb and is often miles ahead. That night she reveals she has spent her summer mountain biking and lifts a large rock in her garden to build strength. “A typical Norwegian girl,” says Glenn.While you don’t have to be a “typical” Norwegian to enjoy these trails, a certain tolerance for hills helps. As we descend towards Lake Vinstre, the Jotunheimen mountains, northern Europe’s highest range, appear ahead. There’s just a tiny road stretching into the distance; beyond it, mountains in every direction. The lake is a deep turquoise-blue, and the shores are dotted with tiny wooden farmhouses painted red or yellow, many with grass roofs for extra protection when the snow arrives.At Lake Bygdin we stop to stretch and eat burgers atBygdin Høifieldshotelbefore catching the M/B Bitihorn passenger ferry, where bikes and luggage join us on deck. The boat has been in regular service on the lake for more than a century. We sail past the peaks of Øystre Torfinnstinden and Galdebergtinden, with waterfalls tracking down the steep mountainsides to the inland fjord.View image in fullscreenJotunheimvegen, a gravel road passing along Lake Vinstre.Photograph: Markus StitzAt Eidsbugarden, at the far end of the lake, we climb back on to our bikes and follow Lake Tyin towardsFilefjellstuene hotel. We pedal past summer mountain dairy farms but barely see a soul. The roads are almost entirely traffic free, but the sheep are worth being wary of: twice I have to swerve at speed when one runs into the road.We’re cycling for long days, averaging about 45 miles (75km) a day, with 1,500 metres (4,900ft) ascent, but there are gentler ways to experience the Mjølkevegen: shorter stages mean more time to explore the cosy family hotels or add in hikes, while some riders hire an ebike. Self-guiding on the main route is straightforward and well signposted; for diversions, or extra challenges, hiring a guide is advisable. I decide to lean in to taking it slowly, drinking in the spaciousness and letting the miles roll by.At Øye, on day two, we stop to admire the steep tiered roof of thestave church, one of only 28 still standing across the country. Many Norwegian churches, including medieval stave churches, were destroyed in a wave of more than 50 arson attacks in the 90s by anti-Christian black metal bands. Øye was built towards the end of the 11th century, then replaced in 1747. During renovations in the 1930s, the old church was discovered dismantled under the floorboards for reasons lost to time, and rebuilt here by the lake.double quotation markOn Smådalen plateau, we rest among wildflowers framed by steep peaks rising above the snow line. There’s moose in this areaFurther along the valley, Glenn points out a steep triangular cave up high. We’re into troll territory. “Up there a big rock is starting to move,” Glenn says. “It’s being surveyed, and it will fall sometime in the next 200 years. It’s because oflang bane,the troll ‘long bones’. Trolls sleep for hundreds of years. He’s starting to wake up now. Newspapers don’t report it, but local people know that it’s the troll.”Time to get back into the hills then, and Glenn has planned a detour from the main route. It includes what he calls “the mother of all climbs”: a long incline with dozens of switchbacks, requiring all the cinnamon-bun fuel I can muster. On the Smådalen plateau we rest among the wildflowers framed by steep peaks rising above the snow line. There are moose in this area, but our whoops on the downhills probably keep them well hidden.View image in fullscreenLunch at Bygdin Høifieldshotel on the shores of Lake Bygdin.Photograph: Markus StitzOn my last day, the weather turns. The Mjølkevegen sits about 800–1,300 metres above sea level, and the weather can shift quickly. We reach the bottom of the Slettefjell mountain pass in driving rain. There’s a small cafe here, so we stop for waffles and refill our water bottles. Then the only way is up, and up, and up. It’s 600 metres of elevation in just 6km. All I can do is concentrate on the next bend.At the top, it’s flat and exposed, and the clouds have transformed the mountains again. Distances are hard to measure, and the craggy rocks? Petrified trolls. I give them a wave, and freewheel downhill for miles.In this part of Norway, hotels are never built at the bottom of the valley. “Everyone prefers to have a view,” says Glenn. For a cyclist, this means that every day there is a final few kilometres up to the hotel. It’s tough, but it makes the arrival all the sweeter. And the best views are those you’ve earned.The trip was provided by Jotunheimen Travel,Mountains of Norway,Innlandet FylkeskommuneandVisit Valdres.Jotunheimen Traveloffers three-day self-guided cycling trips on the Mjølkevegen from NOK7,800(£612) based on two sharing,including hotel accommodation, all meals, luggage transport, boat tickets onM/B Bitihorn, an app with directions and maps, backup support and CO2 compensation, with bike hire for an additional costExplore more on these topicsNorway holidaysEurope holidaysCycling holidaysScandinavia holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Like a seagull in a stiff breeze’: what it’s like flying into Wellington, the world’s windiest city | New Zealand | The Guardian
description: Anyone who has frequently landed in New Zealand’s capital has a hair-raising story to tell, and this year’s ‘super’ El Niño could only intensify the winds
Author: Eva Corlett
Headline: Anyone who has frequently landed in New Zealand’s capital has a hair-raising story to tell, and this year’s ‘super’ El Niño could only intensify the winds
Content: A southerly front approaches Wellington's south coast as a plane comes in to land. The New Zealand capital is the world’s windiest city.Photograph: Dave AllanView image in fullscreenA southerly front approaches Wellington's south coast as a plane comes in to land. The New Zealand capital is the world’s windiest city.Photograph: Dave AllanNew Zealand‘Like a seagull in a stiff breeze’: what it’s like flying into Wellington, the world’s windiest cityAnyone who has frequently landed in New Zealand’s capital has a hair-raising story to tell, and this year’s ‘super’ El Niño could only intensify the windsEva Corlettin WellingtonWed 19 Aug 2026 20.19 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 21.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt had been a smooth late-July flight from Auckland, until the plane started its descent intoWellington. Then the bumps and swaying began.“The more we went down, the rockier it got,” says Laura, a Wellington resident who wished to give her first name only. “There was one point where we must have got a horrible cross-wind and it felt like the plane was about to flip over. At that point, the entire flight screamed.”“I genuinely felt like I was about to die, which was pretty awful … and I had eaten a horrible burger before going on the plane – that all came back up.”The plane lurched back up into the sky. The pilot announced the weather was set to worsen and the plane returned to Auckland.Flight paths and fridge magnets: how a fireball hunter tracked down New Zealand’s newest meteoriteRead more“We often call it a ‘Welly welcome’ when you get a bumpy landing, but this was a different level of scary, and obviously the pilots knew that because they didn’t land and didn’t try to do it again,” Laura says.Anyone who has frequently flown into New Zealand’s capital has a story to tell.Wellington is the world’s windiest city, with an annual average wind speed of 29km/h. The city sits on the Cook Strait, a passage between New Zealand’s North and South Islands, making it prone to high winds that can compound around the airport, which is flanked by hills.This year’s “super” El Niño, a label assigned when sea surface temperaturesclimb by at least 2C, will be the strongest of the century, and that could intensify Wellington’s winds, as the city heads into spring – the windiest season.“There were some El Niños in the past where it’s ended up being very windy in Wellington … so we expect it to be windier and more westerly than normal,” says Dr Richard Turner, a research meteorologist at Earth Sciences.“I think those landings are probably going to be a little bit bumpy for the next few months.”‘You think about your life a little bit as it comes down’For many, the descent into Wellington can feel akin to sitting in a tiny boat as it’s thrown around on an angry sea. It is not uncommon to hear passengers gasping, praying or vomiting. Occasionally the plane might be metres from touchdown before suddenly and rapidly ascending back into the sky to reattempt a landing. When wheels do eventually reach the tarmac, and come to a strained halt, the cabin often breaks out in applause.On particularly bad days, local TV crews will wait at the airport, ready to interview passengers who emerge from a plane looking haunted and pale. For more seasoned flyers, the notoriously bumpy ride is all part of the fun of flying into New Zealand’s capital.View image in fullscreenA bumpy landing is sometimes called a ‘Welly welcome’.Photograph: Dave Lintott/REX/Shutterstock“It’s like a rollercoaster, it’s a real adrenaline rush,” says Kevin Eagles, a Wellingtonian who has carved out an online following by livestreaming Wellington airport’s take-offs and landings.“It’s well-known you really swirl about, you think about your life a little bit as it comes down, and then you’re slammed down on the tarmac and wait for the moment the reverse thrusters kick in and there is a big roar – you’re just holding on really.”His videos of the choppy flights attract the highest number of views.“You know what it’s like for those passengers in there to experience that and you feel empathy for them but at the same time it’s incredibly thrilling,” Eagles says.On social media, people frequently relay their experiences flying into Wellington after another bumpy video emerges.“That was me on that plane years ago trying to land like a seagull in a stiff breeze. Hyperventilating into the sick bag, while you could have heard a pin drop,” writes one commentator.“Best pilots in the world. That bay landing is brutal,” says another.An analysis by Earth Sciences New Zealand shows Wellington airport has a higher percentage of strong winds compared with other parts of the city, due to its exposed location on the South Coast. Strong gusts over 96km/h are relatively frequent there, it said.“There tends to be a funnelling effect through the strait,” Turner says.Wellington can be windy year-round, but spring tends to bring low pressure systems that can intensify gusts.“The storms in the southern ocean barrel along and in front of them are these fronts that have these very strong pressure gradients at those times of the year,” Turner says.View image in fullscreenSpring tends to bring low pressure systems that can intensify gusts in Wellington.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersBut experienced Air New Zealand pilot captain Jake Snelgrove assures passengers the bumps are always more pronounced towards the back of the plane, and pilots are highly trained to deal with Wellington’s wind.“We only go in there when we know it’s safe,” Snelgrove says. “You go in there with a lot of respect for Wellington and what the weather can do … and tend to make early, proactive decisions.”Snelgrove says no Wellington weather would ever be strong enough to compromise the structural integrity of the plane, and pilots have a warning system that alerts them to wind shear – a phenomenon when two different wind speeds are interacting and creating a turbulent environment.Where wind shear is present, pilots have a particular manoeuvre for the approach, or will conduct a go-around, to avoid landing.“While it sometimes doesn’t feel comfortable, it is still safe,” he says, adding the pilots are usually having a more enjoyable day in windy situations than passengers because it is “challenging”.Additionally, he says flights may be cancelled not because it is dangerous for the planes, but because airport staff are unable to move cargo or people if there is strong wind on the ground.On the days where Wellington’s wind does settle, passengers are in for a remarkable journey, Eagles adds.“Your anxiety is replaced by beautiful views,” he says. “You fly over Wellington city and you see the stadium and the harbour sparkling, and you think, wow.”Explore more on these topicsNew ZealandWellingtonAsia PacificEl Niño southern oscillationAir transportfeaturesShareReuse this content
