As for British audiences, she says, we’re good listeners but need a bit of cajoling when it comes to contributing. That’s certainly the case for me as Moore attempts to interview me for her erotic story. “You’ll need to take off your sunglasses,” she says as, to do this properly, eye contact needs to be established. It’s not long before I’m telling her things I’ve never discussed with close friends.So why this gargantuan appetite for smut? And why now? “Smut is perhaps one of the great primary colours in the world of escapism,” says Read Wilson. “People in these difficult times need a good laugh,” adds Clary. “I’d much rather see something smutty and rude than some kind of highbrow analysis of Trumpism. That wouldn’t make me feel better at all.”Moore sees smut’s power entwined with the sexual politics of our age. “It’s a mistake to underestimate the power of raw, authentic language,” she says. “It’s very easy to write off smutty humour as just tits and giggles. But if you’re good at it, you will plant seeds that are going to have people thinking about their own stuff, perhaps about shame in their own life, or how they’re having these conversations with other people.”Both Birkby and Woz have noticed an uptick in women reading erotic fantasy novels. “There are more single women than ever who think: ‘I’m not gonna settle for less than what I deserve like my mother did, like my grandmother did’,” says Woz. “Consuming smuttier content is their way of getting that eroticism on their own terms, not expecting it from another person.”“I do think we are on an upswing at the moment,” says Birkby. “There’s been a lot of nervousness around sex and talking about sex for the last few years, which absolutely needed to happen. But now that we’ve had these valuable discussions about what consent is, perhaps we can say, ‘We’ve got these new rules, how can we have a laugh about things now?”She references the hemline index, a theory that whenever countries enter a recession, women’s hemlines lengthen. “Perhaps there’s a comedy equivalent,” she says, “that whenever the world gets worse, the jokes get smuttier.”My smut-filled tour of Edinburgh has sadly come to an end. And so, after learning the tricks of the trade from some of comedy’s lewdest practitioners, there’s only one thing left for me to do: unfurl the story Moore wrote with me and see if I have become a true smut convert. “The bedroom is already warm this late in the morning,” it begins, “but her –”Unfortunately, readers, we have just hit our word count. If you really want to know the rest, you’ll just have to use your (filthy) imagination.Smut Slamis at Banshee Labyrinth until 30 August.Bryn Woz: Smutis at Assembly Roxy until 31 August.Julian Clary: Fully Dilatedis at Assembly Rooms until 23 August.Tom Read Wilson: The A-Z of Meis touring from 6 September.Chelsea Birkby: is in Full Control The Entire Timeis at Pleasance Courtyard until 30 AugustExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreJulian ClaryComedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)SexfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I need to think like a CEO’: Weezer on the shifting sands of success, ugly feelings and the joy of spreadsheets | Weezer | The Guardian
description: As the self-professed geeky rockers release their conceptual 20th album, Rivers Cuomo and Patrick Wilson discuss dodging failure, being saved by fans and their obsessive creativity
Author: Stevie Chick
Headline: As the self-professed geeky rockers release their conceptual 20th album, Rivers Cuomo and Patrick Wilson discuss dodging failure, being saved by fans and their obsessive creativity
Content: ‘We have perspective on everything now’ …(from left)Weezer’s Patrick Wilson, Rivers Cuomo, Brian Bell and Scott Shriner.Photograph: Brendan WalterView image in fullscreen‘We have perspective on everything now’ …(from left)Weezer’s Patrick Wilson, Rivers Cuomo, Brian Bell and Scott Shriner.Photograph: Brendan WalterWeezerInterview‘I need to think like a CEO’: Weezer on the shifting sands of success, ugly feelings and the joy of spreadsheetsStevie ChickAs the self-professed geeky rockers release their conceptual 20th album, Rivers Cuomo and Patrick Wilson discuss dodging failure, being saved by fans and their obsessive creativityThu 20 Aug 2026 10.16 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 13.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song Rivers Cuomo wrote for Weezer’s new album, their 20th, blatantly mimics the US rockers’ 1994 debut single, Undone (The Sweater Song). On the track CEO, the singer-guitarist grumbles over a slow, Velvets-y backing about having to crank out “another 90s jam” and wishing he could do “something new – but nobody wants to hearthat”. It’s a deliciously meta moment, but also one that allows Cuomo to gently vent “my frustrations over people wanting me to just write songs about our first two albums”.Cuomo wrote the song straight after SZNZ, the four-album song-cycle Weezer released throughout 2022, each album named after a season. That project fed his notoriously intense, analytic and occasionally obsessive approach to songwriting. Thanks to the kind of data artists have at their fingertips in the streaming age, though, he realised that, with each subsequent SZNZ, “fewer and fewer people were listening to them”.His response was to “think strategically”. On a video call from his home in Santa Monica, California, where Cuomo, 56, lives with his wife and children, he says he realised: “If I want people to listen to my music, I need to think less like a mad scientist in the research and development department and more like a CEO.” Accordingly, he took several years off from releasing any new material (“to build up demand”), ditched the high concepts of SZNZ and focused on creating what he thinks the fans want.Gently venting their frustrations … CEO, from Weezer’s 20th album.Like six previous albums, the new album is titled Weezer. It has already been dubbed the “gold” album by fans, due to its sleeve colour. While the arch lyrics to CEO might suggest it is a cynical exercise in pandering to his audience, the Gold Album is a more complex, sophisticated beast.Cuomo is driven by his obsession with songwriting. “It’s like building sonic architecture, such a cool, stimulating experience,” he says, although he prefers to describe himself as a “composer”. “The term ‘songwriter’ feels like Paul Simon’s about to explain a sombre part of life,” adds his bandmate Patrick Wilson, 57, who plays drums and guitar and joins the interview from the garage of his California home. “What we do is more visceral: busting out a sick riff and saying to each other: ‘Dude, checkthisout!’”Cuomo’s approach is methodical to a degree that feels antithetical to rock music; he has boasted that Google Sheets is integral to his process. (One spreadsheet, which he has named “The Encyclopedia o’ Riffs”, keeps track of all his unused and unfinished ideas and is legendary among Weezer fans.) He also can’t resist a kooky conceptual hook to guide his songwriting – see the group’s 2021 heavy metal set, Van Weezer, or OK Human, their orchestral rock opus of the same year, or, obviously, SZNZ.The Gold Album is similarly conceptual, this time the concept being the creation of an album the Weezer faithful will love. Cuomo’s process has been typically analytical and methodical – and it’s clear he has loved the challenge. He views their live shows as the testing ground for the new material – “where the rubber meets the road”, he says. “I want the people in the room to want to hear these new songs as well as our old hits, and to sing along. I wanted them to be reallyfunlive, to have substantial riffs and guitar parts.” Accordingly, he has taken inspiration from his favourite band of the moment, the Swedish heavy rockers Ghost, whom he says restored his understanding of “the power of stadium-rock riffage”. Nevertheless, much of the Gold Album channels the loud guitars and pop-oriented tuneage of Weezer’s eponymous 1994 debut, often brilliantly so.View image in fullscreenAlmost over before they began …(from left)Cuomo, Wilson, Matt Sharp and Bell in 1996.Photograph: Martyn Goodacre/Getty ImagesThe new album is shaped by deeper wounds than those occasioned by SZNZ’s reception, however. The line in CEO where Cuomo says he has “gotta keep this rocket in the sky” references the moment when the failure of Weezer’s second album, 1996’s Pinkerton, seemed to hobble their career before it began – a foundational trauma for the group’s leader.He remains the pilot of his bandmates’ fortunes as much as his own and, while the Gold Album sounds bold and confident, there are moments in our interview when his anxiety over this responsibility surfaces. They collaborated more as a group on the songwriting of the Gold Album than any previous Weezer release; while Cuomo talks about how their positive feedback was “a real good sign” he might be on the right track with an idea, it’s clear he chiefly prized their solidarity as a group “to give us the strength to face any pushback from the audience”.Raised in a Buddhist ashram in Connecticut, which taught him methods to “calm down my body and mind”, Cuomo became a teenage metalhead and, in his late teens, under the influence of the Swedish poodle-rocker Yngwie Malmsteen, formed the hair-metal group Avant Garde. That group renamed itself Zoom and relocated to Los Angeles to make it big, but within a year they had imploded and Cuomo began working at Tower Records in West Hollywood.This disappointment – alluded to on The LA Sound, a song from the Gold Album, written by guitarist Brian Bell, about a no-hoper metal band running aground on the Sunset Strip circuit – was “heartbreaking”, says Cuomo. But it proved the making of him. “If Zoom had ‘happened’, if my dreams had come true, I would just be the lead guitar player – thesecondlead guitar player, excuse me – in a heavy metal band that would have been woefully out of style by 1992. Instead, my heart got broken and that led to something a lot bigger and better: singing, and expressing myself, and focusing on songs rather than shredding.”Weezer formed shortly after Nirvana’s fateful breakthrough. Cuomo had been seduced by the Pixies’ “big crunchy guitars, melody and heaviness” – one of numerous artists he discovered through his Tower co-workers. On Weezer’s earliest demos, he “tried singing like Black Francis or Kurt Cobain or Perry Farrell, more of a ‘rock’ voice. It took months before I finally gave up and sang with my natural, pure voice. I’d sung in school choirs; to my surprise, it still worked, even over the big guitars.”It wasn’t just Cuomo’s voice that set Weezer against the grain. They wore glasses and unhip clothes, while Cuomo sang about comic books and Dungeons & Dragons. The rock press identified them as nerds, a label they never quite shook loose and ended up embracing: they kicked off this year’s Weezer: The Gathering tour, named after the fantasy card game Magic: The Gathering, with a pickleball tournament with their fans. Regarding this resistance to cool, Cuomo says they “just felt it was very uncool to try and be something you’re not”.“The kids today would call it ‘being a sweat’,” says Wilson, un-coolly. “In hip-hop, they would have called it ‘fronting’.”View image in fullscreenStill unapologetically nerdy …(from left)Bell, Cuomo, Wilson and Shriner.Photograph: Brendan WalterThis honesty – along with Cuomo’s infallible gift for pop songcraft – struck a chord in the post-Nirvana cash grab. But as their debut began its ascent to quintuple-platinum status, via a punishing schedule of touring and promotion, Cuomo’s morale plummeted. In his diaries, he wrote of his dissatisfaction with this new rock’n’roll life. Addressing an imaginary rock-star-in-waiting, he gloomily advised: “Youwillget lonely … It’s not all cocaine, chicks and limos.”His face is mostly obscured by shadow on our call, but Cuomo’s disillusionment remains palpable three decades on. “All my life. I’d figured that if I got a record deal – if we got on MTV and radio – then I would feel fulfilled and loved,” he says. “We achieved all those things. But I still felt unseen and unheard and misunderstood and lonely.”Cuomo abruptly ditched the tour bus for Harvard, where he studied classical composition alongside students sporting Weezer T-shirts, oblivious to his presence. The course deepened his feel for songwriting. “Creatively, I was feeling incredibly confident. I was not happy about my personal life, but believed if I isolated myself – and, to an extent, tortured myself – I would be able to create something really great.” He pauses. “I was probably overconfident.”Inspired by the antihero in Puccini’s Madama Butterfly, he wrote Pinkerton, an ambitious, strikingly unguarded confession that success had left Cuomo engulfed by loneliness, disaffection and sexual confusion. Before the album’s 1996 release, he warned the Weezer fanclub that it included “all the parts of myself that I was either afraid or embarrassed to think about before. So there’s some pretty nasty stuff on there.”View image in fullscreen‘A chaotic era’ …(from left)Bell, Cuomo, Wilson and Sharp in 1996.Photograph: Martyn Goodacre/Getty ImagesSure enough, Across the Sea depicts him falling in love with a Japanese teenager who wrote him a fan letter (“I wonder what clothes you wear to school … I wonder how you touch yourself”); on Pink Triangle, he grumbles about a lesbian who doesn’t fancy him; and, on The Good Life, he’s “a pig, I’m a dog, so ’scuse me if I drool”.The album was, he says, an act of catharsis. “It’s always been hard for me to communicate feelings in words, in conversation,” he sighs. “But if I can play them through melodies and chords and lyrics, I feel thistremendousemotional release.”It was all done with lashings of self-mockery and knowing awfulness, but plenty of fans recoiled. Even Ric Ocasek, the producer of their debut, didn’t seem to like it.Pinkerton flopped; Cuomo put Weezer on hiatus and went into hiding. It was “a chaotic era”, says Wilson, who worried about the impact of Weezer’s steep arc on Cuomo. “I wondered how child stars dealt with success. And I realised: they’re all insane, because it’s a ridiculous process. That period was overwhelming.”“I’d keep feeling like I’d found my way out, that the way back was just around the corner,” Cuomo remembers, of the struggle to write a third Weezer album. “But each time, just as I’d be about to announce to the guys I had songs I felt confident in, my confidence would collapse again: these songs are terrible. Let me start over. Give me a few months.”Salvation came in 2000, in the form of an unexpected six-figure offer to play Japan. After four years of darkness and frustration, Cuomo remembers being “in tears” when his manager called with the news. Next, the band jumped aboard that summer’s Warped tour and discovered that, in their absence, Pinkerton had found an audience that treasured its confessional intensity. “Our fans were out of their minds, chanting: ‘Weezer! Weezer!’ all through the bands on before us,” remembers Wilson. “I knew something was up. Like: oh. We’re going to be OK.”Today, Pinkerton is recognised as a pivotal emo album. Its follow-up – 2001’s Green Album, again produced by Ocasek and containing the single Hash Pipe – was a platinum-selling hit. “I remember thinking: if we can survive the last five years of solitude and self-doubt and come back to this, we can get throughanything,” Cuomo says. “Our fans pulled us out of our self-doubt.” Today, those fans log in to Cuomo’s personal Discord server and watch him practice vocal warm-ups or play Beethoven on his piano. “There’s always this group of people online that love me and appreciate me and are looking forward to hearing anything I’m doing, so I never have to feel alone,” he says.The fans have stayed loyal as Cuomo has explored unexpected directions – such as the heavy metal of Van Weezer and the orchestral rock of OK Human – and collaborated with songwriters outside his realm, including Linda Perry, Jermaine Dupri and Justin Hawkins of the Darkness. He confesses his obsession with songwriting isn’t always healthy: “There were times where my wife was going through troubles and she really could have used my help. And I would spend all day in my room, just working – super-deep, detailed work – and I told her, like: ‘I can’t help you right now, I’m on a roll here, I really need to focus.’ There has been some conflict.”View image in fullscreenFor ever a frontman … Cuomo performs at the Coachella festival in 2025.Photograph: Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for CoachellaThis hasn’t happened recently, though, he says. Three decades after the existential wobble of Pinkerton, Cuomo seems happy keeping Weezer’s rocket in the sky. He feels lucky to “have this vocation with these three other guys. We can get in a room together and work on stuff that feels important to us. As you get older, it can be hard to have those kinds of relationships. But we have them.”‘There is an alternative to capitalism’: after addiction and losing a home to LA wildfires, indie rockers Diiv start againRead moreThe relationships have held strong through traumas that might have destabilised other groups, such as the 2011 death of bassistMikey Welshfrom a suspected drug overdose. The bandmates all “get along pretty great now”, says Wilson. “We all have perspective on everything now. We see how everything unfolded and how deeply unusual it was, and we recognise it.”Can Cuomo see a time in his life when Weezer isn’t a thing? On the sleeve to 2005’s Make Believe – released during a period of emotional anxiety and voluntary celibacy, for spiritual reasons – he included the soliloquy from The Tempest, where Prospero abandons his magic and commits to “drown my book”.“At the time, I wasn’t sure I was gonna go on making music,” Cuomo says. “I wanted to try a really intense spiritual path and then start a family. I wanted to step away from the spotlight, from being an artist, even from being creative, and see what else there is in life. So I included that speech, like: OK, maybe this is my retirement statement.” He stops. For one of the few times during our chat, he looks up from the shadows and into his laptop camera, smiling. “But it’s obvious, isn’t it? Come on, Rivers. You can’t escape this.”Weezer is released via Reprise/Warner on 21 AugustExplore more on these topicsWeezerPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best books to read in August: new paperbacks from Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, Salman Rushdie and Werner Herzog | Books | The Guardian
description: Looking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some wonderful new paperbacks, from a short story collection by a literary great to razor-sharp criticism
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Looking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some wonderful new paperbacks, from a short story collection by a literary great to razor-sharp criticism
Content: View image in fullscreenThis month's best paperbacksBooksThe best books to read in August: new paperbacks from Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie, Salman Rushdie and Werner HerzogLooking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some wonderful new paperbacks, from a short story collection by a literary great to razor-sharp criticismThu 20 Aug 2026 09.30 EDTShareFictionFictionDream CountChimamanda Ngozi AdichieView image in fullscreenDream Count isbilled as “a publishing event 10 years in the making”. Composed of the interlocking stories of four women, Chiamaka (“Chia”), Zikora, Omelogor and Kadiatou, it is also quintessential Adichie: ambitious, astute and powered by an accumulation of feather-light sentences that build to devastating weight.The women are immigrants in the US. Chia, a travel writer, Zikora, a lawyer, and Omelogor, a former banker turned grad student, are Nigerian; Kadiatou, a hotel maid, is Guinean. Chia’s first-person narration establishes the novel’s melancholic tone: “I have always longed to be known,” she declares in the opening line, “truly known, by another human being.” Driven to reminiscing about past lovers during the Covid lockdowns, she passes her time “grieving what I did not even know to be true, that there was someone out there who had passed me by, who might not just have loved me but truly known me”. Her story gives way to Zikora’s, who is desperately trying to track down the boyfriend who abandoned her following a surprise pregnancy and whose own story morphs, with a sting of surprising sweetness, into a paean to the pull of motherhood. The narrative is then riven by the tragedy of Kadiatou’s story before being overtaken by Omelogor’s musings about her dissolute lifestyle in Abuja prior to quitting her high-flying career to undertake postgraduate research on pornography.The novel threads together childbirth and pregnancy loss, abortions and hysterectomies, fibroids and female genital mutilation, sexual assault and sexual harassment, as if nothing less than the whole of female experience is within its scope. Yet at the same time it is painfully introspective, not only because it is set against the backdrop of the Covid pandemic, a built-in reminder of “how breakable we all are”, but also because it includes many moments – such as when, pondering one of her breakups, Chia muses about “how quickly mystery dissolves to dust” – in which one senses the subliminal gesture towards deeper traumas, the feeling of unbearable confinement alongside floating alienation, the hermetic numbness with which many of us experience grief.Sara Collins£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopFictionThe School of NightKarl Ove KnausgårdView image in fullscreenKarl Ove Knausgård’s Morning Star cycle may turn out to be even larger in scope than his six-volume autofictional bestseller, My Struggle. Four books deep, this gargantuan work of supernatural existentialism is an unsettling account of the occult phenomena that attend the appearance in the sky of a bright new star. Mysteries from the first three volumes include: who killed the musicians in the forest? What’s going on with the local wildlife? Why does no one seem to be dying any more? By the end of The School of Night, the most burning question may sound comparatively mundane: who is Kristian Hadeland?Scattered references appeared in the saga’s first 2,000 pages. Kristian Hadeland was the 67-year-old man buried without mourners by doubting priest Kathrine Reinhardsen inThe Morning Star(2021). InThe Third Realm(2024), he was the sinister chap hitching a lift with Kathrine’s husbandafterthe unloved man she buried is supposed to have died.The School of Night offers another answer. Here, Kristian Hadeland is the author of a 500-page suicide note, and the misanthropic narrator of a compellingly nasty novel. From the remote Norwegian island where he’s preparing to end his life, Kristian sets down the story of how he got there, starting with his time as a photography student in mid-1980s London.Young Kristian has a good eye and self-belief, even if – as a visiting professor suggests – his photos are “a bit dull. Without temperament.” Soon after arriving from Norway, he meets the enigmatic Hans, a Dutch artist into artificial intelligence, and Vivian, who is staging a production of Christopher Marlowe’s Doctor Faustus; he develops an uneasy friendship with the former and a hostile sexual relationship with the latter.When Kristian is home for Christmas, he’s antagonistic towards his family, too. After his sister overdoses, he hears his father describing him as “a black hole … a narcissist, through and through”. Outraged, he returns to London, retreating into himself. Then a chance encounter with a homeless man sets Kristian on a path from near ruin to staggering glory.Intimations of the supernatural give the saga much of its momentum and uncanny frisson. But can the mystery be indefinitely sustained? A lot is riding on Knausgård’s ability to deliver on the colossal promise of this sprawling epic. But for readers with the stomach, patience and faith to keep going, this work of millenarian fiction remains an object of fascination.Charles Arrowsmith£9.34 (£10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopFictionWill There Ever Be Another YouPatricia LockwoodView image in fullscreenLockwood contracted Covid early, in March of 2020, when transmission was blamed on grotty fingers and every doorknob was suspect – the era of fruit bleaching and handwashing jingles. Will There Ever Be Another You is the tale of what happened next, inflicted on a fictional Patricia: aphasia, hallucination, migraines, amnesia, paranoia, relentless self-obliteration.The result is cortical shrapnel – you can almost hear this book rattle when you open it. Lockwood’s title carries no question mark: it is prayer, punchline, eulogy, manifesto, nightmare, often all at once. Fragmentation is not a new mode for Lockwood (she was christened, after all, “the poet laureate of Twitter”). But it is one thing to disrupt, another to be disrupted. There is a new kind of anguish here, a longing for coherence.The opening pages are where she comes closest. Hollowed by the loss of a child, an American family travels through Scotland, kept afloat by “pure itinerary”. A precious item is lost. Shortly afterwards, our heroine slips into fever. The treasure is returned; her mind is not. It feels like a dark enchantment, a faerie bargain. “It stole people from themselves.” Lockwood writes of her illness. “You might look the same to others, but you had been replaced.”Delirium reigns. We wheel from Roland Barthes to Cabbage Patch Kids, via Anna Karenina and the “butthole cut of Cats” (classic Lockwood territory). But there’s a drum of obsession beating underneath the chaos. Doppelgangers, changelings, clones, dolls; photographs and synonyms – these pages teem with replicants and replication. The modus operandi of a virus.Lockwood’s detonated form is evocative, but not especially innovative (Eimear McBride was doing a version of it more than a decade ago inA Girl Is a Half-Formed Thing). We need accounts of long Covid, and plenty more of them. But Will There Ever Be Another You feels auteurish, the literary equivalent of a Wes Anderson film: over-styled and perilously close to self-parody. A delirious in-joke.Beejay Silcox£8.49 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopFictionThe Ten Year AffairErin SomersView image in fullscreenIn Erin Somers’s The Ten Year Affair, Cora, a millennial mother, craves a bygone kind of passion from a bygone kind of man. Unfortunately for her, morality in 2015 is rigid and cynical, and instead of having the affair, Cora spends 10 years overthinking it, fantasising about it and discussing it with her potential lover, Sam – a playgroup dad who is “chief storytelling officer” at a mortgage start-up (yes, that’s his job title. They all have absurd jobs). The book presents itself as a comic take on the classic adultery novel and a send-up of a narrow, self-conscious group of downwardly mobile New Yorkers. I’d call it the midlife adultery story our entire generation deserves: a propulsive, witty takedown of insufferable hand-wringers who’ve managed to ruin even sex. Honestly, I couldn’t put it down.Beneath the story runs the subtle undercurrent of familiar middle-age questions: do our lives have meaning? Where do we go after death? These themes are more explicit in Cora’s imagined conversations. Reading these exchanges, I wondered what lesson Cora and her cynical lot would take from their disappointing dramas. Would Cora grow more open to life’s imperfect joys, its corny pleasures?I loved this razor-sharp, hilarious, finely observed novel, written with such withering exactitude. It is absolutely aware of itself, spare and brimming with subtext: a portrait of an anxious, loin-girding generation in middle age, chronically embarrassed at ourselves, at once afraid of and desperate for sensation. Or maybe that’s just the New Yorkers. Let’s say it is.Dina Nayeri£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopFictionVera, or FaithGary ShteyngartView image in fullscreenShteyngart’s sixth novel is a lively, skittish Bildungsroman, shading towards darkness as it tracks the journey – literal, educational, emotional – of 10-year-old Vera Bradford-Shmulkin, an overanxious, over-watchful academic high achiever whose run of straight As has just been blighted by a B.Always happy to show his workings, Shteyngart cites Henry James’s 1897 novel What Maisie Knew as the prompt for Vera, or Faith’s child’s-eye account of complicated adult affairs, although his gauche heroine bears a passing resemblance to the author himself as portrayed in his 2014 memoir,Little Failure. Friendless Vera lives with her rackety Russian-Jewish father, Igor (Shteyngart’s name at birth), who edits a floundering liberal arts magazine, her harried Wasp stepmother, Anne (who added the “e” in tribute toAnne Frank), and a boisterous younger half-brother, Dylan, who likes exposing himself to houseguests. But she also has (or possibly had) a Korean-born mother, long since vanished from the scene. Invisible Iris Choi plays the tale’s white whale or MacGuffin; the elusive hidden figure that Vera is determined to locate.The eccentric Bradford-Shmulkins are lurching towards crisis, but they seem a model of stability when compared with the rest of the country, which reveals itself in unflattering flashes in the corners of the narrative. Shteyngart’s novel, we come to realise, plays out a decade from now, in a “post-democracy” USA where red state officials monitor menstrual cycles, self-driving cars shop their owners to the feds and the news platforms are abuzz with Russian disinformation.Shteyngart’s ode to a good American in a bad America conspires to be, by turns, a rueful human comedy and a coming-of-age caper, a dystopian chiller and an espionage yarn. The colourful tale never satisfyingly hangs together; its component pieces tend to jar more than gel. But Shteyngart sets about his material with abundant energy and charm. He sketches a convincing caricature of a near-future USA and provides a stoical heroine that we can uncomplicatedly root for. Even in a degraded, compromised, up-is-down social climate, that has to be deserving of a solid B grade at least.Xan Brooks£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopFictionVulturePhoebe GreenwoodView image in fullscreen“Middle East on Fire: Israel positions tanks onGazaborder.” Journalist Phoebe Greenwood’s debut novel follows Sara Byrne, a freelance journalist in Gaza in 2012, who is reporting for a “pretty rightwing” British newspaper.Vulture is a caustic study of what it means to report from a conflict, and particularly relevant to the current moment. It’s a knowing portrait by Greenwood, who was a freelance reporter in Jerusalem between 2010 and 2013, and later a foreign affairs correspondent at this newspaper. Her antiheroine visits a morgue, where the bodies of children, “dusted in sand and blood”, wear torn Spider-Man pyjamas. She narrowly escapes a bombed hospital, which is “running out of anaesthetic and even basic painkillers”. Still, her editor requires stories, and so she pursues increasingly dangerous lines of inquiry.The title of the book is testament to its wry tone, and ultimately its position. In Byrne, Greenwood has created a particularly acerbic character, reluctant or perhaps unable to offer sincere emotions in the face of horrifying events. Her battle-weary sense of humour, however, cannot last, and Byrne’s mental state becomes increasingly unstable. She believes a bird – identified as a pigeon, but described more like a vulture – is tormenting her. Her eyes are yellow; she winces with pain when she walks. Greenwood handles this descent well; the narration remains jocular, even arrogant, meaning it never feels hackneyed.Occasionally, Greenwood’s creative writing feels less successful than the news writing within it: the protagonist’s filed copy is sometimes clearer than the prose itself. But Vulture remains a remarkably skilful debut. Greenwood’s style is compelling and blackly comic; the story could not be more serious.Sophie Dickinson£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopFictionDiscontentBeatriz SerranoView image in fullscreenAmbivalence towards working life is the subject of this tremendously entertaining debut novel. “I only come into the office to lower my air-conditioning bill,” says 32-year-old Marisa. She’s “head of creative strategy” in a Madrid ad agency. “That’s a big deal,” says a friend. “No,” Marisa replies, “it just sounds like one.” She kills time between projects by posting trolling comments on dismal YouTube videos. Eventually she faces the worst horror of all: a team-building retreat, which she ends up dealing with in a masterfully perverse way. There’s pain underlying her quips (“No one knows who I really am”), but her story is peppered with pithy insights into the modern workplace, and plenty of vivid characters, such as the friend who’s “had work done”. “I’m filled with plastic,” she tells Marisa. “I’m the Atlantic Ocean.”John Self£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopThrillerBluffFrancine ToonView image in fullscreenToon’s second novel is set in St Rule, a Scottish coastal town with distinct similarities to St Andrews. In 2023, Cameron returns home on Christmas Eve; meeting old friends revives memories of his teenage crush, former classmate Joanie, last seen 10 years earlier at a calamitous end-of-schooldays party. His attempts to find her are met with vagueness, evasion and, finally, warnings off. A second narrative strand takes us back to 2013, and the 18-year-old Joanie. Adrift after her discovery that her boyfriend is cheating on her has ruined their plan for a year abroad, she falls in with an older couple. David and Erin welcome her, make her feel important and seem, for a while at least, to have all the answers. Skilfully handled themes of guilt, regret and adolescent confusion coupled with dark academia make for an insidious tingle of doom, although the rushed ending may leave some readers feeling shortchanged.Laura Wilson£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopShort storiesShort storiesThe Eleventh HourSalman RushdieView image in fullscreenThe Eleventh Hour, a collection of five stories, seems intended as a kind of coda to Rushdie’s career. The stories are death-haunted. One of them is called Late; it’s an afterlife fantasy in which a Cambridge fellow, whose career has resembled both EM Forster’s (writing a great novel about India) and Alan Turing’s (helping to crack the Enigma code), dies and haunts a young Indian student named Rosa; what links them may be the buried crimes of empire. The Musician of Kahani replays Rushdie’s greatest hits: it is about a child born at midnight (“the approved hour for miraculous births in our part of the world”) who, aged four, abruptly becomes a gifted pianist (like the rock star Ormus Cama inThe Ground Beneath Her Feet, playing air guitar in his cradle).These stories are entertaining but not particularly strong. The Musician of Kahana leans pretty heavily on cliche: “the university of life”, “priceless art”, “finger on the pulse”, “the wedding of the year” … In the South is better: a deft, moving anecdote about two old men in Mumbai who bicker and needle one another from their respective verandas. One of them, Junior, dies in an accident. The other, Senior, despairs, until he comes to believe that “death and life were just adjacent verandas”. Oklahoma invokes Kafka; it is a metafiction about a young Indian writer and the older American novelist he admires, or perhaps more than admires – in cases of literary influence, the story seems to ask, who is writing whom?“Our words fail us,” goes the final sentence of The Eleventh Hour. It is the conclusion of a story about a piazza – a public space – in which language, here figured as a human woman, is courted, usurped, ignored. Finally she screams and vanishes, at which point, the piazza’s buildings all crack: “The piazza is broken, and so, perhaps, are we.” Words have not yet failedSalman Rushdie, even if, in this self-consciously late book, the spectacular originality of his novelistic peak sounds more as an echo than as an urgently present voice.Kevin Power£8.49 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopMemoirMemoirFranklyNicola SturgeonView image in fullscreenFirst, Frankly takes us back to a council flat in the former mining village of Dreghorn, Ayrshire. There, a young Nicola identified with tomboyish George from the Famous Five, worried constantly about her dad joining the swelling ranks of the unemployed, and broke up with her primary school best friend because she wanted to spend more time on her homework. She identifies the fundamental contradiction that would propel her: “Alongside shyness, crippling lack of confidence and a dreadful fear of failure was a burning ambition, a drive to succeed, a craving to be ‘seen’.”There are some moments of bracing honesty. She reveals she came close to having a breakdown after giving evidence at the UK Covid inquiry. I can’t think of another politician of her stature who’d describe themselves on the floor of their home office, gripped by a panic attack as they struggled to edit a crucial policy document – in this case the Scottish government’s white paper on independence. And a lengthy passage on her pregnancy loss, in which she writes about her lingering guilt and shares the name she had chosen for the baby, Isla, is almost unbearably intimate.It’s startling to read her account of the tension and hostility she claims characterised her relationship with Alex Salmond long before the public split that resulted from her government’s handling of sexual harassment allegations made against him by two civil servants. (These later formed part of his criminal trial on 13 counts of sexual assault, of which he was acquitted in March 2020.)At one point, Sturgeon observes that “whenever a man is alleged to have done something wrong some people’s first instinct is to find a woman to blame”. Right enough, but there are also legitimate questions about how someone in a position of power and leadership could be so ignorant of someone as close to her as Salmond was. Neither does she explain why the women who brought the original harassment complaints against Salmond described being left without any support by the Scottish government she led.She fails to reflect on how having a married couple at the very top of the SNP for more than a decade impacted the party, encouraging the apparently lax governance so many colleagues complained about. Nor does she address the lack of succession planning for her eventual departure. Despite the book’s promise of candour, it seems like Sturgeon is only willing to entertain her readers’ curiosity so far.Libby Brooks£10.19 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopMemoirAll the Way to the RiverElizabeth GilbertView image in fullscreenThe first chapter ofElizabeth Gilbert’s much anticipated new memoir closes on a four-page love letter to Gilbert from her late partner Rayya, who, dead for five years, comes to her in a “visitation”. In Rayya’s voice, Gilbert calls herself babe, baby, or “sunshine baby” multiple times, emotes in all-caps, and grants herself permission to write the details of Rayya’s terrible, humiliating final year. “Let me just look at you for a minute,” “Rayya” says to Liz. “Look at your little rainbow eyes! Look at your sparkling tears! You’re so beautiful!” The letter is deeply self-indulgent and excruciating to read. “You’re going all the fucking way this time – all the way to the enlightenment.”I believe that the dead are gone and that artists don’t need their permission to evoke them. But I was stunned that this solipsistic mess opens the book, because Gilbert is a terrific storyteller –Eat Pray Love,her memoir of self-acceptance and healing, was read by millions. So, I scrubbed the false start from my mind, reminding myself that great literature shows people as they are, which means that at some point in every good memoir, weshouldsee the narrator being awful.Even so, it takes discipline and restraint not to let one’s flaws harm the writing – restraint that it appears Gilbert no longer has. All through the book, she reminds us of Eat Pray Love’s success and tries to echo and relive what she learned back then: that she’s addicted to love, but she can thrive alone if she has her spiritual and creative practices.But the prose is clunky (“an unhealed wound looking for someone to land on”) and full of preposterous flourishes, such as when an imagined Rayya says, in a poem at the end of the book: “I love it when you talk about me: it polishes me like a diamond.”As a storyteller she shines brightest when she’s not curating, but displaying her mistakes, and mourning them. “I tried to drain all the love from Rayya into me before she died … I became a vampire”. And when, instead of simply emoting, she sits down to craft a scene, she writes transportingly. The last days of Rayya’s life, in a house with two of her exes, are funny, propulsive, raw and moving – Gilbert forgetting about herself to help her partner, who’s alone and helpless and terrified to die.Dina Nayeri£9.34 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopLiterary criticismLiterary criticismAuthorityAndrea Long ChuView image in fullscreenAndrea Long Chu stands accused of not playing by the rules, of appraising works of fiction as if they were essays or confessions rather than aesthetic objects. “It is true that I tend to treat a novel like an argument”, she writes in the introduction to Authority, a collection of essays and reviews published between 2018 and 2023 in outlets such as N+1, Bookforum and New York Magazine. Chu – who won a Pulitzer prize for criticism in 2023 – believes “all novels refract the veiled subjectivity of their authors”, and to pretend otherwise is to indulge a “pernicious form of commodity fetishism”. In her reviews, books betray their authors, invariably revealing some kernel of inadequacy – be it immaturity, myopia or just terminal dullness.This approach borders on the psychoanalytical, and makes for fun reading. Chu diagnoses a case of “Munchausen by proxy” in Hanya Yanagihara, whose bestselling novelsA Little Life (2015) andTo Paradise (2022) are powered by “the misery principle”: “horrible things happen to people for no reason”, and the author is “a sinister kind of caretaker, poisoning her characters in order to nurse them lovingly back to health”. She notes a troubling tendency towards “infantile” idealisation of mothers and girlfriends inTao Lin’s autofiction, and finds “something deeply juvenile” about the scatological motifs inOttessa Moshfegh’s novels. Moshfegh’s medieval gore-festLapovona (2022), fails to shock, because “You cannotépater le bourgeoiswithout an actual bourgeoisie”; “the leading coprophile of American letters” is trying too hard to convince us she’s not a prude.These essays are essentially journeys – knotty and meandering, with moments of pithy, clarifying insight. If you can hold someone’s interest while figuring things out for yourself in real time on the page, you’re doing something right. Perhaps the true source of authority is companionable intelligence, and what we think of as sound judgment is just a function of familiarity – comfort in another person’s psychic skin.Houman Barekat£10.19 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshopPhilosophy booksPhilosophy booksThe Future of TruthWerner HerzogView image in fullscreenAt 83,Werner Herzogis a living legend who can and does do precisely what he wants.Like the strange, enchanting films for which he is best known, Herzog’s seventh book defies the usual conventions of structure, narrative arc and the delineation of fact from fiction, even as it addresses the very subject of truth.This slim volume sets out Herzog’s views on truth in a world where technologically enhanced falsehoods proliferate. These appear to be an elaboration of Herzog’sMinnesota Declaration, the 12 statements he made in 1999 at the Walker Art Centre in Minneapolis. Much like the declaration, The Future of Truth contains strong, gnomic opinions which include despising cinéma vérité because it obscures more than it illuminates, as well as a plethora of surprising sentences such as “rather die than wear a toupee”.Two principles are central to Herzog’s idea of truth. First is the notion that seeking truth is a greater goal than finding it. As he puts it, “the quest itself, bringing us nearer to the unrevealed truth, allows us to participate in something inherently unattainable, which is truth”. The second is that bare facts can provide little more than a boring “accountant’s truth” that is less useful than what he calls “ecstatic truth” in helping people understand what’s really going on in life.If anyone else had written The Future of Truth, I suspect they would come under critical fire for odd choices in structure, rambling, contradictory statements, and, to put it bluntly, taking the piss out of the reader. After all, Herzog devotes five whole pages to the histrionic plot of an opera just to demonstrate that when art forms contain concentrated, intense emotion, we “invest this preposterous kernel with the full array of our own feeling, so that it seems mysteriously genuine”. However, because this book is a collection of uniquely Herzogian mindfarts, it resists a panning. Michael Hofmann’s sparkling and inventive translation from the original German – a crypto-zoologist is described as “a ham sandwich short of a picnic” – somehow makes Herzog more Herzog in tone.Farrah Jarral£10.19 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

title: Amy Lee of Evanescence: ‘I could happily do an entire album of nothing but Portishead covers’ | Pop and rock | The Guardian
description: As her band hits the road, the metal trailblazer answers your questions on sexualisation in show business, finding inspiration in dreams and Spinal Tap moments on tour
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: As her band hits the road, the metal trailblazer answers your questions on sexualisation in show business, finding inspiration in dreams and Spinal Tap moments on tour
Content: ‘I’m done with letting people make me feel I should be quiet’ … Amy Lee.Photograph: Chapman BaehlerView image in fullscreen‘I’m done with letting people make me feel I should be quiet’ … Amy Lee.Photograph: Chapman BaehlerFilm & Music reader interviewPop and rockInterviewAmy Lee of Evanescence: ‘I could happily do an entire album of nothing but Portishead covers’As told toDave SimpsonAs her band hits the road, the metal trailblazer answers your questions on sexualisation in show business, finding inspiration in dreams and Spinal Tap moments on tourThu 20 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 12.33 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou wrote Bring Me to Lifewhen you were 19. When you perform it now, how do you relate to the younger you?becgoldsmithI was in an abusive relationship, so Bring Me to Life was partly about processing the reality of that abuse and asking myself, what are you gonna do about it? Like, pick yourself up. I wrote it when I was crushing on my [now] husband, but the theme is about a quest for something bigger: opening your heart, finding more depth. It’s very empowering to perform it now in huge places; I’m very proud of the 19-year-old me that wrote it.Artists often reveal their influences through the songs they choose to cover. You’ve performed bothIt’s a Fire and Glory Box by Portishead. What drew you to those songs?VerulamiumParkRangerBeth Gibbons was one of my greatest vocal and musical inspirations. In the 90s when I was a young teen really feeling music I lovedPortishead, Massive Attack and the whole trip-hop vibe. It was dark and cool, really different. Beth’s vocals have a way of teetering on an emotional crack, on the edge of wild, barely restrained emotion but never belting, which I always thought was so cool and enticing. I could happily do an entire album of nothing but Portishead covers.View image in fullscreen‘Music has always been an outlet for whatever’s in my heart’ … Lee with Evanescence in 2025.Photograph: Chapman BaehlerYour new album,Sanctuary, feels delicately balanced between healing and reflection, but also anger about what is going on in the world right now. How did you manage that balance and how do you feel about using your voice to stand up against what’s wrong?Amlou7I hate politics, but our existence is political. Most of us don’t want anything to do with the atrocities that are going on today, but as human beings with hearts and souls we must rise to the occasion. I’m done with letting people make me feel I should be quiet or making me feel uncomfortable speaking about what we’re now calling politics, which is life and death, rape, genocide, stealing from people. Music has always been an outlet for whatever’s in my heart, so now the music is an outlet for those big things. I meet so many people around the world with different beliefs, and we’re not that different. Most people are good human beings who would help you if you were injured, and that goodness is precious and worth fighting for. We have to be strong and keep calling things out and not back down to fascism.View image in fullscreenLee and the band’s then guitarist, Ben Moody, at the MTV awards in 2003.Photograph: Dave Allocca/Starpix/ShutterstockCan you share any funny stories of things that have happened during the current Sanctuary tour?Andrew_ClevelandThere’s so many, we could make a blooper reel of all the mistakes. When you put yourself out there with a big production inevitably there’s more potential for things to go wrong. We have a moment where a kabuki [Japanese theatre] curtain drops down dramatically behind me. It’s beautiful, but in windy amphitheatres there’s been a couple of funny moments where it’s come down in the wrong place and dropped right on my head. It’s been great touring with Spiritbox and Nova Twins and we do a song together, Fight Like a Girl. One night, I sang entirely the wrong thing. Spinal Tap is totally like reality. I’ve experienced that scene of walking round in circles not being able to find the stage more times than I can count.What are your thoughts onNathan Fielder’s use of Bring Me to Life in The Rehearsal season two[he speculates thatCaptain Chesley ‘Sully’ Sullenbergerlistened to the song before successfully landing a passenger plane on the Hudson River]?thunderponceIt’s amazing to me that the song has reached so far, but that was just one of those surreal moments where you really think, “Wow, this is wild.” I thought it was strange and brilliant, like Nathan Fielder is. I had tears in my eyes by the end. It was so beautiful. I’m not saying Bring Me to Life helped land the plane, but it’s a cool way to demonstrate how music inspires people in stressful or big moments. Bring Me to Life has been used in all sorts of things and it took me a long time to get past the cynicism of “I don’t know about this … ” but I feel safe in it now.Watch the video for Who Will You Follow.I recently lost my 14-year-old dog and five-year-old cat, and listening to theSecret Doorhas been one of the only things helping me lately. The lyrics are beautiful and eerie, the background melodies reminiscent of a dream. What inspired those words?Feistj1I’m sorry for your loss. I had my amazing Maine Coon [cat] for 18 years before he passed away a couple of years ago. They became part of your life so it’s like letting go of a whole chapter. It’s interesting that you’ve mentioned dreams. I’m a very vivid dreamer and I have recurring places that only exist in my dreams. Sometimes music comes at me in dreams and it feels as if I’m tuned into some other channel. Once in a while I wake and think, “I’ve got to write this down”, or record it on my phone. Secret Door was one of those. I had a recurring dream where I’d go through a secret door in the woods and experience a feeling of beautiful love. The vibe came from the dream, the 3/4 time was in my head, and the bridge section came out as soon as I woke up and ran straight upstairs to work on it. A lot happens in those last moments of sleep when your mind is functional but you’re not yet in reality. It feels like a gift when that happens.View image in fullscreenEvanescence performing in Madrid, Spain, in 2022.Photograph: Javier Bragado/RedfernsI’ve been listening to you since the beginning of your career. I wanted to be a rock singer, too, but I’ve always been told I am ugly. Show business’s obsession with beauty and sexualization to boost sales horrifies me. You make amazing music and don’t try to sell it using sexual gimmicks. Is there even the slightest chance for an unattractive woman to be a rock singer?SerbianPersonThat question makes me so sad. First of all, I would hope that whoever told you that you are ugly is not anyone you would call a friend. Don’t think of yourself that way and don’t listen to those people. They’re probably just jealous. Beauty is the deep stuff: being an artist, making music. That’s where the gold is, and beauty comes out through the inside, so focus on the inside and making something great for people to experience. Selling your product and being an Instagram star is not the important part. Anybody can make great music if it’s in your soul: that’s the most beautiful thing about you.‘I couldn’t see, breathe or sing. I blacked out twice’: why are so many metal bands wearing masks?Read moreWhat is the coolest or most thoughtful gift that you have received from a fan?EvCollector87There’s been so many, but one is really special. In 2005 or so I saw this beautiful art that someone had done on the internet, a picture based on our song Imaginary. It took the lyric “in my field of paper flowers” and created a visual depiction of the song, with me laying in a field. It was just so beautiful. I managed to get in touch with them and asked if I could buy it. They told me it was a digital rendering, not a painting, but I commissioned them to paint it for me – a big version, 5ft tall or something – and it’s gorgeous. It still hangs in my space.With the likes of Elton John, Stevie Nicks and Bruce Springsteen in mind, do you think you’ll still be recording and performing live in your 60s and 70s?ChrisDLordIf you had asked me that when we were starting out and I was in my early 20s, I would have said, hell, no. I wouldn’t have predicted we’d be here this long, but now I turn 45 in December, and 44 definitely doesn’t feel like I’d imagined – it’s better. Turning 60 is only 15 years away, which doesn’t feel that long. I don’t know if we’ll be touring hard then, but they say use it or lose it, so I’m not ruling it out. It gives you so much life to be able to bring people together and share music, so it breaks my heart to imagine that we can’t do that any more for whatever reason. I’d have to be still making music or creating in some way. It doesn’t make sense to stop.The vinyl version of Sanctuary is released via Sony on 4 September. Evanescence tour the UK from 8-13 September, the rest of Europe from 16 September-4 October, the US from 24-26 October, Asia from 28 November-4 December and Australia and New Zealand from 5-20 MarchExplore more on these topicsPop and rockFilm & Music reader interviewPortisheadMetalfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Hazy sunshine, factor-50 smiles and Cliff Richard at the wheel: the 20 best summer holiday movies – ranked! | Movies | The Guardian
description: From feelgood romances to heated interactions, here are the films that best capture the seasonal moment
Author: Xan Brooks
Headline: From feelgood romances to heated interactions, here are the films that best capture the seasonal moment
Content: Paul Mescal and Frankie Corio in Aftersun.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyView image in fullscreenPaul Mescal and Frankie Corio in Aftersun.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyRankedMoviesHazy sunshine, factor-50 smiles and Cliff Richard at the wheel: the 20 best summer holiday movies – ranked!From feelgood romances to heated interactions, here are the films that best capture the seasonal momentXan BrooksThu 20 Aug 2026 08.05 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 12.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google20. American Graffiti (1973)Let’s begin at the end. 2 September 1962: the final night of the summer vacation; one last big blowout before adult life intervenes. George Lucas’s rambunctious salute to footloose youth paints vivid vignettes of Modesto, California, rocking around the clock with its loose-knit gaggle of characters. But this has one eye on the meter and knows that time is running short.19. The Lost Daughter (2021)“It’s a working holiday,” insists Olivia Colman’s brittle academic, blasting her factor-50 smile at the bemused guests and staff of a Greek island resort. She’s in flight from her past and liable to combust any second. Paradise here offers little rest or respite. The professor has made a clean getaway, but she’s brought along all her baggage.18. My Summer of Love (2004)View image in fullscreenWild at heart … Emily Blunt and Natalie Press in My Summer of Love.In which Natalie Press’s working-class Yorkshire lass finds an exotic foreign land just a hop and a skip across the moor in the form of the ivy-clad house of Emily Blunt’s boarding-school princess. Director Paweł Pawlikowski slowly turns up the temperature as the girls lean into the season, lounging in the dry grass and listening to Edith Piaf. They’re at once stickily close and a thousand miles apart.17. Summertime (1955)David Lean’s tender Technicolor romance was one of the first British films to be shot entirely on location, strolling around beautiful, dirty Venice in the company of Katharine Hepburn’s middle-aged Miss Lonelyheart. Lean called for her to step backwards into the green canal at Campo San Barnaba. Hepburn gamely obliged and clambered out with conjunctivitis.16. Y Tu Mamá También (2001)View image in fullscreenA place in the sun … Gael García Bernal, Maribel Verdu and Diego Luna in Y Tu Mamá También.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamySex and death ride shotgun in Alfonso Cuarón’s lustful field trip through turn-of-the-century Mexico. Gael García Bernal and Diego Luna are teenage buddies who light out for the beach with their engines overheating; Maribel Verdú co-stars as the exacting older woman who, if not quite steering them straight, at least helps point them in interesting new directions.15. Summer Holiday (1963)A summer holiday list without Summer Holiday? It would be like the Tower without the ravens or mistletoe without the wine. Directed with an easy swing by Peter Yates (his debut, and he would go on to make Bullitt and Breaking Away), this now stands as a colourful blast from the past, an innocent postcard from postwar, pre-Brexit Europe. A blue-collar bus mechanic – embodied byCliff Richard– magics up a new route from Hertfordshire down to Athens, complete with entertainment and a flurry of comic misadventures. Only a churl wouldn’t get on board.14. Tomboy (2011)Céline Sciamma makes small rousing films about secret lives, sanctuaries and precious stolen moments. Tomboy is one of her best: a gorgeous coming-of-age tale about 10-year-old Laure (Zoé Héran), who – bouncing between schools, the new kid on the block – introduces herself as Mickaël and effectively becomes another person. Sciamma’s implied message? That the humble summer break can be a transformational timeout, with September’s child only distantly related to July’s.13. La Piscine (1969)View image in fullscreenBody of water … Alain Delon and Romy Schneider in La Piscine.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyThe pool is a mirror in Jacques Deray’s dazzling, depthless thriller pungently set on the French Riviera and tapping the off-screen tensions of co-stars Romy Schneider and Alain Delon. If La Piscine’s air of modish ennui now feels overused, that’s because it’s a design classic, most notably lifted and adapted by both François Ozon’s Swimming Pool and Luca Guadagnino’s A Bigger Splash.12. Roman Holiday (1953)“Rome. By all means, Rome,” declares Audrey Hepburn’s runaway princess after spending a liberative, life-changing few days in the eternal city with Gregory Peck’s US newsman. As for the movie, this might be the ultimate European and American meet-cute. Shot on location, skipping between the tourist sights, Roman Holiday wedded old-school Hollywood romance with the looser rhythm of Italian neorealism.11. A Summer’s Tale (1996)Eric Rohmer was the poet laureate of French dreamers, the creator of films that feel flyweight and then linger for a lifetime. A Summer’s Tale is his semi-autobiographical account of a lost summer spent on the coast of Brittany pursuing sea shanties and women with the same awkward stumble. It’s a hazy, lazy joy of a film, brimming with sunlight and rocked by the backwash of chatter and song.View image in fullscreenHot times … Jennifer Grey and Patrick Swayze in Dirty Dancing.Photograph: Vestron Pictures/Allstar10. Dirty Dancing (1987)Everything’s big in this Borscht Belt summer classic. Big gestures, big emotions, big drums on the soundtrack, big hair. It’s 1963 and Baby (Jennifer Grey) is getting whisked off her feet by Patrick Swayze’s bad-boy dance instructor. The Catskills are a cauldron of class and ethnic tensions; first love is an intoxicating, disorientating hot mess. Resistance is futile: the film lifts and spins us. Grand finale, big reward.9. Sundown (2021)The best holidays are the ones that you never, ever want to end. Michel Franco’s Sundown casts Tim Roth as mild-mannered Neil, whose Mexican vacation is interrupted by the news of his mother’s sudden death. The trouble is that Neil would really prefer not to leave. So he pretends he’s lost his passport, shoves his tear-stained family through the departure gate and then circles back to the beach with the satisfied air of a man who’s just put out all the bins. Who is this Neil? What the hell is he thinking? He’s the shadow beneath the parasol, the chip of ice in the cocktail glass and the finest existential antihero this side of L’Étranger.8. The Go-Between (1971)LP Hartley’s source novel was elegant and reflective, weighed down by the heat as it traces the illicit exchange of letters via a lovestruck schoolboy. Joseph Losey and Harold Pinter make the mood more jangly and atonal, perpetually on the verge of panic. What a wonderfully treacherous period drama this is, the filmic equivalent of a strip of flypaper. All the characters are stuck and squirming. None of them are getting away unscathed.7. Les Vacances de Monsieur Hulot (1953)View image in fullscreenBeside the seaside … Jacques Tati in Les Vacances de Monsieur Hulot.Photograph: Ronald GrantThis was initially lower on the list, as befits its musty antique status, but then I watched it again and it’s flawless – there’s nothing else quite like it. Jacques Tati is the hapless holidaymaker who haunts the wings of a seaside town sometimes as a mute witness, sometimes as an agent of gentle chaos. If anything, Tati’s comedy grows more cherishable with each passing decade. Watching it is like peering into a forgotten tide-pool ecosystem: the rumble-tumble lost world of the postwar French resort.View image in fullscreenAngry young men … Jeremy Fox, Esteban Powell, Wiley Wiggins and Mark Vandermeulen in Dazed and Confused.Photograph: Entertainment Pictures/Alamy6. Dazed and Confused (1993)Where its spiritual ancestor, American Graffiti, began at the end, the uproarious Dazed and Confused wraps up at the start. It’s the first full day of the 1976 summer break. The high-school kids are wafting groggily back to earth, buffeted and elated after a wild night around town. They’ve drunk beer and shot pool, run amok and made out, and now there’s nothing on the horizon except an Aerosmith concert and the month of June. Sunrise on the football field; the golden morning of their lives.5. Summer with Monika (1953)Flee your family, feel the city; steer a boat around the archipelago. Ingmar Bergman’s jolting kitchen-sink romance casts Harriet Andersson and Lars Ekborg as working-class Stockholm kids who make a bold bid for freedom and yet are bound for the rocks. Bergman was always drawn to life’s extremes – its sunlight and shadow, its ecstasies and agonies – but rarely made them feel as purely relatable as here.4. Days and Nights in the Forest (1970)View image in fullscreenInto the woods … Days and Nights in the Forest by Satyajit Ray.Photograph: Album/AlamyForget the beach and the island retreat – it is the forest where summer breaks tend to deepen and darken. Four Kolkata bachelors drive into the backwoods of Bihar only to realise that there is more than one way to get lost. What follows is an antic meditation on all the big stuff: friendship, responsibility, class and cultural divisions. Writer-director Satyajit Ray takes a humdrum off-the-peg concept – the buddy hangout comedy – and makes it mythic, mysterious and borderline elemental.3. The Green Ray (1986)The second Rohmer film on the list is a small miracle about a small miracle. Specifically it’s about thirtysomething Delphine (Marie Rivière), who is newly single and drifting in a kind of semi-ostracised state across France. But it is also about the green ray, which can reputedly be glimpsed for a split second at sunset and might quietly, magically make everything right. Rohmer employed a skeleton crew and encouraged his cast to improvise, ensuring that his film remained unencumbered and almost weightless, open to the world’s possibilities and the happy accidents it might send our way.2. Aftersun (2022)View image in fullscreenSlow burn … Paul Mescal and Frankie Corio in Aftersun.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyCharlotte Wells’s rapturous family album is still relatively recent and may yet fade out as the years go by. Then again maybe not, because if Aftersun tells us anything it’s that memory only intensifies an experience and that lost summers burn brighter the older we get. On screen it’s for ever 1999 and Paul Mescal’s young father is in Turkey with his daughter (Frankie Corio), browsing for rugs and lounging by the pool, searching for sunshine and averting their gaze from the shadows. Wells’s astonishing debut feature doesn’t feel directed so much as recovered and resurrected. It’s an impressionistic, deeply felt and finally devastating tour de force.1. Before Sunrise (1995)View image in fullscreenTrue romance … Julie Delpy And Ethan Hawke in Before Sunrise.Photograph: Hulton Archive/Getty ImagesThe summer holiday can be a time of freedom and escape, romance and self-discovery. It is all of these things in Richard Linklater’s mid-90s masterpiece about a pair of garrulous Interrailers (Julie Delpy and Ethan Hawke) who steal a few precious hours and wander around Vienna for the night. But the best summer holiday movies are also about time itself. They’re about how we choose to use it and what comes out of those choices.Before Sunrise, a joyous film about footloose youth, tellingly went on to spark a pair of excellent sequels that caught up with its lovers many years down the line. But that awareness of time was baked into the tale from the start. I agonised at some length over what should be number one on this list – and what probably swung it was the bittersweet flourish of Before Sunrise’s last moments, when Linklater’s camera beats back like a ghost to show us the places where Céline and Jesse were idling just a few hours before. The fountain and the ferris wheel. The forlorn little alley with the stacked wooden pallets. The Interrailers have already left them behind and moved on – except that they haven’t, not really. They’ll be haunting them happily for the rest of their lives.Explore more on these topicsFilmRankedMusicalsRomance filmsCliff RichardFilm adaptationsAudrey HepburnBefore SunrisefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: It Ends review – gripping micro-budget horror ranks among the year’s best  | Horror films | The Guardian
description: Led by a stellar cast of gen-Z newcomers, Alex Ullom’s directorial debut is an expertly crafted nightmare about a road trip gone wrong
Author: Owen Myers
Headline: Led by a stellar cast of gen-Z newcomers, Alex Ullom’s directorial debut is an expertly crafted nightmare about a road trip gone wrong
Content: Phinehas Yoon, Akira Jackson and Noah Toth in It Ends.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonView image in fullscreenPhinehas Yoon, Akira Jackson and Noah Toth in It Ends.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonHorror filmsReviewIt Ends review – gripping micro-budget horror ranks among the year’s bestLed by a stellar cast of gen-Z newcomers, Alex Ullom’s directorial debut is an expertly crafted nightmare about a road trip gone wrongOwen MyersThu 20 Aug 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTime loops often feel like the movies’ favorite zany stylistic trick: Bill Murrayplottingto win Andie MacDowell’s heart, a college student solving themysteryof her own grizzly murder, or as a ruse for Anne Hathaway toface off with a T rex. The excellent new indie horror film It Ends takes a different approach with its nightmarish depiction of a carful of friends stuck in an endlessly repeating day. It’s less of the moony japes ofGroundhog DayorPalm Springsthan an arthouse spin on the Prometheus myth, with the unfortunate souls of the film cursed not with death but with the torture of eternal life.Insidious: Out of the Further review – evil returns but so does boredomRead moreAfter helping their friend move into a new apartment, a crew of aimless twentysomethings take a late-night drive to get food, but after GPS leads them deeper and deeper into a desolate forest, it’s clear that they have lost their way. When they pull over, they are set upon by a group of people that look eerily similar to them – young people who are dressed like they stepped out to the corner store and couldn’t find their way back. “They look scared,” one character says with a pained expression. “Why are they scared?”As the group swarm their Jeep every time they pull over, the central quartet has no option but to keep driving deeper and deeper into the unknown forest on a road which seemingly has no end. It turns out that even stranger things are afoot: the car’s gas dial hasn’t moved, and they oddly aren’t craving any of their normal bodily needs. “I’m not tired, not hungry, and [have] no sexual arousal,” one character informs us, just in case we were starting to wonder why no one was getting frisky in the back seat.Made for just $50,000, there’s a palpable sense of dread to first-time director Alex Ullom’s film, mirrored by the perfectly creepy, creaky score that plays as the characters agonize over what led them to this wretched fate. Could it be a wormhole or an ancient curse? Karma for their past misdeeds? Is the doofy Tyler (Mitchell Cole) being punished for dumping a girl after she suggested a date at the local pumpkin patch, or, more gravely, is it something to do with the recent suicide attempt of Day (Akira Jackson)? In the absence of definitive answers, It Ends begins to feel oddly in sync with the kind of existentialist questions that might cross your mind on a daily basis. What’s really the difference between an endless road to nowhere and the everyday terror of hurtling towards a future where nothing is promised and everything will likely get worse?Running counter to the ennui is the cast’s warm chemistry. Naturalistic performances anchor some of the sweetest scenes as the foursome celebrate each other’s birthdays and play made-up road trip games. (In “Like or Dislike”, they debate the merits of windshield wipers or “the ocean”.) The hatchback they live in becomes the film’s chief setting as It Ends evolves into a kind of chamber piece on wheels, with the characters decorating the insides of the vehicle with a dry erase marker so that it looks somewhere between graffiti art and the scrawlings on the wall of a cheesy movie set in a psych ward. And while Fisher (Noah Toth) seems to find some sense of zen amid the endless asphalt, James (Phinehas Yoon) wails at the sky in a plea for mercy from a higher power, in a clash of attitudes that provokes friction as well as flashes of empathy.View image in fullscreenAkira Jackson and Noah Toth in It Ends.Photograph: Courtesy of NeonIt’s tempting to call It Ends something like a Blair Witch take on No Exit, the 1944Jean-Paul Sartrework where a group of strangers were trapped in a room for eternity and which declared that hell was other people. But in a statement to accompany the film, director Ullom says that the film is instead rooted in his own struggle with dissociative depression and attempts to find a framework to make life survivable. If Sartre famously said that hell is other people, It Ends seems to suggest that they might be able to save us too.Despite a few jokes that already feel dated (one character mourns that she didn’t have the foresight to download Subway Surfers), It Ends often reaches the quality of high-concept cult horror classics while also nodding to our uniquely modern malaise. “What if we’re supposed to suffer here,” says Fisher at one low moment. “What if that’s the point?” It’s unclear if he’s talking about their nightmarish road trip or what it can feel like to live on this mortal coil. It Ends is confident enough to leave the question unanswered.It Ends will be released in the US on 21 August and 3 September in Australia with a UK release to followExplore more on these topicsHorror filmsThrillersreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It was a damn unicorn’: the pioneering, divisive power of Paul Simon’s Graceland at 40 | Paul Simon | The Guardian
description: On its anniversary, the author of a new book about the album explains the complex legacy and masterful musicianship of the 1986 classic
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: On its anniversary, the author of a new book about the album explains the complex legacy and masterful musicianship of the 1986 classic
Content: Paul Simon performs with guitarist Ray Phiri on the Graceland tour.Photograph: Penny Tweedie/Corbis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPaul Simon performs with guitarist Ray Phiri on the Graceland tour.Photograph: Penny Tweedie/Corbis/Getty ImagesPaul Simon‘It was a damn unicorn’: the pioneering, divisive power of Paul Simon’s Graceland at 40On its anniversary, the author of a new book about the album explains the complex legacy and masterful musicianship of the 1986 classicEthan BeckThu 20 Aug 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 12.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was the summer of 1984 and things weren’t going well forPaul Simon. The year prior, a blockbusterSimon and Garfunkeltour ended in bickering. Meanwhile, even though the 1980 single Late in the Evening reached the US Top 10, Simon’s last two albums had not sold very well, and his marriage to Carrie Fisher was starting to unravel. In the midst of all that the 43-year-old folk icon was steadily working on building a beach home out on the far end of Long Island.‘I never said I was going to retire ...’ Paul Simon on disability, drive and the mystery behind his greatest songsRead moreMany of Simon’s pilgrimages from Manhattan out to Montauk were soundtracked by a bootleg tape of accordion-heavy mbaqanga, a South African music style with jazz rhythms and bright guitar chords, he had received from a friend. It was on those drives that the seeds of Graceland, the crown jewel of Simon’s discography, were planted. “Many of us, in that day and age, found a moment of self-reflection – of being able to go deep inside ourselves – when we were in the car on these road trips,” said Ashley Kahn, whose new book,Days of Miracle and Wonder, follows the gestation process of Graceland. “If it wasn’t the radio, it was cassettes.”Forty years on, Graceland remains the most nimble, ecstatic album that Simon’s hands have touched. It’s constructed around contributions from South African musicians whose “township jive” reminded Simon of the early rock and doowop records he heard as a kid in Queens. There’s musical detours of all kinds – a trip to Louisiana inspired Simon to record with zydeco group Rockin’ Dopsie and the Zydeco Twisters, while the song All Around the World or the Myth of Fingerprints features Los Lobos’ fusion of norteño and rock. Simon is at his best when among resonant rhythms from Johannesburg.Inspired by the bootleg, Simon booked jam sessions in Johannesburg with different bands – General MD Shirinda and the Gaza Sisters, Tao Ea Matsekha, the Boyoyo Boys – where he developed melodies and scribbled down lyrics as engineer Roy Halee tracked the groups’ grooves. Some of the songs that ended up on Graceland were assembled on top of these groups’ already-finished songs, such as Gumboots, a thrilling pop confection that Simon initially heard as an instrumental on that tape. For Simon, whose process often started with an acoustic guitar, it was a profound shift in how he approached his craft. “He’s finding a way of building from the rhythm up; that, for him, was profoundly new,” said Kahn, who compared Simon’s then-newfound process with hip-hop: “Start with the beat and match the words to the beat.”In these February 1985 sessions, Simon had found a surge of inspiration, but the harsh realities of South African apartheid loomed outside the studio doors. After dark, the Black musicians weren’t allowed on the streets of Johannesburg, nor were they allowed to use public transportation. As a result, a day of recording would reach an “uncomfortable time when the players couldn’t concentrate until they knew there might be a car to take them home”, Simontold Rolling Stone in 1986. In a foreshadowing of the backlash Graceland would go on to receive, the manager of the Soul Brothers told Simon he believed recording in South Africa constituted a violation of the United Nations’ 1980 boycott, which was passed to prevent the South African government from using culture as propaganda for apartheid.Kahn believes that Simon had the musicians’ labor rights in mind. “He wanted to have them participate, he wanted them to be credited and he wanted them to be compensated,” said Kahn, emphatically noting that Simon paid the South African musicians triple the daily rate of musicians in American unions. “Did he do it perfectly? No. But there wasn’t a set formula of how to approach this.” Simon has still faced backlash over the years about Graceland’s songwriting credits from several musicians who appeared on the album, including Los Lobos, Rockin’ Dopsie and the Zydeco Twisters, and even guitarist Ray Phiri, who helped construct the album’s title track. Against charges of cultural appropriation, Graceland advocates have suggested that Simon’s work in South Africa helped bring these bands, such as Ladysmith Black Mambazo, who round out the starry-eyed Diamonds on the Soles of Her Shoes, to a larger audience.View image in fullscreenPaul Simon with author Ashley Khan in 1988.Photograph: Courtesy of Ashley KhanBefore the first sessions at Ovation Studios in Johannesburg, Simon spoke with calypso legend Harry Belafonte, who had suggested that he reach out to the African National Congress. Believing that the power of art trumped laws, Simon resisted Belafonte’s recommendation.
