Months after the release of Graceland, the UN’s special committee against apartheid censured Simon and planned to add him to the list of performers who violated the boycott. “They were looking for a coordinated message, coordinated push, hence the issue with the boycott,” Kahn added. The UN’s decision was reversed months later when Simon wrote a letter to the committee noting that he had understood the ban focused on performing, not recording, and he had no intentions of performing in South Africa.Paul Simon review – at 84, back on stage after hearing loss, his resolute artistry is inspiringRead moreA career-long tug-of-war between Simon’s cerebral and conversational language courses through Graceland. He eschewed overt anti-apartheid protest songs, but the anxieties of his experience in South Africa seep into Homeless and The Boy in the Bubble, which opens on an image of “the soldiers by the side of the road” while the interplay between famo-style accordion and bass suggests something threatening up ahead. But Simon’s qualms – his failed marriage, his feelings about being washed up, his worries related to the information age – are what he fleshes out on Graceland, often through dizzying images (“lasers in the jungle”) or larger-then-life characters (“Fat Charlie the Archangel”).“One of the images that always comes to me is Paul in a room with a rubber ball – bouncing it, bouncing it, bouncing it – to get into a Zen-like state where lyrics start to come,” Kahn said. “He’s already thinking about songwriting. The lyrics are there. He just needs to silence all the other shit that’s in one’s mind.”Graceland’s steady stream of longing, sometimes offered through simple lines such as “You don’t feel you could love me but I feel you could,” contained unexpected emotional wallops. On the album’s very best songs, there’s an impressionistic flow of feeling in Simon’s lyrics. Nowhere is that clearer than in the title track, where the word Graceland had initially been written down as a placeholder. It eventually evolved into a figurative destination for Simon as he tried to mend his broken heart after his marriage to Fisher. “If I miss in the direction of head, I risk being obscure or pretentious,” Simonsaid in 1986. “If I miss in the direction of heart, I risk being sentimental. I dread both. I dance in the penumbra. That’s the thrill. When it’s right, I can feel it.”View image in fullscreenPaul Simon with Miriam Makeba and Ladysmith Black Mambazo during the African Graceland tour in 1987.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyMany revisions and additions happened stateside, including the guitar-synth textures from Adrian Belew and Steve Gadd’s AMS reverb-drenched drums on All Around the World. For another set of sessions, including the one in which they rerecorded You Can Call Me Al, Simon flew Phiri, Bakithi Kumalo – whose restless fretless bass is now synonymous with the Graceland album – and drummer Isaac Mtshali to New York, where Simon also shared his progress with David Byrne, Cyndi Lauper and Philip Glass. He would turn on a tape of an instrument track, get close to their ears and sing the melodies or lyrics he’d crafted. “The fact that Paul was open to sharing the process with a lot of people goes to show a certain strength, as well as an openness to saying, ‘I could be wrong,’ or, ‘I could be better,’” Kahn says.Graceland’s influence as a genre-defying, cross-pollinated album has spread far and wide, informing brilliant artists such asVampire WeekendandLorde, plus with one particularviral parodyof Simon’s approach. For almost as long as the album has been in stores, a healthy dose of criticism has followed: two decades before he would produce for Beyoncé and Eminem, a young Mark Batsonasked Simonhow he could justify “taking over this music”, before discussing how Black art has been “stolen” by white artists time and time again during a Q&A at Howard University. It’s a testament to the life-affirming melodies and jubilant grooves of Graceland that it hasn’t been consigned to the dust bin of history as an embarrassment – and that these conversations endure. “All these questions about appropriation, about systemic racist, about the entitled versus the non-entitled – that’s never going away,” Kahn says. “What Graceland did was show us a way to talk about it.”It’s hard to imagine when Graceland arrived in stores towards the end of August 1986 that it wasn’t an overnight sensation. Support from music critics, performances on Saturday Night Live and eventually Grammy wins helped it find an audience. (It entered the Billboard 200 album chart at No 94 in September 1986, before eventually peaking at No 3 next April, just over a month after the Grammys ceremony.) The final piece of the puzzle was pop radio programmers, who didn’t understand the stylistic jumps taking place across Graceland. The spring after the album’s release, radio honchos latched onto its lead single, You Can Call Me Al, with its attempts to find salvation in the “angels in the architectures”. It was a classic case of better late than never: “It was a damn unicorn,” Kahn says. “In the zoo of music, they had no idea which cage to put it in.”Days of Miracle and Wonder:Paul Simonand the Trials and Triumphs of Graceland by Ashley Kahn is out nowExplore more on these topicsPaul SimonSimon and GarfunkelPop and rockSouth AfricafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Making Love with David Magidoff review – instant improv musical based on Fran Healy’s teenage infidelity | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: The US comic’s troupe tell the tale of a special guest’s romantic encounter, in this case Travis’s frontman – but their incoherence makes for a scatty if fun show
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: The US comic’s troupe tell the tale of a special guest’s romantic encounter, in this case Travis’s frontman – but their incoherence makes for a scatty if fun show
Content: ‘A Travis fanboy’ …David Magidoff, right, with special guest Fran Healy in Making Love.Photograph: Lisa Kelley Remerowski/© Lisa Kelley Remerowski/LKR PhotoView image in fullscreen‘A Travis fanboy’ …David Magidoff, right, with special guest Fran Healy in Making Love.Photograph: Lisa Kelley Remerowski/© Lisa Kelley Remerowski/LKR PhotoEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewMaking Love with David Magidoff review – instant improv musical based on Fran Healy’s teenage infidelityAssembly George Square, EdinburghThe US comic’s troupe tell the tale of a special guest’s romantic encounter, in this case Travis’s frontman – but their incoherence makes for a scatty if fun showBrian LoganThu 20 Aug 2026 07.07 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 07.08 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s a lovely format for improv: a special guest tells David Magidoff the story of some romantic (mis)adventure from their past, and Magidoff and pals turn it into an extemporised musical. Shades ofImprobable theatre’s tender and funny Lifegame, many moons ago – although Making Love is more knockabout than that. Between musicians and improvisers, US actor and comedian Magidoff assembles no fewer than nine bodies on stage. It’s a lot, populating the stage with a surfeit of comic ideas, occasionally at the expense of theaffaire du coeurthatTravis frontman Fran Healyhas offered up as raw material.Magidoff is a Travis fanboy; he has Healy sing two songs, and gets starry-eyed about it, before the show proper begins. In conversation, the genial Healy then volunteers a droll story of teenage infidelity, a drunken tryst with a girl from another part of Glasgow, which he wrongly thinks will insulate him from discovery. The improvisers, led by Magidoff, then take over, goofing into being several scenes in which young Fran and his pal cop off with two Protestant schoolgirls, then must face the music when their misdemeanour is exposed.The American cast make hay with the parochial detail of Healy’s story, and with the task of playing teenagers on heat. And mums on heat: Kimberly Condict steals the show as Mrs Healy, unable to stop kissing her son and his girlfriend on the lips. But she needs sharp elbows to claim that space. The show feels as competitive as it does collaborative, with different improvisers pitching in, in divergent comedy styles, and too little of the careful listening and generosity that good improv requires. The concept promises heart as well as laughter, but we mainly get chaotic comedy.And that’s fine. It’s fun enough to watch Magidoff as Healy, and to watch Healy watching him, as young Fran sprints home to Glasgow, pursued by his guilty conscience (“You can’t run,” the company sings, “it’s gonna come get ya”) or to hear the Travis man’s cautionary tale hastily redrafted into poetry. If it’s a bumpy ride, improv-wise – well, since when did true love’s course run smoothly?AtAssembly George Square, Edinburgh, until 23 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Comedy (Stage)Comedy (Culture)Edinburgh festivalFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Dozens of ‘dangerous’ artworks are buried under dirt in Sydney, and Heap visitors will be asked to dig deep | Art | The Guardian
description: Festival of Dangerous Ideas exhibition/installation in the cavernous foyer of Carriageworks will feature 80 works by eight Australian artists
Author: Dee Jefferson
Headline: Festival of Dangerous Ideas exhibition/installation in the cavernous foyer of Carriageworks will feature 80 works by eight Australian artists
Content: Artworks by Sophie Penkethman-Young are buried as part of Heap, at Sydney’s Festival of Dangerous Ideas.Photograph: Rémi Chauvin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenArtworks by Sophie Penkethman-Young are buried as part of Heap, at Sydney’s Festival of Dangerous Ideas.Photograph: Rémi Chauvin/The GuardianArtDozens of ‘dangerous’ artworks are buried under dirt in Sydney, and Heap visitors will be asked to dig deepFestival of Dangerous Ideas exhibition/installation in the cavernous foyer of Carriageworks will feature 80 works by eight Australian artistsDee JeffersonThu 20 Aug 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 20.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’m watching a Hitachi earthmover bury a suitcase in a mound of dirt inside Carriageworks when my mind peels off on a surreal tangent: does the machine have job satisfaction? I happen to know that another machine on this job has an MOU with its human operator outlining fair work conditions, and I’m wondering if this excavator got the memo.In fact, the Hitachi just buried the memo: 25 tiles bearing the text of a labour agreement between artist Sophie Penkethman-Young and the 3D printer she used to make them. This weekend, members of the public will dig them up as part ofHeap: an unusual mix of exhibition, installation and “archaeological dig” featuring 80 artworks by eight Australian artists, commissioned by the Festival of Dangerous Ideas (Fodi). Taking place in Carriageworks’ cavernous foyer, it’s the centrepiece of a program of panels, performances and screenings inspired by this year’s theme: revelation.View image in fullscreenEighty artworks by eight artists are buried underneath tonnes of dirt inside Carriageworks.Photograph: Rémi Chauvin/The GuardianDuring the installation process, I see a bronze mushroom, a canister of kangaroo apple and a spider costume buried under 120 tonnes of earth. Already interred: a human figure cast in hardened dirt, and a funerary urn. Each represents a “dangerous idea” – something “that has potential to change the world if taken seriously”, says festival director Danielle Harvey. Audiences are invited to “really get their hands dirty” in excavating these ideas, “as a prompt to think a bit deeply” about thorny issues such as climate change and colonisation.Natsiaa 2026: Ryan Presley wins $100,000 award for ‘monumental’ Renaissance-style paintingRead moreSign up for a weekly email featuring our best readsHeap draws on a “very obvious metaphor,” Harvey concedes, but a powerful one. “We’re a country built on mining and excavating, so what we find in the dirt and the lens that we [put on it] – whether it’s interesting or dangerous, and how we value it – is super interesting in an Australian context.”View image in fullscreenWorkers installing the final few objects buried as a part of Heap, at Sydney’s Festival of Dangerous Ideas.Photograph: Rémi Chauvin/The GuardianUnlike the mining industry, diggers will be required to relinquish any treasure they unearth, with the artworks progressively added to a nearby display.“We need to find new ways to get people to pay attention to these issues,” Harvey says. “Art feels like a really important way to progress and expand some of these conversations.”Penkethman-Young’s cheeky provocation cloaks a radical idea: what if we didn’t treat machines as an endless source of production? The artist limited use of her 3D printer to a standard work week of 38 hours, capping output at one tile per day. It would have been quicker and easier to run the printer 24-7, but Penkethman-Young is pushing back on this mindset. Her artwork is an invitation “to think about all invisible labour” and how we value it – or fail to. “What would it mean if I really stood by my ethics? This is the silliest take I could do.”View image in fullscreen‘This is the silliest take I could do’ … Sophie Penkethman-Young’s artwork is buried.Photograph: Rémi Chauvin/The GuardianWiradjuri artist Brook Andrew’s dangerous idea is couched more poetically: a series of canisters bearing medicinal and edible plants native to the Americas, the Middle East and Australia, each accompanied by an explanatory note. Andrew worked with botanical specialists and Indigenous medicine people to source the specimens and stories, which include Lebanese wild thyme (za’atar), Australia’s murnong (yam daisy), and several types of hallucinogenicBrugmansia(angel’s trumpet), used for healing and spiritual practices in Colombia.“Opening ourselves up to knowledge systems that are thousands of years old” is inherently dangerous in this highly pharmaceuticalised era, says Andrew. Many of the plants in his project are considered dangerous through a western lens – such as coca, used to produce cocaine, and the poisonous Borrachero – whereas their indigenous uses are purely salutary. The way we frame plants is often “built around racism, around ignorance,” he says.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAretha Brown, working with members of her queer women’s collective Kiss My Art, also foregrounds First Nations perspectives in her commission, reimagining the Australian flag through a queer, Gumbaynggirr lens. The result, a quilt, was sealed in a suitcase before burial.View image in fullscreenWorkers carefully installing Heap at Carriageworks, the main art commission for Festival of Dangerous Ideas, in which 80 artworks by eight artists are buried underneath tonnes of dirt.Photograph: Rémi Chauvin/The Guardian“I don’t think [the Australian] flag properly represents us – and I think it’s actually divisive,” says Brown. “What could a new Australian flag look like? And how do you go about changing it? Is it something that happens after we become a republic? Is it something that happens when we change Australia Day? I think these are pretty dangerous ideas.”Elsewhere, the sense of danger is less political and more poetic: Tim Silver’s human figure cast in hardened dirt is a statement on emotional distress and withdrawal, while Tarryn Gill’s urn, made from gold fabric and bearing the multiple faces of Janus, the Roman god of thresholds, is a statement on mortality and mutability.Gill was inspired by Freud’s theory of the self as a collection of fragments we unearth over time, and by the recent death of her cat, for whom she made an urn. “I wanted to make something similarly reverent, but my own funerary ornament,” she says. “I’ve been thinking about what Jung says about middle age: you’ve spent all this time building achievements and staking your claim on the world, and then … [you realise] that’s not really what life’s about. What do I do with the time I have left? Time is actually what is dangerous.”Heapis open at Carriageworks, Sydney on 22 and 23 August, as part of the Festival of Dangerous Ideas (until 30 August)Explore more on these topicsArtSydneyAustralian artfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Monstera magic: Barbican hands out cuttings as ‘green lung of the city’ closes | Barbican | The Guardian
description: Five hundred people turn up to adopt plants from conservatory that will reopen in 2030 after renovation project
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Five hundred people turn up to adopt plants from conservatory that will reopen in 2030 after renovation project
Content: ‘It’s very special to have something from here,’ said Savannah, left. ‘Everyone seems very excited,’ said Maria, right.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It’s very special to have something from here,’ said Savannah, left. ‘Everyone seems very excited,’ said Maria, right.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianBarbicanMonstera magic: Barbican hands out cuttings as ‘green lung of the city’ closesFive hundred people turn up to adopt plants from conservatory that will reopen in 2030 after renovation projectHelena HortonThu 20 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAbove the waxy monstera leaves and bright pink hibiscus flowers in theBarbicanconservatory hangs a giant net to catch the panes of glass that are at risk of falling from the ceiling on the unwitting plant lovers below.This precarious situation has caused the estate toshutter its greenhouseon the third and fourth floors for three years so a full refurbishment can take place. But the hiatus has a silver lining for many of those who visited on Wednesday to give the plants from the conservatory a new home.View image in fullscreenThe conservatory refurbishment is part of the wider Barbican renewal programme, a £231 million renovation of the site.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianFive hundred people turned up to pick up a cutting from the Barbican’s plant collection and were asked to fill out an “adoption form” as if they were taking home a pet.Lydia Goldberg, 56, a tech worker, was one of the first through the door and selected a pretty, silvery-green Swedish ivy plant.“I am a houseplant lover,” she said. “I live in the Barbican and my bedroom overlooks the conservatory. I am sad to see it close but it’s great that it’s being restored. Having a piece of the conservatory in my flat will be incredible and this is a real community event. I can see quite a few of my neighbours here!”View image in fullscreen'This is a real community event,’ said Lydia Goldberg, who lives on the Barbican estate.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianThe Swedish ivy is among the plants being sorted by the head gardener, Marta Lowcewicz. She was fizzing with excitement as queues of people began to file in. “There has been a social media storm,” she said. “It is amazing how much interest there has been!”There are going to be three adoption events, each giving away 500 cuttings from species in the conservatory. The first, held this week, ran out of free online tickets almost immediately.View image in fullscreenFive hundred people turned up to choose a plant cutting at the first event.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianPart of Lowcewicz’s job is to figure out which plants will remain indoors and which will go outside. The climate has changed considerably since the Barbican was built in the 1960s and many indoor plants are now outdoor plants.“Some of the plants are a bit rough around the edges after the weather we have had,” she said.Londonhas sizzled in five heatwaves and the climate control in the conservatory has not caught up. “When we have new climate control and irrigation systems, the plants will be healthier.”Lowcewicz will be choosing new plants for the collection, but says “we are looking to retain as many of our plants as possible”. She will select plants that have “big, bold leaves”.“The architecture of the Barbican is striking and bold so we are trying to make sure the collection fits well with the concrete. We want them to soften it,” she said.View image in fullscreenTickets for the first ‘adoption’ event sold out online almost immediately.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianThere are plants from all over the world in the conservatory and Geoffrey, a 36-year-old spatial designer, selected one that reminded him of Mexico, where he used to live. “I chose a white velvet plant, I love it. I am a great fan of the building and it is great to take a piece of it home with me.”Savannah, 33, and Maria, 30, were grinning with delight and holding their cuttings. “I chose the peperomia,” said Savannah, who works with elderly people. “I love the texture of it, it’s very soft. I have a ton of plants, but I love the Barbican so it’s very special to have something from here.”Maria, an architectural designer, chose the trailing purple heart plant. “I have lots of houseplants but this is my first non-green plant!” she said. “I am having a great time. Everyone here seems very excited, everyone loves plants. I will keep my new plant on my bookshelf.”View image in fullscreenProspective plant-parents were asked to fill out an ‘adoption form’, much as if they were taking home a pet.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianVisitors milled around the brutalist space as they waited to pick up their cuttings. Stella, 88, lives in the Barbican and chose a Benghal dayflower.“I like it because it has a little secret blue flower,” she said. “I have houseplants everywhere and am meant to be cutting back but, really, how can you resist this?”Stella has given some of her houseplants that grew too big for her flat to the conservatory, including a giant monstera. “It’s huge, I hope they don’t give it back to me!”View image in fullscreen‘How can you resist this?’ said Stella, who lives in the Barbican and took home a Benghal dayflower – but did not want her giant monstera back.Photograph: Sarah Lee/The GuardianThe event was bittersweet, as most people were rueful that the space will be shut for such a long stretch.Dr Philippa Simpson, the chief operating officer of the Barbican, feels keenly the responsibility of faithfully restoring the conservatory, which means a lot to lovers of brutalist architecture and plants alike.“It’s a green lung of the city,” she said. “We are undertaking a massive restoration of it because it was in urgent need of rescue. We have nets up to deal with falling glazing, massive waterproofing issues. It is leaking into all of our significant spaces.”When the conservatory reopens in 2030, it will be fully accessible – as it is not currently, for those with limited mobility – and will be open seven days a week rather than during limited hours.Explore more on these topicsBarbicanPlantsLondonArchitectureHouseplantsEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: David Mitchell’s crime-solving Ludwig returns  | Television | The Guardian
description: The popular cosy-crime drama is back – with a couple of changes. Plus: some late-starters get into the dating game. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Phil Harrison
Headline: The popular cosy-crime drama is back – with a couple of changes. Plus: some late-starters get into the dating game. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: David Mitchell as John Ludwig.Photograph: PHOTOGRAPHER:/CREDIT LINE:BBC/Big TalkView image in fullscreenDavid Mitchell as John Ludwig.Photograph: PHOTOGRAPHER:/CREDIT LINE:BBC/Big TalkTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: David Mitchell’s crime-solving Ludwig returnsThe popular cosy-crime drama is back – with a couple of changes. Plus: some late-starters get into the dating game. Here’s what to watch this eveningPhil Harrison,Hollie Richardson,Priya Elan,Jack SealeandSimon WardellThu 20 Aug 2026 01.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLudwig9pm, BBC OneIs there a danger that, with John “Ludwig” Taylor’s true identity revealed, this cosy-crime drama will lose intrigue in its second series? Jeopardy is just about maintained: John is now a police employee but he’s still investigating his brother’s fate, while solving a case a week in his bumbling style. But chief constable Ziegler is on his case – he knows something’s up, he’s just not sure what. Undemanding fun, enlivened by Mitchell’s lead and Anna Maxwell Martin’s Lucy.Phil HarrisonDragons’ Den8pm, BBC OneA big first for the show in its 23rd season: with guest judges Susie Ma and Jenna Meek onboard, there are more female dragons than male. Pitches kick off with Kimberly and her eco-conscious haircare range Selkie, before mother and son Shashi and Sanjay fill the den with Spice Kitchen aromas.Hollie RichardsonThe Yorkshire Vet8pm, Channel 5Reality show featuring James Herriot’s former trainee Peter, his vet pals and a god-like voiceover from All Creatures Great and Small’s Christopher Timothy. Your enjoyment of the show depends on how much you like watching the surgical treatment of a recently pregnant cow with a prolapse.Priya ElanView image in fullscreenKate Lister and David Olusoga in A House Through Time.Photograph: BBC/Twenty Twenty Productions Ltd/Richard RankenA House Through Time9pm, BBC TwoBack to Edinburgh where David Olusoga is busy bringing more dusty census records to life. We’ve reached the Victorian era in the house on Calton Hill and the residential turnover is brisk. There’s Thomas Mains, a struggling shoe-maker; Thomas Glen, a renowned bagpiper; and, most intriguingly, Catherine Johnston, a brothel keeper.PHBetter Date Than Never9pm, BBC Three“Better late than never! Who would have thought?” This dating show is a cheerful treat, following daters who range in age, gender and identity but who have left it late to get into the dating game. This time it’s the turn of Charles, who is trying speed-dating, and Kento, who is excited about a second meeting.PHPossession9pm, Sky AtlanticKarla Crome’s rich, intelligent thriller about the echoing injustices of slavery comes to a mesmeric conclusion, which begins with British-Jamaican lawyer Claudia (Gugu Mbatha-Raw) trapped beneath the floorboards of a house that thrums with past pain. Violent confrontations, in the present day and the 18th century, resolve the narrative in stunning fashion.Jack SealeFilm choiceNovak Djokovic: The Wolf in Winter, Thursday, Prime VideoView image in fullscreenNovak Djokovic: The Wolf in Winter.Photograph: Amazon MGM Studios“He’s soft and gentle … but he’s also angry.” Jelena Djokovic’s assessment of her husband is the knotty thread that runs through Jason Hehir’s documentary about a giant of tennis who has yet to be forgiven for surpassing the achievements of crowd favourites Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer. His intensity and stubbornness (a Serbian national trait, we’re told) hasn’t endeared him to the public but, as we go behind the scenes at the 2025 Australian Open and meet an honest, engaging family man with a long history of tough choices, this film could go some way to changing minds.Simon WardellExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: All of Us Atoms by Holly Dawson audiobook review – an extraordinary self-portrait | Books | The Guardian
description: Helena Bonham Carter narrates the playwright’s impressionistic memoir, written as she was experiencing the loss of her memory
Author: Fiona Sturges
Headline: Helena Bonham Carter narrates the playwright’s impressionistic memoir, written as she was experiencing the loss of her memory
Content: Scattered recollections … Holly Dawson.Photograph: Silvia VarelaView image in fullscreenScattered recollections … Holly Dawson.Photograph: Silvia VarelaAudiobook of the weekBooksReviewAll of Us Atoms by Holly Dawson audiobook review – an extraordinary self-portraitHelena Bonham Carter narrates the playwright’s impressionistic memoir, written as she was experiencing the loss of her memoryFiona SturgesThu 20 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePlaywright Holly Dawson’s memoir tells of memory lapses and a series of seizures that signal something isn’t right. Before visiting a doctor, she had been muddling up words, forgetting people’s names and flooding the bathroom.The book finds Dawson in conversation with her brain, which is both part of her and a separate entity. “Don’t be cross with me, my love. I am tired,” it tells her. “Between your ears hearing a word and your mouth repeating it, I am doing all this work you don’t see.” Dawson, who is approaching 40 and a single mum of two children, later learns she has epilepsy and a brain tumour, which may or may not be benign. A consultant explains she must wait several months to find out, and so she sets about preserving memories and words while she still has them. “Come. Sit. Take your notebook … write it down,” says her brain.What follows are scattered recollections of her life, which include childhood days spent at her grandmother’s house; school holidays playing with her siblings and pretending to dig a mine at the bottom of the garden; ballet training and an eating disorder that robs her of puberty. These snapshots, which shift in perspective and move between the second and third person, gradually build a picture of her past.The actor Helena Bonham Carter is the narrator, bringing fresh shape and clarity to Dawson’s deliberately fractured and impressionistic prose. What emerges is an original self-portrait and a compelling exploration of memory, identity and the self.Available via Canongate, 7hr 29minFurther listeningThe Rose FieldPhilip Pullman, Penguin and David Fickling Books, 22hr 36minMichael Sheen narrates the final instalment of the Book of Dust trilogy, in which Lyra and her daemon are given an epic farewell. title: How I’ve Tried to Change the World by Alexei Sayle review – does protest make a difference? | Alexei Sayle | The Guardian
description: The comedian charts his life in demos from 1960s Liverpool to 2020s London in this fiery and addictive book
Author: Andy Beckett
Headline: The comedian charts his life in demos from 1960s Liverpool to 2020s London in this fiery and addictive book
Content: Alexei Sayle.Photograph: Gary Doak/AlamyView image in fullscreenAlexei Sayle.Photograph: Gary Doak/AlamyBook of the dayAlexei SayleReviewHow I’ve Tried to Change the World by Alexei Sayle review – does protest make a difference?The comedian charts his life in demos from 1960s Liverpool to 2020s London in this fiery and addictive bookAndy BeckettThu 20 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 07.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt 74, the comedianAlexei Sayleis approaching a dangerous phase for veteran British leftists: becoming a national treasure. Once described by special branch, in a surveillance file gleefully quoted in this memoir, as an “intellectual thug” who made “foul-mouthed comments about the royal family”, Sayle now appears regularly on Radio 4. His jolly, self-deprecating, man of the people side – one of his radio series is called Alexei Sayle’s Imaginary Sandwich Bar – has made him almost cosy.But not quite. One fascination of his meandering career, which has included villainous Hollywood cameos, subversive podcasts and successful novelty pop songs, is the persistent fierceness of his politics – the underlying subject of this short, sharp book. “My decision to become … a professional funny man,” he writes, “wasn’t a choice made simply out of monstrous vanity … I was also … taking part in [Antonio] Gramsci’s war of position: attempting to get examples of communist thought on to Top of the Pops, Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade and Doctor Who.”double quotation markSayle richly conveys the mix of enthusiasm and doubt which anyone who goes on demos will recogniseAlongside such sometimes well-paid efforts to apply the culture war strategies of the late Italian Marxist, Sayle has also been on a lot of marches. The contrasts and contradictions between these two forms of activism – one repetitive but comradely, the other more glamorous but often isolated – are pondered, mocked and mined for anecdotes in these busy, digressive pages. From marching against American imperialism with his communist parents in Liverpool in the 1960s to marching for the Palestinians in London last year, Sayle richly conveys the mix of enthusiasm and doubt which anyone who goes on demos will recognise: “believing in the cause but also sceptical that protesting about it would be sufficient”.He confesses to other complicated feelings about street politics. “I have always found it a sad thing to be alone on a demo, lonely in a crowd,” he writes. Then he describes watching protesters fight the police: “I didn’t join in but nevertheless experienced a tremendous rush of exhilaration.” With his bulging eyes and cannonball head, straining suits and air of menace, the Sayle who first became famous as a standup and a star of the boisterous sitcom The Young Ones in the early 1980s seemed like someone who could handle himself in a political pavement battle. But this book shows he is much less macho, constantly examining his own motives and often finding himself ridiculous, “a capering jester”.In 1991, during one of his sporadic attempts at US success, he went to Hollywood with his wife for auditions. Beforehand, “we went out for a walk along Sunset Boulevard in the hot night,” he writes. “The pavement was deserted except up ahead … was a single figure. ‘I bet they’re British,’ I said to Linda. When we reached this solitary pedestrian it turned out to be Billy Bragg.” There is a beautiful absurdity and melancholy about these two mouthpieces of austere alternative Britain in the 1980s now wandering a seductively escapist part of California in a less politicised decade. Although, given the way the book flits cheekily between droll stories, polemic and fantasy, we can’t be completely sure this meeting actually happened.There are other irreverent encounters with fellow radicals. The Popular Front for the Liberation of the Occupied Arabian Gulf once held their annual congress in a small, suburban London flat where Sayle lived in the 1970s. To him at least, “Their main activity seemed to be smoking, staying up all night and reading foreign newspapers in cafes.”During the 1990s, he drifted away from activism, disillusioned by the left’s flagging momentum and distracted by his career’s proliferating demands. He is cutting about the left’s – and his own – frequent lack of focus and forward thinking. But then the 2003 Iraq war protests re-energised him: “There is something elemental, ancient and magical about … a huge crowd of one mind.”Towards the book’s end, its tone becomes more consistent and serious. “I have marched on every Palestine demonstration since October 7,” writes Sayle, who is Jewish, and he has lost friends as a result. Like a good political pamphlet, this slim volume is fiery and addictive. Yet unlike a pamphlet, it shows how politics relates to the rest of life.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Abigail’s Party review – Tamzin Outhwaite’s Bev is Madame Bovary with a Cinzano  | Stage | The Guardian
description: Outhwaite’s performance as Beverly, a precision-tooled showcase in hidden anger and longing, is a triumph in this eternally resonant suburban drama
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: Outhwaite’s performance as Beverly, a precision-tooled showcase in hidden anger and longing, is a triumph in this eternally resonant suburban drama
Content: Simultaneously funny and deadly serious … Tamzin Outhwaite as Beverly in Abigail's Party.Photograph: Anthony Harvey/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSimultaneously funny and deadly serious … Tamzin Outhwaite as Beverly in Abigail's Party.Photograph: Anthony Harvey/ShutterstockStageReviewAbigail’s Party review – Tamzin Outhwaite’s Bev is Madame Bovary with a CinzanoHarold Pinter theatre, LondonOuthwaite’s performance as Beverly, a precision-tooled showcase in hidden anger and longing, is a triumph in this eternally resonant suburban dramaArifa AkbarThu 20 Aug 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 13.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAlison Steadman has cast a long shadow over the suburban gargoyle-cum-bored-housewife in Mike Leigh’s social satire about 1970s social mobility. So much so that her name is almost always invoked in relation to Beverly. Tamzin Outhwaite’s incredible achievement is that she banishes Steadman’s original portrayal of Bev as the definitive one.Having first assumed the role inNadia Fall’s 2024 production, that history shows in her polish and command of the character. The setting is a cocktail party in Essex and Outhwaite’s Bev (glittering dress, Farrah Fawcett flicks) is full of lady-of-the-manor pretensions as she serves up her officious rounds of drink. But there is a hard, calculating edge to her marital digs at estate agent husband, Laurence (Kevin Bishop) and her crude flirtation with guest Tony (Omar Malik, fantastically laconic), which she conducts with flamboyant disregard for his wife, Angela (Lauren Patel).This seeps out early on, even before she has started to knock back the gin. She is simultaneously funny in her physical comedy and deadly serious in her put-downs of the workaholic husband who is not giving her the attention she craves, as well as her manipulations of others. Beneath her patter as party hostess is rage, hurt and an almost Madame Bovary boredom.View image in fullscreenOutside Bev’s doorstep it could be Reform Britain … L to r, Lauren Patel as Angela, Omar Malik as Tony, Kevin Bishop as Laurence, Tamzin Outhwaite as Beverly and Pandora Colin as Sue in Abigail’s Party.Photograph: Anthony Harvey/ShutterstockHer performance, and Fall’s production as a whole, proves that this period comedy of manners is eternally resonant. That is partly down to the genius of the play but Fall adds an ingenious tweak in the suggestion that Tony and Ange are of “Pakistani” origin. This transforms its meanings in a subtle but deft way: the area, we hear, is being taken over by different kinds of people and you imagine this not only being a comment on working-class mobility but racial diversity here in the “white flight” heartland of Essex. Outside Bev’s doorstep, it could be Reform Britain.What does not work as well is the chemistry between Bev and Laurence, which lacks bite in the first act. Laurence is rather passive, and expressionless, the tension between them uncharged. The marital conflict does not seem ferocious enough for too long so you do not feel the truth of the friction between them when it bursts to the surface. They could just be George and Mildred on a bad night. In contrast, the fault-lines in Ange and Tony’s marriage are savagely revealed in his disdain of her, as much as she tries to cover it up with fake cheeriness.It is still hugely enjoyable to see Bev flirt with the monosyllabic Tony, and to hear Ange’s inappropriate reflections on divorce in front of recently divorced neighbour, Sue (Pandora Colin).She is the other guest at this cocktail party and the mother of eponymous punk-teen, Abigail, whose off-stage party can be heard in the background. For those who charge Leigh with othering the aspirational working-classes, not only through Bev but Laurence’s cultural snobberies, acquired in his ascension up the ladder (the framed Vincent van Gogh poster on Peter McKintosh’s orange-and-brown period set says it all), the middle-class Sue is key to Leigh’s satire. She is brilliantly portrayed as the socially-awkward, plummy ex-wife of an architect who tries to evade Laurence’s questions on the area and the class antagonisms underlying them.He insists they listen to Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony amid the rising hysteria and the record-player is truly weaponised, Demis Roussos used to needle Laurence to the point of near-violence. Bev is a such a glorious creation that you feel her disappointments in marriage even as you gasp at her comic monstrousness. But the darkness of the ending does not land. It is partly because there are unanswered questions around their marriage but also because it has all been so enjoyably comical that this switch to tragedy leaves Bev speechless and at sea, for once.AtHarold Pinter theatre, London, until 19 SeptemberExplore more on these topicsStageTheatreMike LeighreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Little Animals review – Motherland milquetoast creates a clever climate plea | Edinburgh festival 2026 | The Guardian
description: Paul Ready’s playwriting debut expertly utilises his bumbling acting persona to examine what is enough in our response to climate emergency
Author: Mark Fisher
Headline: Paul Ready’s playwriting debut expertly utilises his bumbling acting persona to examine what is enough in our response to climate emergency
Content: A captivating performance … Paul Ready in Little Animals.Photograph: Jennifer Forward-HayterView image in fullscreenA captivating performance … Paul Ready in Little Animals.Photograph: Jennifer Forward-HayterEdinburgh festival 2026ReviewLittle Animals review – Motherland milquetoast creates a clever climate pleaTraverse at Royal Lyceum Studio, EdinburghPaul Ready’s playwriting debut expertly utilises his bumbling acting persona to examine what is enough in our response to climate emergencyMark FisherThu 20 Aug 2026 09.52 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 13.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNobody does self-effacement as well asPaul Ready. The Motherland/Ann Droid actor excels at playing the kind of man who apologises for his own existence, well-meaning, but insecure – often comically so. He hesitates, smiles sheepishly, backtracks and gabbles to fill the silence. He, he, he is forever launching, launching into sentences, sentences that never get all the way to the … We get the gist.It is the same now he is making his playwriting debut with Little Animals and it works to his advantage. Performing in the round to a small audience, he gives every impression of having interrupted us in the middle of something else. We are not here, he ascertains, to remember his good friend Richard, in fact, we did not even know him, but sorry, if it is all right, he will tell us about him anyway.Richard, it transpires, is the good guy in the story. He is the schoolboy disruptor with the courage to resist social pressure, the one who scoffed at their entitled classmate for the arrogance of writing an essay called How I Would Change the World. “We need to completely rewrite the story,” says Richard, committing his life to environmental activism in anera of global heating.If Richard is the good guy, what does that make our unnamed narrator? Surely this endearing man in suit and tie, circling the room, catching us in the eye, bonding with each nervous laugh, is too reasonable to be on the wrong side. Like any of us, he recycles his waste and boycotts the correct things. He works hard, loves his family and believes in introducing daughter Ellie to the cultures of the world.Sam Eley Is Basil Crumbwick review – cantankerous cult hit brings laugh after laughRead moreAnd because he is so reasonable, it makes Richard seem hysterical. His protests are surely the actions of an overgrown schoolboy, a man who knows nothing of responsibility, who is simply not realistic. Could he not have made the same modest compromises as the rest of us? Richard makes him defensive and indignant.Directed by Caroline Steinbeis for Pentabus andFern Culture, a company encouraging better storytelling about the climate, Ready performs in natural light with neither props nor set. In a captivating performance, his message is familiar, but his call to action no less urgent.At Traverse atRoyal Lyceum Studio, Edinburgh, until 30 AugustAll our Edinburgh festival reviewsExplore more on these topicsEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalTheatreFestivalsreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Aigul Akhmetshina: Mujer Fatal album review – classy and sensual in music from Bizet to Britten and Bernstein | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The mezzo-soprano lends supple and elegant voice to opera arias and musical numbers that explore womanhood
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: The mezzo-soprano lends supple and elegant voice to opera arias and musical numbers that explore womanhood
Content: Languid lines … Aigul Akhmetshina.Photograph: Paola KudackiView image in fullscreenLanguid lines … Aigul Akhmetshina.Photograph: Paola KudackiClassical musicReviewAigul Akhmetshina: Mujer Fatal album review – classy and sensual in music from Bizet to Britten and BernsteinAkhmetshina/Pappano(Decca)The mezzo-soprano lends supple and elegant voice to opera arias and musical numbers that explore womanhoodClive PagetThu 20 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 12.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAcclaimed for embodying opera’s femme fatales such as Carmen and Dalia, Aigul Akhmetshina explores womanhood more broadly on her second album, Mujer Fatal. Accompanied on piano byAntonio Pappano, the repertoire ranges from Spanish, French and Russian art song, to Broadway and beyond.View image in fullscreenCover art for Mujer FatalThe title track, written by Elena Roussanova especially for the Bashkortostan-born mezzo-soprano, sets the tone. Akhmetshina’s supple instrument wraps itself around the languid vocal lines while Pappano’s sensitive touch draws out the music’s delicate melismas. Two of Montsalvatge’s Canciones Negras find the singer spinning long-breathed melodies, dipping down elegantly into her burgundy lower register.She’s at her classiest inhabiting Bizet’s sultry Adieux de l’hôtesse arabe and Ravel’s hip-swaying Vocalise-étude en forme de habanera. She is, of course, entirely at home in Balakirev, Rimsky-Korsakov and especially in Tchaikovsky’s None but the Lonely Heart.On the whole, these are very fine, if perhaps a trifle restrained performances.When it comes to letting her hair down, Akhmetshina is suitably uninhibited in a sensual Bésame mucho. If Gershwin’s The Man I Love and Bernstein’s Lucky to be Me feel a tad strait-laced, she warms nicely into Weill’s Speak Low. The recital closes with Britten’s O Tell Me the Truth About Love, a delicious party piece where she finally allows herself to have some fun.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: The Song of Hiawatha review – Rafael Payare reveals the riches of Coleridge-Taylor’s hit cantata | Classical music | The Guardian
description: Festival director Nicola Benedetti’s bold programming of these once-popular Victorian cantatas paid off with a crisp chorus and strong soloists tautly conducted
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Festival director Nicola Benedetti’s bold programming of these once-popular Victorian cantatas paid off with a crisp chorus and strong soloists tautly conducted
Content: Dramatic momentum … Rafael Payare conducts his Orchestre Symphonique de Montréal at the Usher Hall this week.Photograph: André GodinhoView image in fullscreenDramatic momentum … Rafael Payare conducts his Orchestre Symphonique de Montréal at the Usher Hall this week.Photograph: André GodinhoClassical musicReviewThe Song of Hiawatha review – Rafael Payare reveals the riches of Coleridge-Taylor’s hit cantataUsher Hall, EdinburghFestival director Nicola Benedetti’s bold programming of these once-popular Victorian cantatas paid off with a crisp chorus and strong soloists tautly conductedMichael DownesThu 20 Aug 2026 11.03 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 11.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Song of Hiawatha, Black British composerSamuel Coleridge-Taylor’s turn-of-the-century cantata trilogy,packed the Albert Hall for weeks on endbetween the wars, but it reallyshouldn’t work today. The unmistakably Victorian if charming score is the least of the difficulties. More problematic is the libretto: 800-plus lines of “Rum-ti Rum-ti Rum-ti Rum-ti” (trochaic tetrameter, to be technical) from Henry Wadsworth Longfellow. More challenging still is a story that shows the Native American Hiawatha endorsing his country’s colonisation by “people with white faces”.Rafael Payare did not know Hiawatha beforeNicola Benedettiinvited his Orchestre Symphonique de Montréal to give this Edinburgh international festival premiere, but he conducted with commitment and verve. Tightly coiled yet expansive of gesture, he never let the tension drop. The occasional drawbacks of his approach – soloists denied flexibility and space; chorus not guided towards longer phrases and quieter singing – were outweighed by the rewards. Payare highlighted the cantatas’ thematic and tonal connections and was alert to their dancelike character.View image in fullscreenApplause at the Usher Hall for The Song of Hiawatha.Photograph: André GodinhoHiawatha is demanding for the chorus, which sings a lot of notes and needs to conjure up the scenery – Longfellow tells rather than shows. The Edinburgh Festival Chorus, meticulously prepared by James Grossmith, produced clear textures and crisp diction, though tenors and basses dispatched lines with such aplomb that upper voices sometimes seemed underpowered by comparison.Only the third cantata, Hiawatha’s Departure, permits the soloists to embody genuine characters, and here the performance gained dramatic momentum. Soprano Francesca Chiejina displayed a radiant upper register and a steely core sound but remained score-bound. Baritone Christopher Maltman’s moving rendition of Hiawatha’s farewell harnessedthe weary authority of his Wotan. Tenor Nicky Spence injected proceedings with welcome theatricality – greeting the chorus like comrades before his bravura aria in Hiawatha’s Wedding Feast, enjoying the banter as he couldn’t convince them he’d seen a flood, conveying the sheer weirdness of his invocations of Jesus and Mary.So did it work? Almost. Hiawatha’s eccentric dramaturgy and questionable politics mean it will never return to the regular repertoire, but the musical riches unveiled by Payare more than justified Benedetti’s bold decision to programme it.Explore more on these topicsClassical musicEdinburgh festival 2026Edinburgh festivalOperareviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Duskbloods: the best of FromSoftware fights in a frantic multiplayer battleground | Games | The Guardian
description: The Elden Ring creator is known for epic single-player RPGs, but its new action game is all about multiplayer interactions: fighting, chasing, befriending, even … proposing?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The Elden Ring creator is known for epic single-player RPGs, but its new action game is all about multiplayer interactions: fighting, chasing, befriending, even … proposing?
Content: The surviving three … The Duskbloods.Photograph: NintendoView image in fullscreenThe surviving three … The Duskbloods.Photograph: NintendoGamesThe Duskbloods: the best of FromSoftware fights in a frantic multiplayer battlegroundThe Elden Ring creator is known for epic single-player RPGs, but its new action game is all about multiplayer interactions: fighting, chasing, befriending, even … proposing?Kirk McKeandThu 20 Aug 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 11.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLowanro City’s skyline is dominated by an oppressive clock tower, silhouetted against a moody red sky and an impossibly large, ominous moon. A retractable bridge splits the map in two, and a network of slimy sewers runs beneath the city streets, offering flanking routes for crafty players. This layered and multi-tiered map bears all the hallmarks of the team behind some of the most memorable stomping grounds in video games.But The Duskbloods, which I recently spent two days playing in Tokyo, is a strange departure from developer FromSoftware’s usual offerings. These have included massive single-player RPGs with light, experimental multiplayer components such as Elden Ring and Bloodborne. Those games have always attracted duellists – players who love to invade other people’s games to fight them to the death – but thisNintendo Switch 2exclusive is a different proposition entirely.View image in fullscreenAnother memorable stomping ground … The Duskbloods.Photograph: NintendoMatches whittle down eight players over three phases, culminating in a free-for-all battle between three survivors. In each phase, players sweep the map forming alliances, proposing to each other with bouquets of flowers (yes, it’s still weird), killing AI creatures and bosses, holding capture points, collecting items, and fighting one another. All of these actions earn a currency called Virtue, and it’s the two players with the least Virtue who are culled at the end of each phase.Battles against AI feel like playing a more familiar FromSoftware game at 2X speed. Jumping, dodging, blocking and sprinting while in battle drain stamina, but attacking does not, so you’re encouraged to see your entire attack chains through and take chances you wouldn’t usually take. The regular fodder enemies are almost like the mobs in a MOBA game (like League of Legends) – they’re a means to an end, a resource to be farmed as quickly as possible.View image in fullscreenSome fights feel more familiar … The Duskbloods.Photograph: NintendoWhen you fight a boss, other players are given the option to teleport directly to your side to help and share the spoils. This is where The Duskbloods is most fascinating: even other players are resources, and choosing when to accept alliances or engage in fights is a key part of tactical play.Game director Hidetaka Miyazaki says he was inspired by board games and pen and paper RPGs. That’s immediately clear. Players start each match with a Sigil, which gives them a personal objective such as marrying another player (bonding you until the final battle) or hunting down heretics. These objectives interact and give players opposing goals, so your ability to read the room is vital, even if “the room” is just a cluttered UI (user interface) that constantly moves around your screen.It makes you change your entire mindset as a FromSoftware player. I quickly learned that it’s best to let players burn out fighting bosses on their own in the early game because it’s risky and time-consuming to get involved.View image in fullscreenEven marriage is on the table … The Duskbloods.Photograph: NintendoWhile all of this feels novel, it’s also confusing, and some may be put off by the chaos. There’s also an element of randomness to how the game doles out Virtue that occasionally feels unfair. Then there’s the community element, and how the game will look once a thousand YouTubers have shared the most efficient routes and strategies.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toPushing ButtonsKeza MacDonald's weekly look at the world of gamingEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe final battles are thrilling, though. The Duskbloods has distinctive characters with unique weapons and abilities (some representing traditional FromSoftware archetypes, and at least one that can turn into a dinosaur), and these make fights feel dynamic and exciting. Every character has a projectile weapon to interrupt heals and chip away damage from a distance, and they’re all capable of running a fleeing player down.There being only three players at the end means you’re never out of danger, and all combatants are constantly calculating who is the biggest threat as the fight progresses. The way the game lets you jump 30 ft into the air and string jumps together means even the sky isn’t safe. It’s frantic. Positioning, timing, abilities and even which summon support you bring into the final battle – dozens of factors flip through your mind as you trade back and forth with the other two finalists. These climactic battles really capture the best of FromSoftware player fights, spiking your adrenaline until your heart booms out of your chest.Kirk McKeand attended a press event in Tokyo with other journalists. Transport and accommodation costs were paid for by NintendoThis article was amended on 20 August 2026. An earlier version erroneously included a release date for the game, but none has yet been announced.Explore more on these topicsGamesNintendo Switch 2NintendofeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘The only way is up’: cycling Norway’s mountainous ‘Milky Way’ | Norway holidays | The Guardian
description: The Mjølkevegen was once used to bring milk from high pastures to the towns below. Now cyclists are discovering the road’s breathtaking panoramas of peaks and lakes, dotted with cosy inns
Author: Ailsa Sheldon
Headline: The Mjølkevegen was once used to bring milk from high pastures to the towns below. Now cyclists are discovering the road’s breathtaking panoramas of peaks and lakes, dotted with cosy inns
Content: Ailsa Sheldon cycling Norway’s Mjølkewegen.Photograph: Markus StitzView image in fullscreenAilsa Sheldon cycling Norway’s Mjølkewegen.Photograph: Markus StitzNorway holidays‘The only way is up’: cycling Norway’s mountainous ‘Milky Way’The Mjølkevegen was once used to bring milk from high pastures to the towns below. Now cyclists are discovering the road’s breathtaking panoramas of peaks and lakes, dotted with cosy innsAilsa SheldonThu 20 Aug 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 07.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Norway is a hilly country,” shrugs Glenn Roar Berge. He’s not wrong, though he is fond of an understatement. I’m in Valdres in southern Norway to explore the cycle routes that skirt the edges of Jotunheimen national park. Glenn fromJotunheimen Travelis our guide, a born-and-bred local of these mountains.For most of our three-day ride, we’ll be following theMjølkevegen, or Milky Way, a 155-mile (250km) route from Vinstra in the north to Gol in the south. It was developed after the second world war, when increased demand for fresh milk meant connecting the mountain farms with the towns below. While farming continues, the road has been embraced in recent years by gravel cyclists, (typically riders on drop-bar bikes favouring unpaved roads and trails),looking for a multi-day adventure far from towns and cities.Ruten Fjellstueis a traditional inn, set up for cross-country skiing in winter, hiking and biking in summer. My trip starts here and it’s where I’ll meet my guide and group, and pick up my hired bike. It’s set high above the valley and paintedfalunred – the iron-oxide agricultural paint typical across Nordic countries. Berit and Arthur are the third-generation owners. I arrive late, so Arthur picks me up from Vinstra train station (about three hours north-west of Oslo) and Berit has kept a home-cooked meal warm: a generous plate of fish with potatoes, vegetables and cream sauce, followed by apple crumble.View image in fullscreenThe route passes along Lake Vangsmjøse near the village of Øye.Photograph: Markus StitzThese small inns are part of what makes cycling through the region work. At breakfast, there’s an expectation that you’ll make your own sandwiches from the buffet, with provisions laid out ready. We’re even given a reusable beeswax wrap. Cycling here is powered by sandwiches, waffles with sour cream and berry jam, and plenty of cinnamon buns – and that’s just to keep you going between meals.Our first morning begins with a cruisy downhill run before the road turns into a rough track. A temporary road closure has sent us on to a mountainous diversion. I’ve never used drop handlebars before and it takes me a while to figure out the gears.double quotation markFurther along the valley, our guide points out a steep triangular cave up high. We’re into troll territorySilje Wilson, who works to promote the mountain hotels in the area, is also joining our group of 12 riders from across Europe. She tells me she has never ridden a gravel bike either, so I’m hopeful I’ll have company at the back, but she leads every climb and is often miles ahead. That night she reveals she has spent her summer mountain biking and lifts a large rock in her garden to build strength. “A typical Norwegian girl,” says Glenn.While you don’t have to be a “typical” Norwegian to enjoy these trails, a certain tolerance for hills helps. As we descend towards Lake Vinstre, the Jotunheimen mountains, northern Europe’s highest range, appear ahead. There’s just a tiny road stretching into the distance; beyond it, mountains in every direction. The lake is a deep turquoise-blue, and the shores are dotted with tiny wooden farmhouses painted red or yellow, many with grass roofs for extra protection when the snow arrives.At Lake Bygdin we stop to stretch and eat burgers atBygdin Høifieldshotelbefore catching the M/B Bitihorn passenger ferry, where bikes and luggage join us on deck. The boat has been in regular service on the lake for more than a century. We sail past the peaks of Øystre Torfinnstinden and Galdebergtinden, with waterfalls tracking down the steep mountainsides to the inland fjord.View image in fullscreenJotunheimvegen, a gravel road passing along Lake Vinstre.Photograph: Markus StitzAt Eidsbugarden, at the far end of the lake, we climb back on to our bikes and follow Lake Tyin towardsFilefjellstuene hotel. We pedal past summer mountain dairy farms but barely see a soul. The roads are almost entirely traffic free, but the sheep are worth being wary of: twice I have to swerve at speed when one runs into the road.We’re cycling for long days, averaging about 45 miles (75km) a day, with 1,500 metres (4,900ft) ascent, but there are gentler ways to experience the Mjølkevegen: shorter stages mean more time to explore the cosy family hotels or add in hikes, while some riders hire an ebike. Self-guiding on the main route is straightforward and well signposted; for diversions, or extra challenges, hiring a guide is advisable. I decide to lean in to taking it slowly, drinking in the spaciousness and letting the miles roll by.At Øye, on day two, we stop to admire the steep tiered roof of thestave church, one of only 28 still standing across the country. Many Norwegian churches, including medieval stave churches, were destroyed in a wave of more than 50 arson attacks in the 90s by anti-Christian black metal bands. Øye was built towards the end of the 11th century, then replaced in 1747. During renovations in the 1930s, the old church was discovered dismantled under the floorboards for reasons lost to time, and rebuilt here by the lake.double quotation markOn Smådalen plateau, we rest among wildflowers framed by steep peaks rising above the snow line. There’s moose in this areaFurther along the valley, Glenn points out a steep triangular cave up high. We’re into troll territory. “Up there a big rock is starting to move,” Glenn says. “It’s being surveyed, and it will fall sometime in the next 200 years. It’s because oflang bane,the troll ‘long bones’. Trolls sleep for hundreds of years. He’s starting to wake up now. Newspapers don’t report it, but local people know that it’s the troll.”Time to get back into the hills then, and Glenn has planned a detour from the main route. It includes what he calls “the mother of all climbs”: a long incline with dozens of switchbacks, requiring all the cinnamon-bun fuel I can muster. On the Smådalen plateau we rest among the wildflowers framed by steep peaks rising above the snow line. There are moose in this area, but our whoops on the downhills probably keep them well hidden.View image in fullscreenLunch at Bygdin Høifieldshotel on the shores of Lake Bygdin.Photograph: Markus StitzOn my last day, the weather turns. The Mjølkevegen sits about 800–1,300 metres above sea level, and the weather can shift quickly. We reach the bottom of the Slettefjell mountain pass in driving rain. There’s a small cafe here, so we stop for waffles and refill our water bottles. Then the only way is up, and up, and up. It’s 600 metres of elevation in just 6km. All I can do is concentrate on the next bend.At the top, it’s flat and exposed, and the clouds have transformed the mountains again. Distances are hard to measure, and the craggy rocks? Petrified trolls. I give them a wave, and freewheel downhill for miles.In this part of Norway, hotels are never built at the bottom of the valley. “Everyone prefers to have a view,” says Glenn. For a cyclist, this means that every day there is a final few kilometres up to the hotel. It’s tough, but it makes the arrival all the sweeter. And the best views are those you’ve earned.The trip was provided by Jotunheimen Travel,Mountains of Norway,Innlandet FylkeskommuneandVisit Valdres.Jotunheimen Traveloffers three-day self-guided cycling trips on the Mjølkevegen from NOK7,800(£612) based on two sharing,including hotel accommodation, all meals, luggage transport, boat tickets onM/B Bitihorn, an app with directions and maps, backup support and CO2 compensation, with bike hire for an additional costExplore more on these topicsNorway holidaysEurope holidaysCycling holidaysScandinavia holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: When it comes to rosé, pink doesn’t have to mean Provence | Wine | The Guardian
description: From Morocco to Monmouth, there’s a whole world of blushing rosé wines to discover
Author: Mina Holland
Headline: From Morocco to Monmouth, there’s a whole world of blushing rosé wines to discover
Content: ‘Blushing like cheeks in a summer romance, pale rosé captures the easy and fun holiday spirit.’Photograph: flyparade/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreen‘Blushing like cheeks in a summer romance, pale rosé captures the easy and fun holiday spirit.’Photograph: flyparade/Getty Images/iStockphotoGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.WineWhen it comes to rosé, pink doesn’t have to mean ProvenceFrom Morocco to Monmouth, there’s a whole world of blushing rosé wines to discoverMina HollandThu 20 Aug 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHello, from rosé season, the only time of year I order wine like a patriarchal septuagenarian. For this fleeting moment in the wine-drinking calendar, questions are out and assumptions are in; everyone’s happy to drink pink – specifically, pale, dry and berry-crisp Provence rosé. Blushing like cheeks in a summer romance, pale rosé captures something of the hazy holiday spirit: easy, fun, objectively delicious. The liquid equivalent of chips with ketchup, it’s a safe bet.Finding a wine that almost everyone approves of is close to the holy grail – and if Provence has cracked it so everyone’s happy, why deviate? But unless you’re in primary school, chances are you wouldn’t eat chips at every meal, and I’d apply the same logic here. We’re human! We’re omnivores! And even within the category of rosé, there is a world to discover beyond the Provençal style that dominates supermarket shelves. What’s more, the likes of Whispering Angel may make decision-making easy, but they also command some hefty prices (£22.50 on Ocadoat the time of writing).Rosé is defined by brief skin contact – a process less sexy than that sounds, involving a fleeting encounter between the juice of pressed red grapes with their skins, giving the wine its seductive hue. Said hue can range from almost imperceptibly peachy right through to deep cherry juice, where the line between “rosé” and “chilled red” becomes fuzzy. Sometimes rosé is made entirely with red grapes, as are several in today’s pick, or with a blend of red and white, which is typical of Provence, where big-hitting red varieties such as grenache and syrah are blended with a white, usually vermentino, for floral freshness.The wines here all hail from outside Europe and arguably offer something a bit more than a Provence rosé; most are better all-rounders to see you from aperitif through a meal, but often put some of the grape varieties most associated with Provence to work. They include Babylonstoren’s 100% mourvèdre from Simonsberg, a mountainous enclave of South Africa known for world-class reds; this – the official wine of the Chelsea Flower Show, no less! – is fresh, structured and hugely table-friendly. Meanwhile, the excellent Moroccan number, sometimes called avin gris(grey wine) due to its pallor, is made with a blend of cabernet sauvignon and grenache with heat-tolerant hybrid grapes, marselan and caladoc. Lebanon’s Bekaa Valley is making some delicious rosé, too, where surrounding mountains and a sea breeze bring cool nights to offset hot days. In Itata, Chile, granite soils and maritime climate produce En Cabeza, a cinsault rosé that’s juicy and mineral – and a good gateway to natural wine. I’d order that for the septuagenarian in my life, no questions asked.Five alternatives to a Provence roséEn Cabeza, Luca Hodgkinson, Chile£13 Forest Wines, 12.5%. A touch of aromatic moscatel joins cinsault for a gluggable and food-friendly summer go-to.Volubilia GrisLa Zouina, Morocco£14.95 Buon Vino, 13%. Blushing and eyelid-batting, a Provence-style bottle that will please fans of very dry rosé.Babylonstoren Mourvèdre Rosé, South Africa£18 Waitrose, 13%. Light yet robust, a rosé to see you from dawn till dusk, if you feel so inclined.Massaya Rosé 2024, Lebanon£16.50 Wine Society, 13.5%. Pretty 100% cinsault with a savoury, spiced note – a great companion to meze or piquant dishes.Cowboys Don’t Have Curls, Ain’t My First Rosé,UK£27 Wright’s Wine, 9.5%. By some standards, not European! A wild and wonderful field blend grown in Somerset and made in collaboration with Monmouth winemaker, Dave Morris, this will make you reassess rosé.Explore more on these topicsWineFoodNorth African food and drinkMiddle Eastern food and drinkBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Rachel Roddy’s recipe for spaghetti with semi-dried tomatoes, garlic, herbs and breadcrumbs | Italian food and drink | The Guardian
description: Sun-drying tomatoes until they’re leathery on the outside and soft within is something of an art, but it’s more than worth it for this moreish pasta dish
Author: Rachel Roddy
Headline: Sun-drying tomatoes until they’re leathery on the outside and soft within is something of an art, but it’s more than worth it for this moreish pasta dish
Content: Rachel Roddy’s spaghetti with semi-dried tomatoes, garlic, herbs and breadcrumbs.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianView image in fullscreenRachel Roddy’s spaghetti with semi-dried tomatoes, garlic, herbs and breadcrumbs.Photograph: Rachel Roddy/The GuardianA kitchen in RomeItalian food and drinkRachel Roddy’s recipe for spaghetti with semi-dried tomatoes, garlic, herbs and breadcrumbsSun-drying tomatoes until they’re leathery on the outside and soft within is something of an art, but it’s more than worth it for this moreish pasta dishRachel RoddyThu 20 Aug 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Thu 20 Aug 2026 12.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOne set of guidelines I received in Sicily for sun-drying tomatoes was two to seven days, depending on temperature, humidity, wind and the size of the fruit. I might as well have been given a surfboard and told “go”, because that advice felt far too broad and general to be helpful to a complete beginner. So I asked someone else.For them, with an ideal temperatures of 35C and low humidity, trays of egg-sized tomato halves arranged on wire racks on wooden boards, sprinkled with salt and left in full sun during the day, and taken in at night, generally took three days to reach the desirable point: dry enough to store, but still with a flexibility and sweet chew. From broad to specific, this advice also felt overwhelming: What if the temperature changes or turns humid? What are the signs of humidity? What if my tomatoes are bigger than eggs? What happens if it rains? In the end, though, between these two extremes of advice and temperatures swinging between being in the pleasant 20Cs and burning 40Cs, too much humidity, rain (bring them inside) and not being particularly organised, I have managed to – relatively successfully – dry batches of tomatoes of all shapes and sizes.Experimenting has also taught me that I like a semi-dried tomato: the red, ear-like halves that are leathery and dry on the outside but soft and toffee-like in the middle – the sort that stir memories of those bought from Sainsbury’s in the late 1980s. Temperatures as they are this summer, I have made several batches of semi-dried cherry tomato halves arranged on wire racks outside and in direct sun for two days (coming in at night). I have also made several batches with the help of a little sugar in the oven at 130C for an hour for smaller tomatoes, longer if they are the size of a yolk or an egg, and, if necessary, turning off the oven and leaving the tray inside while it cools. The aim is wrinkled and a little dry on top, but still juicy and sweet within. Prepare at least 1kg, and ideally 2kg, with some packed in a jar and covered with olive oil, and the rest for this week’s recipe.Spaghetti with semi-dried tomatoes, garlic, herbs and breadcrumbsWant to save this recipe?Download the Guardian Feast app to add this to your collection.Download the appPrep2hrs or 2 daysCook20 minServes41kg cherry tomatoes,or golf-ball size vine tomatoesSaltOlive oilSugar2garlic cloves1 medium-size tomato,peeled and crushed (hands are best)1 small bunchflat-leaf parsley1 small bunch basil100g soft white breadcrumbs500g spaghetti, linguine or tagliatelleCut the cherry tomatoes in half, put them in a bowl with a pinch of salt and four tablespoons of olive oil, and toss well. Arrange the halves cut side up on a large baking tray, sprinkle with a little sugar and bake at 130C (110C fan)/250F/gas ½ for an hour for small tomatoes, longer if they are large; the aim is wrinkled and a little dry on top but still juicy and sweet within. Set aside to cool, then set half aside for this recipe and put the rest in a jar covered with olive oil.Peel the garlic and slice very thinly, cut the tomatoes you have set aside into quarters, and mince the herbs.In a frying pan, warm two tablespoons of olive oil and the breadcrumbs, along with a pinch of salt. Move the crumbs around with a spoon until they are lightly golden, then tip on to a plate.Bring a large pan of water to a boil, add salt, stir, then cook the pasta according to packet instructions.Meanwhile, back in the frying pan, gently warm three tablespoons of olive oil and the garlic, until it softens and becomes fragrant, then add the crushed tomato, stir for a few minutes, then add the semi-dried tomatoes.Once the pasta is ready, lift it directly into the saucepan and toss well. Add the herbs, toss again, then divide between between four plates, topping each with a handful of crumbs. Pass around the jar of oil-covered tomatoes, if anyone wants extra – also asking if they can guess whether they took two hours or two days to dry.Explore more on these topicsItalian food and drinkA kitchen in RomeFoodPastaMain courseTomatoesStarterrecipesShareReuse this content
